body: ## Part One · Book One: The Story of One Little Family · Chapter I · Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov

Alexei Fyodorovich Karamazov was the third son of a landowner of our district, Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov, so well known in his day (and still remembered among us) because of his tragic and dark end, which came about exactly thirteen years ago and which I shall tell of in its place. For now I will say of this “landowner” (as he was called among us, though all his life he hardly lived on his estate at all) only that he was a strange type, yet one met fairly often: precisely the type of a man not only worthless and depraved but at the same time muddle-headed; but one of those muddle-headed men who know very well how to manage their little property affairs, and only those, it seems. Fyodor Pavlovich, for example, began with almost nothing; he was the smallest of landowners; he ran about dining at other people’s tables and angled to become a hanger-on; and yet at the moment of his death he turned out to have as much as a hundred thousand roubles in ready money. And at the same time he went on all his life being one of the most muddle-headed cranks in the whole of our district. I repeat: this is not stupidity; most of these cranks are rather clever and cunning; it is precisely muddle-headedness, and a special, national kind of it.

He was married twice, and he had three sons: the eldest, Dmitry Fyodorovich, by his first wife, and the other two, Ivan and Alexei, by his second. Fyodor Pavlovich’s first wife came from a fairly rich and distinguished noble family, the Miusovs, who were also landowners in our district. Exactly how it came about that a girl with a dowry, and a beautiful girl besides, and moreover one of those lively clever girls who are so common among us in the present generation but who were already appearing in the last one, could marry such a worthless “weakling”, as everyone called him then, I will not undertake to explain at length. After all, I once knew a young lady, still of the “romantic” generation before last, who after several years of mysterious love for a certain gentleman, whom, by the way, she could always have married in the most peaceful way, ended nevertheless by inventing insurmountable obstacles for herself, and on a stormy night threw herself from a high bank, like a cliff, into a rather deep and swift river and perished in it, decidedly out of her own caprice, solely in order to resemble Shakespeare’s Ophelia; and indeed, if that cliff, so long since chosen and loved by her, had not been so picturesque, if there had been only a prosaic flat bank in its place, perhaps the suicide would not have happened at all. This is a true fact, and one must suppose that in our Russian life, in the last two or three generations, not a few such facts, or facts of the same kind, have taken place. In the same way the act of Adelaida Ivanovna Miusova was without doubt an echo of foreign influences, and also the irritation of a captive mind. Perhaps she wanted to assert a woman’s independence, to go against social conventions, against the despotism of her relations and family; and an obliging imagination persuaded her, let us suppose for only a moment, that Fyodor Pavlovich, in spite of his status as a hanger-on, was all the same one of the boldest and most mocking men of that epoch of transition to everything better, whereas he was only a wicked buffoon and nothing more. What made it more piquant was that the affair was carried out by an elopement, and this greatly attracted Adelaida Ivanovna. As for Fyodor Pavlovich, even by his social position he was very well prepared then for all such escapades, for he passionately wished to make his career by any means whatever; and to attach himself to a good family and take a dowry was very tempting. As for mutual love, there seems to have been none at all, either on the bride’s side or on his, in spite of Adelaida Ivanovna’s beauty. So that this was perhaps the only case of its kind in the life of Fyodor Pavlovich, a most sensual man all his life, ready in an instant to cling to any skirt whatever, if only it beckoned to him. And yet this woman alone made no particular impression on him from the passionate side.

Immediately after the elopement Adelaida Ivanovna saw in a flash that she felt nothing for her husband but contempt. So the consequences of the marriage showed themselves with extraordinary swiftness. Although the family even fairly soon became reconciled to the event and gave the runaway her dowry, the most disorderly life and endless scenes began between the spouses. It was said that the young wife showed incomparably more nobility and loftiness in it than Fyodor Pavlovich, who, as is now known, pinched all her money from her at once, as much as twenty-five thousand, as soon as she received it, so that from then on those thousands simply sank, as far as she was concerned, as if into the water. The little village and the rather good town house which had also formed part of her dowry he tried for a long time, with all his might, to transfer to his own name by means of some suitable deed, and he would surely have succeeded, if only from the contempt and disgust, so to speak, which he aroused in his wife every minute by his shameless extortions and beggings, simply from her weariness of soul, just so that he would leave her alone. But fortunately Adelaida Ivanovna’s family stepped in and restrained the grabber. It is positively known that there were frequent fights between the spouses, but, according to tradition, it was not Fyodor Pavlovich who did the beating but Adelaida Ivanovna, a hot-tempered, bold, dark-skinned, impatient lady, gifted with remarkable physical strength. At last she abandoned the house and ran away from Fyodor Pavlovich with a seminary-trained teacher who was perishing of poverty, leaving the three-year-old Mitya on Fyodor Pavlovich’s hands. Fyodor Pavlovich instantly set up a whole harem in the house and the most dissolute drinking, and in the intervals drove round almost the whole province, complaining tearfully to everyone of Adelaida Ivanovna for leaving him, and in doing so he told such details as a husband should be far too ashamed to tell about his married life. Above all, it seemed to please him and even to flatter him to play before everyone his ridiculous part of the injured husband, and even to paint the details of his injury with embellishments. “One would think you had been given a promotion, Fyodor Pavlovich, you are so pleased, in spite of all your grief,” the mockers used to say to him. Many even added that he was glad to appear in a refurbished role as a buffoon, and that he deliberately pretended not to notice his comic position, so as to make the laughter louder. Who knows, though; perhaps it was naive in him. At last he managed to find the traces of his runaway. The poor woman turned out to be in Petersburg, where she had moved with her seminarist and where she had thrown herself recklessly into the fullest emancipation. Fyodor Pavlovich at once began to bustle and prepare to go to Petersburg; what for? he did not know himself, of course. Really, perhaps he would have gone then; but, having taken this decision, he at once considered himself especially entitled, to keep up his spirits before the journey, to plunge again into the most boundless drinking. And it was just at this time that his wife’s family received the news of her death in Petersburg. She had died somehow suddenly, in some garret, of typhus according to some accounts, and according to others supposedly of hunger. Fyodor Pavlovich learned of his wife’s death while drunk; they say he ran out into the street and began to shout, raising his hands to heaven in joy: “Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart”; and according to others he sobbed like a little child, so much that, they say, it was pitiful even to look at him, in spite of all the disgust he aroused. It is very possible that both happened, that is, that he rejoiced at his liberation and wept for his liberator, all at once. In most cases people, even villains, are much more naive and simple-hearted than we generally conclude about them. And so are we ourselves.
## Chapter II · He Gets Rid of His First Son

Of course, one can imagine what kind of upbringer and father such a man could be. With him as a father, exactly what was bound to happen did happen: that is, he abandoned his child by Adelaida Ivanovna entirely and completely, not out of malice towards him or from any wounded conjugal feelings, but simply because he forgot about him completely. While he was wearying everyone with his tears and complaints and had turned his house into a den of debauchery, the three-year-old boy Mitya was taken into his care by a faithful servant of the house, Grigory, and if he had not looked after him then, perhaps there would have been no one even to change the child’s little shirt. Besides, it so happened that the child’s relations on his mother’s side also seemed to forget him at first. His grandfather, that is, Mr Miusov himself, Adelaida Ivanovna’s father, was no longer alive then; his widow, Mitya’s grandmother, who had moved to Moscow, had fallen seriously ill; the sisters had all married; so that Mitya had to spend almost a whole year with the servant Grigory, living with him in the servants’ cottage. However, even if his papa had remembered him (he could not really have been unaware of his existence), he himself would have sent him back to the cottage, since the child would after all have been in the way of his debauchery. But it so happened that a cousin of the late Adelaida Ivanovna returned from Paris, Pyotr Alexandrovich Miusov, who afterwards lived abroad for many years on end, a very young man still at that time, but a man exceptional among the Miusovs, enlightened, metropolitan, foreign, and moreover a European all his life, and at the end of his life a liberal of the forties and fifties. In the course of his career he had been in touch with many of the most liberal people of his epoch, both in Russia and abroad; he had known personally both Proudhon and Bakunin, and he especially liked to remember and tell, already near the end of his wanderings, of the three days of the February revolution in Paris in forty-eight, hinting that he himself had almost taken part in it on the barricades. This was one of the most gratifying memories of his youth. He had an independent fortune, by the old reckoning about a thousand souls. His excellent estate lay just outside our little town and bordered on the land of our famous monastery, with which Pyotr Alexandrovich, while still very young, as soon as he received his inheritance, at once began an endless lawsuit over the rights to some fishing in the river or some wood-cutting in the forest, I don’t know exactly, but he even considered it his civic and enlightened duty to begin a lawsuit against the “clericals”. Hearing all about Adelaida Ivanovna, whom of course he remembered and had once even noticed, and learning that Mitya had been left behind, he took up this business, in spite of all his youthful indignation and contempt for Fyodor Pavlovich. That was when he first became acquainted with Fyodor Pavlovich. He declared to him straight out that he would like to take the child’s upbringing upon himself. He used to tell long afterwards, as a characteristic trait, that when he began talking to Fyodor Pavlovich about Mitya, the latter for some time looked as if he did not understand at all what child was being talked about, and even seemed surprised that he had a little son somewhere in the house. Even if there was exaggeration in Pyotr Alexandrovich’s story, there must still have been something like the truth in it. But in fact Fyodor Pavlovich all his life loved to pose, suddenly to play some unexpected part before you, and above all sometimes without any need at all, even to his own direct harm, as in the present case, for instance. This trait, however, is characteristic of a very great many people, even very clever ones, not only of Fyodor Pavlovich. Pyotr Alexandrovich pursued the matter warmly and was even appointed guardian of the child (together with Fyodor Pavlovich), because after all a small property had been left by the mother: a house and an estate. Mitya did indeed move to this cousin once removed, but the latter had no family of his own, and since he himself, as soon as he had settled and secured the income from his estates, hastened back to Paris for a long time, he entrusted the child to one of his aunts, a certain Moscow lady. It so happened that, once he had settled in Paris, he too forgot the child, especially when that same February revolution came, which so struck his imagination and which he could never forget all his life. And the Moscow lady died, and Mitya passed to one of her married daughters. It seems that he afterwards changed his nest a fourth time as well. I will not enlarge on this now, all the more since there will be much more to tell about this first-born of Fyodor Pavlovich, and for now I shall limit myself only to the most necessary facts about him, without which I cannot even begin my novel.

In the first place, this Dmitry Fyodorovich was the only one of Fyodor Pavlovich’s three sons who grew up in the conviction that he did after all have some property, and that when he came of age he would be independent. His boyhood and youth passed in a disorderly way: he did not finish at the gymnasium; he then got into a military school; then he found himself in the Caucasus, was promoted, fought a duel, was reduced to the ranks, was promoted again, caroused a great deal and comparatively spent a fair amount of money. He did not begin to receive money from Fyodor Pavlovich until he came of age, and until then he ran into debt. He first knew and saw Fyodor Pavlovich, his father, only after he came of age, when he came to our parts on purpose to have it out with him about his property. It seems he did not like his parent even then; he stayed with him only a short time and left quickly, having managed only to get a certain sum from him and to enter into a certain arrangement with him about further receipts of income from the estate, of which (a remarkable fact) he did not on that occasion manage to get from Fyodor Pavlovich either the income or the value. Fyodor Pavlovich noticed then, from the very first (and this should be remembered), that Mitya had an exaggerated and false idea of his property. Fyodor Pavlovich was very pleased by this, having his own special calculations in view. He concluded only that the young man was frivolous, wild, passionate, impatient, a carouser, and that if only he could snatch something for the time being, he would at once calm down, if only for a short while, of course. And this is what Fyodor Pavlovich began to exploit: that is, he got off with small handouts, with sums sent from time to time, and in the end it came about that when, some four years later, Mitya, losing patience, appeared in our little town a second time to settle his affairs with his parent once and for all, it suddenly turned out, to his greatest amazement, that he had absolutely nothing left, that it was even hard to reckon up, that he had already drawn in money the whole value of his property from Fyodor Pavlovich and perhaps was even in debt to him himself; that by such and such deals, which he himself had wished to enter into at such and such a time, he had no right to demand anything more, and so on and so on. The young man was stunned, suspected falsehood and deceit, was almost beside himself and seemed to lose his mind. It was this very circumstance that led to the catastrophe whose account will make up the subject of my first introductory novel, or rather its outward side. But before I go on to this novel, I must also tell about Fyodor Pavlovich’s other two sons, Mitya’s brothers, and explain where they came from.
## Chapter III · The Second Marriage and the Second Children

Fyodor Pavlovich, having got the four-year-old Mitya off his hands, very soon afterwards married a second time. This second marriage lasted about eight years. He took this second wife of his, also a very young person, Sofya Ivanovna, from another province, where he had gone on some small contracting business, in company with some little Jew. Though Fyodor Pavlovich caroused and drank and made scenes, he never stopped investing his capital, and always arranged his little affairs successfully, though of course almost always somewhat basely. Sofya Ivanovna was one of the “little orphans”, without family since childhood, the daughter of some obscure deacon, brought up in the rich house of her benefactress, educator and tormentor, a distinguished old general’s widow, the widow of General Vorokhov. I do not know the details, but I have only heard that the ward, meek, gentle and uncomplaining, was once taken down from a noose which she had hung on a nail in the storeroom, so hard was it for her to bear the caprices and eternal reproaches of this old woman, who was apparently not wicked but had become simply a most intolerable petty tyrant from idleness. Fyodor Pavlovich offered his hand; inquiries were made about him and he was driven away; and then once again, as in his first marriage, he proposed an elopement to the little orphan. It is very, very possible that she would not have gone with him for anything if she had learned more details about him in time. But it was in another province; and what could a sixteen-year-old girl understand, except that it was better to go into the river than to stay with her benefactress? So the poor thing exchanged a benefactress for a benefactor. This time Fyodor Pavlovich did not get a penny, because the general’s widow was angry, gave nothing, and besides cursed them both; but he had not counted on getting anything this time; he had been captivated only by the remarkable beauty of the innocent girl and, above all, by her innocent look, which struck him, a sensualist and until then a depraved lover only of coarse female beauty. “Those innocent little eyes slashed my soul like a razor then,” he used to say afterwards, giggling nastily in his own way. However, in a depraved man even this may have been only a sensual attraction. Having received no reward, Fyodor Pavlovich did not stand on ceremony with his wife, and taking advantage of her being, so to speak, “guilty” before him, and of his having almost “taken her down from the noose”, taking advantage moreover of her phenomenal meekness and lack of response, he trampled underfoot even the most ordinary decencies of marriage. Bad women came to the house, right there with the wife present, and orgies were held. As a characteristic trait I will report that the servant Grigory, a gloomy, stupid and stubborn reasoner, who had hated the former mistress, Adelaida Ivanovna, this time took the side of the new mistress, defended her and quarrelled with Fyodor Pavlovich on her account in a way almost impermissible for a servant, and once even broke up an orgy and drove out by force all the disorderly women who had come. Later the unhappy young woman, frightened from her very childhood, developed something like a nervous women’s illness, found most often among common village women, who for this illness are called klikushi, shriekers. From this illness, with terrible hysterical fits, the sick woman at times even lost her reason. She bore Fyodor Pavlovich, however, two sons, Ivan and Alexei, the first in the first year of the marriage and the second three years later. When she died, the boy Alexei was in his fourth year, and though it is strange, I know that he remembered his mother all his life afterwards, as if through a dream, of course. After her death almost exactly the same thing happened to both boys as to the first, Mitya: they were completely forgotten and abandoned by their father and ended up with the same Grigory, in his cottage too. It was in the cottage that the old tyrant, the general’s widow, the benefactress and educator of their mother, found them. She was still alive, and all that time, all eight years, she had not been able to forget the offence done to her. All those eight years she had had the most exact information, secretly, about the life of her “Sofya”, and hearing how ill she was and what outrages surrounded her, she had two or three times said aloud to her hangers-on: “It serves her right; God has sent it to her for her ingratitude.”

Exactly three months after Sofya Ivanovna’s death the general’s widow suddenly appeared in our town in person and went straight to Fyodor Pavlovich’s lodging, and she stayed in the little town only about half an hour, but she did a great deal. It was evening then. Fyodor Pavlovich, whom she had not seen for all eight years, came out to her a little drunk. They relate that instantly, without any explanations, as soon as she saw him, she gave him two good resounding slaps in the face and three times tugged him by his forelock from top to bottom; then, without adding a word, she went straight to the cottage to the two boys. Noticing at the first glance that they were unwashed and in dirty linen, she at once gave Grigory himself another slap and announced to him that she was taking both children away with her; then she led them out just as they were, wrapped them in a rug, put them in her carriage and took them off to her own town. Grigory bore this slap like a devoted slave, did not say a rude word, and when he saw the old lady to her carriage, he bowed to her from the waist and said impressively that “God will repay you for the orphans.” “You’re a blockhead all the same!” the general’s widow shouted to him as she drove off. Fyodor Pavlovich, having thought the whole thing over, found that it was a good thing, and afterwards did not refuse his formal consent on a single point regarding the children’s upbringing by the general’s widow. As for the slaps he had received, he went round the whole town himself telling of them.

It so happened that the general’s widow too died soon afterwards, having, however, stipulated in her will a thousand roubles for each of the two little ones “for their education, and that all this money be spent on them without fail, but so that it lasts right up to their coming of age, because such a handout is more than enough for such children, and if anyone wishes otherwise, let him loosen his own purse strings,” and so on and so on. I have not read the will myself, but I have heard that there was something strange in it of this kind, and far too peculiarly expressed. The chief heir of the old woman, however, turned out to be an honest man, the provincial marshal of nobility of that province, Yefim Petrovich Polenov. Having exchanged letters with Fyodor Pavlovich and guessed in a flash that one would never extract money from him for the upbringing of his own children (though he never refused outright, but only always dragged things out in such cases, sometimes even pouring out sentiments), he took a personal interest in the orphans and especially grew fond of the younger of them, Alexei, so that for a long time the boy even grew up in his family. I ask the reader to note this from the very beginning. And if the young men owed their upbringing and education for their whole lives to anyone, it was precisely to this Yefim Petrovich, a most noble and humane man, of a kind rarely met. He kept the little ones’ thousand each, left by the general’s widow, untouched, so that by the time they came of age it had grown with interest to two thousand each; and he brought them up at his own expense, and of course spent much more than a thousand on each of them. I will not enter now either into a detailed account of their childhood and youth, but will indicate only the most important circumstances. About the elder, Ivan, I will report only that he grew up a somewhat gloomy boy, shut up in himself, far from timid, but as if he had grasped already at ten years old that they were growing up after all in someone else’s family and on someone else’s charity, and that their father was a man of such a kind that it was shameful even to speak of him, and so on and so on. This boy very soon, almost in infancy (so it was said at least), began to show some extraordinary and brilliant aptitude for learning. I do not know exactly, but it somehow came about that he parted from Yefim Petrovich’s family when he was hardly thirteen, going to one of the Moscow gymnasiums and boarding with a certain experienced and, at that time, famous teacher, a childhood friend of Yefim Petrovich. Ivan himself used to say afterwards that it all came, so to speak, from Yefim Petrovich’s “ardour for good deeds”, carried away by the idea that a boy of genius ought also to be brought up by an educator of genius. However, neither Yefim Petrovich nor the educator of genius was alive any longer when the young man, having finished the gymnasium, entered the university. Since Yefim Petrovich had made poor arrangements, and the receipt of the children’s own money bequeathed by the tyrannical general’s widow, which had grown from one thousand to two with interest, was delayed by various formalities and delays quite unavoidable among us, the young man had a very hard time of it in his first two years at the university, since he was forced all that time to feed and keep himself and to study at the same time. It must be noted that he did not even want to make an attempt then to write to his father: perhaps out of pride, out of contempt for him, or perhaps as a result of cold, sound reasoning, which told him that he would not get any even slightly serious support from his papa. However that may be, the young man did not lose his head in the least, and managed to find work, first giving lessons at twenty kopecks, and then running round the newspaper offices and supplying little articles of ten lines about street incidents, signed “Eyewitness”. These little articles, they say, were always composed so curiously and piquantly that they quickly caught on, and in this alone the young man showed all his practical and intellectual superiority over that numerous, eternally needy and unhappy part of our student youth of both sexes, who in the capitals, as a rule, knock from morning to night at the doors of various newspapers and journals, unable to think of anything better than the eternal repetition of the same request for translations from French or copying. Having become acquainted with the editorial offices, Ivan Fyodorovich never afterwards broke his connections with them, and in his last years at the university he began to publish very talented reviews of books on various specialised subjects, so that he even became known in literary circles. However, only quite recently had he happened suddenly to attract special attention in a much wider circle of readers, so that very many people noticed and remembered him all at once. It was a rather curious incident. Having already left the university and preparing to go abroad on his two thousand, Ivan Fyodorovich suddenly published in one of the big newspapers a strange article which attracted the attention even of non-specialists, and above all on a subject apparently quite unfamiliar to him, since he had graduated in natural science. The article was written on the question of ecclesiastical courts, which was being raised everywhere at that time. Examining certain opinions already given on this question, he also stated his own personal view. The main thing was in the tone and in the remarkable unexpectedness of the conclusion. And yet many of the churchmen decidedly took the author for one of their own. And suddenly, alongside them, not only the secularists but even the atheists themselves began to applaud from their side. In the end some shrewd people decided that the whole article was only an insolent farce and a mockery. I mention this incident especially because the article in due course made its way also into our famous monastery near the town, where people were interested in the question of ecclesiastical courts that had arisen; it made its way there and produced complete bewilderment. Learning the author’s name, they were interested too that he was a native of our town and the son of “that very Fyodor Pavlovich”. And then suddenly, at that very time, the author himself appeared among us.

Why Ivan Fyodorovich came to us then, I remember asking myself even then, with a kind of almost uneasiness. This so fateful arrival, which served as the beginning of so many consequences, long remained for me, almost always, an unclear affair. Judging in general, it was strange that a young man so learned, so proud and cautious in appearance, should suddenly appear in such a disgraceful house, to such a father, who had ignored him all his life, did not know him and did not remember him, and though he would certainly not have given him money for anything and in any case if his son had asked him, had nevertheless been afraid all his life that his sons, Ivan and Alexei, would also come some day and ask for money. And here the young man settles in the house of such a father, lives with him a month and another, and the two get along as well as could be. This last especially surprised not only me but many others too. Pyotr Alexandrovich Miusov, of whom I have already spoken above, a distant relation of Fyodor Pavlovich through his first wife, happened to be with us again at that time, on his estate near the town, having come from Paris, where he had now settled for good. I remember that it was precisely he who wondered most of all, having become acquainted with the young man, who interested him extremely and with whom he sometimes crossed swords in learning, not without inner pain. “He is proud,” he said to us about him then; “he will always earn himself a kopeck; even now he has money for going abroad; what does he want here? It is clear to everyone that he has not come to his father for money, because in any case his father won’t give it. He doesn’t like drinking wine and debauchery, and yet the old man can’t do without him, they have got on so well!” That was true; the young man even had a visible influence on the old man; the latter almost began at times to obey him, as it were, though he was extremely and even sometimes spitefully wilful; he even began at times to behave more decently...

Only later was it explained that Ivan Fyodorovich had come partly at the request and on the business of his elder brother, Dmitry Fyodorovich, whom he also knew and saw for the first time in his life at almost this same time, on this same visit, but with whom, however, he had entered into correspondence even before coming from Moscow, over an important matter which concerned Dmitry Fyodorovich more. What this matter was the reader will learn fully in detail in due course. Nevertheless, even when I already knew about this special circumstance, Ivan Fyodorovich still seemed enigmatic to me, and his arrival among us still inexplicable.

I will add that Ivan Fyodorovich had at that time the air of a mediator and peacemaker between his father and his elder brother, Dmitry Fyodorovich, who had then started a big quarrel and even a formal lawsuit against his father.

This little family, I repeat, came together then for the first time in their lives, and some of its members saw each other for the first time in their lives. Only the youngest son, Alexei Fyodorovich, had already been living among us for a year before this, and so had arrived among us before all his brothers. It is about this very Alexei that it is hardest of all for me to speak in my present introductory account, before bringing him on the stage in the novel. But I shall have to write a preface about him too, at least to explain beforehand one very strange point, namely: I am forced to present my future hero to the readers, from the first scene of his novel, in the cassock of a novice. Yes, he had already been living for a year in our monastery then, and seemed to be preparing to shut himself up in it for the rest of his life.
## Chapter IV · The Third Son, Alyosha

He was only twenty then (his brother Ivan was in his twenty-fourth year, and their elder brother Dmitry in his twenty-eighth). First of all I declare that this young man, Alyosha, was not a fanatic at all, and, in my opinion at least, not even a mystic at all. I will say beforehand my full opinion: he was simply an early lover of humanity, and if he took up the monastic road, it was only because at that time it alone struck him and presented to him, so to speak, the ideal way out for his soul, which was struggling out of the darkness of worldly malice towards the light of love. And this road struck him only because on it he had met then what was, in his opinion, an extraordinary being: our famous monastery elder Zosima, to whom he became attached with all the ardent first love of his insatiable heart. However, I do not dispute that he was very strange even then, having begun so even from the cradle. By the way, I have already mentioned about him that, though he was left without his mother when only in his fourth year, he remembered her all his life afterwards, her face, her caresses, “just as if she were standing before me alive”. Such memories can be retained (everyone knows this) even from an earlier age, even from the age of two, but only standing out all one’s life like points of light out of the darkness, like a corner torn from a huge picture which has all faded and vanished except this one little corner. So it was exactly with him: he remembered one evening, a summer evening, quiet, an open window, the slanting rays of the setting sun (the slanting rays were what he remembered most of all), in the corner of the room an icon, before it a lighted lamp, and before the icon, on her knees, his mother, sobbing as if in hysterics, with shrieks and cries, seizing him in both arms, embracing him tightly till it hurt and praying for him to the Mother of God, holding him out from her embrace in both hands towards the icon as if under the protection of the Mother of God... and suddenly the nurse runs in and snatches him from her in fright. There is a picture! Alyosha remembered his mother’s face too at that moment: he used to say that it was frenzied but beautiful, as far as he could remember. But he rarely liked to confide this memory to anyone. In childhood and youth he was not very expansive and even not very talkative, but not from mistrust, not from timidity or sullen unsociability, quite the contrary, but from something else, from a kind of inner preoccupation, personal to himself, not concerning others, but so important to him that because of it he as if forgot others. But he loved people: he seemed all his life to live with complete faith in people, and yet no one ever considered him either a simpleton or a naive person. There was something in him that said and suggested (and did so all his life afterwards) that he did not want to be a judge of people, that he would not take condemnation upon himself and would not condemn for anything. It even seemed that he allowed everything, without condemning in the least, though often grieving very bitterly. More than that, in this sense he had gone so far that no one could either surprise or frighten him, and this even in his very earliest youth. Coming to his father in his twentieth year, positively into a den of filthy debauchery, he, chaste and pure, only withdrew silently when it was unbearable to look, but without the slightest sign of contempt or condemnation of anyone at all. And his father, once a hanger-on and therefore a man sensitive and quick to take offence, who at first received him mistrustfully and sullenly (“he is very silent, they say, and reasons a lot to himself”), soon ended, however, by beginning to hug and kiss him terribly often, no more than two weeks or so later, with drunken tears, it is true, in tipsy sentimentality, but evidently having come to love him sincerely and deeply, and as such a man as he had of course never managed to love anyone...

And indeed everyone loved this young man wherever he appeared, and this from his very earliest childhood. Finding himself in the house of his benefactor and educator, Yefim Petrovich Polenov, he so attached everyone in that family to himself that they decidedly considered him there almost as their own child. And yet he had entered that house at such an infant age that one could never expect in a child calculating cunning, wiliness, or the art of ingratiating oneself and pleasing, the knack of making oneself loved. So the gift of arousing special love towards himself he contained, so to speak, in his very nature, artlessly and directly. It was the same with him at school, and yet, it would seem, he was precisely one of those children who arouse the mistrust of their schoolfellows, sometimes mockery, and perhaps even hatred. He would, for instance, fall into thought and as if withdraw. From his very childhood he loved to go off into a corner and read books, and yet his schoolfellows came to love him so much that he could decidedly be called the general favourite all the time he was at school. He was rarely playful, even rarely merry, but everyone, looking at him, saw at once that this was not at all from any sullenness in him; that, on the contrary, he was even-tempered and serene. Among those of his own age he never wanted to put himself forward. Perhaps for that very reason he was never afraid of anyone, and yet the boys at once understood that he was not at all proud of his fearlessness, but looked as if he did not even understand that he was brave and fearless. He never remembered an offence. It happened that an hour after an offence he would answer the offender or begin talking with him himself with such a trusting and serene air, as if nothing had passed between them at all. And it was not that he had the air of having forgotten the offence by chance or forgiven it on purpose; he simply did not consider it an offence, and this decidedly captivated and conquered the children. There was only one trait in him which in all the classes of the gymnasium, from the lowest to the highest, aroused in his schoolfellows a constant wish to tease him, not out of malicious mockery, but because it amused them. This trait in him was a wild, frenzied modesty and chastity. He could not hear certain words and certain conversations about women. These “certain” words and conversations, unfortunately, cannot be rooted out in schools. Boys pure in soul and heart, still almost children, very often like to talk among themselves in the classroom, and even aloud, about such things, pictures and images as even soldiers will not always talk about; what is more, soldiers do not know and understand much of what is already familiar in this line to such young children of our educated and higher society. There is perhaps no moral depravity here yet; there is no real, depraved, inner cynicism either; but there is an outward one, and this is often considered among them something even delicate, subtle, dashing and worthy of imitation. Seeing that “Alyoshka Karamazov” quickly stopped his ears with his fingers when they began talking “about that”, they would sometimes deliberately crowd round him and, pulling his hands away from his ears by force, shout filth into both his ears, while he struggled, slid down to the floor, lay down, covered himself up, and all this without saying a word to them, without cursing, bearing the offence in silence. In the end, however, they left him alone and no longer teased him as a “little girl”; more than that, they looked at him in this respect with pity. By the way, in class he always stood among the best in his studies, but was never marked first.

When Yefim Petrovich died, Alyosha stayed two more years at the provincial gymnasium. Yefim Petrovich’s inconsolable widow, almost immediately after his death, went off to Italy for a long stay with her whole family, which consisted entirely of persons of the female sex, and Alyosha ended up in the house of two ladies whom he had never seen before, some distant relations of Yefim Petrovich, but on what terms he did not know himself. A characteristic trait of his too, and very much so, was that he never cared at whose expense he lived. In this he was the complete opposite of his elder brother, Ivan Fyodorovich, who had struggled in poverty his first two years at the university, feeding himself by his own labour, and had felt bitterly from his very childhood that he was living on someone else’s bread, with a benefactor. But this strange trait in Alexei’s character, it seems, could not be condemned very severely, because anyone who got to know him even a little became sure at once, when the question arose, that Alexei was certainly one of those young men, something like holy fools, who, if a whole fortune were suddenly to fall into their hands, would not hesitate to give it away at the first request, either to a good cause or perhaps even simply to a clever rogue, if he asked him for it. And in general he seemed not to know the value of money at all; not in the literal sense, of course. When he was given pocket money, which he himself never asked for, he either did not know for whole weeks what to do with it, or was terribly careless with it, and it vanished from him in an instant. Pyotr Alexandrovich Miusov, a man very particular about money and bourgeois honesty, once, later on, having observed Alexei, pronounced the following aphorism about him: “Here, perhaps, is the only man in the world whom you could suddenly leave alone and without money in the square of an unknown city of a million inhabitants, and he would not perish for anything or die of hunger and cold, because he would be fed in an instant, settled in an instant, and if he were not settled, he would settle himself in an instant, and it would cost him no effort and no humiliation, and it would be no burden to the one who settled him; on the contrary, perhaps they would consider it a pleasure.”

He did not finish the course at his gymnasium; he still had a whole year to go when he suddenly announced to his ladies that he was going to his father on a certain matter that had come into his head. They were very sorry for him and did not want to let him go. The journey cost very little, and the ladies did not allow him to pawn his watch, a present from his benefactor’s family before they went abroad, but supplied him lavishly with means, even with new clothes and linen. He gave half the money back to them, however, declaring that he absolutely wanted to travel third class. Arriving in our little town, he made no direct answer to his parent’s first questions, “Why exactly have you come, without finishing the course?”, but was, they say, unusually thoughtful. It soon came out that he was looking for his mother’s grave. He even admitted then himself that this was the only reason he had come. But this hardly exhausted the whole reason for his coming. Most probably he did not know himself then, and could not for anything have explained, what exactly had as if suddenly risen from his soul and irresistibly drawn him onto some new, unknown, but already inevitable road. Fyodor Pavlovich could not show him where he had buried his second wife, because he had never been to her grave since the coffin was covered with earth, and with the passing of years he had quite forgotten where she had been buried...

A word about Fyodor Pavlovich. For a long time before this he had not lived in our town. Three or four years after his second wife’s death he went off to the south of Russia and ended up in Odessa, where he lived for several years on end. He first became acquainted, by his own account, “with a lot of Jews, Jewlings, Jewkins and little Jewlets”, and ended up by being received not only among the Jews but “even among the Hebrews”. One must suppose that it was in this period of his life that he developed a special skill in scraping together and squeezing out money. He came back to our little town for good only about three years before Alyosha’s arrival. His former acquaintances found him terribly aged, though he was not at all such an old man yet. He conducted himself not so much more nobly as somehow more insolently. There appeared, for example, in the former buffoon an insolent need to make buffoons of others. He liked to behave outrageously with the female sex not only as before but even, as it were, more repulsively. Soon he became the founder of many new taverns around the district. It was evident that he had perhaps a hundred thousand, or only a little less. Many of the townspeople and of the inhabitants of the district at once got into debt to him, against the safest securities, of course. In the very last period he had somehow grown flabby, had begun somehow to lose his evenness and self-control, had fallen even into a kind of frivolity, would begin one thing and end with another, somehow sprawled about, and got drunk more and more often; and if it had not been for the same footman Grigory, who had also aged considerably by that time and looked after him sometimes almost like a tutor, then perhaps Fyodor Pavlovich would not have lived without special trouble. Alyosha’s arrival seemed to affect him even on the moral side, as if something had awakened in this prematurely old man of what had long since been stifled in his soul. “Do you know,” he often began to say to Alyosha, looking at him closely, “that you are like her, the shrieker?” That was what he called his late wife, Alyosha’s mother. It was the footman Grigory who at last showed Alyosha the grave of the “shrieker”. He took him to our town cemetery and there, in a remote corner, showed him an inexpensive but neat cast-iron slab, on which there was even an inscription with the name, rank, age and year of death of the deceased, and at the bottom there was even engraved a kind of quatrain, from the old cemetery verses commonly used on the graves of people of the middling sort. To his surprise, this slab turned out to be Grigory’s doing. It was he himself who had put it up over the grave of the poor “shrieker”, at his own expense, after Fyodor Pavlovich, whom he had pestered many times with reminders about this grave, had at last gone off to Odessa, waving his hand not only at graves but at all his memories. Alyosha showed no particular emotion at his mother’s grave; he only listened to Grigory’s solemn and sensible account of the putting up of the slab, stood with his head bowed, and went away without uttering a word. Since then, perhaps for the whole year, he had not even been to the cemetery. But this little episode had its effect on Fyodor Pavlovich too, and a very original one. He suddenly took a thousand roubles and took it to our monastery for prayers for the soul of his wife, but not the second, not Alyosha’s mother, not the “shrieker”, but the first, Adelaida Ivanovna, who used to beat him. In the evening of that day he got drunk and abused the monks to Alyosha. He himself was far from being a religious man; a man who had perhaps never put a five-kopeck candle before an icon. Strange impulses of sudden feelings and sudden thoughts come over such subjects.

I have already said that he had grown very flabby. His physiognomy by that time presented something that bore sharp witness to the character and essence of the whole life he had lived. Besides the long, fleshy little bags under his small eyes, always insolent, suspicious and mocking, besides a multitude of deep little wrinkles on his small but fat little face, there hung under his sharp chin a big Adam’s apple, fleshy and oblong like a purse, which gave him a kind of repulsively sensual look. Add to this a carnivorous, long mouth, with plump lips, from under which small stumps of black, almost decayed teeth could be seen. He spluttered every time he began to speak. He himself, however, liked to joke about his face, though it seems he remained pleased with it. He especially pointed to his nose, not very big, but very thin, with a strongly pronounced hump: “A real Roman one,” he used to say; “together with the Adam’s apple, the real physiognomy of an ancient Roman patrician of the time of the decline.” He seemed proud of this.

And fairly soon after finding his mother’s grave, Alyosha suddenly announced to him that he wanted to enter the monastery and that the monks were ready to admit him as a novice. He explained that this was his extraordinary wish and that he was asking his solemn permission as his father. The old man already knew that the elder Zosima, who was living out his days in the monastery hermitage, had made a special impression on his “quiet boy”.

“That elder, of course, is the most honest monk they have,” he said, having listened to Alyosha in silence and thoughtfully, though hardly at all surprised by his request. “Hm, so that’s where you want to go, my quiet boy!” He was half drunk, and suddenly smiled his long, half-drunken smile, not without cunning and drunken slyness. “Hm, and you know I had a presentiment that you would end up with something just like this, can you imagine it? That is just where you were heading. Well, why not; you have your own two little thousands, there’s a dowry for you, and I will never leave you, my angel, and I’ll pay in for you now whatever is due, if they ask. Well, and if they don’t ask, why should we push ourselves on them, eh? After all, you spend money like a canary, two little grains a week... Hm. You know, at one monastery there is a little settlement outside the town, and everyone there knows that only ‘monastery wives’ live in it, that is what they call them there, thirty wives or so, I think... I’ve been there, and you know, it is interesting, in its own way of course, in the sense of variety. The only bad thing is the dreadful Russianism; there are no French girls at all yet, though there might be, the means are excellent. They’ll get wind of it and come. Well, but here there is nothing, here there are no monastery wives, but about two hundred monks. Honest. Fasters. I confess... Hm. So you want to go to the monks? And you know, I am sorry for you, Alyosha, truly, would you believe it, I have come to love you... However, here is a convenient opportunity: you will pray for us sinners; we have sinned far too much, sitting here. I have kept thinking: who will ever pray for me? Is there such a person in the world? My dear boy, I am terribly stupid on that score, perhaps you don’t believe it? Terribly. You see: stupid as I am, I keep thinking about it, keep thinking, now and then, of course, not all the time. It is impossible, I think, that the devils should forget to drag me off to them with hooks when I die. Well, so I think: hooks? And where do they get them? What are they made of? Iron? Where are they forged? Do they have some kind of factory down there? Why, the monks in the monastery there probably suppose that in hell, for example, there is a ceiling. And I am ready to believe in hell, only without a ceiling; it comes out more delicate, as it were, more enlightened, more Lutheran, that is. And in essence isn’t it all the same: with a ceiling or without a ceiling? Why, that is where the damned question lies! Well, and if there is no ceiling, then there are no hooks either. And if there are no hooks, then everything goes by the board, which again is improbable: who then will drag me off with hooks, because if they don’t drag me off, then what will happen, where is there any justice in the world? Il faudrait les inventer, one would have to invent them, those hooks, for me on purpose, for me alone, because if you knew, Alyosha, what a shameless wretch I am!..”
“Yes, there are no hooks there,” Alyosha said quietly and seriously, looking closely at his father.

“Just so, just so, only the shadows of hooks. I know, I know. It is like a certain Frenchman’s description of hell: ‘J’ai vu l’ombre d’un cocher, qui avec l’ombre d’une brosse frottait l’ombre d’un carrosse’: ‘I saw the shadow of a coachman, who with the shadow of a brush was rubbing the shadow of a carriage.’ How do you know, my dear, that there are no hooks? Stay with the monks a while, and you will sing a different tune. But then, go, get to the truth there, and come and tell me: it will be easier to go to the other world after all, if you know for certain what is there. And it will be more proper for you at the monks’ than with me, with a drunken old man and with girls... though nothing will touch you, as nothing touches an angel. Well, perhaps nothing will touch you there either; that is why I am allowing you, because I am hoping for that last. The devil hasn’t eaten your wits. You will burn out and go out, get cured and come back. And I will wait for you: why, I feel that you are the only man on earth who has not condemned me, my dear boy, I feel it, I can’t help feeling it!..”
And he even began to whimper. He was sentimental. He was wicked and sentimental.
## Book Three: The Sensualists · Chapter I · In the Servants’ Quarters

Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov’s house stood far from the very centre of the town, but not quite on the outskirts either. It was rather dilapidated, but had a pleasant appearance: one storey, with an attic room, painted grey, with a red iron roof. It could still stand a very long time, however; it was roomy and cosy. There were many little storerooms in it, many hiding places and unexpected little staircases. There were rats in it, but Fyodor Pavlovich was not altogether angry with them: “All the same it’s not so boring in the evenings when you are left alone.” And he really did have the habit of sending the servants off to the lodge for the night and locking himself up alone in the house all night. This lodge stood in the yard; it was large and solid; Fyodor Pavlovich had decided that the kitchen should be there too, though there was a kitchen in the house: he did not like the smell of cooking, and the food was carried across the yard winter and summer. In general the house had been built for a large family: five times as many masters and servants could have been housed in it. But at the time of our story only Fyodor Pavlovich and Ivan Fyodorovich lived in the house, and in the servants’ lodge only three servants: old Grigory, old Marfa, his wife, and the servant Smerdyakov, still a young man. I must say a little more in detail about these three persons in service. About old Grigory Vasilievich Kutuzov, however, we have already said enough. He was a firm and unswerving man, going stubbornly and in a straight line towards his point, if only that point, for some reason (often amazingly illogical), stood before him as an unalterable truth. Generally speaking, he was honest and incorruptible. His wife, Marfa Ignatievna, although she had bowed without question to her husband’s will all her life, pestered him terribly, for example, immediately after the emancipation of the serfs, to leave Fyodor Pavlovich and go to Moscow and start some little business there (they had some little money put by); but Grigory decided then and there, once and for all, that the woman was talking nonsense, “because every woman is dishonest”, but that they ought not to leave their former master, whatever he might be himself, “because that is now their duty”.
“Do you understand what duty is?” he said, turning to Marfa Ignatievna.
“I understand about duty, Grigory Vasilievich, but what duty we have to stay here, that I don’t understand at all,” Marfa Ignatievna answered firmly.
“Then don’t understand, but that’s how it will be. Be quiet from now on.”

And so it came out: they did not leave, and Fyodor Pavlovich fixed them a wage, a small one, and paid the wage. Grigory knew besides that he had an indisputable influence over his master. He felt it, and it was true: the cunning and stubborn buffoon Fyodor Pavlovich, very firm of character “in some things in life”, as he himself put it, was, to his own surprise, even rather weak of character in some other “things in life”. And he knew himself in which, knew and feared much. In some things in life one had to keep one’s ears pricked, and it was hard without a faithful man, and Grigory was the most faithful of men. It even happened that Fyodor Pavlovich might many times in the course of his career have been beaten, and beaten painfully, and it was always Grigory who rescued him, though each time he read him a lecture afterwards. But beatings alone would not have frightened Fyodor Pavlovich: there were higher cases, and even very subtle and complex ones, when Fyodor Pavlovich himself would perhaps not have been able to define that extraordinary need for a faithful and close person which he would sometimes suddenly, instantly and incomprehensibly, begin to feel in himself. These were almost morbid cases: most depraved, and in his sensuality often cruel, like a wicked insect, Fyodor Pavlovich would suddenly feel in himself at times, in drunken moments, a spiritual fear and a moral shock, which echoed in his soul almost, so to speak, physically. “At those times my soul seems to be fluttering in my throat,” he used to say sometimes. It was just at such moments that he liked to have near him, close by, perhaps not in the same room but in the lodge, a man like that, devoted, firm, not at all like himself, not depraved, who, though he saw all this dissipation going on and knew all the secrets, would still allow it all out of devotion, would not oppose it, and above all would not reproach him or threaten him with anything, either in this world or in the next; and in case of need would even defend him; from whom? From someone unknown, but terrible and dangerous. The point was precisely that there should certainly be another man, an old and friendly one, so that in a sick moment he could call him, only in order to look into his face, perhaps to exchange a word, even a quite irrelevant one; and if the man was all right and not angry, then the heart was somehow easier, and if he was angry, well, then it was sadder. It happened (though extremely rarely) that Fyodor Pavlovich even went at night to the lodge to wake Grigory, so that he would come to him for a minute. Grigory would come, and Fyodor Pavlovich would talk about the most complete trifles and soon let him go, sometimes even with a little mockery and a little joke, and he himself, with a spit, would go to bed and sleep the sleep of the righteous. Something of this kind happened to Fyodor Pavlovich after Alyosha’s arrival too. Alyosha had “pierced his heart” by the fact that he “lived, saw everything and condemned nothing”. More than that, he brought with him something unheard of: a complete absence of contempt for him, the old man; on the contrary, a constant gentleness and a perfectly natural, straightforward affection for him, who had deserved it so little. All this was a complete surprise for the old rake and man without a family, quite unexpected for him, who had until then loved only “filth”. After Alyosha left he admitted to himself that he had understood something which until then he had not wanted to understand.

I have already mentioned at the beginning of my story how Grigory hated Adelaida Ivanovna, Fyodor Pavlovich’s first wife and the mother of his first son, Dmitry Fyodorovich, and how, on the contrary, he defended his second wife, the shrieker Sofya Ivanovna, against his master himself and against anyone who took it into his head to say a bad or frivolous word about her. In him sympathy for this unhappy woman had turned into something sacred, so that even twenty years later he would not have borne, from whomever it came, even a bad hint about her, and would at once have retorted to the offender. In appearance Grigory was a cold and grave man, not talkative, letting out weighty, unfrivolous words. In the same way it would have been impossible to make out at first glance whether he loved his uncomplaining, obedient wife or not, and yet he really did love her, and she of course understood it. This Marfa Ignatievna was a woman not only far from stupid, but perhaps cleverer than her spouse, at least more sensible than he in everyday matters, and yet she submitted to him without a murmur and without answering back, from the very beginning of their marriage, and indisputably respected him for his spiritual superiority. It is remarkable that all their lives they talked very little to each other, except about the most necessary and current things. The grave and majestic Grigory always thought over all his affairs and cares alone, so that Marfa Ignatievna had long since understood once and for all that he did not need her advice at all. She felt that her husband valued her silence and acknowledged her intelligence for it. He had never beaten her, except just once, and then only lightly. In the first year of Adelaida Ivanovna’s marriage to Fyodor Pavlovich, once in the country, the village girls and women, still serfs then, had been gathered in the manor yard to sing and dance. They began “In the meadows”, and suddenly Marfa Ignatievna, still a young woman then, sprang out in front of the chorus and did the “Russian dance” in a special manner, not in the village way, like the women, but as she had danced when she was a house serf girl at the rich Miusovs’ in their private manor theatre, where the actors were taught to dance by a dancing master brought from Moscow. Grigory saw how his wife had danced, and at home in their cottage, an hour later, he taught her a lesson, pulling her hair a little. But with that the beatings ended once and for all and were never repeated even once in all their lives, and Marfa Ignatievna swore off dancing from then on.

God had not given them children; there had been one baby, and he had died. But Grigory evidently loved children, and did not even hide it, that is, was not ashamed to show it. When Adelaida Ivanovna ran away he took Dmitry Fyodorovich into his arms, a boy of three, and fussed over him for almost a year, combed him with a comb himself, even washed him in a tub himself. Afterwards he took trouble over Ivan Fyodorovich and Alyosha too, for which he got a slap in the face; but I have already told all about that. As for his own baby, it gladdened him only with hope while Marfa Ignatievna was still pregnant. When it was born, it struck his heart with grief and horror. The point is that this boy was born with six fingers. Seeing this, Grigory was so crushed that he not only kept silent right up to the very day of the christening, but went out into the garden on purpose to be silent there. It was spring, and for all three days he dug beds in the kitchen garden. On the third day the baby was to be christened; by this time Grigory had worked something out. Entering the cottage, where the clergy had gathered and the guests had come and, finally, Fyodor Pavlovich himself, who had come in person as godfather, he suddenly announced that the child “ought not to be christened at all”; he announced it not loudly, did not enlarge on it in words, barely squeezed out word by word, and only looked dully and intently at the priest as he did so.
“Why so?” the priest inquired with merry surprise.
“Because it... is a dragon...” muttered Grigory.
“What do you mean, a dragon, what dragon?”
Grigory was silent for some time.
“A confusion of nature has occurred...” he muttered, though very unclearly, yet very firmly, and evidently not wishing to say any more.

They laughed, and of course the poor little baby was christened. Grigory prayed zealously at the font, but did not change his opinion of the newborn. However, he did not hinder anything; only for all the two weeks that the sickly boy lived he hardly looked at him, did not even want to notice him, and for the most part went out of the cottage. But when two weeks later the boy died of thrush, he himself laid him in the little coffin, looked at him with deep anguish, and when they filled in the shallow little grave, he knelt down and bowed to the ground before the little grave. After that, for many years, he never once mentioned his child, and Marfa Ignatievna never once recalled her child in his presence, and when she happened to talk to anyone about her “little one”, she talked in a whisper, even if Grigory Vasilievich was not there. According to Marfa Ignatievna’s observation, from that very grave he began to occupy himself chiefly with “the divine”; he read the Lives of the Saints, mostly silently and alone, each time putting on his big round silver spectacles. He rarely read aloud, except perhaps in Lent. He loved the Book of Job; he had got hold somewhere of a copy of the sayings and sermons of “our God-bearing father Isaac the Syrian”, read it stubbornly and for many years, understood almost absolutely nothing in it, but perhaps for that very reason valued and loved this book most of all. Quite recently he had begun to listen to and look into the Khlyst sect, an opportunity for which had turned up in the neighbourhood; he was evidently shaken, but did not see fit to go over to the new faith. His reading “in the divine”, of course, gave his physiognomy still greater gravity.

Perhaps he was inclined to mysticism. And then, as if on purpose, the event of the birth of his six-fingered baby and its death coincided exactly with another very strange, unexpected and original event, which left on his soul, as he himself once put it afterwards, “a seal”. It so happened that on the very day they buried the six-fingered little one, Marfa Ignatievna, waking in the night, heard what sounded like the crying of a newborn child. She was frightened and woke her husband. He listened and remarked that it was more likely someone moaning, “a woman, it seems”. He got up and dressed; it was a fairly warm May night. Coming out onto the porch, he heard clearly that the moans were coming from the garden. But the garden was locked for the night with a padlock from the yard side, and there was no getting into it except by this entrance, because a strong and high fence ran round the whole garden. Returning home, Grigory lit a lantern, took the garden key and, paying no attention to the hysterical horror of his wife, who still insisted that she heard a child crying and that it must be her boy crying and calling her, silently went into the garden. There he clearly made out that the moans were coming from their little bathhouse, which stood in the garden, not far from the gate, and that it really was a woman moaning. Opening the bathhouse, he saw a sight before which he stood stupefied: a holy fool of the town, who wandered the streets and was known to the whole town, nicknamed Lizaveta Smerdyashchaya, Stinking Lizaveta, had got into their bathhouse and had just given birth to a baby. The baby lay beside her, and she was dying beside it. She said nothing, if only because she did not know how to speak. But all this ought to be explained separately.
## Chapter II · Stinking Lizaveta

There was one special circumstance here which deeply shook Grigory, finally confirming in him a certain unpleasant and loathsome earlier suspicion. This Lizaveta Smerdyashchaya was a girl of very small stature, “four feet and a little”, as many of the pious old women of our little town touchingly remembered after her death. Her twenty-year-old face, healthy, broad and ruddy, was completely that of an idiot; the look of her eyes was fixed and unpleasant, though meek. All her life, summer and winter, she went barefoot and in nothing but a hempen shift. Her almost black hair, extremely thick and curly like a ram’s, sat on her head like some kind of enormous cap. Besides, it was always soiled with earth and mud, with little leaves, splinters and shavings stuck in it, because she always slept on the ground and in the mud. Her father was a homeless, ruined and sickly tradesman, Ilya, who drank heavily and had lived for many years as a sort of labourer with some well-to-do employers, also tradespeople of ours. Lizaveta’s mother had died long ago. The eternally sickly and spiteful Ilya used to beat Lizaveta inhumanly when she came home. But she came home rarely, because she lived as a dependant all over the town, as a holy fool, a person of God. Both Ilya’s employers and Ilya himself, and even many of the compassionate townspeople, merchants and merchants’ wives chiefly, tried more than once to dress Lizaveta more decently than in a shift alone, and towards winter they always put a sheepskin coat on her and boots on her feet; but she would usually let them put everything on her without a word, then go off and somewhere, chiefly on the porch of the cathedral church, would certainly take off everything given her, whether a kerchief, a skirt, the sheepskin, the boots; she left everything on the spot and went away barefoot and in her shift as before. It once happened that a new governor of our province, making a tour of inspection through our little town, was much offended in his best feelings on seeing Lizaveta, and though he understood that she was a “holy fool”, as was reported to him, he nevertheless pointed out that a young girl wandering about in nothing but a shift offended decency, and so this must not happen in future. But the governor went away, and Lizaveta was left as she was. At last her father died, and by that very fact she became still dearer to all the pious people in the town, as an orphan. Indeed, everyone seemed even to love her; even the boys did not tease or hurt her, and our boys, especially at school, are a mischievous lot. She went into strangers’ houses, and no one drove her out; on the contrary, everyone would be kind to her and give her a half-kopeck. They would give her a half-kopeck, she would take it and at once carry it off and drop it into some church or prison collection box. If they gave her a bagel or a loaf at the market, she would certainly go and give the bagel or loaf to the first child she met, or else stop one of our richest ladies and give it to her; and the ladies even accepted it with joy. She herself lived on nothing but black bread and water. She would go into a rich shop, sit down; expensive goods lay there, and money too; the owners never watched her; they knew that even if thousands of roubles were laid out before her and forgotten, she would not take a kopeck of them. She rarely went into church; she slept either on church porches or, having climbed over someone’s wattle fence (we still have many wattle fences instead of board fences even today), in someone’s kitchen garden. She came home, that is, to the house of the employers with whom her late father had lived, about once a week, and in winter she came every day, but only for the night, and slept either in the passage or in the cowshed. People marvelled that she could stand such a life, but she was used to it; though she was small, she was of extraordinarily strong build. Some of our gentry maintained that she did all this only out of pride, but somehow that did not fit: she could not even say a word, and only rarely moved her tongue and mumbled; what pride was there in that? And so it happened that once (this was a long time ago), on a bright and warm September night, at full moon, very late by our standards, a tipsy band of our gentry out on a spree, five or six fine fellows, were returning home from the club “by the back ways”. On both sides of the lane ran a wattle fence, behind which stretched the kitchen gardens of the adjoining houses; and the lane came out onto a footbridge across our long, stinking puddle, which among us it is the custom to call a river sometimes. By the fence, in the nettles and burdock, our company caught sight of Lizaveta asleep. The gentlemen, who had had a drop, stopped over her with guffaws and began to make jokes with every possible lack of restraint. One young gentleman suddenly had a completely eccentric question come into his head on an impossible subject: “Could anyone at all, they say, regard such a beast as a woman, now for instance,” and so on. They all decided with proud disgust that one could not. But Fyodor Pavlovich happened to be in this little crowd, and he instantly jumped forward and decided that one could regard her as a woman, even very much so, and that there was even something piquant of a special kind in it, and so on and so on. True, at that time he was even far too deliberately pushing himself forward among us in his part of buffoon; he liked to jump forward and amuse the gentry, apparently as an equal of course, but in fact as a complete lout before them. This was precisely the very time when he had received the news from Petersburg of the death of his first wife, Adelaida Ivanovna, and when, with crape on his hat, he was drinking and behaving so outrageously that some people in the town, even among the most dissolute, were sickened at the sight of him. The band, of course, roared with laughter at this unexpected opinion; one of the band even began egging Fyodor Pavlovich on, but the rest began spitting even more, though still with excessive merriment, and at last they all went off on their way. Afterwards Fyodor Pavlovich swore that he too had gone away then with all the rest; perhaps that is exactly how it was; no one knows for certain and no one ever did; but five or six months later the whole town began talking with sincere and extraordinary indignation about Lizaveta’s going about pregnant; they asked and inquired: whose sin was it, who was the offender? And it was just then that a strange rumour suddenly spread through the whole town that the offender was this very Fyodor Pavlovich. Where did this rumour come from? Of that band of revelling gentlemen only one participant remained in the town by that time, and he an elderly and respectable state councillor, with a family and grown-up daughters, who would certainly not have spread anything even if there had been something; the other participants, some five men, had left by then. But the rumour pointed straight at Fyodor Pavlovich and went on pointing. Of course he did not even much protest: he would not even have bothered to answer some petty merchants or tradesmen. He was proud then, and did not talk except in his own company of officials and nobles, whom he amused so much. It was at this time that Grigory stood up energetically and with all his might for his master, and not only defended him against all these slanders, but entered into quarrels and arguments on his behalf and convinced many. “She herself, the low creature, is to blame,” he said positively, and the offender was none other than “Karp with the screw” (that was the name of a terrible convict well known to the town at that time, who had escaped by then from the provincial prison and was living secretly in our town). This guess seemed plausible; people remembered Karp; they remembered precisely that on those very nights, towards autumn, he had been roaming the town and had robbed three people. But this whole incident and all this talk not only did not turn general sympathy away from the poor holy fool, but everyone began to guard and protect her even more. A merchant’s widow, Kondratieva, a well-to-do woman, even arranged to take Lizaveta into her house at the end of April, intending not to let her out until her confinement. They watched her without sleeping, but it so happened that in spite of all the watchfulness, on the very last day, in the evening, Lizaveta suddenly slipped away secretly from Kondratieva’s and turned up in Fyodor Pavlovich’s garden. How in her condition she climbed over the high and strong garden fence remained a sort of riddle. Some insisted that she had been “carried over”, others that “something had carried her over”. Most probably it all happened in a very ingenious but natural way, and Lizaveta, who knew how to climb wattle fences into strangers’ kitchen gardens to sleep in them, somehow got up onto Fyodor Pavlovich’s fence too, and jumped down from it into the garden, though to her own harm, in spite of her condition. Grigory rushed to Marfa Ignatievna and sent her to help Lizaveta, and he himself ran for an old midwife, a tradeswoman, who happened to live not far off. They saved the baby, but by dawn Lizaveta was dead. Grigory took the baby, brought it into the house, sat his wife down and laid it on her knees, right at her breast: “A child of God, an orphan, is everyone’s kin, and ours all the more. Our little dead one has sent us this one, and this one was born of the devil’s son and a righteous woman. Feed him, and weep no more.” And so Marfa Ignatievna brought up the child. He was christened and named Pavel, and as for his patronymic, everyone, of their own accord, without being told, began calling him Fyodorovich. Fyodor Pavlovich did not object to anything and even found it all amusing, though he went on with all his might denying everything. The town liked his having taken in the foundling. Later Fyodor Pavlovich invented a surname for the foundling too: he called him Smerdyakov, after his mother’s nickname, Lizaveta Smerdyashchaya. And this Smerdyakov became Fyodor Pavlovich’s second servant, and at the beginning of our story he was living in the lodge with old Grigory and old Marfa. He was employed as a cook. I really ought to add something about him specially, but I am ashamed to distract my reader’s attention so long to such ordinary servants, and so I pass on to my story, hoping that Smerdyakov will somehow come in of himself in the further course of the tale.
## Chapter III · The Confession of a Passionate Heart, in Verse

Alyosha, having heard his father’s order, which the old man had shouted to him from the carriage as he drove away from the monastery, stayed for some time where he was in great perplexity. Not that he stood like a post; that never happened to him. On the contrary, for all his uneasiness he managed at once to go to the Father Superior’s kitchen and find out what his papa had done upstairs. Then, however, he set off, hoping that on the way to the town he would somehow manage to solve the problem that was troubling him. I will say beforehand: he was not in the least afraid of his father’s shouts and his order to move home “with your pillows and mattress”. He understood only too well that the order to move, given aloud and with such a show of shouting, had been given “in a fit of enthusiasm”, so to speak even for effect, rather like a tradesman of their little town who, carousing not long ago at his own name-day party, and in front of his guests, getting angry because they would not give him any more vodka, suddenly began smashing his own crockery, tearing his own and his wife’s clothes, breaking his furniture and, finally, the windows in the house, and all again for effect; and of course something of the same kind had happened now with his papa. The next day, of course, the carousing tradesman, sobered up, regretted the broken cups and plates. Alyosha knew that the old man too would certainly let him go back to the monastery the next day, perhaps even today. And besides he was completely sure that his father, whomever else he might wish to offend, would not wish to offend him. Alyosha was sure that no one in the whole world would ever wish to offend him; not only would not wish to, but could not. For him this was an axiom, given once and for all, without reasoning, and in this sense he went forward without any hesitation.
