But at this moment another fear was stirring in him, a fear of quite another kind, and all the more tormenting because he could not have defined it himself: namely a fear of a woman, and precisely of Katerina Ivanovna, who had so insistently begged him, in the note passed to him that morning by Madame Khokhlakova, to come and see her for some reason. This request, and the necessity of certainly going, had at once planted a tormenting feeling in his heart, and all morning, the further it went, the more and more painfully this feeling had been aching in him, in spite of all the scenes and adventures that had followed in the monastery, and just now at the Father Superior’s, and so on and so on. He was not afraid because he did not know what she would talk to him about and what he would answer her. And it was not women in general that he feared in her: he knew little of women, of course, but still all his life, from his very infancy until the monastery, he had lived with them alone. He was afraid of this woman, of Katerina Ivanovna herself precisely. He had been afraid of her from the very time he first saw her. He had seen her only once or twice, perhaps three times, and had even once happened to exchange a few words with her. He remembered her image as that of a beautiful, proud and imperious girl. But it was not her beauty that tormented him; it was something else. It was precisely this inexplicability of his fear that now increased his fear. This girl’s aims were most noble, he knew it; she was trying to save his brother Dmitry, who was already guilty before her, and trying out of sheer magnanimity alone. And yet, in spite of his recognition of this and of the justice which he could not help rendering to all these beautiful and magnanimous feelings, a chill ran down his spine the nearer he came to her house.

He reckoned that he would not find his brother Ivan Fyodorovich, who was so close to her, at her house: brother Ivan would surely be with their father now. Still more surely he would not find Dmitry there, and he had a presentiment why. So their conversation would take place alone. He would have very much liked to see his brother Dmitry before this fateful conversation, and run in to see him. Without showing him the letter, he could have exchanged a few words with him. But brother Dmitry lived far away and was surely not at home now either. Having stood still for a minute, he finally made up his mind. Crossing himself with a habitual, hurried sign of the cross, and at once smiling at something, he set off firmly towards his terrible lady.

He knew her house. But if he had gone by the High Street, then across the square, and so on, it would have been rather far. Our small town is extraordinarily spread out, and the distances in it are sometimes quite large. Besides, his father was waiting for him, might not have forgotten his order yet, might turn capricious, and so he had to hurry so as to manage both here and there. As a result of all these considerations he decided to shorten the way by going by the back ways, and he knew all these passages in the little town like the five fingers of his hand. By the back ways meant almost without roads, along deserted fences, sometimes even climbing over strangers’ wattle fences, passing through strangers’ yards, where, however, everyone knew him and everyone greeted him. By this way he could come out onto the High Street in half the distance. At one point he even had to pass very close to his father’s house, namely past the garden next to his father’s, which belonged to a small, dilapidated, crooked little house with four windows. The owner of this little house was, as Alyosha knew, a tradeswoman of the town, an old woman without legs, who lived with her daughter, formerly a civilised housemaid in the capital, who until recently had lived in nothing but generals’ households and had now come home a year ago because of the old woman’s illness, and showed off in smart dresses. This old woman and her daughter, however, had fallen into terrible poverty and even went every day next door to Fyodor Pavlovich’s kitchen for soup and bread. Marfa Ignatievna poured them out some willingly. But the daughter, coming for soup, had not sold a single one of her dresses, and one of them even had a very long train. Alyosha had learned of this last circumstance, quite by chance of course, from his friend Rakitin, to whom absolutely everything in their little town was known, and having learned it, he of course forgot it at once. But now, coming level with the neighbour’s garden, he suddenly remembered precisely that train, quickly raised his drooping and thoughtful head, and... suddenly came upon a most unexpected encounter.

Behind the wattle fence in the neighbour’s garden, perched on something, leaning out to his chest, stood his brother Dmitry Fyodorovich, making signs to him with his hands with all his might, calling him and beckoning to him, evidently afraid not only to shout but even to say a word aloud, lest he be heard. Alyosha at once ran up to the fence.

“It’s good that you looked round yourself, or else I nearly shouted to you,” Dmitry Fyodorovich whispered to him joyfully and hurriedly. “Climb in here! Quickly! Ah, how splendid that you’ve come. I was just thinking about you...”

Alyosha was glad himself, and was only puzzled how to get over the fence. But “Mitya” caught his elbow with a mighty hand and helped him jump. Gathering up his cassock, Alyosha leapt over with the agility of a barefoot town boy.
“Well done, come on!” broke from Mitya in a rapturous whisper.

“Where to?” Alyosha whispered too, looking round on all sides and seeing himself in a completely empty garden, in which there was no one but the two of them. The garden was small, but the owner’s little house still stood at least fifty paces from them. “But there’s no one here; why are you whispering?”

“Why am I whispering? Ah, the devil take it,” Dmitry Fyodorovich suddenly shouted at the top of his voice, “why am I whispering? Well, you see for yourself how a confusion of nature can suddenly come about. I am here in secret, keeping watch on a secret. The explanation later; but, knowing that it’s a secret, I suddenly started talking secretly too, and whispering like a fool, when there’s no need. Come on! Over there! Until then, be quiet. I want to kiss you!

> Glory to the Highest in the world,
> Glory to the Highest in me!..
I was just repeating that, sitting here, before you came...”

The garden was about an acre in size, or a little more, but planted with trees only round the edges, along all four fences: apple trees, maple, lime, birch. The middle of the garden was empty, laid down to a meadow, from which several hundredweight of hay were mown in summer. The owner let the garden out from the spring for a few roubles. There were also beds of raspberries, gooseberries and currants, also all along the fences; vegetable beds close to the house, started only recently, however. Dmitry Fyodorovich led his guest to the corner of the garden furthest from the house. There, among thickly growing limes and old bushes of currant and elder, guelder rose and lilac, there suddenly appeared something like the ruins of a very ancient green summer house, blackened and lopsided, with latticed walls, but with a covered roof, under which one could still shelter from the rain. God knows when the summer house had been built, by tradition about fifty years before, by some owner of the little house at that time, Alexander Karlovich von Schmidt, a retired lieutenant colonel. But everything had already rotted; the floor had decayed, all the floorboards were loose, the wood smelled of damp. In the summer house stood a green wooden table, dug into the ground, and round it ran benches, also green, on which one could still sit. Alyosha had noticed his brother’s rapturous state at once, but on entering the summer house he saw half a bottle of brandy and a little glass on the table.
“It’s brandy!” Mitya burst out laughing. “And you are already looking: ‘drinking again’? Don’t believe the phantom.

> Do not believe the empty, lying crowd,
> forget your doubts...

I am not drinking; I am only ‘savouring’, as that swine of yours Rakitin says, who will become a state councillor and will always say ‘savouring’. Sit down. I would like to take you, Alyoshka, and press you to my breast, so as to crush you, because in the whole world... really... re-al-ly... (take it in! take it in!) I love only you!”
He uttered this last line in a kind of almost frenzy.

“Only you, and one more, a ‘low woman’, with whom I have fallen in love, and with that I am done for. But to fall in love does not mean to love. One can fall in love and hate. Remember that! Now, while I am merry, I’m talking! Sit down here at the table, and I’ll sit beside you, and look at you, and talk all the time. You will be silent all the time, and I will talk all the time, because the time has come. But then, you know, I have decided that I really must speak quietly, because here... here... the most unexpected ears may turn up. I’ll explain everything; it has been said: to be continued. Why have I been longing for you, thirsting for you now, all these days, and now? (I have dropped anchor here for five days already.) All these days? Because I will tell everything to you alone, because I must, because you are needed, because tomorrow I fly down from the clouds, because tomorrow life will end and begin. Have you ever felt, have you ever seen in a dream, how one falls from a mountain into a pit? Well, now I am falling, and not in a dream. And I am not afraid, and don’t you be afraid. That is, I am afraid, but it is sweet to me. That is, not sweet, but rapture... Well, the devil, it makes no difference, whatever happens. A strong spirit, a weak spirit, a woman’s spirit, whatever happens! Let us praise nature: look how much sun there is, how clear the sky, all the leaves are green, it is still quite summer, four o’clock in the afternoon, the stillness! Where were you going?”
“I was going to Father, but first I meant to call on Katerina Ivanovna.”

“To her and to Father! Ooh! A coincidence! Why, what else did I call you for, what else did I want you for, hunger and thirst for with all the curves of my soul and even my ribs? Precisely to send you to Father from me, and then to her, to Katerina Ivanovna, and so be done both with her and with Father. To send an angel. I could have sent anyone, but I needed to send an angel. And here you are going to her and to Father yourself.”
“Did you really mean to send me?” broke from Alyosha, with a pained expression on his face.
“Stop, you knew it. And I see that you understood everything at once. But be quiet, be quiet for now. Don’t pity me and don’t cry!”
Dmitry Fyodorovich stood up, fell to thinking and put a finger to his forehead.
“She called you herself, she wrote you a letter or something, that’s why you were going to her; otherwise would you have gone?”
“Here is the note,” Alyosha took it out of his pocket. Mitya quickly ran through it.

“And you came by the back ways! O gods! I thank you for directing him by the back ways, so that he fell into my hands like the golden fish to the old fool of a fisherman in the fairy tale. Listen, Alyosha, listen, brother. Now I mean to tell everything. For one must tell someone at least. I have told an angel in heaven already, but I must tell an angel on earth too. You are an angel on earth. You will listen, you will judge, and you will forgive... And that is just what I need, for someone higher to forgive me. Listen: if two beings suddenly tear themselves away from everything earthly and fly into the extraordinary, or at least one of them does, and before that, flying away or perishing, he comes to the other and says: do this and that for me, something which is never asked of anyone, but which can be asked only on one’s deathbed; then surely the other will not refuse to do it... if he is a friend, if he is a brother?”
“I will do it, but tell me what it is, and tell me quickly,” said Alyosha.

“Quickly... Hm. Don’t hurry, Alyosha: you are hurrying and worrying. There is no need to hurry now. Now the world has come out onto a new street. Eh, Alyosha, what a pity you have never thought your way to rapture! But then, what am I saying to him? You, not thought your way to it! What am I saying, blockhead that I am:
> Be noble, O man!
Whose verse is that?”

Alyosha resolved to wait. He understood that all his business really was, perhaps, here alone now. Mitya fell to thinking for a minute, leaning his elbow on the table and resting his head on his palm. Both were silent.

“Lyosha,” said Mitya, “you alone won’t laugh! I would like to begin... my confession... with Schiller’s hymn to joy. An die Freude! To Joy! But I don’t know German; I know only that it is an die Freude. And don’t think I am babbling drunk either. I am not drunk at all. Brandy is brandy, but I need two bottles to get drunk:

> And ruddy-faced Silenus
> upon his stumbling ass;

and I haven’t drunk a quarter of a bottle, and I am not Silenus. Not Silenus, but silent-strong, because I have taken a decision for ever. Forgive me the pun; you must forgive me much today, not only a pun. Don’t worry, I am not spreading it thin, I am talking business and I’ll come to the business in a moment. I won’t drag it out of my soul like a miser. Wait, how does it go...”
He raised his head, fell to thinking, and suddenly began rapturously:

> Timid, naked and wild, the troglodyte
> hid in the caves of the rocks;
> the nomad wandered over the fields
> and laid the fields waste.
> The hunter, with spear and arrows,
> ran fearsome through the woods...
> Woe to those cast by the waves
> upon inhospitable shores!
> From the heights of Olympus
> Mother Ceres comes down in search
> of her stolen Proserpina:
> the world lies wild before her.
> No shelter and no welcome
> anywhere for the goddess there;
> and nowhere does a temple
> bear witness to the worship of the gods.
> The fruit of the fields and the sweet grapes
> do not shine at the feasts;
> only the remains of bodies smoke
> upon the bloody altars.
> And wherever Ceres turns
> her sorrowful eye there,
> everywhere she sees man
> in deep humiliation!
Sobs suddenly broke from Mitya’s breast. He seized Alyosha’s hand.

“Friend, friend, in humiliation, in humiliation even now. Man has a terrible lot to bear on earth, terribly many misfortunes! Don’t think that I am only a lout in an officer’s rank who drinks brandy and goes in for debauchery. I, brother, think of almost nothing else, of this humiliated man, if only I am not lying. God grant that I am not lying now and not praising myself. I think about this man because I am such a man myself.

> That man may rise in soul
> out of his baseness,
> let him enter for ever into a union
> with his ancient mother, the earth.

But here is the whole point: how am I to enter into a union with the earth for ever? I don’t kiss the earth, I don’t cut open her breast; what, am I to become a peasant or a shepherd boy? I walk on and don’t know: have I fallen into stench and shame, or into light and joy? There is the trouble, for everything in the world is a riddle! And whenever I happened to sink into the very, very deepest shame of debauchery (and that is all that ever happened to me), I always read this poem about Ceres and about man. Did it reform me? Never! Because I am a Karamazov. Because if I fly into the abyss, I fly straight, head down and heels up, and I am even pleased to be falling in such a humiliating position, and I count it beauty for myself. And in the very depth of that shame I suddenly begin a hymn. Let me be accursed, let me be low and vile, but let me too kiss the hem of the garment in which my God is clothed; let me be following the devil at the same time, but I am still your son too, O Lord, and I love you, and I feel the joy without which the world cannot stand and be.

> Eternal joy gives drink
> to the soul of God’s creation;
> by the secret power of ferment
> it sets the cup of life aflame;
> it lured the little grass to the light,
> unfolded chaos into suns,
> and poured them out in spaces
> beyond the stargazer’s reach.
> At the breast of kindly nature
> all that breathes drinks joy;
> all creatures, all peoples
> she draws after her;
> she gave us friends in misfortune,
> the juice of the grape, the Graces’ garlands,
> to insects, sensual lust...
> and the angel stands before God.

But enough of verses! I have shed tears, and you let me weep. Let it be foolishness at which everyone will laugh, but not you. There, your little eyes are shining too. Enough of verses. I want to tell you now about ‘insects’, about those whom God endowed with sensual lust:
> To insects, sensual lust!

I, brother, am that very insect, and it was said of me specially. And all of us Karamazovs are the same, and in you, angel, that insect lives and raises storms in your blood. Storms, because sensual lust is a storm, more than a storm! Beauty is a terrible and dreadful thing! Terrible because it cannot be defined, and it cannot be defined because God has set nothing but riddles. Here the shores meet, here all contradictions live together. I am very uneducated, brother, but I have thought about this a lot. There are terribly many mysteries! Far too many riddles weigh down man on earth. Solve them as you can and come out of the water dry. Beauty! What I can’t bear, besides, is that a man, even one of the highest heart and of lofty mind, begins with the ideal of the Madonna and ends with the ideal of Sodom. What is still more terrible is when a man who already has the ideal of Sodom in his soul does not renounce the ideal of the Madonna either, and his heart burns with it, and truly, truly burns, as in his young, blameless years. No, man is broad, even too broad; I would narrow him. The devil knows what to make of it, that’s what! What seems shame to the mind is all beauty to the heart. Is there beauty in Sodom? Believe me that it is in Sodom that it sits for the vast majority of people; did you know that secret or not? What is terrible is that beauty is not only a terrible but also a mysterious thing. Here the devil is fighting with God, and the battlefield is the hearts of men. But then, everyone talks about where it hurts him. Listen, now to the business itself.”
## Chapter IV · The Confession of a Passionate Heart, in Anecdotes

“I caroused there. Father said earlier that I paid several thousand at a time for seducing girls. That is a swinish phantom, and it never happened; and what did happen did not, properly speaking, need money for ‘that’. With me money is an accessory, the fever of the soul, the setting. Today this is my lady; tomorrow a little street girl is in her place. I amuse both the one and the other, I throw money about by the handful, music, din, gypsy girls. If need be, I give it to her too, because they take it, they take it eagerly, that must be admitted, and they are pleased and grateful. Fine ladies loved me; not all, but it happened, it happened; but I always loved the little back lanes, the remote and dark little corners behind the square: there are adventures there, surprises there, nuggets in the mud. I am speaking allegorically, brother. In our little town there were no such lanes in the material sense, but there were moral ones. But if you were what I am, you would understand what these mean. I loved debauchery, and I loved the shame of debauchery too. I loved cruelty: am I not a bedbug, a wicked insect? It has been said: a Karamazov! Once the whole town went on a picnic; we went in seven troikas; in the dark, in winter, in the sledge, I began to press the hand of a neighbouring girl, and I forced kisses on that girl, an official’s daughter, poor, sweet, meek, uncomplaining. She allowed it; she allowed a lot in the dark. She thought, poor thing, that I would come the next day and make her an offer (they valued me above all as a suitor, you see); and after that I never said a word to her, not half a word for five months. I saw how her little eyes followed me from a corner of the ballroom whenever there was dancing (and with us there is nothing but dancing); I saw how they burned with a little flame, a flame of meek indignation. This game amused only the insect’s sensuality which I was feeding in myself. Five months later she married an official and went away... angry, and still loving, perhaps. Now they live happily. Note that I told no one, did not disgrace her; though I am low in my desires and love baseness, I am not dishonourable. You are blushing; your eyes have flashed. Enough of this filth for you. And all this was still only so-so, little Paul de Kock flowers, though the cruel insect was already growing, already spreading in my soul. Here, brother, there is a whole album of memories. God send them health, the darlings. When I broke off with them, I liked not to quarrel. And I never gave one away, never disgraced a single one. But enough. Did you really think I called you here only for this rubbish? No, I will tell you something more curious; but don’t be surprised that I am not ashamed before you, and even seem glad.”
“You say that because I blushed,” Alyosha remarked suddenly. “I didn’t blush at your words or for your deeds, but because I am the same as you.”
“You? Well, that’s going a bit far.”

“No, not far,” said Alyosha warmly. (Evidently the thought had long been in him.) “It is all the same steps. I am on the very lowest, and you are above, somewhere on the thirteenth. That is how I see the matter, but it is all one and the same, quite of the same kind. Whoever has stepped on the lowest step will certainly step on the highest all the same.”
“So one shouldn’t step at all?”
“Whoever can, should not step at all.”
“And can you?”
“I think not.”

“Be quiet, Alyosha, be quiet, my dear; I want to kiss your little hand, just like that, out of tenderness. That rogue Grushenka is a connoisseur of people; she told me once that some day she would eat you up. I’m quiet, I’m quiet! From the abominations, from the field fouled by flies, let us pass to my tragedy, also a field fouled by flies, that is, by every baseness. The point is that though the old man lied about the seducing of innocents, yet essentially, in my tragedy, that is how it was, though it happened only once, and even then it didn’t come off. The old man, who reproached me with a fable, doesn’t know of this very thing: I never told anyone; I’ll tell you first now, except Ivan of course; Ivan knows everything. He knew it long before you. But Ivan is a grave.”
“Ivan is a grave?”
“Yes.”
Alyosha was listening extremely attentively.

“In that line battalion, you see, though I was an ensign, I was all the same as if under supervision, like some exile. And the little town received me terribly well. I threw a lot of money about; they believed I was rich, and I believed it myself. But then I must have pleased them with something else too. Though they shook their heads, really they loved me. My lieutenant colonel, an old man already, suddenly took a dislike to me. He found fault with me; but I had a hand to back me, and besides, the whole town stood up for me, so he couldn’t find much fault. I was to blame myself too: I deliberately did not show him proper respect. I was proud. This stubborn old man, not at all a bad man and the most good-natured of hosts, had once had two wives, both dead. One, the first, was of some simple family and left him a daughter, simple too. In my time she was already a girl of about twenty-four and lived with her father together with an aunt, her late mother’s sister. The aunt was speechless simplicity, and the niece, the lieutenant colonel’s elder daughter, was lively simplicity. I like to say a good word when I remember: never, my dear, have I known a more charming woman’s character than that girl’s; her name was Agafya, just imagine, Agafya Ivanovna. And she was not at all bad-looking, in the Russian taste: tall, buxom, full-bodied, with beautiful eyes; her face, let us say, a little coarse. She did not marry, though two men proposed; she refused, and did not lose her cheerfulness. I became friends with her; not in that way, no, it was pure there, but just as friends. I often made friends with women quite sinlessly, as friends. I chatter such frank things with her that, ooh! and she only laughs. Many women love frankness, note that, and besides, she was a maiden, which amused me very much. And here is something else: she could not possibly have been called a young lady. They lived with her father, she and her aunt, somehow voluntarily lowering themselves, not putting themselves on a level with the rest of society. Everyone loved her and needed her, because she was an excellent dressmaker: she had a talent; she did not ask money for her services, she did it out of kindness, but when she was given presents she did not refuse to accept them. The lieutenant colonel, though, he was something else! The lieutenant colonel was one of the very first persons in our place. He lived in style, received the whole town, suppers, dances. When I arrived and joined the battalion, the whole little town was talking about how the lieutenant colonel’s second daughter would soon be coming to us from the capital, a beauty of beauties, who had only just left a certain aristocratic institute in the capital. This second daughter is this very Katerina Ivanovna, and she was by the lieutenant colonel’s second wife. And this second wife, already dead, came from a distinguished family, some big general’s house, though, as I know for certain, she too brought the lieutenant colonel no money at all. So she came with relations, and that was all; perhaps some expectations, but nothing in hand. And yet, when the institute girl arrived (on a visit, not for good), our whole little town seemed to come to life again; our most distinguished ladies, two Excellencies, a colonel’s wife, and everyone, everyone after them, at once took her up, snatched at her, began to entertain her; queen of balls, of picnics; they cooked up tableaux vivants for the benefit of some governesses. I am silent, I carouse; just then I pulled off a trick that set the whole town buzzing. I see that once she measured me with her eyes; it was at the battery commander’s; but I didn’t go up to her then: I disdain to make her acquaintance, so to speak. I went up to her a little later, also at a party; I began to talk; she barely looked at me, pursed her contemptuous little lips; well, I thought, wait, I’ll have my revenge! I was a most dreadful boor on most occasions then, and I felt it myself. Above all I felt that ‘Katenka’ was not exactly an innocent institute girl, but a person of character, proud and truly virtuous, and above all with intelligence and education, and I had neither one nor the other. You think I meant to make her an offer? Not in the least; I simply wanted revenge, because I was such a fine fellow and she didn’t feel it. And meanwhile, carousing and havoc. At last the lieutenant colonel put me under arrest for three days. Just at that time Father sent me six thousand, after I had sent him a formal renunciation of everything and anything, that is, we are ‘quits’, so to speak, and I won’t demand anything more. I understood nothing then: I, brother, until my very arrival here, and even until these very last days, and perhaps even until today, understood nothing about all these money disputes between Father and me. But to the devil with that; that comes later. And then, having received these six thousand, I suddenly learned for certain, through a little letter from a friend, of a most curious thing for me: namely, that people were displeased with our lieutenant colonel, that they suspected him of irregularities; in a word, that his enemies were preparing a little treat for him. And indeed the divisional commander arrived and gave him a dressing down like nothing on earth. Then a little later he was ordered to send in his resignation. I won’t tell you how it all came about in detail; he really did have enemies; only suddenly there was an excessive coolness in the town towards him and his whole family; everyone suddenly drew back, as it were. And here my first trick came off: I meet Agafya Ivanovna, with whom I had always kept up our friendship, and I say: ‘But you know, your papa is short of four thousand five hundred roubles of government money.’ ‘What are you saying, why do you say that? The general was here not long ago, it was all there...’ ‘It was then, but now it isn’t.’ She was terribly frightened: ‘Don’t frighten me, please; whom did you hear it from?’ ‘Don’t worry,’ I say, ‘I won’t tell anyone, and you know that on this score I am a grave; but here is what I wanted to add on this score, also by way, so to speak, of “just in case”: when they demand the four thousand five hundred from your papa and he doesn’t have it, then rather than go to trial and then be sent to serve as a private in his old age, better send me your institute girl then, secretly; money has just been sent to me; I’ll fork out the four thousand to her, perhaps, and keep the secret sacredly.’ ‘Ah, what a scoundrel you are,’ she says (she said just that), ‘what a wicked scoundrel! How dare you!’ She went away in terrible indignation, and I shouted after her once more that the secret would be kept sacredly and inviolably. These two women, that is, Agafya and her aunt, I will say in advance, turned out in this whole story to be pure angels, and they truly adored this sister, this proud girl, Katya; they humbled themselves before her, they were her maids... Only Agafya went and passed this thing on to her then, that is, our conversation. I learned all this afterwards as well as I know my five fingers. She didn’t hide it, and of course that was just what I wanted.

“Suddenly a new major arrives to take over the battalion. He takes it over. The old lieutenant colonel suddenly falls ill, can’t move, stays at home two days, doesn’t hand over the government money. Our doctor Kravchenko insisted that he really was ill. Only here is what I knew thoroughly, in secret, and for a long time: that every time the authorities had inspected the money, after that, and this had gone on for about four years running, the sum vanished for a while. The lieutenant colonel lent it to a most reliable man, a merchant of ours, an old widower, Trifonov, a bearded man in gold spectacles. He would go to the fair, do whatever business he needed to there, and at once return the money intact to the lieutenant colonel, and at the same time bring back presents from the fair, and with the presents a little interest. Only this time (I learned all this then quite by chance from a youngster, Trifonov’s slobbering little son, his son and heir, the most depraved boy the world ever produced), this time, I say, Trifonov, coming back from the fair, returned nothing. The lieutenant colonel rushed to him: ‘I never received anything from you, and could not have received anything’: that was the answer. Well, so our lieutenant colonel sits at home, his head tied up in a towel; all three of them are putting ice on the crown of his head; suddenly an orderly arrives with the book and an order: ‘Hand over the government money, at once, immediately, within two hours.’ He signed; I saw that signature in the book afterwards; he got up, said he was going to put on his uniform, ran to his bedroom, took his double-barrelled hunting gun, loaded it, rolled in a soldier’s bullet, took the boot off his right foot, braced the gun against his chest and began feeling for the trigger with his foot. But Agafya already suspected; she had remembered my words of that time; she stole up and spied on him in time: she burst in, threw herself on him from behind, embraced him; the gun went off upwards into the ceiling; no one was hurt; the others ran in, seized him, took away the gun, held him by the arms... I learned all this afterwards down to the last detail. I was sitting at home then; it was twilight, and I was just about to go out; I had dressed, combed my hair, scented my handkerchief, taken my cap, when suddenly the door opens and there before me, in my lodging, is Katerina Ivanovna.

“Strange things do happen: no one in the street noticed then how she came to me, so in the town it simply vanished without a trace. I was renting a lodging from two officials’ widows, very ancient old women; they waited on me; respectful women; they obeyed me in everything, and at my order they both kept silent afterwards like cast-iron posts. Of course I understood everything at once. She came in and looked straight at me; her dark eyes looked resolutely, insolently even, but in her lips and around her lips, I see, there is irresolution.

“‘My sister told me that you would give four thousand five hundred roubles if I came for them... to you myself. I have come... give me the money!..’ She couldn’t hold out; she choked, took fright, her voice broke, and the corners of her lips and the lines around her lips trembled. Alyoshka, are you listening or asleep?”
“Mitya, I know you will tell the whole truth,” Alyosha said in agitation.

“That is just what I will tell. If it’s the whole truth, then this is how it was; I won’t spare myself. My first thought was a Karamazov one. Once, brother, a phalanx spider bit me, and I lay in a fever from it for two weeks; well, so now too, suddenly, I feel the spider bite me in the heart, the wicked insect, do you understand? I measured her with my eye. Have you seen her? She is a beauty, you know. But it was not for that that she was beautiful then. She was beautiful at that moment because she was noble and I was a scoundrel, because she was in the grandeur of her magnanimity and her sacrifice for her father, and I was a bedbug. And on me, a bedbug and a scoundrel, she wholly depends, wholly, all round, soul and body. She is hemmed in. I will tell you straight: this thought, the thought of the spider, so seized my heart that it almost bled away from sheer languor. It would seem there could be no struggle at all: I should act precisely like a bedbug, like a wicked tarantula, without any pity... It even took my breath away. Listen: of course I would have gone the very next day to ask for her hand, so as to end all this in the noblest way, so to speak, and so that no one would know of it or could know. Because, though I am a man of low desires, I am honest. And suddenly at that same second someone whispered in my ear: ‘But tomorrow, when you come with an offer of your hand, such a girl will not even come out to you, but will tell the coachman to throw you out of the yard. “Go and disgrace me through the whole town, I’m not afraid of you!”’ I glanced at the girl; my voice had not lied: of course, that is just how it will be. They will throw me out by the scruff of the neck; one can judge by her face already. Spite boiled up in me; I wanted to play the vilest, piggish, shopkeeper’s trick: to look at her with a sneer, and right there, while she is standing before you, to stun her with the intonation that only a little shopkeeper knows how to put into it:

“‘Four thousand, is it! Why, I was joking, what are you thinking of? You have reckoned too credulously, madam. A couple of hundred, perhaps, even with pleasure and willingly, but four thousand is not the kind of money, miss, to be thrown away on such frivolity. You have been pleased to trouble yourself for nothing.’

“You see, I would have lost everything, of course; she would have run away; but it would have come out infernal, vengeful; it would have been worth all the rest. I would have howled all my life afterwards from remorse, but only to pull off that little trick now! Would you believe it, never has this happened to me with any woman, not a single one, that at such a moment I looked at her with hatred; and here I swear by the cross: I looked at that one then for three or five seconds with terrible hatred, with that very hatred from which to love, to the maddest love, is only a hair’s breadth! I went to the window, put my forehead to the frozen glass, and I remember that the ice burned my forehead like fire. I didn’t keep her long, don’t worry; I turned round, went to the table, opened the drawer and took out a five-thousand five-per-cent bond made out to bearer (it was lying in my French dictionary). Then I silently showed it to her, folded it, gave it to her, opened the door to the passage for her myself, and, stepping back a pace, bowed to her from the waist with a most respectful, most heartfelt bow, believe me! She trembled all over, looked at me intently for a second, turned terribly pale, well, white as a tablecloth, and suddenly, also without saying a word, not impulsively but so softly, deeply, quietly, she bent right down and fell straight at my feet, her forehead to the ground, not like an institute girl, but like a Russian! She jumped up and ran. When she ran out I was wearing my sword; I drew the sword and wanted to stab myself right there; why, I don’t know; it was terrible foolishness, of course, but it must have been from rapture. Do you understand that one can kill oneself from a certain kind of rapture? But I didn’t stab myself; I only kissed the sword and put it back in its sheath, which, by the way, I need not have mentioned to you. And even now, I think, in telling about all the struggles, I have laid it on a bit thick, to praise myself. But let it be, let it be so, and the devil take all spies of the human heart! That is the whole of my former ‘incident’ with Katerina Ivanovna. So now brother Ivan knows about it, and you, and that’s all!”

Dmitry Fyodorovich got up, took a step and another in agitation, took out his handkerchief, wiped the sweat from his forehead, then sat down again, but not in the place where he had sat before, but in another, on the bench opposite, by the other wall, so that Alyosha had to turn right round to him.
## Book Five: Pro and Contra · Chapter I · The Engagement

Madame Khokhlakova again met Alyosha first. She was in a hurry: something important had happened: Katerina Ivanovna’s hysterics had ended in a fainting fit, then had come “a terrible, dreadful weakness; she lay down, rolled up her eyes and began to rave. Now there is fever; they have sent for Herzenstube, sent for the aunts. The aunts are here already, but Herzenstube isn’t yet. Everyone is sitting in her room and waiting. Something will happen, and she is unconscious. And what if it is brain fever!”

Exclaiming this, Madame Khokhlakova had a seriously frightened look: “This is serious now, serious!” she added to every word, as if everything that had happened to her before had not been serious. Alyosha listened to her with sorrow; he began to tell her his own adventures, but she interrupted him at the first words: she had no time; she asked him to sit with Lise and wait for her at Lise’s.

“Lise, dearest Alexei Fyodorovich,” she whispered to him almost in his ear, “Lise surprised me strangely just now, but she moved me too, and so my heart forgives her everything. Imagine, as soon as you had gone, she suddenly began sincerely repenting that she had supposedly laughed at you yesterday and today. But she didn’t laugh, she was only joking. But she repented so seriously, almost to tears, that I was surprised. She never repented seriously before when she laughed at me, it was always in jest. And you know, she laughs at me every minute. And now she is serious; now everything has turned serious. She values your opinion extremely, Alexei Fyodorovich, and if you can, don’t be offended with her and don’t hold it against her. I do nothing but spare her myself, because she is so clever; would you believe it? She was saying just now that you were the friend of her childhood, ‘the most serious friend of my childhood’; imagine that, the most serious; and what about me? She has extremely serious feelings on that score, and even memories, and above all these phrases and little words, these most unexpected little words, so that you never expect it, and suddenly out it jumps. Not long ago about a pine tree, for instance: there was a pine tree in our garden in her early childhood, perhaps it is still standing, so there is no need to speak in the past tense. Pine trees are not people, they don’t change for a long time, Alexei Fyodorovich. ‘Mama,’ she says, ‘I remember that pine as if in a dream’, that is, ‘a pine tree from a dream’; she put it somehow differently, because there is a muddle here; ‘pine’ is a silly word, but only she told me something so original about it that I absolutely won’t undertake to repeat it. And I’ve forgotten it all anyway. Well, goodbye; I am very shaken, and I am surely going out of my mind. Ah, Alexei Fyodorovich, twice in my life I have gone out of my mind, and they treated me. Go to Lise. Cheer her up, as you always do so charmingly. Lise,” she called, going up to her door, “here I have brought you Alexei Fyodorovich, whom you insulted so, and he is not in the least angry, I assure you; on the contrary, he is surprised that you could think so!”
“Merci, maman; come in, Alexei Fyodorovich.”

Alyosha went in. Lise looked somehow embarrassed and suddenly blushed all over. She was evidently ashamed of something, and, as always happens in such cases, began very, very quickly to talk about something quite irrelevant, as if that irrelevant thing were all that interested her at that moment.

“Mama has just suddenly told me, Alexei Fyodorovich, the whole story about those two hundred roubles and about your errand... to that poor officer... and told me the whole of that dreadful story of how he was insulted, and, you know, though Mama tells things very muddle-headedly... she keeps skipping about... I listened and cried. Well, what happened, did you give him the money, and how is that unhappy man now?..”

“That’s just it, I didn’t give it to him, and there is a whole story to it,” answered Alyosha, as if for his part most concerned of all precisely that he had not given the money; and yet Lise noticed perfectly well that he too was looking aside and evidently also trying to talk about something irrelevant. Alyosha sat down at the table and began to tell her, but from the very first words he completely stopped being embarrassed and in his turn carried Lise away. He was speaking under the influence of strong feeling and of a recent extraordinary impression, and he managed to tell it well and in detail. Even before, back in Moscow, in Lise’s childhood, he had liked to come to her and tell her now what had just happened to him, now something he had read, now memories of the childhood he had lived. Sometimes they even dreamed together and made up whole stories between the two of them, but mostly merry and funny ones. Now it was as if they had both suddenly been carried back to the old Moscow days, two years before. Lise was extremely moved by his story. Alyosha managed to paint the image of “Ilyushechka” before her with warm feeling. And when he had finished, in every detail, the scene of how that unhappy man trampled the money, Lise clasped her hands and cried out with uncontrollable feeling:
“So you didn’t give him the money, so you just let him run away! My God, you should at least have run after him yourself and caught him up...”
“No, Lise, it is better that I didn’t run,” said Alyosha; he got up from his chair and walked about the room with a preoccupied air.
“How better, why better? Now they are without bread and will perish!”

“They won’t perish, because the two hundred roubles won’t pass them by all the same. He will take them tomorrow anyway. Tomorrow he will certainly take them,” said Alyosha, pacing in thought. “You see, Lise,” he went on, suddenly stopping in front of her, “I made a mistake myself here, but even the mistake turned out for the better.”
“What mistake, and why for the better?”

“Here is why: he is a cowardly man and weak in character. He is so worn out, and very kind. Now I keep thinking: why did he suddenly take such offence and trample the money? Because, I assure you, until the very last moment he did not know that he would trample it. And it seems to me that he took offence at a lot of things here... and it could not have been otherwise in his position... In the first place, he took offence just because he rejoiced too much over the money in front of me and did not hide it from me. If he had rejoiced but not very much, had not shown it, had begun to put on airs, like others, when taking money, to make faces, well, then he might still have borne it and accepted it; but he rejoiced too truthfully, and that is what is offensive. Ah, Lise, he is a truthful and kind man; that is the whole trouble in such cases! All the time he was talking then, his voice was so weak, so faint, and he talked so very quickly, kept giggling a sort of little laugh, or else was crying... really, he was crying, he was in such raptures... and he talked about his daughters... and about the post that would be given him in another town... And as soon as he had poured out his soul, he suddenly felt ashamed of having shown me his whole soul like that. So he immediately came to hate me. And he is one of those terribly shamefaced poor people. Above all, he took offence because he had accepted me as his friend too quickly and surrendered to me too quickly; first he flew at me, frightened me, and then suddenly, as soon as he saw the money, he began to embrace me. Because he did embrace me; he kept touching me with his hands. It was precisely in that position that he must have felt all that humiliation, and just then I made that mistake, a very important one: I suddenly told him that if he didn’t have enough money to move to another town, he would be given more, and that I myself would even give him as much as he liked out of my own money. That suddenly struck him: why, he thinks, did I too jump forward to help him? You know, Lise, it is terribly hard for an injured man when everyone starts looking at him as his benefactors... I have heard this; the elder told me so. I don’t know how to express it, but I have often seen it myself. And I feel exactly the same way myself, you know. And the main thing is that though he did not know until the very last moment that he would trample the notes, he still had a presentiment of it, certainly he did. That is why his rapture was so strong, because he had a presentiment... And so, though all this is so bad, still it is for the better. I even think it is for the very best; it could not have been better...”
“Why, why could it not have been better?” exclaimed Lise, looking at Alyosha in great surprise.

“Because, Lise, if he had not trampled the money but had taken it, then, coming home, within an hour or so he would have wept over his humiliation; that is certainly what would have happened. He would have wept, and perhaps tomorrow he would have come to me at dawn and thrown the notes at me, perhaps, and trampled them as he did earlier. But now he has gone away terribly proud and triumphant, though he knows that he has ‘ruined himself’. And so now nothing is easier than to make him accept those same two hundred roubles no later than tomorrow, because he has already proved his honour, thrown down the money, trampled it... He could not have known when he trampled it that I would bring it to him again tomorrow. And yet he needs that money terribly, you know. Though he is proud now, still, even today he will be thinking about what help he has lost. At night he will think about it even more, he will dream about it, and by tomorrow morning he will perhaps be ready to run to me and ask forgiveness. And that is just when I shall appear: ‘Here,’ I’ll say, ‘you are a proud man, you have proved it; well, now take it, forgive us.’ And that is when he will take it!”
Alyosha said “And that is when he will take it!” with a kind of rapture. Lise clapped her hands.
“Ah, that’s true, ah, I have suddenly understood it terribly! Ah, Alyosha, how do you know all this? So young, and he already knows what is in the soul... I would never have thought of it...”

“The main thing now is to convince him that he is on an equal footing with all of us, in spite of his taking money from us,” Alyosha went on in his rapture, “and not only on an equal footing, but even on a higher footing...”
“‘On a higher footing’, charming, Alexei Fyodorovich, but go on, go on!”
“That is, I didn’t put it right... about a higher footing... but that doesn’t matter, because...”

“Ah, it doesn’t matter, it doesn’t matter, of course it doesn’t matter! Forgive me, Alyosha, dear... You know, until now I hardly respected you... that is, I respected you, but on an equal footing, and now I shall respect you on a higher footing... Dear, don’t be angry that I am ‘being witty’,” she took up at once with strong feeling. “I am silly and little, but you, you... Listen, Alexei Fyodorovich, isn’t there in all this reasoning of ours, that is, yours... no, better ours... isn’t there contempt for him, for that unhappy man... in our analysing his soul like this now, as if from above, eh? In our having decided so surely now that he will take the money, eh?”

“No, Lise, there is no contempt,” Alyosha answered firmly, as if he had already been prepared for this question. “I thought about it myself on the way here. Consider, what contempt can there be, when we ourselves are just the same as he is, when everyone is just the same as he is? Because we are just the same, no better. And even if we were better, we would still be the same in his place... I don’t know about you, Lise, but I consider that in many ways I have a petty soul. And his is not petty; on the contrary, it is very delicate... No, Lise, there is no contempt for him here at all! You know, Lise, my elder once said: one must look after people all the time as one looks after children, and some of them as one looks after the sick in hospitals...”
“Ah, Alexei Fyodorovich, ah, my dear, let us look after people as one looks after the sick!”
“Let us, Lise; I am ready, only I am not quite ready myself; sometimes I am very impatient, and at other times I have no eyes. Now you are different.”
“Ah, I don’t believe it! Alexei Fyodorovich, how happy I am!”
“How good that you say that, Lise.”

“Alexei Fyodorovich, you are wonderfully good, but sometimes you are a sort of pedant... and yet, you look, and you are not a pedant at all. Go and look at the door, open it quietly and see whether Mama is listening,” Lise whispered suddenly in a kind of nervous, hurried whisper.
Alyosha went, opened the door a little and reported that no one was listening.

“Come here, Alexei Fyodorovich,” Lise went on, blushing more and more, “give me your hand, like this. Listen, I must make you a great confession: I did not write you yesterday’s letter in jest, but seriously...”
And she covered her eyes with her hand. It was evident that she was very ashamed to make this confession. Suddenly she seized his hand and impetuously kissed it three times.
“Ah, Lise, that’s splendid,” Alyosha exclaimed joyfully. “And I was quite sure that you wrote it seriously.”

“Sure, imagine that!” She suddenly pushed his hand away, without letting it go out of hers, however, blushing terribly and laughing a little happy laugh. “I kiss his hand, and he says ‘that’s splendid’.” But she reproached him unjustly: Alyosha too was in great confusion.
“I would like always to please you, Lise, but I don’t know how to do it,” he muttered somehow, blushing too.

“Alyosha, dear, you are cold and impudent. You see, sir? He has been pleased to choose me as his wife and has left it at that! He was already sure that I wrote it seriously; what do you think of that! But that is impudence, that’s what!”
“But is it bad that I was sure?” Alyosha suddenly laughed.

“Ah, Alyosha, on the contrary, it is terribly good,” Lise looked at him tenderly and happily. Alyosha stood there, still holding his hand in hers. Suddenly he bent down and kissed her right on the lips.
“What’s this? What’s the matter with you?” cried Lise. Alyosha was completely at a loss.
“Well, forgive me if it was wrong... Perhaps it was terribly stupid of me... You said I was cold, so I went and kissed you... Only I see it came out stupid...”
Lise laughed and covered her face with her hands.
“And in that dress!” broke from her between laughs; but suddenly she stopped laughing and became quite serious, almost stern.

“Well, Alyosha, we will wait a while with kisses, because neither of us knows how to do it yet, and we still have a very long time to wait,” she concluded suddenly. “Tell me instead why you are taking me, such a fool, a sick little fool, you, so clever, so thoughtful, so observant? Ah, Alyosha, I am terribly happy, because I am not worthy of you at all!”

“You are, Lise. In a few days I shall leave the monastery altogether. Going out into the world, one must marry; that much I know. That is what he told me to do too. Whom could I take better than you... and who would take me, except you? I have already thought it over. In the first place, you have known me since childhood, and in the second, you have very many gifts that I don’t have at all. Your soul is merrier than mine; above all, you are more innocent than I, and I have already touched on much, on very much... Ah, you don’t know, but I too am a Karamazov! What does it matter that you laugh and joke, and at me too; on the contrary, laugh, I am so glad of it... But you laugh like a little girl, and inside yourself you think like a martyr...”
“Like a martyr? How so?”

“Yes, Lise; your question earlier, whether there is contempt in us for that unhappy man, because we are dissecting his soul like that: that is a martyr’s question... you see, I can’t express it at all, but whoever has such questions is capable of suffering himself. Sitting in your chair, you must have thought a great deal already...”

“Alyosha, give me your hand; why are you taking it away?” Lise said in a little voice weakened by happiness, somehow fallen. “Listen, Alyosha, what will you wear when you leave the monastery, what kind of suit? Don’t laugh, don’t be angry, it is very, very important to me.”
“I haven’t thought about the suit yet, Lise, but I’ll wear whatever you like.”
“I want you to have a dark blue velvet jacket, a white piqué waistcoat and a soft grey felt hat... Tell me, did you really believe earlier that I didn’t love you, when I disowned yesterday’s letter?”
“No, I didn’t believe it.”
“Oh, unbearable man, incorrigible!”
“You see, I knew that you... I think you love me, but I pretended to believe you, that you don’t love me, so that it would be... more convenient for you...”

“Worse still! Both worst and best of all. Alyosha, I love you terribly. Earlier, before you came, I made a wish: I’ll ask him for yesterday’s letter, and if he calmly takes it out and gives it back to me (as one can always expect of him), then it means he doesn’t love me at all, feels nothing, and is simply a stupid and unworthy boy, and I am lost. But you left the letter in your cell, and that encouraged me: isn’t it true that you left it in your cell because you had a presentiment that I would demand the letter back, so as not to give it? Is that it? It is, isn’t it?”
“Oh, Lise, not at all; why, the letter is with me now, and it was with me earlier too, in this pocket; here it is.”
Laughing, Alyosha took out the letter and showed it to her from a distance.
“Only I won’t give it to you; look at it from my hands.”
“What? So you lied earlier; you, a monk, and you lied?”

“Perhaps I lied,” Alyosha laughed too; “I lied so as not to give you the letter. It is very dear to me,” he added suddenly, with strong feeling, and blushing again; “it is for ever, and I will never give it to anyone!”
Lise looked at him in delight.
“Alyosha,” she began to babble again, “look at the door; isn’t Mama listening?”
“Very well, Lise, I’ll look; only wouldn’t it be better not to look, eh? Why suspect your mother of such baseness?”

“What baseness? Baseness in what? Her listening to her daughter, that is her right, not baseness,” Lise flared up. “You may be sure, Alexei Fyodorovich, that when I am a mother myself and have a daughter like me, I shall certainly listen to her.”
“Really, Lise? That isn’t good.”

“Ah, my God, what baseness is there in it? If it were some ordinary society conversation and I listened in, that would be baseness, but here one’s own daughter has locked herself in with a young man... Listen, Alyosha, know that I shall spy on you too, as soon as we are married, and know too that I shall unseal all your letters and read everything... You had better be forewarned of that...”
“Yes, of course, if so...” Alyosha muttered, “only it isn’t good...”

“Ah, what contempt! Alyosha, dear, let us not quarrel from the very first time; I had better tell you the whole truth: of course it is very bad to listen at doors, and of course I am wrong and you are right, but all the same I shall listen.”
“Do. You won’t spy out anything of that kind in me,” Alyosha laughed.
“Alyosha, and will you obey me? That must be decided beforehand too.”
“With great willingness, Lise, and without fail, only not in the most important thing. In the most important thing, if you disagree with me, I shall still do as my duty tells me.”

“That is how it should be. Then know that I, on the contrary, am ready not only to obey in the most important thing, but to give way to you in everything, and I swear it to you now: in everything and for all my life,” Lise cried ardently, “and this with happiness, with happiness! More than that, I swear to you that I shall never listen in on you, never once, and shall not read a single letter of yours, because you are right and I am not. And though I shall want terribly to listen, I know it, still I won’t, because you consider it ignoble. You are like my Providence now... Listen, Alexei Fyodorovich, why have you been so sad all these days, yesterday and today? I know that you have worries and troubles, but I see besides that you have some special sadness, a secret one perhaps, eh?”
“Yes, Lise, there is a secret one too,” Alyosha said sadly. “I see that you love me, since you have guessed it.”
“What sadness? About what? Can you tell me?” Lise said with timid entreaty.
“I’ll tell you later, Lise... afterwards...” Alyosha was embarrassed. “Now, perhaps, it would not even be understood. And I might not even be able to say it myself.”
“I know, besides, that your brothers and your father are tormenting you?”
“Yes, my brothers too,” said Alyosha, as if in thought.
“I don’t like your brother Ivan Fyodorovich, Alyosha,” Lise remarked suddenly.
Alyosha noted this remark with some surprise, but did not take it up.

“My brothers are destroying themselves,” he went on, “and my father too. And they are destroying others along with them. Here is ‘the earthy Karamazov force’, as Father Paissy put it the other day: earthy and violent and unhewn... I don’t even know whether the spirit of God moves above this force. I know only that I too am a Karamazov... I am a monk, a monk? Am I a monk, Lise? You said something just now about my being a monk?”
“Yes, I did.”
“And perhaps I don’t even believe in God.”

“You don’t believe, what is the matter with you?” Lise said quietly and carefully. But Alyosha did not answer this. There was in these too sudden words of his something too mysterious and too subjective, perhaps unclear even to himself, but already undoubtedly tormenting him.

“And now, on top of everything, my friend is going, the first man in the world, he is leaving the earth. If you knew, if you only knew, Lise, how bound I am, how welded in soul to this man! And so I shall be left alone... I shall come to you, Lise... From now on we will be together...”
“Yes, together, together! From now on always together, all our lives. Listen, kiss me, I allow it.”
Alyosha kissed her.

“Well, now go, Christ be with you!” (And she made the sign of the cross over him.) “Go quickly to him while he is alive. I see that I have kept you cruelly. I shall pray today for him and for you. Alyosha, we shall be happy! We shall be happy, shan’t we?”
“I think we shall, Lise.”

On leaving Lise, Alyosha did not see fit to go in to Madame Khokhlakova, and, without saying goodbye to her, was about to leave the house. But as soon as he opened the door and came out onto the stairs, from nowhere Madame Khokhlakova herself appeared before him. From her first word Alyosha guessed that she had been waiting for him there on purpose.
“Alexei Fyodorovich, this is terrible. This is childish nonsense and all rubbish. I hope you won’t take it into your head to dream... Foolishness, foolishness and foolishness!” she fell upon him.
“Only don’t tell her that,” said Alyosha, “or she will be upset, and that is bad for her now.”
“I hear the sensible word of a sensible young man. Am I to understand that you agreed with her only because, out of compassion for her sickly state, you did not want to anger her by contradiction?”
“Oh no, not at all; I talked with her quite seriously,” Alyosha declared firmly.
“Seriousness is impossible here, unthinkable; and in the first place I shall not receive you even once now, and in the second I shall go away and take her with me, know that.”
“But why,” said Alyosha, “it is still so far off; we shall have to wait a year and a half yet, perhaps.”

“Ah, Alexei Fyodorovich, that is true, of course, and in a year and a half you will quarrel with her and part a thousand times. But I am so unhappy, so unhappy! Let it all be nonsense, but it has struck me down. Now I am like Famusov in the last scene, you are Chatsky, she is Sofya, and imagine, I ran out here onto the stairs on purpose to meet you, and there too everything fateful happened on the stairs. I heard everything; I could hardly stand. So here is the explanation of the horrors of this whole night and of all the hysterics earlier! Love for the daughter and death for the mother. Into the grave with me. Now the second and most important thing: what is this letter she wrote you? Show it to me now, now!”
“No, there is no need. Tell me how Katerina Ivanovna is; I very much need to know.”

“She is still lying delirious; she hasn’t come to; her aunts are here and only sigh and put on airs with me; and Herzenstube came and was so frightened that I didn’t know what to do with him and how to save him; I even wanted to send for a doctor. He was taken away in my carriage. And suddenly, to crown it all, you suddenly come with this letter. True, all this is still a year and a half away. In the name of everything great and holy, in the name of your dying elder, show me that letter, Alexei Fyodorovich, me, her mother! If you like, hold it in your fingers, and I will read it from your hands.”
“No, I won’t show it, Katerina Osipovna; even if she allowed it, I would not show it. I will come tomorrow and, if you like, we will talk about many things, but now, goodbye!”
And Alyosha ran down the stairs into the street.
## Chapter II · Smerdyakov with a Guitar

And indeed he had no time. A thought had flashed into his mind while he was still saying goodbye to Lise. The thought was this: how to catch brother Dmitry now in the most cunning way, since Dmitry was obviously hiding from him? It was no longer early; it was getting on for three in the afternoon. With his whole being Alyosha longed to go to the monastery to his “great” dying man, but the need to see brother Dmitry outweighed everything: with every hour the conviction grew in Alyosha’s mind that a terrible catastrophe was inevitable and about to happen. What exactly the catastrophe consisted in, and what he wanted to say to his brother at this moment, he perhaps could not have defined himself. “Let my benefactor die without me, but at least I shall not reproach myself all my life that perhaps I could have saved something and did not save it, passed by, hurried to my own home. In doing so I shall be doing as his great word bids...”

His plan was to catch brother Dmitry unawares, namely: to climb over that wattle fence as yesterday, go into the garden and sit down in that summer house. “And if he is not there,” thought Alyosha, “then, without telling either Foma or the landladies, I’ll hide and wait in the summer house, even till evening. If he is still keeping watch for Grushenka’s coming, then very possibly he will come to the summer house...” Alyosha, however, did not reason too much about the details of the plan, but he decided to carry it out, even if he did not get to the monastery today...

Everything went without a hitch: he climbed over the fence almost at the same place as yesterday and secretly made his way to the summer house. He did not want to be noticed: both the landlady and Foma (if he was there) might take his brother’s side and obey his orders, and so either not let Alyosha into the garden or warn his brother in time that he was being looked for and asked after. There was no one in the summer house. Alyosha sat down in his place of yesterday and began to wait. He looked round the summer house; for some reason it seemed to him much more dilapidated than yesterday; it seemed so shabby to him this time. The day, however, was just as clear as yesterday. On the green table there was the imprint of a ring, probably from yesterday’s glass of brandy that had been spilled. Empty thoughts of no use to the business, as always during tedious waiting, crept into his head: for instance, why, coming in here now, had he sat down exactly on the very same place where he had sat yesterday, and why not on another? At last he grew very sad, sad from anxious uncertainty. But he had not sat a quarter of an hour when suddenly, somewhere very near, a chord on a guitar was heard. Someone was sitting, or had only just sat down, some twenty paces from him, no further, somewhere in the bushes. A memory suddenly flashed through Alyosha’s mind that yesterday, leaving his brother in the summer house, he had seen, or seemed to glimpse, on his left by the fence, a low old green garden bench among the bushes. So it must be on that that the visitors had now sat down. Who? A man’s voice suddenly began singing a couplet in a sugary falsetto, accompanying himself on the guitar:

> By a force invincible
> I am bound to my sweetheart.
> Lord, have mer-er-cy
> on her and me!
> On her and me!
> On her and me!
The voice stopped. A lackey’s tenor, and the twirl of the song a lackey’s. Another voice, a woman’s this time, suddenly said caressingly and as if timidly, but with great affectation, however:
“Why don’t you come to see us for so long, Pavel Fyodorovich, why do you keep despising us?”

“Not at all, ma’am,” answered the man’s voice, politely but above all with insistent and firm dignity. Evidently the man was the dominant one, and the woman was flirting. “The man, I think, is Smerdyakov,” thought Alyosha, “at least by his voice, and the lady is probably the daughter of the landlady of this little house, who came from Moscow, wears a dress with a train and goes to Marfa Ignatievna for soup...”
“I terribly love any kind of verse, if it is smooth,” the woman’s voice went on. “Why don’t you go on?”
The voice sang again:

> A royal crown,
> if only my sweetheart were well.
> Lord, have mer-er-cy
> on her and me!
> On her and me!
> On her and me!
“Last time it came out even better,” remarked the woman’s voice. “You sang about the crown: ‘if only my little darling were well’. It came out more tenderly that way; you must have forgotten today.”
“Verses are rubbish, ma’am,” Smerdyakov cut her short.
“Oh no, I love a little verse very much.”

“As for verse, ma’am, it is essential rubbish, ma’am. Consider for yourself: who in the world talks in rhyme? And if we all began to talk in rhyme, even by order of the authorities, how much would we say, ma’am? Verses are no business, Marya Kondratievna.”
“How clever you are about everything; how did you come to be so in everything?” the woman’s voice coaxed more and more.

“I could have done more than that, ma’am, I could have known more than that, ma’am, if it were not for my lot from my very childhood. I would have shot dead in a duel the man who told me I was a scoundrel because I was born of Stinking Lizaveta without a father; and they threw it in my face in Moscow too; it crept over there from here, thanks to Grigory Vasilievich. Grigory Vasilievich reproaches me that I rebel against my birth: ‘You,’ he says, ‘opened her womb.’ Womb or no womb, I would have let myself be killed while still in the womb, so as not to come into the world at all, ma’am. They said in the market, and your mama too took it into her head to tell me, in her great indelicacy, that she went about with her hair matted on her head and was only four feet and a lit-tel tall. Why say lit-tel, when one can simply say ‘little’, as all people say it? She wanted to say it tearfully, but that is a peasant’s tear, so to speak, ma’am, the most peasant feelings. Can a Russian peasant have feeling as against an educated man? In his lack of education he cannot have any feeling. From my very childhood, whenever I used to hear ‘lit-tel’, I could have thrown myself at the wall. I hate the whole of Russia, Marya Kondratievna.”
“If you were a little military cadet or a young little hussar, you wouldn’t talk like that; you would draw your sabre and go to defend the whole of Russia.”
“Not only do I not wish to be a military hussar, Marya Kondratievna, but on the contrary I wish for the abolition of all soldiers, ma’am.”
“And when the enemy comes, who will defend us?”

“There is no need at all, ma’am. In the year twelve there was a great invasion of Russia by the Emperor Napoleon, the first French one, the father of the present one, and it would have been a good thing if those same French had conquered us then: an intelligent nation would have conquered a very stupid one, ma’am, and joined it to itself. There would even have been quite different arrangements, ma’am.”

“But are they really so much better over there than ours? I wouldn’t exchange one of our young dandies for three of the youngest Englishmen,” Marya Kondratievna said tenderly, probably accompanying her words at that moment with the most languishing little eyes.
“That is as one fancies, ma’am.”
“And you yourself are just like a foreigner, just like the most noble foreigner; I tell you that through my shame.”

“If you wish to know, as regards depravity those over there and ours are all alike. All rogues, ma’am, but with this difference, that over there they go about in polished boots, while our scoundrel stinks in his poverty and finds nothing bad in it. The Russian people need flogging, ma’am, as Fyodor Pavlovich rightly said yesterday, though he is a madman, with all his children, ma’am.”
“You said yourself that you respect Ivan Fyodorovich so much.”

“And he referred to me as a stinking lackey. He thinks I might rebel; there he is mistaken, ma’am. If I had a certain sum in my pocket, I would have been gone from here long ago. Dmitry Fyodorovich is worse than any lackey in conduct, and in mind, and in his poverty, ma’am, and he can’t do anything at all, and yet, on the contrary, he is respected by everyone. I, let us suppose, am only a soup-maker, but with luck I can open a café-restaurant in Moscow on Petrovka. Because I cook specially, and not one of them in Moscow, except the foreigners, can serve anything specially. Dmitry Fyodorovich is a beggar in torn trousers, ma’am, but let him challenge the very first count’s son to a duel, and the other will go out with him, ma’am; and in what way is he better than me, ma’am? Because he is incomparably stupider than me. How much money he has whistled away without any use, ma’am.”
“I think it must be very nice at a duel,” Marya Kondratievna remarked suddenly.
“In what way, ma’am?”

“It is so terrible and brave, especially when young little officers with pistols in their hands blaze away at each other over some girl. Simply a picture. Ah, if only girls were allowed to watch, I would want terribly to see it.”
“It is good when he is aiming himself, but when they are aiming right at his own snout, then it is the stupidest feeling, ma’am. You would run from the spot, Marya Kondratievna.”
“Would you really run?”
But Smerdyakov did not condescend to answer. After a minute’s silence the chord sounded again, and the falsetto poured out the last couplet:

> However hard I try
> I shall go far away,
> to enjoy li-i-ife
> and live in the capital!
> I shall not grieve.
> I shall not grieve at all,
> I don’t even intend to grieve at all!

Here something unexpected happened: Alyosha suddenly sneezed; on the bench they instantly fell quiet. Alyosha got up and went towards them. It was indeed Smerdyakov, dressed up, pomaded and very nearly curled, in polished boots. The guitar lay on the bench. And the lady was Marya Kondratievna, the landlady’s daughter; she wore a light blue dress with a train four feet long; the girl was still young and would not have been bad-looking, but she had a very round face and dreadful freckles.
“Will brother Dmitry be back soon?” said Alyosha as calmly as possible.
Smerdyakov slowly rose from the bench; Marya Kondratievna rose too.
“How should I be informed about Dmitry Fyodorovich; it would be another matter if I were employed as his watchman?” Smerdyakov answered quietly, distinctly and disdainfully.
“But I was simply asking whether you knew,” Alyosha explained.
“I know nothing about his whereabouts, and I don’t wish to know, sir.”
“But my brother told me precisely that it is you who let him know everything that goes on in the house, and that you promised to let him know when Agrafena Alexandrovna comes.”
Smerdyakov slowly and imperturbably raised his eyes to him.
“And how were you pleased to get in this time, since the gate here has been bolted for an hour?” he asked, looking intently at Alyosha.
“I came from the lane over the fence straight into the summer house. You will forgive me for it, I hope,” he turned to Marya Kondratievna. “I needed to catch my brother quickly.”

“Ah, how could we be offended with you,” Marya Kondratievna drawled, flattered by Alyosha’s apology, “since Dmitry Fyodorovich too often comes to the summer house this way; we don’t even know, and there he is already sitting in the summer house.”
“I am looking for him very much now; I would very much like to see him, or to learn from you where he is now. Believe me, it is on business very important for him himself.”
“He doesn’t tell us,” Marya Kondratievna babbled.

“Though I come here as an acquaintance,” Smerdyakov began again, “he has oppressed me inhumanly even here with his incessant questioning about the master: what, he says, and how are things with him, who comes and who leaves, and can’t I tell him something else? Twice he even threatened me with death.”
“With death? How?” Alyosha was surprised.

“And is that anything to him, sir, with his character, which you yourself were pleased to observe yesterday, sir? If, he says, I let Agrafena Alexandrovna in and she spends the night here, you will be the first not to live. I am very much afraid of him, sir, and if I weren’t even more afraid, I ought to report him to the town authorities. God knows what he may even do, sir.”
“The other day he told him: ‘I’ll pound you in a mortar,’” added Marya Kondratievna.
“Well, if it’s a mortar, that is perhaps only talk...” Alyosha remarked. “If I could meet him now, I could say something to him about this too...”

“Here is the only thing I can tell you,” Smerdyakov said, as if he had suddenly thought of it. “I come here as an old neighbourly acquaintance, and why shouldn’t I come, sir? On the other hand, Ivan Fyodorovich sent me at dawn today to Dmitry Fyodorovich’s lodging in Lake Street, without a letter, sir, so that Dmitry Fyodorovich should come without fail, by word of mouth, to the tavern here in the square, to dine together, sir. I went, sir, but I did not find Dmitry Fyodorovich at his lodging, sir, and it was already eight o’clock. ‘He was here,’ they say, ‘but he’s gone out’: those were the very words his landlords told me. It is as if there is some conspiracy between them, sir, a mutual one, sir. And now, perhaps, at this very moment, he is sitting in that tavern with his brother Ivan Fyodorovich, since Ivan Fyodorovich did not come home to dinner, and Fyodor Pavlovich dined alone an hour ago and has now gone to lie down. I beg you most earnestly, however, not to tell him anything about me and what I have told you, sir, for he will kill me for nothing, sir.”
“Brother Ivan invited Dmitry to the tavern today?” Alyosha asked again quickly.
“Just so, sir.”
“To the Capital City tavern, in the square?”
“That very one, sir.”
“That is very possible!” Alyosha exclaimed in great agitation. “Thank you, Smerdyakov; that is important news; I’ll go there at once.”
“Don’t give me away, sir,” Smerdyakov said after him.
“Oh no, I’ll turn up at the tavern as if by chance; don’t worry.”
“But where are you going? I’ll open the gate for you,” Marya Kondratievna began to call.
“No, it’s nearer this way; I’ll go over the fence again.”

The news shook Alyosha terribly. He set off for the tavern. It was improper for him to go into a tavern in his dress, but to inquire on the stairs and call them out, that was possible. But just as he came up to the tavern, a window suddenly opened and brother Ivan himself shouted down to him from the window:
“Alyosha, can you come in here to me now or not? You’d do me a terrible favour.”
“I certainly can, only I don’t know how, in my clothes.”
“But I am in a private room; go up to the porch; I’ll run down to meet you...”
A minute later Alyosha was sitting beside his brother. Ivan was alone and having dinner.
## Chapter III · The Brothers Get Acquainted

Ivan, however, was not in a private room. It was only a place by the window, screened off, but those sitting behind the screens could not be seen by others all the same. This room was the entrance room, the first one, with a sideboard against the side wall. Waiters kept darting through it every minute. Of the customers there was only one little old man, a retired military man, drinking tea in a corner. But in the other rooms of the tavern all the usual tavern bustle was going on: calls for the waiter, the uncorking of beer bottles, the click of billiard balls; an organ was droning. Alyosha knew that Ivan almost never went to this tavern and was no lover of taverns in general; so he must be here, Alyosha thought, only in order to meet brother Dmitry by arrangement. And yet brother Dmitry was not there.

“I’ll order you fish soup or something; you don’t live on tea alone, do you?” cried Ivan, apparently terribly pleased to have caught Alyosha. He himself had already finished his dinner and was drinking tea.
“Let’s have fish soup, and then tea too; I’m hungry,” said Alyosha cheerfully.
“And cherry jam? They have it here. Do you remember how you loved cherry jam at Polenov’s when you were little?”
“You remember that? Let’s have the jam too; I still love it.”
Ivan rang for the waiter and ordered fish soup, tea and jam.

“I remember everything, Alyosha; I remember you until you were eleven; I was in my fifteenth year then. Fifteen and eleven: that is such a difference that brothers of those ages are never companions. I don’t know whether I even loved you. When I went to Moscow, for the first years I didn’t even think of you at all. Then, when you came to Moscow yourself, I think we met only once somewhere. And here I have been living four months now, and until now we haven’t said a word to each other.
