I am leaving tomorrow, and I was just thinking, sitting here: how can I see him, to say goodbye; and you come walking past.”
“And did you very much want to see me?”

“Very much. I want to get acquainted with you once and for all, and to acquaint you with me. And then say goodbye. In my opinion it is best to get acquainted before parting. I saw how you looked at me all these three months; there was a kind of unbroken expectation in your eyes, and that is just what I can’t stand; that is why I didn’t come up to you. But in the end I learned to respect you: the little fellow, I thought, stands firm. Note that, though I am laughing now, I am speaking seriously. You do stand firm, don’t you? I love such firm people, whatever they stand on, even if they are such little boys as you. Your expectant look was not at all repulsive to me in the end; on the contrary, at last I came to love your expectant look... You seem to love me for some reason, Alyosha?”

“I do love you, Ivan. Brother Dmitry says of you: Ivan is a grave. I say of you: Ivan is a riddle. You are a riddle to me even now, but I have already grasped something in you, and only since this morning!”
“What is that?” laughed Ivan.
“You won’t be angry?” Alyosha laughed too.
“Well?”
“That you are just as young a man as all other young men of twenty-three, just as young, youthful, fresh and fine a boy; well, a greenhorn of a boy, in short! What, have I hurt you very much?”

“On the contrary, you have struck me by a coincidence!” Ivan cried cheerfully and warmly. “Would you believe that after our meeting at her place this morning I have been thinking of nothing but that, of my twenty-three-year-old greenness, and now you suddenly guess it exactly and begin with that very thing. I was just sitting here, and do you know what I was saying to myself: if I didn’t believe in life, if I lost faith in the woman I love, lost faith in the order of things, were convinced even that everything, on the contrary, is a disorderly, damned and perhaps devilish chaos, if all the horrors of human disillusionment struck me, still I would want to live, and once I have set my lips to this cup I won’t tear myself away from it until I have drained it all! However, by thirty I shall probably drop the cup, even if I haven’t drunk it all, and go away... I don’t know where. But until I am thirty, I know this firmly, my youth will overcome everything: every disillusionment, every disgust with life. I have asked myself many times: is there in the world such despair as would overcome in me this frenzied and perhaps indecent thirst for life? And I have decided that there seems to be none, that is, again, until those thirty years, and then I won’t want it myself; so it seems to me. Some consumptive snotty moralists often call this thirst for life base, especially the poets. It is partly a Karamazov trait, it’s true, this thirst for life in spite of everything; it certainly sits in you too; but why is it base? There is still a terrible amount of centripetal force on our planet, Alyosha. One wants to live, and I live, even if it is against logic. I may not believe in the order of things, but the sticky little leaves that open in the spring are dear to me, the blue sky is dear to me, some person is dear to me, whom sometimes, would you believe it, you love without knowing why; some human deed is dear to me, in which one has perhaps long since stopped believing, and yet out of old habit one honours it with one’s heart. Here, they have brought your fish soup; eat it and good health to you. The fish soup is splendid; they cook well here. I want to go to Europe, Alyosha; I shall go from here; and of course I know that I shall be going only to a graveyard, but to the most, the most precious graveyard, that’s what! Precious dead lie there; every stone over them speaks of such ardent past life, of such passionate faith in their deed, in their truth, in their struggle and in their science, that I know beforehand I shall fall on the ground and kiss those stones and weep over them, while at the same time convinced with all my heart that it has all long been nothing but a graveyard and nothing more. And I shall weep not from despair, but simply because I shall be happy in the tears I shed. I shall get drunk on my own tenderness. I love the sticky spring leaves, the blue sky, that’s what! It is not the mind here, not logic; here one loves with one’s insides, with one’s belly; one loves one’s first young strength... Do you understand anything of my rubbish, Alyoshka, or not?” Ivan suddenly laughed.

“I understand it only too well, Ivan: one wants to love with one’s insides and one’s belly; you put that beautifully, and I am terribly glad that you want so much to live,” exclaimed Alyosha. “I think that everyone must love life above everything in the world.”
“Love life more than its meaning?”

“Certainly so: love it before logic, as you say; certainly before logic, and only then shall I understand its meaning too. That is what I have long been dimly seeing. Half your work is done, Ivan, and won: you love to live. Now you must try for your second half, and you are saved.”
“You are saving me already, but perhaps I wasn’t perishing! And what is it, your second half?”
“It is that you must raise your dead, who perhaps never died at all. Well, let’s have tea. I’m glad we are talking, Ivan.”

“I see you are in a kind of inspiration. I terribly love such professions de foi, professions of faith, from such... novices. You are a firm man, Alexei. Is it true that you want to leave the monastery?”
“It is true. My elder is sending me into the world.”

“Then we shall see each other again in the world; we shall meet before thirty, when I begin to tear myself away from the cup. Now Father doesn’t want to tear himself away from his cup until seventy; he even dreams of eighty, he said so himself; with him it is far too serious, though he is a buffoon. He has taken his stand on his sensuality as if on a rock too... though after thirty, it is true, there is perhaps nothing else to stand on but that... But to seventy is base; better to thirty: one can keep ‘a shade of nobility’, deceiving oneself. Have you seen Dmitry today?”

“No, I haven’t, but I saw Smerdyakov.” And Alyosha told his brother quickly and in detail about his meeting with Smerdyakov. Ivan suddenly began to listen with great concern; he even asked about some things again.
“Only he asked me not to tell brother Dmitry what he had said about him,” Alyosha added.
Ivan frowned and fell to thinking.
“Is it because of Smerdyakov that you are frowning?” asked Alyosha.
“Yes, because of him. To the devil with him; I really did want to see Dmitry, but now there’s no need...” Ivan said reluctantly.
“And are you really leaving so soon, brother?”
“Yes.”
“And what about Dmitry and Father? How will it end between them?” Alyosha said anxiously.

“You and your same old rigmarole! What have I to do with it? Am I my brother Dmitry’s keeper, or what?” Ivan began to snap irritably, but suddenly smiled somehow bitterly. “Cain’s answer to God about his murdered brother, eh? Perhaps that is what you are thinking at this moment? But, the devil take it, I can’t really stay here as their keeper, can I? I have finished my business and I am going. You don’t think, do you, that I am jealous of Dmitry, that I have been trying all these three months to take his beauty Katerina Ivanovna away from him? Eh, the devil, I had my own business. I have finished my business and I am going. I finished my business this morning; you were a witness.”
“This morning, at Katerina Ivanovna’s?”

“Yes, at hers; and I got free all at once. And what of it? What business is Dmitry of mine? Dmitry has nothing to do with it. I had only my own business with Katerina Ivanovna. You know yourself that, on the contrary, Dmitry behaved as if he were in a conspiracy with me. I didn’t ask him at all, and he solemnly handed her over to me himself and gave us his blessing. It is all quite laughable. No, Alyosha, no; if you knew how light I feel now! I was sitting here having dinner, and would you believe it, I was going to ask for champagne to celebrate my first hour of freedom. Pah, almost half a year, and suddenly, all at once, I have thrown it all off. Well, did I even suspect yesterday that if one wanted to, it would cost nothing to end it!”
“Are you talking about your love, Ivan?”

“Love, if you like, yes; I fell in love with a young lady, an institute girl. I tormented myself over her, and she tormented me. I sat over her... and suddenly it all flew off. This morning I spoke with inspiration, but I went out and burst out laughing; do you believe it? No, I mean it literally.”
“And even now you speak of it so cheerfully,” Alyosha remarked, gazing into his face, which had indeed suddenly brightened.

“But how was I to know that I didn’t love her at all! He-he! And so it turned out that I don’t. And yet how I liked her! How I liked her even this morning, when I was making my speech. And do you know, I like her terribly even now, and yet how easy it is to go away from her. Do you think I am showing off?”
“No. Only perhaps it wasn’t love.”

“Alyoshka,” laughed Ivan, “don’t go reasoning about love! It isn’t proper for you. This morning, this morning you jumped in, ah! I even forgot to kiss you for it... And how she tormented me! Truly I was sitting at the breaking point. Oh, she knew that I loved her! She loved me, not Dmitry,” Ivan insisted cheerfully. “Dmitry is only a strain she puts herself under. Everything I said to her this morning is the real truth. But the whole point, the most important point, is that she needs perhaps fifteen or twenty years to realise that she doesn’t love Dmitry at all, but loves only me, whom she torments. And perhaps she will never realise it, even after today’s lesson. Well, so much the better: I got up and left for ever. By the way, how is she now? What happened there after I left?”
Alyosha told him about the hysterics and that she seemed to be unconscious now and delirious.
“Isn’t Khokhlakova lying?”
“I think not.”
“I must find out. No one has ever died of hysterics, though. And let it be hysterics; God sent woman hysterics out of love. I shan’t go there at all. Why push in again.”
“But you told her this morning that she had never loved you.”
“I did that on purpose. Alyoshka, shall I order champagne? We’ll drink to my freedom. No, if you knew how glad I am!”
“No, brother, better not drink,” Alyosha said suddenly. “Besides, I feel somehow sad.”
“Yes, you have been sad for a long time; I have seen it for a long time.”
“So you will certainly go tomorrow morning?”

“Morning? I didn’t say morning... But then, perhaps in the morning. Would you believe it, I dined here today solely so as not to dine with the old man, he has become so repulsive to me. Because of him alone I would have left long ago. And why are you so worried about my going? You and I have still God knows how much time before I go. A whole eternity of time, immortality!”
“If you are leaving tomorrow, what eternity is there?”

“But what has that to do with you and me?” laughed Ivan. “We shall still have time to talk over what is ours, what we came here for. Why are you staring in surprise? Answer: what did we meet here for? To talk about my love for Katerina Ivanovna, about the old man and Dmitry? About going abroad? About the fatal situation of Russia? About the Emperor Napoleon? Is that it, is it for that?”
“No, not for that.”

“So you understand yourself what for. Others have one thing, but we greenhorns have another; first of all we must solve the everlasting questions; that is our concern. All young Russia is talking now only about the eternal questions. Precisely now, when the old men have all suddenly taken to practical questions. What did you look at me in expectation for all these three months? To ask me: ‘What is your creed, or have you none at all?’ That is what your three months of looks came to, Alexei Fyodorovich, isn’t it?”
“Perhaps it is,” smiled Alyosha. “You aren’t laughing at me now, brother?”

“I, laughing? I don’t want to grieve my little brother, who has looked at me for three months in such expectation. Alyosha, look straight at me: I am just such a little boy as you are myself, only not a novice. How do Russian boys go about things until now? Some of them, I mean? Here, for instance, is this stinking tavern; they meet here and sit down in a corner. They never knew each other before in their lives, and when they leave the tavern they won’t know each other again for forty years; well, and what will they talk about while they have caught a moment in the tavern? About the world questions, nothing less: is there a God, is there immortality? And those who don’t believe in God, well, they will talk about socialism and anarchism, about remaking all humanity on a new pattern; and that comes to the same devil; still the same questions, only from the other end. And a great many, a great many of the most original Russian boys do nothing but talk about the eternal questions among us in our time. Isn’t that so?”

“Yes, for real Russians the questions of whether there is a God and whether there is immortality, or, as you say, the questions from the other end, are of course the first questions and come before everything, and so they should,” said Alyosha, still gazing at his brother with the same quiet and searching smile.

“Here is the thing, Alyosha: to be a Russian is sometimes not at all clever, but still it is impossible to imagine anything stupider than what Russian boys busy themselves with now. But there is one Russian boy, Alyoshka, whom I love terribly.”
“How nicely you led up to that,” Alyosha suddenly laughed.
“Well, tell me then where to begin; give the order yourself: with God? Does God exist, is that it?”
“Begin with whatever you like, even from ‘the other end’. You proclaimed yesterday at Father’s that there is no God,” Alyosha looked at his brother searchingly.

“Yesterday at dinner at the old man’s I teased you with that on purpose, and I saw how your little eyes lit up. But now I am not at all averse to talking it over with you, and I say so very seriously. I want to become close to you, Alyosha, because I have no friends; I want to try. Well, just imagine, perhaps I too accept God,” laughed Ivan; “that’s unexpected for you, eh?”
“Yes, of course, if only you are not joking even now.”

“‘Joking’. They said at the elder’s yesterday that I was joking. You see, my dear, there was an old sinner in the eighteenth century who declared that if there were no God, he would have to be invented: s’il n’existait pas Dieu, il faudrait l’inventer. And man really has invented God. And what is strange, what would be marvellous, is not that God really exists; what is marvellous is that such a thought, the thought of the necessity of God, could creep into the head of such a wild and wicked animal as man, so holy is it, so touching, so wise, and so much does it do honour to man. As for me, I have long since resolved not to think about whether man created God or God created man. I won’t, of course, go through all the modern axioms of Russian boys on this score, all derived from European hypotheses; because what is a hypothesis there is at once an axiom for a Russian boy, and not only for the boys but perhaps for their professors too, because Russian professors among us now are very often the same Russian boys. And so I bypass all the hypotheses. What is our task now, yours and mine? The task is for me to explain to you as quickly as possible my essence, that is, what kind of man I am, what I believe in and what I hope for; isn’t that so, isn’t it? And so I declare that I accept God simply and directly. But here is what must be noted, however: if God exists and if he really did create the earth, then, as we know perfectly well, he created it according to Euclidean geometry, and the human mind with a notion of only three dimensions of space. And yet there have been and still are geometers and philosophers, even some of the most remarkable, who doubt whether the whole universe, or, still more broadly, all being, was created only according to Euclidean geometry; they even dare to dream that two parallel lines, which according to Euclid can never meet on earth, might perhaps meet somewhere in infinity. I have decided, my dear, that if I cannot understand even this, then how can I understand about God? I humbly admit that I have no ability to solve such questions; I have a Euclidean, earthly mind, and so how are we to decide about what is not of this world? And I advise you too never to think about it, friend Alyosha, and above all about God: does he exist or not? All these are questions entirely unsuited to a mind created with a notion of only three dimensions. And so I accept God, and not only willingly, but, what is more, I accept his wisdom too, and his purpose, which are completely unknown to us; I believe in the order, in the meaning of life; I believe in the eternal harmony in which we are all supposed to merge; I believe in the Word, towards which the universe is striving and which itself ‘was with God’ and which itself is God; well, and so on and so on, and so forth to infinity. Many words have been made up on this score. It seems I am on the right road already, eh? Well, then imagine that in the final result I do not accept this world of God’s, and though I know that it exists, I don’t admit it at all. It is not God that I don’t accept, understand that; it is the world created by him, God’s world, that I don’t accept and cannot agree to accept. I will make a reservation: I am convinced, like a child, that suffering will be healed and smoothed over, that the whole offensive comedy of human contradictions will vanish like a pitiful mirage, like the nasty invention of the feeble and puny, atom-like Euclidean human mind; that at last, in the world’s finale, at the moment of eternal harmony, something will happen and appear so precious that it will suffice for all hearts, for the soothing of all indignation, for the redemption of all the villainies of men, of all the blood they have shed; it will suffice not only to make it possible to forgive but even to justify everything that has happened with men; let it, let all this come and appear, but I don’t accept it and don’t want to accept it! Even if the parallel lines meet and I see it myself: I shall see and say that they have met, and still I won’t accept it. That is my essence, Alyosha; that is my thesis. I have told you this seriously. I deliberately began this conversation of ours as stupidly as it could be begun, but I have brought it round to my confession, because that is all you need. It wasn’t God you needed; you only needed to find out what your beloved brother lives by. And I have told you.”
Ivan ended his long tirade suddenly with a kind of special and unexpected feeling.
“And why did you begin ‘as stupidly as it could be begun’?” asked Alyosha, looking at him thoughtfully.

“Well, in the first place, if only for the Russianism of it: Russian conversations on these subjects are all conducted as stupidly as they could be. And in the second place, again: the stupider, the closer to the point. The stupider, the clearer. Stupidity is brief and artless, while intelligence wriggles and hides. Intelligence is a scoundrel, but stupidity is straightforward and honest. I have brought the matter round to my despair, and the more stupidly I have presented it, the better for me.”
“Will you explain to me why you ‘don’t accept the world’?” said Alyosha.

“Of course I will explain; it’s no secret; that is what I was leading up to. My little brother, it is not you I want to corrupt and move from your foundation; perhaps I want to heal myself by you,” Ivan smiled suddenly, quite like a meek little boy. Alyosha had never seen such a smile on him before.
## Book Five, Chapter IV · Rebellion

“I have a confession to make to you,” Ivan began. “I have never been able to understand how one can love one’s neighbours. It is precisely one’s neighbours, in my view, that it is impossible to love; only those far away, perhaps. I read somewhere once about John the Merciful, a saint, that when a hungry, frozen passer-by came to him and asked to be warmed, he lay down with him in his bed, put his arms round him and began breathing into his mouth, which was festering and foul from some terrible disease. I am convinced he did it out of the strain of a lie, out of a love ordered by duty, out of a penance he had loaded on himself. For a man to be loved he has to hide; the moment he shows his face, love is gone.”

“Elder Zosima spoke about that more than once,” Alyosha remarked. “He also said that a man’s face often keeps people who are not yet practised in love from loving him. But there is a great deal of love in mankind all the same, almost like Christ’s love. I know that myself, Ivan…”

“Well, I don’t know it yet, and I can’t understand it, and countless people are with me there. The question is whether it comes from people’s bad qualities or whether it is simply their nature. In my opinion Christ’s love for people is, in its way, a miracle impossible on earth. True, he was God. But we are not gods. Suppose, for instance, that I can suffer deeply; another person can never know how deeply I suffer, because he is someone else and not me, and besides, a man rarely agrees to recognise another as a sufferer (as if it were a rank). Why won’t he, do you think? Because, say, I smell bad, because I have a stupid face, because I once trod on his foot. Then there is suffering and suffering. Degrading suffering, suffering that humiliates me, hunger for instance, my benefactor will still allow me; but suffering a little higher, for an idea for instance, no, that he allows only in rare cases, because he will look at me and suddenly see that I don’t have at all the face that, in his fancy, a man suffering for such and such an idea ought to have. And so he at once withdraws his kindness from me, and not even out of a wicked heart. Beggars, especially noble beggars, ought never to show themselves in the street; they should ask for alms through the newspapers. One can love one’s neighbour in the abstract, and sometimes even from a distance, but close up almost never. If everything were as it is on the stage, in the ballet, where the beggars come on in silken rags and torn lace and beg for alms while dancing gracefully, well, then one might admire them. Admire them, but still not love them. But enough of that. I only needed to put you where I stand. I meant to speak of the suffering of mankind in general, but let us rather keep to the sufferings of children alone. That cuts the scale of my argument by about ten times, but better to keep to children. All the worse for me, of course. But, in the first place, children can be loved even close up, even dirty ones, even ugly ones (though it seems to me that children are never ugly). In the second place, I won’t speak of grown-ups because, besides being disgusting and undeserving of love, they have their retribution: they ate the apple and knew good and evil and became ‘as gods’. They are still eating it. But the little ones have eaten nothing and are not yet guilty of anything. Do you love children, Alyosha? I know you do, and you will understand why I want to speak only of them now. If they too suffer terribly on earth, then of course it is for their fathers, they are punished for their fathers who ate the apple; but that is reasoning from another world, and the human heart here on earth cannot understand it. An innocent cannot suffer for another, and such an innocent at that! Wonder at me, Alyosha: I love little children terribly too. And note this: cruel people, passionate, carnivorous people, Karamazovs, sometimes love children very much. Children, while they are children, up to seven years old for instance, stand terribly far from people, as if they were quite another creature with another nature. I knew a robber in prison. In the course of his career, slaughtering whole families in the houses he broke into at night to rob, he had happened to cut the throats of several children as well. But sitting in prison he loved them strangely. He did nothing but look out of the prison window at the children playing in the yard. He taught one little boy to come and stand under his window, and the boy became great friends with him… You don’t know why I am telling you all this, Alyosha? My head aches somehow, and I am sad.”
“You speak with a strange look,” Alyosha remarked uneasily, “as if you were in some sort of madness.”

“By the way, a Bulgarian in Moscow was telling me lately,” Ivan Fyodorovich went on, as though not listening to his brother, “how the Turks and Circassians there in Bulgaria commit atrocities everywhere, fearing a general rising of the Slavs: they burn, they cut throats, they violate women and children, they nail prisoners to fences by the ears and leave them so till morning, and in the morning they hang them, and so on; it is impossible even to imagine it all. People sometimes speak of man’s ‘bestial’ cruelty, but that is terribly unjust and insulting to the beasts: a beast can never be so cruel as a man, so artfully, so artistically cruel. A tiger simply gnaws and tears; that is all he knows how to do. It would never enter his head to nail people up by the ears for the night, even if he could. These Turks, among other things, tortured children with relish, from cutting them out of their mothers’ wombs with a dagger to tossing nursing babies into the air and catching them on a bayonet before their mothers’ eyes. It was doing it before the mothers’ eyes that made the chief sweetness of it. But here is one little picture that interested me greatly. Imagine: a nursing baby in the arms of its trembling mother, and round them the Turks who have come in. They have thought up an amusing bit of fun: they pet the baby, they laugh to make it laugh; they succeed, the baby laughs. At that moment a Turk points a pistol at it, four inches from its face. The little boy laughs with joy, stretches out his little hands to grab the pistol, and suddenly the artist pulls the trigger right in his face and shatters his little head… Artistic, isn’t it? By the way, they say the Turks are very fond of sweet things.”
“Brother, what is all this for?” asked Alyosha.
“I think that if the devil doesn’t exist, and man has therefore created him, he has created him in his own image and likeness.”
“In that case, just as he did God.”

“You are wonderfully good at turning words round, as Polonius says in Hamlet,” Ivan laughed. “You have caught me out; so be it, I’m glad. A fine God yours is, if man created him in his own image and likeness. You asked just now what all this is for. You see, I am a lover and collector of certain little facts, and, would you believe it, I write down and collect from the newspapers and from people’s stories, from wherever I can, a certain kind of anecdote, and I already have a good collection. The Turks have gone into the collection, of course, but they are all foreigners. I have home-grown specimens too, even better than the Turkish ones. You know, with us it is more beating, more the birch and the lash, and that is national: nailed-up ears are unthinkable with us, we are Europeans after all, but the birch, the lash, that is something of our own and cannot be taken from us. Abroad nowadays they seem hardly to beat at all; manners have been purified, or else the laws have been arranged so that a man no longer dares to flog a man. But they have made up for it with something else, also purely national, as ours is, and so national that with us it seems almost impossible, though it does seem to be taking root here too, especially since the religious movement in our high society. I have a charming little pamphlet, translated from the French, about how in Geneva, quite recently, only five years ago, they executed a villain and murderer called Richard, a young fellow of twenty-three, I think, who repented and was converted to the Christian faith at the very foot of the scaffold. This Richard was someone’s illegitimate child, whom his parents, when he was a little thing of six, made a present of to some Swiss mountain shepherds, and they raised him to use him for work. He grew up among them like a little wild animal. The shepherds taught him nothing; on the contrary, at seven they were already sending him out to graze the flock, in the wet and the cold, almost without clothes and almost without feeding him. And of course nobody who did this thought twice about it or repented of it; on the contrary, each considered himself fully in the right, because Richard had been given to them as a thing, and they did not even think it necessary to feed him. Richard himself testifies that in those years, like the prodigal son in the Gospel, he longed terribly to eat even the mash they gave to the pigs being fattened for sale; but they would not give him even that, and beat him when he stole from the pigs. And so he spent his whole childhood and youth, until he grew up and, having gained his strength, went out to steal for himself. The savage began to earn money as a day labourer in Geneva, drank what he earned, lived like a monster, and ended by killing some old man and robbing him. He was caught, tried and sentenced to death. They don’t go in for sentiment there. And in prison he is at once surrounded by pastors, members of various Christian brotherhoods, charitable ladies and the rest. In prison they taught him to read and write, began expounding the Gospel to him, worked on his conscience, persuaded him, pressed him, nagged him, squeezed him, and at last he solemnly confesses his crime himself. He was converted; he wrote to the court himself that he was a monster and that at last he had been found worthy of having the Lord enlighten him too and send him grace. All Geneva was stirred, all charitable and pious Geneva. Everything that was highest and best brought up rushed to him in prison. They kiss Richard, they embrace him: ‘You are our brother, grace has come down upon you!’ And Richard himself only weeps with tender feeling: ‘Yes, grace has come down upon me! Before, all my childhood and youth, I was glad of the pigs’ food, and now grace has come down on me too, I am dying in the Lord!’ ‘Yes, yes, Richard, die in the Lord; you have shed blood and must die in the Lord. You may not be guilty of not knowing the Lord at all when you envied the pigs their food and were beaten for stealing it from them (which was very wrong of you, for stealing is not allowed), but you have shed blood and must die.’ And so the last day comes. Richard, unstrung, weeps and does nothing but repeat every minute: ‘This is the best of my days, I am going to the Lord!’ ‘Yes,’ cry the pastors, the judges and the charitable ladies, ‘this is your happiest day, for you are going to the Lord!’ The whole crowd moves towards the scaffold behind the shameful cart in which Richard is carried, in carriages, on foot. They reach the scaffold. ‘Die, our brother,’ they cry to Richard, ‘die in the Lord, for grace has come down upon you too!’ And so, covered with his brothers’ kisses, brother Richard was dragged up onto the scaffold, laid on the guillotine, and they chopped his head off in brotherly fashion, because grace had come down upon him too. No, that is characteristic. The pamphlet was translated into Russian by some Lutheranising Russian philanthropists of high society and sent out free with the newspapers and other publications for the enlightenment of the Russian people. The thing about Richard is good because it is national. With us, though it would be absurd to cut off a brother’s head only because he has become our brother and grace has come down upon him, we have, I repeat, something of our own that is almost as good. With us it is a historical, immediate and intimate delight in the torment of beating. Nekrasov has a poem about how a peasant whips a horse across the eyes, ‘across its meek eyes’. Who hasn’t seen that? It is a Russianism. He describes how a feeble little nag with too much piled on it has got stuck with its cart and can’t pull it out. The peasant beats it, beats it in a fury, beats it at last not knowing what he is doing; drunk with beating, he flogs it painfully, past counting: ‘Even if you haven’t the strength, pull, die but pull!’ The nag strains, and he begins to lash it, defenceless as it is, across its weeping, its ‘meek eyes’. Beside itself, it gives a jerk and pulls the cart out and goes on, trembling all over, not breathing, somehow sideways, with a sort of skip, somehow unnaturally and shamefully. In Nekrasov it is horrible. But that is only a horse, and God himself gave us horses to be flogged. So the Tatars explained it to us, and left us the knout as a keepsake. But one can flog people too. And so an intelligent, educated gentleman and his lady flog their own little daughter, a child of seven, with birch rods. I have it written down in detail. Papa is glad that the twigs have knots in them: ‘it will sting more,’ he says, and so he begins to ‘sting’ his own daughter. I know for certain there are floggers who grow more heated with every stroke, to the point of voluptuousness, literal voluptuousness, more and more with each stroke that follows, in a progression. They flog for a minute, they flog at last for five minutes, they flog for ten minutes, further, harder, faster, more stinging. The child screams; the child at last cannot scream, she is choking: ‘Papa, papa, papa dear, papa dear!’ By some devilish, indecent chance the case comes to court. A lawyer is hired. Our Russian people long ago named the lawyer ‘a hired conscience’. The lawyer shouts in his client’s defence: ‘The matter is so simple, a family matter, an ordinary one; a father has flogged his daughter, and, to the shame of our times, it has come to court!’ The jury, convinced, retire and bring in an acquittal. The public roars with joy that the torturer has been acquitted. Ah, I wasn’t there; I would have bellowed a proposal to found a scholarship in the torturer’s name! Charming pictures. But about children I have still better ones; I have collected a great, great deal about Russian children, Alyosha. A little girl of five was hated by her father and mother, ‘most respectable people of rank, educated and well brought up’. You see, I affirm once more, positively, that there is a peculiar trait in many people: a love of torturing children, but children only. Towards all other members of the human race these same torturers behave even kindly and gently, like educated and humane Europeans, but they are very fond of tormenting children; they even love children in that sense. It is precisely the defencelessness of these creatures that tempts the torturers, the angelic trustfulness of a child who has nowhere to go and no one to turn to: that is what inflames the vile blood of the torturer. In every man, of course, a beast lies hidden: the beast of rage, the beast of lustful excitement at the cries of the tortured victim, the beast let off the chain with nothing to hold it, the beast of diseases picked up in debauchery, gout, a bad liver and the rest. These educated parents subjected that poor five-year-old girl to every kind of torture. They beat her, flogged her, kicked her, not knowing why themselves; they turned her whole body into bruises. At last they reached the height of refinement: in the cold, in the frost, they locked her up all night in the privy, and because she did not ask to be taken out at night (as if a child of five, sleeping her sound angelic sleep, could learn to ask at that age), for that they smeared her whole face with her excrement and made her eat it, and it was the mother, the mother who made her! And this mother could sleep while at night the moans of the poor little child locked up in that vile place could be heard! Do you understand that, when a little creature who cannot even grasp what is being done to her beats her torn little breast with her tiny fist in that vile place, in the dark and the cold, and weeps her bloody, unresentful, meek little tears to ‘dear God’ to protect her? Do you understand this nonsense, my friend and my brother, my humble novice of God, do you understand why this nonsense is so necessary and was created? Without it, they say, man could not even have lived on earth, for he would not have known good and evil. Why know this devilish good and evil, when it costs so much? Why, the whole world of knowledge is not worth that child’s little tears to ‘dear God’. I am not speaking of the sufferings of grown-ups; they ate the apple, and the devil take them, let the devil take them all, but these, these! I am torturing you, Alyoshka; you don’t look yourself. I’ll stop if you like.”
“Never mind, I want to be tortured too,” Alyosha muttered.

“One more, just one more little picture, and that only out of curiosity, because it is so very characteristic, and above all I have only just read it in one of our collections of antiquities, the Archive or Antiquity, I must look it up; I have even forgotten where I read it. It was in the darkest days of serfdom, at the beginning of the century, and long live the liberator of the people! There was at that time, at the beginning of the century, a general, a general with great connections and a very rich landowner, but one of those (even then, it seems, very few) who, when they retired from the service, were all but convinced that they had earned the right of life and death over their subjects. There were such men then. Well, the general lives on his estate of two thousand souls, puffed up, treating his small neighbours as his hangers-on and buffoons. He has kennels with hundreds of hounds and nearly a hundred huntsmen, all in uniform, all mounted. And one day a house serf’s boy, a little boy only eight years old, threw a stone in play and hurt the paw of the general’s favourite hound. ‘Why is my favourite dog lame?’ He is told that this very boy threw a stone at it and hurt its paw. ‘Ah, so it was you,’ the general looked him over. ‘Take him!’ They took him, took him from his mother; he spent the whole night in the lock-up. In the morning, at first light, the general rides out in full dress for the hunt, mounts his horse, with his hangers-on, his dogs, his kennelmen and huntsmen round him, all mounted. The house serfs are gathered round for their edification, and in front of them all, the guilty boy’s mother. The boy is brought out of the lock-up. A gloomy, cold, misty autumn day, a famous day for hunting. The general orders the boy to be undressed; the child is stripped stark naked; he shivers, he is out of his mind with fear, he dares not make a sound… ‘Drive him!’ the general commands. ‘Run, run!’ the kennelmen shout at him; the boy runs… ‘At him!’ the general yells, and sets the whole pack of borzois on him. He hunted him down before his mother’s eyes, and the hounds tore the child to pieces!… I believe the general was put under guardianship. Well… what is to be done with him? Shoot him? Shoot him for the satisfaction of our moral feelings? Speak, Alyoshka!”
“Shoot him!” Alyosha said quietly, raising his eyes to his brother with a pale, somehow twisted smile.
“Bravo!” Ivan yelled in a kind of rapture. “If you said it, then… What a hermit! So that is the little devil sitting in your heart, Alyoshka Karamazov!”
“I said something absurd, but…”

“That’s just it, the ‘but’…” Ivan shouted. “Know this, novice: absurdities are only too necessary on earth. The world stands on absurdities, and without them perhaps nothing would ever have happened in it at all. We know what we know!”
“What do you know?”

“I understand nothing,” Ivan went on as if in delirium, “and I don’t want to understand anything now. I want to stay with the fact. I decided long ago not to understand. If I want to understand something, I shall at once betray the fact, and I have decided to stay with the fact…”
“Why are you testing me?” Alyosha cried out with sorrowful strain. “Will you tell me at last?”
“Of course I’ll tell you; that is what I have been leading up to. You are dear to me; I don’t want to let you go, and I won’t give you up to your Zosima.”
Ivan was silent for a minute; his face suddenly became very sad.

“Listen to me. I took only children to make it clearer. Of the other human tears with which the whole earth is soaked from its crust to its centre I won’t say a word; I have narrowed my theme on purpose. I am a bedbug, and I admit in all humility that I cannot understand at all why everything is arranged as it is. People themselves are to blame, it seems: they were given paradise, they wanted freedom and stole fire from heaven, knowing themselves that they would become unhappy; so there is no need to pity them. Oh, with my pitiful, earthly, Euclidean mind, all I know is that there is suffering, that no one is guilty, that everything follows from everything else directly and simply, that everything flows and finds its level. But that is only Euclidean nonsense; I know that, don’t I, and I cannot agree to live by it! What is it to me that no one is guilty and that I know it? I need retribution, or else I shall destroy myself. And retribution not somewhere and some time in infinity, but here on earth, and so that I see it myself. I have believed; I want to see it for myself, and if I am dead by that hour, then let them raise me up, for if it all happens without me it will be too unfair. Surely I didn’t suffer so that I, my crimes and my sufferings, should manure the soil of some future harmony for somebody else. I want to see with my own eyes the hind lie down beside the lion and the murdered man rise up and embrace his murderer. I want to be there when everyone suddenly learns why it all was as it was. All the religions on earth are built on this longing, and I believe. But then there are the children, and what am I to do with them then? That is the question I cannot resolve. For the hundredth time I repeat: there are a multitude of questions, but I have taken only the children, because here what I need to say is irrefutably clear. Listen: if everyone must suffer in order to buy eternal harmony with suffering, what have children to do with it, tell me, please? It is quite incomprehensible why they too should have had to suffer, and why they should buy harmony with sufferings. Why should they too fall into the material and manure with themselves some future harmony for someone? I understand solidarity in sin among people; I understand solidarity in retribution too; but there is no solidarity in sin with children, and if the truth really is that they too share with their fathers in all their fathers’ crimes, then of course that truth is not of this world and is beyond my understanding. Some joker will say, perhaps, that the child would have grown up anyway and had time to sin; but there, he didn’t grow up; at eight years old he was hunted down by dogs. Oh, Alyosha, I am not blaspheming! I do understand what a shaking of the universe it must be when everything in heaven and under the earth flows into one voice of praise and everything living and that has lived cries out: ‘Thou art just, O Lord, for thy ways are revealed!’ When the mother embraces the torturer who had her son torn to pieces by his dogs, and all three cry out with tears, ‘Thou art just, O Lord,’ then of course the crown of knowledge will have come and everything will be explained. But that is just where the comma is; that is what I cannot accept. And while I am on earth I hasten to take my own measures. You see, Alyosha, it may really happen that when I myself live to see that moment, or rise again to see it, I too shall perhaps cry out with the rest, looking at the mother embracing her child’s torturer, ‘Thou art just, O Lord!’ But I don’t want to cry out then. While there is still time, I hasten to protect myself, and so I renounce the higher harmony altogether. It is not worth the tears of even that one tortured child who beat her breast with her little fist and prayed in her stinking kennel, with her unredeemed tears, to ‘dear God’! It is not worth it, because her tears were left unredeemed. They must be redeemed, or there can be no harmony. But with what, with what will you redeem them? Is it possible? By their being avenged? But what do I care for their being avenged, what do I care for a hell for the torturers, what can hell put right when those children have already been tortured? And what sort of harmony is it, if there is hell? I want to forgive, I want to embrace; I don’t want more suffering. And if the sufferings of children went to make up the sum of sufferings needed to buy truth, then I declare in advance that the whole of truth is not worth such a price. I don’t want, in the end, the mother to embrace the torturer who had her son torn to pieces by dogs! She dare not forgive him! If she wants to, let her forgive him for herself, let her forgive the torturer her own immeasurable mother’s suffering; but the sufferings of her torn child she has no right to forgive; she dare not forgive the torturer, even if the child himself forgave him! And if that is so, if they dare not forgive, where is the harmony? Is there in the whole world a being who could forgive and would have the right to? I don’t want harmony; out of love for mankind I don’t want it. I would rather remain with my suffering unavenged. I would rather remain with my unavenged suffering and my unappeased indignation, even if I were wrong. Besides, they have priced harmony too high; it is beyond our means to pay so much for admission. And so I hasten to give back my entrance ticket. And if I am an honest man, I am bound to give it back as far in advance as I can. That is what I am doing. It is not God I don’t accept, Alyosha; I only most respectfully return him the ticket.”
“That is rebellion,” Alyosha said quietly, lowering his eyes.

“Rebellion? I would rather not have had that word from you,” Ivan said with feeling. “Can one live by rebellion? And I want to live. Tell me yourself, straight out; I call on you, answer me: imagine that you yourself are building the edifice of human destiny with the aim of making people happy in the end, of giving them peace and rest at last, but that for this it was necessary and unavoidable to torture to death only one tiny creature, that very child who beat her breast with her little fist, and to found that edifice on her unavenged tears. Would you agree to be the architect on those terms? Tell me, and don’t lie!”
“No, I wouldn’t agree,” Alyosha said quietly.

“And can you admit the idea that the people for whom you are building would themselves agree to accept their happiness on the unjustified blood of a little tortured child, and, having accepted it, remain happy for ever?”

“No, I can’t admit it. Brother,” Alyosha said suddenly, his eyes flashing, “you asked just now whether there is in the whole world a being who could forgive and would have the right to. But there is such a being, and he can forgive everything, everyone and everything and for everything, because he himself gave his innocent blood for all and for everything. You have forgotten him, and it is on him that the edifice is founded, and it is to him that they will cry out: ‘Thou art just, O Lord, for thy ways are revealed.’”

“Ah, that is ‘the only sinless one’ and his blood! No, I haven’t forgotten him; on the contrary, I have been wondering all this time why you were so long in bringing him out, for usually in arguments all your people put him forward first of all. You know, Alyosha, don’t laugh: I once made up a poem, about a year ago. If you can waste another ten minutes with me, I’ll tell it to you.”
“You wrote a poem?”

“Oh no, I didn’t write it,” Ivan laughed, “and I have never in my life composed even two lines of verse. But I made up this poem and remembered it. I made it up with passion. You will be my first reader, that is, my first listener. Why indeed should an author lose even one listener?” Ivan smiled. “Shall I tell it or not?”
“I am listening hard,” said Alyosha.
“My poem is called ‘The Grand Inquisitor’. An absurd thing, but I want to tell it to you.”
## Book Five, Chapter V · The Grand Inquisitor

“You see, even here I can’t do without a preface, a literary preface, I mean. Damn it!” Ivan laughed. “And what kind of author am I? Look: my story takes place in the sixteenth century, and back then (you must remember this from school) it was the custom in poetry to bring the powers of heaven down to earth. I won’t even mention Dante. In France the law clerks, and the monks in the monasteries too, used to put on whole performances with the Madonna on stage, and angels, and saints, and Christ, and God himself. All of it was very naive in those days. In Victor Hugo’s Notre-Dame de Paris, in the Paris of Louis XI, to celebrate the birth of the Dauphin, an edifying play is put on for the people, free of charge, in the great hall of the town hall, called The Good Judgement of the Most Holy and Gracious Virgin Mary, and she appears in person and pronounces her good judgement. Here in Moscow, in the old days before Peter the Great, almost the same sort of plays were put on now and then, especially from the Old Testament. And besides plays, all sorts of tales and verses went round the world in which saints, angels and all the powers of heaven took part as they were needed. In our monasteries too they translated and copied such poems, and even wrote them, and when? Under the Tatars.

“There is one little monastery poem, for instance (from the Greek, of course), called The Descent of the Mother of God into Hell, with scenes as bold as anything in Dante. The Mother of God visits hell, and the Archangel Michael is her guide through the torments. She sees the sinners and their sufferings. Among them, by the way, there is one most remarkable class of sinners in a burning lake: those who sink so deep in the lake that they can never swim up again, ‘these God forgets’, an expression of extraordinary depth and power. And the Mother of God, shaken and weeping, falls before the throne of God and begs mercy for everyone in hell, everyone she has seen there, without distinction. Her conversation with God is tremendously interesting. She pleads, she will not go away, and when God points to the nail-pierced hands and feet of her Son and asks, ‘How can I forgive his torturers?’, she commands all the saints, all the martyrs, all the angels and archangels to fall down with her and pray for mercy for all, without distinction. In the end she wins from God a respite from torment every year, from Good Friday to Trinity Sunday, and the sinners in hell at once thank the Lord and cry out to him: ‘Thou art just, O Lord, in thy judgement.’

“Well, my little poem would have been of that kind if it had appeared in those days. He appears on my stage. True, he says nothing in the poem; he only appears and passes by. Fifteen centuries have gone by since he promised to come in his kingdom, fifteen centuries since his prophet wrote, ‘Behold, I come quickly.’ ‘But of that day and that hour knoweth no man, not even the Son, but the Father only,’ as he said himself while still on earth. But humanity awaits him with the same faith as before, and the same tenderness. Oh, with even greater faith, for fifteen centuries have passed since heaven stopped giving pledges to man:

> Believe what the heart tells you;
> heaven gives no pledges.
— Schiller, ‘Longing’ (as Ivan quotes it)

“Nothing but faith in what the heart has said! True, there were many miracles then. There were saints who worked miraculous cures; to some righteous men, so their Lives say, the Queen of Heaven came down in person. But the devil does not sleep, and doubt had already begun among men about the truth of these miracles. Just then, in the north, in Germany, a terrible new heresy appeared. A great star, ‘burning as it were a lamp’ (that is, a church), ‘fell upon the fountains of waters, and they were made bitter’. These heresies blasphemously denied miracles. But those who remained faithful believed all the more ardently. The tears of humanity rose up to him as before; people waited for him, loved him, hoped in him, longed to suffer and die for him as before. So many centuries had humanity prayed with faith and fire, ‘O Lord God, appear to us’, so many centuries had it called to him, that in his immeasurable compassion he resolved to come down to those who prayed. He had come down before, he had visited some of the righteous, the martyrs and holy hermits while they were still on earth, as is written in their Lives. Our own Tyutchev, who believed deeply in the truth of his words, proclaimed that

> Bowed beneath the burden of the cross,
> through all of you, my native land,
> in the form of a servant, the King of Heaven
> has walked, blessing as he went.
— Tyutchev, ‘These Poor Villages’

“And I tell you that this was certainly so. And now he wished to appear, even for a moment, to the people: to the tormented, suffering, foully sinful people, who loved him like children. My story takes place in Spain, in Seville, at the most terrible time of the Inquisition, when fires were lit every day throughout the land to the glory of God, and

> in splendid acts of faith
> they burned the wicked heretics.
— Polezhaev

“Oh, of course, this was not the coming in which he will appear, as he promised, at the end of time in all his heavenly glory, the coming that will be sudden, ‘as the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even unto the west’. No, he wanted only to visit his children for a moment, and precisely there, where the fires of the heretics had just been crackling. In his boundless mercy he walks once more among men, in the same human form in which he walked among them for three years fifteen centuries before. He comes down into the hot squares of the southern city, in which, only the day before, in a ‘magnificent auto-da-fé’, in the presence of the king, the court, the knights, the cardinals and the loveliest ladies of the court, before the whole population of Seville, the Cardinal Grand Inquisitor had burned almost a hundred heretics at once, ad majorem gloriam Dei, for the greater glory of God.

“He appeared quietly, unnoticed, and yet (this is the strange thing) everyone recognises him. That could be one of the best passages in the poem: why exactly they recognise him. The people are drawn to him by an irresistible force, they surround him, they grow into a crowd round him, they follow him. He walks among them in silence with a quiet smile of infinite compassion. The sun of love burns in his heart, rays of Light, Enlightenment and Power stream from his eyes and, pouring over the people, shake their hearts with answering love. He stretches out his hands to them, he blesses them, and from touching him, even only his clothes, there comes a healing power. Here an old man, blind from childhood, cries out from the crowd, ‘Lord, heal me, so that I too may see you,’ and something like scales falls from his eyes, and the blind man sees him. The people weep and kiss the ground where he walks. Children throw flowers in front of him, sing and cry out to him, ‘Hosanna!’ ‘It is he, it is he himself,’ they all repeat. ‘It must be he, it can be no one but he.’

“He stops on the steps of the cathedral of Seville at the very moment when a small open white coffin is being carried into the church, with weeping. In it lies a girl of seven, the only daughter of a prominent citizen. The dead child lies covered in flowers. ‘He will raise your child,’ people shout from the crowd to the weeping mother. The cathedral priest who has come out to meet the coffin looks on in bewilderment and frowns. But now the mother of the dead child cries out. She throws herself at his feet. ‘If it is you, raise my child!’ she cries, stretching out her hands to him. The procession stops; the little coffin is set down on the steps at his feet. He looks with compassion, and his lips once more softly say, ‘Talitha cumi’, ‘and the damsel arose’. The girl rises in the coffin, sits up and looks round, smiling, with wide, astonished eyes. In her hands is the bunch of white roses she lay with in the coffin.

“There is confusion among the people, shouting, sobbing, and at that very moment the Cardinal Grand Inquisitor himself crosses the square in front of the cathedral. He is an old man of nearly ninety, tall and straight, with a withered face and sunken eyes, in which there is still a gleam like a spark of fire. Oh, he is not in his splendid cardinal’s robes, the ones he paraded in yesterday before the people when the enemies of the Roman faith were burned; no, at this moment he wears only his old, coarse monk’s cassock. At a certain distance behind him follow his grim assistants and servants and the ‘holy’ guard. He stops in front of the crowd and watches from a distance. He has seen everything: he has seen them set the coffin down at his feet, he has seen the girl rise, and his face has darkened. He knits his thick grey brows, and his eyes flash with an ominous fire. He stretches out his finger and orders the guards to seize him. And such is his power, so well trained, submissive and tremblingly obedient are the people to him, that the crowd at once parts before the guards, and they, amid the deathly silence that has suddenly fallen, lay hands on him and lead him away. At once the whole crowd, as one man, bows to the ground before the old Inquisitor; he blesses the people in silence and passes on. The guards bring the prisoner to a cramped, gloomy, vaulted prison in the ancient building of the Holy Office and lock him in.

“The day passes, and the dark, hot, ‘breathless’ night of Seville comes on. The air ‘smells of laurel and lemon’. In the deep darkness the iron door of the prison suddenly opens, and the old Grand Inquisitor himself slowly comes in with a lamp in his hand. He is alone; the door is locked behind him at once. He stops at the entrance and looks into his face for a long time, a minute or two. At last he quietly comes closer, sets the lamp on the table and says to him:

“‘Is it you? You?’ But, getting no answer, he quickly adds: ‘Don’t answer. Be silent. And what could you say? I know too well what you would say. And you have no right to add anything to what you said before. Why have you come to get in our way? For you have come to get in our way, and you know it. But do you know what will happen tomorrow? I do not know who you are, and I do not want to know, whether you are he or only his likeness; but tomorrow I will condemn you and burn you at the stake as the worst of heretics, and the very people who kissed your feet today will rush, at a single sign from me, to rake up the coals for your fire. Do you know that? Yes, perhaps you do know it,’ he added, lost in thought, not taking his eyes off his prisoner for a moment.”

“I don’t quite understand, Ivan, what this is,” said Alyosha, who had listened all this time in silence, smiling. “Is it just wild fantasy, or some mistake on the old man’s part, some impossible mix-up?”

“Take it as the second, if you like,” laughed Ivan, “if modern realism has spoiled you so much that you can’t stand anything fantastic. You want a mix-up: let it be a mix-up. It’s true,” he laughed again, “the old man is ninety, and he could long ago have gone mad over his idea. The prisoner might have struck him by his appearance. It might simply be delirium, the vision of an old man of ninety before his death, inflamed by the auto-da-fé of the day before, with its hundred burnt heretics. But isn’t it all the same to you and me whether it’s a mix-up or wild fantasy? The point is only that the old man has to speak out, that at last, after ninety years, he speaks out and says aloud what he has kept silent about for ninety years.”
“And the prisoner is silent too? He looks at him and doesn’t say a word?”

“That’s how it has to be, in any case,” laughed Ivan again. “The old man himself tells him that he has no right to add anything to what he said before. If you like, that is the most basic feature of Roman Catholicism, in my opinion at least: ‘Everything,’ they say, ‘was handed over by you to the Pope, so everything is now in the Pope’s hands, and you might as well not come at all now, or at least don’t get in the way for the time being.’ They don’t only say it, they write it, the Jesuits at any rate. I have read it in their theologians myself.

“‘Have you the right to reveal to us even one of the mysteries of the world you have come from?’ my old man asks him, and answers for him: ‘No, you have not; so as not to add to what was said before, and so as not to take away from people the freedom you stood up for so much when you were on earth. Everything you might reveal now would encroach on people’s freedom of faith, because it would come as a miracle, and the freedom of their faith was dearer to you than anything, even then, fifteen hundred years ago. Wasn’t it you who said so often then, “I will make you free”? Well, now you have seen these “free” men,’ the old man adds suddenly with a thoughtful smile. ‘Yes, this business has cost us dear,’ he goes on, looking at him sternly, ‘but we have finished it at last, in your name. For fifteen centuries we have been tormented by this freedom, but now it is over, and over for good. You don’t believe that it is over for good? You look at me meekly and do not even deign to be angry with me? But know that now, today, these people are more certain than ever before that they are completely free, and yet they themselves brought us their freedom and laid it humbly at our feet. But it was we who did that; and is that what you wanted, that kind of freedom?’”
“Again I don’t understand,” Alyosha broke in. “Is he being ironic? Is he laughing?”

“Not in the least. He is counting it as a merit, for himself and his kind, that at last they have overcome freedom and have done it in order to make people happy. ‘For only now’ (he is talking about the Inquisition, of course) ‘has it become possible to think for the first time of people’s happiness. Man was made a rebel; can rebels be happy? You were warned,’ he says to him. ‘You had no lack of warnings and signs, but you did not listen to the warnings; you rejected the only way by which people could be made happy. But, fortunately, when you left, you handed the work over to us. You promised, you confirmed it with your word, you gave us the right to bind and to loose, and of course you cannot even think of taking that right away from us now. Why, then, have you come to get in our way?’”
“And what does it mean, ‘no lack of warnings and signs’?” asked Alyosha.
“That is exactly the main thing the old man has to say.

“‘The terrible and intelligent spirit, the spirit of self-destruction and non-being,’ the old man goes on, ‘the great spirit spoke with you in the wilderness, and we are told in the books that he “tempted” you. Is that so? And could anything truer be said than what he told you in his three questions, which you rejected, and which the books call “temptations”? And yet if ever there was a real, thundering miracle on earth, it was on that day, the day of those three temptations. The miracle lay precisely in the appearance of those three questions.

“‘Imagine, just as an experiment, that the three questions of the terrible spirit had been lost from the books without a trace, and had to be restored, thought up and composed anew to be put back in the books, and for this all the wise men of the earth were gathered together: rulers, high priests, scholars, philosophers, poets. And they were given the task: think up, compose three questions, which must not only be equal to the size of the event but must also express, in three words, in only three human sentences, the whole future history of the world and of humanity. Do you think that all the wisdom of the earth, united together, could think up anything even remotely equal in strength and depth to the three questions that were actually put to you then by the powerful and intelligent spirit in the wilderness? From those questions alone, from the miracle of their appearing, one can see that one is dealing not with a passing human mind but with an eternal and absolute one. For in those three questions the whole subsequent history of mankind is, as it were, brought together into one whole and foretold, and three images are revealed in which all the insoluble historical contradictions of human nature on all the earth will meet. It could not be seen so clearly then, because the future was unknown; but now that fifteen centuries have passed, we see that everything in those three questions was so well guessed and foretold, and has come true so completely, that nothing more can be added to them or taken away.

“‘Decide for yourself who was right: you, or the one who questioned you then? Remember the first question. Its meaning, if not its words, was this: “You want to go into the world, and you go empty-handed, with some promise of freedom which men, in their simplicity and their innate unruliness, cannot even understand, which they fear and dread, for nothing has ever been more unbearable for man and for human society than freedom! But do you see these stones in this bare, scorching wilderness? Turn them into bread, and mankind will run after you like a flock, grateful and obedient, though forever trembling that you will withdraw your hand and your bread will stop.” But you did not want to take away man’s freedom, and you rejected the offer, for what kind of freedom is it, you reasoned, if obedience is bought with bread? You replied that man does not live by bread alone. But do you know that in the name of that very earthly bread the spirit of the earth will rise up against you and fight with you and defeat you, and everyone will follow him, crying, “Who is like unto this beast? He has given us fire from heaven!” Do you know that centuries will pass, and mankind will proclaim through the mouth of its wisdom and science that there is no crime, and therefore no sin, but only hungry people? “Feed them first, then ask them to be virtuous!” That is what they will write on the banner they will raise against you, and with which your temple will be destroyed.

“‘In place of your temple a new building will rise; the terrible Tower of Babel will be raised again, and though this one will not be finished either, any more than the first, still you could have spared people this new tower and cut their sufferings short by a thousand years, for it is to us they will come, after tormenting themselves for a thousand years with their tower! They will seek us out again, under the earth, in the catacombs, where we shall be hiding (for we shall be persecuted and tortured again), they will find us and cry out to us: “Feed us, for those who promised us fire from heaven have not given it.” And then we shall finish building their tower, for the one who finishes it is the one who feeds them, and only we shall feed them, in your name, and we shall lie that it is in your name. Oh, never, never will they feed themselves without us! No science will give them bread while they remain free. In the end they will bring their freedom to our feet and say to us: “Make us your slaves, but feed us.” They will understand at last that freedom and enough earthly bread for everyone are unthinkable together, for never, never will they be able to share among themselves! They will be convinced, too, that they can never be free, because they are weak, vicious, worthless and rebellious.

“‘You promised them the bread of heaven, but, I repeat, can it compare in the eyes of the weak, forever vicious and forever ignoble race of men with earthly bread? And if thousands and tens of thousands follow you for the sake of the bread of heaven, what will become of the millions and tens of thousands of millions of creatures who will not have the strength to give up earthly bread for the bread of heaven? Or are only the tens of thousands of the great and strong dear to you, while the remaining millions, numerous as the sand of the sea, who are weak but love you, must serve only as material for the great and strong? No, the weak are dear to us too. They are vicious and rebellious, but in the end they will become obedient. They will marvel at us and think us gods, because we, by standing at their head, have agreed to endure freedom and to rule over them, so terrible will it become for them at last to be free! But we shall say that we obey you and rule in your name. We shall deceive them again, for we shall not let you come near us any more. In that deception our suffering will lie, for we shall have to lie.

“‘That is what the first question in the wilderness meant, and that is what you rejected in the name of freedom, which you put above everything. And yet that question held the great secret of this world. Had you accepted the “loaves”, you would have answered the universal and everlasting anguish of man, both as an individual and as the whole of mankind, which is: “Whom shall I bow down to?” There is no care more constant and more agonising for a man who is left free than to find, as quickly as possible, someone to bow down to. But man seeks to bow down to something that is beyond dispute, so far beyond dispute that all men at once would agree to bow down to it together. For the care of these pitiful creatures is not only to find something that I or someone else can bow down to, but to find something that everyone will believe in and bow down to, and it must be everyone together. This need for a shared worship is the chief torment of every man, and of all mankind, since the beginning of time. For the sake of this shared worship they have killed each other with the sword. They have made gods and called out to each other: “Give up your gods and come and worship ours, or death to you and your gods!” And so it will be until the end of the world, even when the gods have disappeared from the world: they will fall down before idols all the same.

“‘You knew, you could not but know this fundamental secret of human nature, but you rejected the only absolute banner that was offered to you to make everyone bow down to you without dispute: the banner of earthly bread. And you rejected it in the name of freedom and the bread of heaven. And look what you did next. And all again in the name of freedom! I tell you, man has no care more agonising than to find someone to whom he can hand over, as quickly as possible, the gift of freedom with which this unhappy creature is born. But only the one who sets their conscience at rest can take possession of men’s freedom. With bread you were given a banner beyond dispute: give bread, and man will bow down, for nothing is more beyond dispute than bread. But if at the same time someone else takes possession of his conscience, oh, then he will even throw away your bread and follow the one who has seduced his conscience. In that you were right. For the secret of human existence is not just to live, but to have something to live for. Without a firm idea of what he lives for, man will not agree to live; he would rather destroy himself than stay on earth, even if he were surrounded by bread.

“‘That is so. But what happened? Instead of taking possession of men’s freedom, you increased it even more! Did you forget that peace, and even death, are dearer to man than free choice in the knowledge of good and evil? Nothing is more seductive for man than the freedom of his conscience, but nothing is more agonising either. And instead of firm foundations for setting the human conscience at rest once and for all, you chose everything that is exceptional, enigmatic and vague, you chose everything that was beyond men’s strength, and so you acted as though you did not love them at all, and who did this? The one who came to give his life for them! Instead of taking possession of men’s freedom, you multiplied it, and burdened the spiritual kingdom of man with its torments forever. You wanted man’s free love, so that he would follow you freely, enticed and captivated by you. In place of the firm ancient law, man was from now on to decide for himself, with a free heart, what is good and what is evil, having only your image before him as a guide. But did you not think that he would in the end reject and dispute even your image and your truth, if he were weighed down with so terrible a burden as freedom of choice? They will cry out at last that the truth is not in you, for it was impossible to leave them in more confusion and torment than you did, leaving them so many cares and insoluble problems. So you yourself laid the foundation for the destruction of your own kingdom, and you should not blame anyone else for it.

“‘And yet, was that what was offered to you? There are three powers, only three powers on earth, that can conquer and hold captive forever the conscience of these weak rebels, for their own happiness. These powers are miracle, mystery and authority. You rejected all three, and set the example yourself. When the terrible and wise spirit set you on the pinnacle of the temple and said to you, “If you want to know whether you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written that the angels will catch him and bear him up, and he will not fall and be dashed to pieces, and then you will know whether you are the Son of God, and you will prove how great your faith in your Father is,” you listened, and rejected the offer, and did not give in, and did not throw yourself down. Oh, of course, you acted proudly and magnificently there, like God; but men, that weak, rebellious race, are they gods? Oh, you understood then that if you had taken just one step, made just one movement to throw yourself down, you would at once have tempted the Lord and lost all your faith in him, and been dashed to pieces against the earth you had come to save, and the intelligent spirit who tempted you would have rejoiced. But, I repeat, are there many like you? And could you really have supposed for one moment that men, too, would be able to withstand such a temptation? Is human nature made to reject miracles and, in the most terrible moments of life, the moments of its deepest, most fundamental and agonising questions of the soul, to remain with only the free decision of the heart?

“‘Oh, you knew that your deed would be kept in the books, would reach the depths of time and the furthest ends of the earth, and you hoped that, following you, man too would stay with God without needing a miracle. But you did not know that as soon as man rejects miracles he will reject God as well, for man seeks not so much God as miracles. And since man cannot bear to be without miracles, he will create new miracles of his own, and he will bow down to the miracles of quacks and the witchcraft of old women, even if he is a rebel, a heretic and an atheist a hundred times over. You did not come down from the cross when they shouted to you, mocking and taunting you, “Come down from the cross and we will believe that it is you.” You did not come down because, again, you did not want to enslave man by a miracle, and you longed for faith that was free, not faith based on a miracle. You longed for free love, not the slavish raptures of a slave before a power that has terrified him once and for all. But here too you judged men too highly, for of course they are slaves, though they were created rebels.

“‘Look around and judge. Fifteen centuries have passed: go and look at them. Whom have you raised up to yourself? I swear, man was made weaker and lower than you thought! Can he, can he do what you did? By respecting him so much you acted as if you had ceased to feel compassion for him, because you asked too much of him, and who did this? The one who loved him more than himself! If you had respected him less, you would have asked less of him, and that would have been closer to love, for his burden would have been lighter. He is weak and base. What does it matter that he now rebels everywhere against our power and is proud of rebelling? It is the pride of a child, a schoolboy. They are little children who have rebelled in class and driven out the teacher. But the children’s glee will come to an end, and it will cost them dear. They will tear down the temples and drench the earth in blood. But the foolish children will see at last that, though they are rebels, they are feeble rebels who cannot bear their own rebellion. Shedding their foolish tears, they will admit at last that the one who made them rebels must have meant to mock them. They will say it in despair, and what they say will be blasphemy, which will make them still more unhappy, for human nature cannot bear blasphemy and in the end always takes revenge for it itself.

“‘So: unrest, confusion and unhappiness, that is the lot of men now, after you suffered so much for their freedom! Your great prophet says, in his vision and his allegory, that he saw all those who took part in the first resurrection, and that there were twelve thousand from each tribe. But if there were so many of them, they were not men but gods. They bore your cross, they endured decades in the hungry, naked wilderness, living on locusts and roots, and of course you can point with pride to these children of freedom, of free love, of their free and magnificent sacrifice in your name. But remember that there were only a few thousand of them, and those were gods; and what about the rest? How are the rest, the weak people, to blame for not being able to endure what the mighty endured? How is the weak soul to blame for not being able to hold such terrible gifts? Did you really come only to the chosen, and for the chosen? But if so, there is a mystery here, and we cannot understand it. And if it is a mystery, then we too had the right to preach mystery and to teach them that it is not the free decision of their hearts that matters, and not love, but the mystery, which they must obey blindly, even against their conscience.

“‘That is what we did. We corrected your work and founded it on miracle, mystery and authority. And people rejoiced that they were led like a flock again, and that the terrible gift that had brought them so much suffering was at last lifted from their hearts. Were we right to teach and act like this, tell me? Did we not love mankind, when we so humbly recognised its weakness, lovingly lightened its burden, and allowed its feeble nature even sin, so long as it was with our permission? Why have you come to get in our way now? And why do you look at me so silently and so deeply with your meek eyes? Be angry! I do not want your love, because I do not love you myself.

“‘And what have I to hide from you? Do I not know whom I am speaking to? Everything I have to say to you, you already know; I can read it in your eyes. And should I hide our secret from you? Perhaps you want to hear it from my own lips. Then listen. We are not with you, but with him: that is our secret! We have not been with you, but with him, for a long time now: eight centuries. Exactly eight centuries ago we took from him what you rejected with indignation, the last gift he offered you when he showed you all the kingdoms of the earth. We took Rome and the sword of Caesar from him, and proclaimed ourselves the only kings of the earth, though even now we have not managed to bring our work to completion. But whose fault is that? Oh, the work is only beginning, but it has begun.
