We shall have long to wait for its completion, and the earth will suffer much more, but we shall get there, and we shall be Caesars, and then we shall think about the universal happiness of mankind.

“‘And yet you could have taken the sword of Caesar even then. Why did you reject that last gift? If you had accepted that third counsel of the mighty spirit, you would have supplied everything that man seeks on earth: someone to bow down to, someone to entrust his conscience to, and a way for everyone to unite at last in one undisputed, common and harmonious anthill; for the need for universal union is the third and last torment of men. Mankind as a whole has always striven to organise itself universally. There have been many great nations with great histories, but the higher these nations were, the more unhappy they were, for they felt more strongly than others the need for a universal union of mankind. The great conquerors, the Tamerlanes and Genghis Khans, swept like a whirlwind across the earth, striving to conquer the universe, but even they, though without knowing it, expressed the same great need of mankind for universal and general union. Had you accepted the world and the purple of Caesar, you would have founded a universal kingdom and given universal peace. For who should rule over men if not those who rule over their consciences and in whose hands their bread is? So we took the sword of Caesar, and in taking it, of course, we rejected you and followed him.

“‘Oh, there will be centuries more of the lawlessness of free thought, of their science and their cannibalism, for having begun to build their Tower of Babel without us, they will end in cannibalism. But then the beast will crawl to us and lick our feet and spatter them with tears of blood from its eyes. And we shall sit upon the beast and raise the cup, and on it will be written: “Mystery!” And then, and only then, will the kingdom of peace and happiness come for men. You are proud of your chosen ones, but you have only the chosen, while we will give rest to all. And more than that: how many of those chosen ones, of the mighty ones who could have become chosen, have grown tired at last of waiting for you, and have carried and will carry the strength of their spirit and the warmth of their hearts to another field, and will end by raising their free banner against you? But it was you yourself who raised that banner. With us, everyone will be happy and will no longer rebel or destroy one another, as they do everywhere under your freedom.

“‘Oh, we shall convince them that they will only become free when they give up their freedom to us and submit to us. And shall we be right, or shall we be lying? They themselves will be convinced that we are right, for they will remember what horrors of slavery and confusion your freedom brought them to. Freedom, the free mind and science will lead them into such thickets and set them before such marvels and insoluble mysteries that some of them, the unruly and fierce, will destroy themselves; others, unruly but feeble, will destroy one another; and the rest, the feeble and unhappy, will crawl to our feet and cry out to us: “Yes, you were right, you alone possessed his secret, and we are coming back to you; save us from ourselves.” Receiving bread from us, they will see clearly, of course, that we take from them the bread they have made with their own hands in order to give it back to them, without any miracle; they will see that we have not turned stones into bread; but truly they will be more glad to receive it from our hands than of the bread itself! For they will remember only too well that before, without us, the very bread they made turned to stones in their hands, and when they came back to us, the very stones turned to bread in their hands. Only too well, only too well will they appreciate what it means to submit once and for all! And until men understand this, they will be unhappy.

“‘And who did most to bring about this misunderstanding, tell me? Who split the flock and scattered it on unknown paths? But the flock will gather again and submit again, and this time once and for all. Then we shall give them quiet, humble happiness, the happiness of weak creatures such as they were made. Oh, we shall persuade them at last not to be proud, for you raised them up and so taught them to be proud; we shall prove to them that they are weak, that they are only pitiful children, but that a child’s happiness is sweeter than any other. They will grow timid and look to us and huddle close to us in fear, like chicks to a hen. They will marvel at us and be in awe of us, and be proud that we are so mighty and so wise that we could tame such a turbulent flock of a thousand million. They will tremble limply before our anger, their minds will grow timid, their eyes will fill with tears like children’s and women’s; but just as easily, at a sign from us, they will pass to cheerfulness and laughter, bright joy and happy children’s songs. Yes, we shall make them work, but in their hours free from work we shall arrange their lives like a children’s game, with children’s songs, in chorus, with innocent dances. Oh, we shall even allow them sin; they are weak and powerless, and they will love us like children for allowing them to sin. We shall tell them that every sin will be redeemed if it is committed with our permission; we allow them to sin because we love them, and as for the punishment for those sins, very well, we shall take it on ourselves. And we shall take it on ourselves, and they will adore us as benefactors who have borne their sins before God. And they will have no secrets from us. We shall allow or forbid them to live with their wives and mistresses, to have or not to have children, all according to how obedient they are, and they will submit to us gladly and joyfully. The most agonising secrets of their conscience, all, all of them they will bring to us, and we shall decide everything, and they will trust our decision gladly, because it will spare them the great worry and the terrible present torment of deciding personally and freely.

“‘And everyone will be happy, all the millions of creatures, except the hundred thousand who rule over them. For only we, we who keep the secret, only we shall be unhappy. There will be thousands of millions of happy babes, and a hundred thousand sufferers who have taken upon themselves the curse of the knowledge of good and evil. Peacefully they will die, peacefully they will fade away in your name, and beyond the grave they will find only death. But we shall keep the secret, and for their own happiness we shall lure them on with the reward of heaven and eternity. For if there were anything in the other world, it would certainly not be for such as they.

“‘They say and prophesy that you will come and conquer again, come with your chosen ones, your proud and mighty ones; but we shall say that they saved only themselves, while we have saved everyone. They say that the harlot who sits upon the beast and holds the mystery in her hands will be put to shame, that the weak will rise up again, tear her purple robe and strip her “vile” body naked. But then I shall stand up and point out to you the thousands of millions of happy babes who have known no sin. And we, who took their sins upon ourselves for their happiness, we shall stand before you and say: “Judge us if you can and if you dare.” Know that I am not afraid of you. Know that I too was in the wilderness, that I too lived on locusts and roots, that I too blessed the freedom with which you blessed mankind, and I was preparing to stand among your chosen ones, among the mighty and strong, thirsting “to make up the number”. But I came to my senses and would not serve madness. I came back and joined the ranks of those who have corrected your work. I left the proud and came back to the humble, for the happiness of the humble. What I say to you will come to pass, and our kingdom will be built. I tell you again: tomorrow you will see this obedient flock, which at the first sign from me will rush to rake the hot coals up to your fire, on which I shall burn you for coming to get in our way. For if anyone has deserved our fire more than all, it is you. Tomorrow I shall burn you. Dixi: I have spoken.’”
Ivan stopped. He had grown heated as he talked, and talked with passion; when he had finished, he suddenly smiled.

Alyosha, who had listened to him all the while in silence, though towards the end, in extreme agitation, he had many times tried to interrupt his brother’s speech and had visibly held himself back, suddenly burst out as if he had sprung from his seat.

“But... that’s absurd!” he cried, flushing. “Your poem is praise of Jesus, not blame... as you meant it to be. And who will believe you about freedom? Is that, is that the way to understand it? Is that the idea in Orthodoxy?... That’s Rome, and not even the whole of Rome, that isn’t true; those are the worst of Catholicism, the inquisitors, the Jesuits!... And there could never be such a fantastic figure as your Inquisitor. What sins of men taken upon themselves? Who are these keepers of the mystery who have taken some curse upon themselves for the happiness of mankind? When has anyone ever seen them? We know the Jesuits, people speak badly of them, but are they what they are in your poem? They’re not like that at all, not at all... They’re simply a Roman army for a future universal earthly kingdom, with the Pontiff of Rome as emperor at its head... that’s their ideal, but without any mysteries or lofty sadness... The simplest lust for power, for filthy earthly goods, for enslavement... like a future serfdom, with themselves as the landowners... that’s all they are. Perhaps they don’t even believe in God. Your suffering Inquisitor is pure fantasy...”

“Wait, wait,” Ivan laughed, “how worked up you are. Fantasy, you say; very well! Of course it’s fantasy. But allow me: do you really think that the whole Catholic movement of the last centuries is nothing but a lust for power, for filthy earthly goods? Is it Father Paissy who teaches you that?”
“No, no, on the contrary, Father Paissy once said something rather like what you say... but of course not that, not that at all,” Alyosha caught himself.

“A precious piece of information, all the same, in spite of your ‘not that at all’. What I am asking you is why your Jesuits and inquisitors have joined together only for vile material goods. Why can’t there be among them even one sufferer, tormented by great sorrow and loving mankind? Look: suppose that among all those who want nothing but material, filthy goods there was even one, just one, like my old Inquisitor, who had himself eaten roots in the wilderness and raged to overcome his flesh so as to make himself free and perfect, who had loved mankind all his life, and who suddenly saw clearly and understood that it is no great moral bliss to reach perfection of the will if at the same time you are convinced that millions of God’s other creatures have been made only as a mockery, that they will never be able to cope with their freedom, that pitiful rebels will never grow into giants to complete the tower, that it was not for such geese that the great idealist dreamed of his harmony. Having understood all this, he went back and joined... the clever people. Couldn’t that happen?”

“Joined whom? What clever people?” cried Alyosha, almost in a passion. “They have no such intelligence, and no such mysteries and secrets... Unless it’s atheism, that’s their whole secret. Your Inquisitor doesn’t believe in God, that’s his whole secret!”

“And what if that is so! At last you’ve guessed it. Yes, that really is so, that really is the whole secret; but isn’t that suffering, at least for a man like him, who has spent his whole life in heroic struggle in the wilderness and has not been cured of his love for mankind? At the end of his days he becomes clearly convinced that only the counsels of the great and terrible spirit could bring these feeble rebels, ‘these unfinished trial creatures made in mockery’, into any kind of bearable order. And so, convinced of this, he sees that he must follow the guidance of the intelligent spirit, the terrible spirit of death and destruction, and for that accept lies and deceit and lead people consciously to death and destruction, deceiving them all the way so that they do not notice where they are being led, so that at least on the way these pitiful blind creatures may think themselves happy. And note: deceit in the name of the one in whose ideal the old man had so passionately believed all his life! Isn’t that a tragedy? And if even one such man stood at the head of that whole army ‘thirsting for power only for filthy goods’, wouldn’t even one be enough to make a tragedy? More than that: one such man at its head would be enough to give the whole Roman enterprise, with all its armies and Jesuits, its real guiding idea, the highest idea of that enterprise. I tell you frankly that I firmly believe that this single man has never been lacking among those at the head of the movement. Who knows, perhaps there have been such single men even among the Popes of Rome. Who knows, perhaps that cursed old man, who loves mankind so stubbornly and in his own way, exists even now in the form of a whole host of such single old men, and not by chance, but as an alliance, a secret league formed long ago to keep the secret, to keep it from the unhappy and feeble people, in order to make them happy. That must exist, and it must be so. I fancy that even the Freemasons have something of the same kind of mystery at their foundation, and that the Catholics hate the Freemasons so much because they see them as competitors, a splitting of the unity of the idea, when there must be one flock and one shepherd... But in defending my idea I am looking like an author who can’t stand your criticism. Enough of this.”

“Perhaps you are a Freemason yourself!” Alyosha suddenly burst out. “You don’t believe in God,” he added, but now with deep sorrow. It seemed to him, besides, that his brother was looking at him mockingly. “How does your poem end?” he asked suddenly, looking at the ground. “Or is it finished?”

“I meant to end it like this. When the Inquisitor falls silent, he waits for some time for his prisoner to answer him. His silence weighs on him. He saw that the prisoner listened to him all the time intently and quietly, looking him straight in the eyes and evidently not wishing to object to anything. The old man would like him to say something, even something bitter and terrible. But suddenly he goes up to the old man in silence and quietly kisses him on his bloodless, ninety-year-old lips. That is his whole answer. The old man shudders. Something stirs at the corners of his mouth; he goes to the door, opens it and says to him: ‘Go, and do not come again... do not come at all... never, never!’ And he lets him out into the dark streets of the city. The prisoner goes away.”
“And the old man?”
“The kiss glows in his heart, but the old man holds to his idea.”
“And you with him, you too?” Alyosha cried sorrowfully. Ivan laughed.

“But this is nonsense, Alyosha; it’s only the senseless poem of a senseless student who never wrote two lines of verse. Why do you take it so seriously? Surely you don’t think I’m going straight off to the Jesuits now, to join the ranks of the men who are correcting his work? Good Lord, what do I care! I told you: I only want to hold out until I’m thirty, and then, dash the cup to the floor!”

“And the sticky little leaves, and the precious graves, and the blue sky, and the woman you love! How will you live, what will you love them with?” Alyosha cried sorrowfully. “With such a hell in your heart and your head, is it possible? No, you are going away precisely to join them... and if not, you will kill yourself; you won’t be able to bear it!”
“There is a strength that can bear anything,” said Ivan, with a cold smile now.
“What strength?”
“The Karamazov strength... the strength of the Karamazov baseness.”
“To drown in depravity, to crush your soul in corruption, yes, yes?”
“Perhaps that too... only till I’m thirty perhaps I’ll escape it, and then...”
“How will you escape it? With what? With your ideas, it’s impossible.”
“Again, in the Karamazov way.”
“So that ‘everything is permitted’? Everything is permitted, is that it, is that it?”
Ivan frowned and suddenly turned strangely pale.

“Ah, you’ve picked up yesterday’s little phrase that offended Miusov so much... and that brother Dmitri so naively jumped in and repeated?” He smiled crookedly. “Yes, perhaps: ‘everything is permitted’, since the word has been said. I don’t take it back. And Mitya’s version isn’t bad either.”
Alyosha looked at him in silence.

“I thought, brother, as I was leaving, that I had you at least in all the world,” Ivan said suddenly, with unexpected feeling, “and now I see that there is no room for me in your heart either, my dear hermit. I won’t renounce the formula ‘everything is permitted’; well, so, will you renounce me for it? Will you?”
Alyosha stood up, went to him and quietly kissed him on the lips without a word.
“Literary theft!” cried Ivan, suddenly passing into a kind of rapture. “You stole that from my poem! Thank you, though. Get up, Alyosha, let’s go; it’s time, for both of us.”
They went out, but stopped at the steps of the tavern.

“Listen, Alyosha,” said Ivan in a firm voice, “if I really do have it in me to love the sticky little leaves, I shall love them only remembering you. It’s enough for me that you are somewhere here, and I shan’t lose the wish to live. Is that enough for you? Take it as a declaration of love, if you like. And now you go to the right and I go to the left, and enough, do you hear, enough. I mean, even if I didn’t leave tomorrow (I think I certainly shall) and we somehow met again, not another word to me on all these subjects. I earnestly beg you. And about brother Dmitri too, I particularly beg you, don’t even bring him up with me ever again,” he added suddenly with irritation. “Everything has been exhausted, everything has been talked over, hasn’t it? And I in my turn will make you a promise for this: when, at thirty, I want to ‘dash the cup to the floor’, then wherever you are I will come once more to talk it over with you... even from America, you may be sure. I’ll come specially. It will be very interesting to see you by then: what will you be like then? You see, a rather solemn promise. And really, perhaps we are saying goodbye for seven years, or ten. Well, go now to your Pater Seraphicus; he’s dying, after all; if he dies without you, you may be angry with me for keeping you. Goodbye; kiss me once more, like that, and go...”

Ivan suddenly turned and went his way, without looking back again. It was like the way brother Dmitri had left Alyosha the day before, though yesterday had been quite different. This strange little observation flashed like an arrow through Alyosha’s sad mind, sad and sorrowful at that moment. He waited a little, looking after his brother. For some reason he suddenly noticed that brother Ivan walked with a kind of sway, and that his right shoulder, seen from behind, looked lower than his left. He had never noticed that before. But suddenly he too turned and almost ran towards the monastery. It was getting very dark, and he felt almost frightened; something new was growing in him, something he could not have explained. The wind rose again, as it had the day before, and the ancient pines rustled gloomily round him as he entered the hermitage wood. He was almost running. “‘Pater Seraphicus’: where did he get that name? Where from?” flashed through Alyosha’s mind. “Ivan, poor Ivan, and when shall I see you now?... Here is the hermitage, Lord! Yes, yes, it is he, it is Pater Seraphicus; he will save me... from him, and forever!”

Several times later in his life he remembered with great bewilderment how he could, after parting from Ivan, so completely forget about his brother Dmitri, whom that very morning, only a few hours before, he had resolved to find without fail, and not to give up until he had, even if it meant not returning to the monastery that night.
## Book Five, Chapter VI · Still a Very Obscure One

And Ivan Fyodorovich, having parted from Alyosha, went home, to Fyodor Pavlovich’s house. But, strange to say, an unbearable anguish suddenly came over him, and, what was more, it grew with every step as he came nearer the house. The strangeness was not in the anguish but in the fact that Ivan Fyodorovich could not for the life of him make out what the anguish consisted of. He had often felt anguish before, and it would have been no wonder if it had come at such a moment, when tomorrow, breaking suddenly with everything that had drawn him here, he was getting ready to turn sharply aside once more and set out on a new, completely unknown road, and again quite alone, as before, hoping for much but not knowing what for, expecting much, far too much, from life, but unable himself to define anything either in his expectations or even in his desires. And yet at this moment, though the anguish of the new and unknown really was in his soul, it was not that at all that tormented him. “Is it disgust for my father’s house?” he thought to himself. “It looks like it, I am so sick of it; and though today I shall cross that vile threshold for the last time, it is disgusting all the same…” But no, it was not that either. Was it the parting with Alyosha and the conversation he had had with him? “For so many years I kept silent with the whole world and would not deign to speak, and suddenly I have reeled off such a heap of nonsense.” Indeed, it might have been the youthful vexation of youthful inexperience and youthful vanity, vexation at not having managed to say what he meant, and with such a being as Alyosha, too, on whom his heart undoubtedly had great designs. Of course that was there too, that vexation; it was bound to be there; but that was not it either, none of it was it. “Anguish to the point of nausea, and I can’t say what I want. Perhaps not think…”

Ivan Fyodorovich tried “not thinking”, but that did not help either. The chief thing that made the anguish vexing and irritating was that it had some accidental, entirely external character: he could feel that. Some being or object stood and stuck up somewhere, the way something sometimes sticks up before your eye, and for a long while, busy with work or in heated talk, you don’t notice it, and yet you are visibly irritated, almost tormented, and at last it occurs to you to remove the offending object, often something very trivial and absurd, some thing left out of its place, a handkerchief fallen on the floor, a book not put back in the bookcase, and so on, and so on. At last, in the foulest and most irritated state of mind, Ivan Fyodorovich reached his father’s house, and suddenly, about fifteen paces from the gate, glancing at it, he guessed at once what had been tormenting and disturbing him so.

On the bench at the gate sat the servant Smerdyakov, enjoying the cool of the evening, and Ivan Fyodorovich understood at the first glance at him that the servant Smerdyakov was sitting in his soul too, and that it was precisely this man his soul could not bear. Everything was suddenly lit up and became clear. Earlier, when Alyosha had told him of his meeting with Smerdyakov, something gloomy and repellent had suddenly pierced his heart and at once roused an answering spite in him. Then, in the course of the conversation, Smerdyakov had been forgotten for a while, yet he had stayed in his soul, and no sooner had Ivan Fyodorovich parted from Alyosha and set off alone for the house than the forgotten feeling quickly began to come to the surface again. “Can this worthless scoundrel really trouble me to such a degree?” he thought with unbearable spite.

The fact was that Ivan Fyodorovich had indeed taken a great dislike to this man of late, and especially in the last few days. He had even begun to notice in himself this growing, almost hatred for the creature. Perhaps the hatred had grown so sharp precisely because at first, when Ivan Fyodorovich had only just come to us, something quite different had happened. At that time Ivan Fyodorovich had suddenly taken a kind of special interest in Smerdyakov and even found him very original. He had himself encouraged him to talk to him, always wondering, however, at a certain muddle-headedness, or rather a certain restlessness of his mind, and not understanding what it was that could so constantly and persistently trouble “this contemplative”. They talked about philosophical questions too, and even about why there was light on the first day when the sun, moon and stars were made only on the fourth, and how one ought to understand that. But Ivan Fyodorovich soon became convinced that the point was not the sun, moon and stars at all; that the sun, moon and stars, though a curious subject, were for Smerdyakov entirely third-rate, and that he wanted something quite different. One way or another, at any rate, a boundless vanity began to show and betray itself, a wounded vanity at that. Ivan Fyodorovich did not like it at all. That was where his aversion began. Later, troubles started in the house: Grushenka appeared, the stories with his brother Dmitri began, there was trouble all round. They talked about that too, but though Smerdyakov always spoke of it with great agitation, again it was impossible to get out of him what he himself wanted in it all. One could even wonder at the illogicality and disorder of some of his wishes, which came out in spite of him and were always equally obscure. Smerdyakov kept asking questions, putting some indirect, obviously contrived questions, but what for he did not explain, and usually at the hottest moment of his own questioning he would suddenly fall silent or pass to something quite different. But the main thing, which finally irritated Ivan Fyodorovich beyond bearing and filled him with such aversion, was a sort of disgusting and peculiar familiarity that Smerdyakov had begun to show him more and more, the further it went. Not that he allowed himself to be impolite; on the contrary, he always spoke extremely respectfully; but things had somehow come about so that Smerdyakov evidently began to consider himself, God knows why, at one with Ivan Fyodorovich in something, and always spoke in a tone as if there were already something agreed between the two of them, something secret, something once said on both sides and known only to the two of them, and not even comprehensible to the other mortals bustling about them. For a long time, however, Ivan Fyodorovich did not understand this real cause of his growing aversion either, and only very lately had he managed to guess what it was. With a squeamish, irritable feeling he wanted to go through the gate now in silence, without looking at Smerdyakov; but Smerdyakov rose from the bench, and from that gesture alone Ivan Fyodorovich guessed in an instant that he wished to have a special conversation with him. Ivan Fyodorovich looked at him and stopped, and the fact that he had stopped like that, and not walked past as he had wanted to a minute before, enraged him till he shook. With anger and disgust he looked at Smerdyakov’s gelded, sunken face, with the hair at the temples combed forward and a little tuft whipped up on top. His left eye, slightly screwed up, winked and grinned, as if to say: “Why are you going? You won’t get by; you see that we two clever men have something to talk over.” Ivan Fyodorovich began to tremble.
“Away, you scoundrel, what company am I for you, you fool!” was on the tip of his tongue, but, to his great surprise, something quite different came off it:

“Is my father asleep or awake?” he said quietly and meekly, unexpectedly to himself, and suddenly, also quite unexpectedly, sat down on the bench. For a moment he felt almost frightened; he remembered that afterwards. Smerdyakov stood facing him, his hands behind his back, and looked at him with assurance, almost sternly.

“Still resting, sir,” he said unhurriedly. (“You spoke first, as it were, not me.”) “I wonder at you, sir,” he added after a pause, lowering his eyes somehow affectedly, putting his right foot forward and playing with the toe of his patent-leather boot.

“Why do you wonder at me?” Ivan Fyodorovich said curtly and sternly, restraining himself with all his might, and suddenly understood with disgust that he felt the most intense curiosity and would not leave here on any account until he had satisfied it.

“Why don’t you go to Chermashnya, sir?” Smerdyakov suddenly raised his eyes and smiled familiarly. “And why I smiled you must understand for yourself, if you are a clever man,” his screwed-up left eye seemed to say.
“Why should I go to Chermashnya?” Ivan Fyodorovich was surprised.
Smerdyakov was silent again.

“Fyodor Pavlovich himself begged you to, sir,” he said at last, without hurry and as if he himself did not value his answer: I am getting off with a third-rate reason, he seemed to say, just to say something.
“Oh, damn it, speak plainly, what do you want?” Ivan Fyodorovich cried out at last angrily, passing from meekness to rudeness.
Smerdyakov drew his right foot back to his left, drew himself up straighter, but went on looking with the same calm and the same little smile.
“Nothing of any substance, sir… just by way of conversation…”

Silence again. They were silent for almost a minute. Ivan Fyodorovich knew that he ought to get up at once and be angry, and Smerdyakov stood before him as if waiting: “Now I’ll see whether you get angry or not.” So at least it seemed to Ivan Fyodorovich. At last he swayed forward to get up. Smerdyakov seemed to catch the moment exactly.

“My position is terrible, Ivan Fyodorovich, sir; I don’t even know how to help myself,” he said suddenly, firmly and distinctly, and sighed with his last word. Ivan Fyodorovich at once sat down again.

“Both of them have quite gone out of their minds, sir, both have come down to the merest childishness, sir,” Smerdyakov went on. “I mean your father, sir, and your brother Dmitri Fyodorovich. Now Fyodor Pavlovich will get up and start pestering me every minute: ‘Why hasn’t she come? Why hasn’t she come?’, and so on right up till midnight, and past midnight too. And if Agrafena Alexandrovna doesn’t come (because maybe she doesn’t mean ever to come at all, sir), then he will go for me again tomorrow morning: ‘Why didn’t she come? Why didn’t she come, when will she come?’, as if I were to blame for it somehow before him. On the other hand there’s this, sir: as soon as it gets dark, and earlier too, your brother turns up next door with a weapon in his hands: ‘Look out, you rogue, you soup-maker: if you miss her and don’t let me know she has come, I’ll kill you before anyone.’ The night passes, and in the morning he too, like Fyodor Pavlovich, starts tormenting me cruelly: ‘Why didn’t she come, will she show herself soon?’, and again I am to blame before him, sir, for his lady not coming. And every day and every hour they both get angrier, sir, so that sometimes I think I shall take my own life from fright, sir. I can’t rely on them, sir.”
“Then why did you get mixed up in it? Why did you start carrying tales to Dmitri Fyodorovich?” Ivan Fyodorovich said irritably.

“And how could I not get mixed up in it, sir? And I didn’t get mixed up in it at all, if you want to know with complete exactness, sir. From the very beginning I kept silent, not daring to object, and he himself appointed me to be his servant Lichard. Since then he only knows one word: ‘I’ll kill you, you rogue, if you let her slip past!’ I am quite certain, sir, that tomorrow I shall have a long fit of the falling sickness.”
“What do you mean, a long fit?”

“A long fit, sir, extremely long, sir. It goes on for several hours, sir, or maybe a day or two. Once it went on with me for about three days; I fell from the attic that time. It stops shaking you, and then it starts again; and for all three days I couldn’t come to my senses. Fyodor Pavlovich sent for Herzenstube, the doctor here, that time, and he put ice on the crown of my head and used another remedy besides… I might have died, sir.”

“But they say you can’t know beforehand that a fit of the falling sickness will come at such and such an hour. How can you say it will come tomorrow?” Ivan Fyodorovich asked with a peculiar, irritable curiosity.
“That’s true, sir, you can’t know beforehand.”
“Besides, you fell from the attic that time.”

“I climb into the attic every day, sir; I can fall from the attic tomorrow too. And if not from the attic, I’ll fall into the cellar, sir; I go down into the cellar every day too, sir, on my own business, sir.”
Ivan Fyodorovich gave him a long look.
“You are spinning something, I see, and I don’t quite understand you,” he said quietly, but somehow menacingly. “Do you mean to pretend tomorrow that you are in a fit for three days? Eh?”

Smerdyakov, who had been looking at the ground and again playing with the toe of his right foot, put his right foot back in its place, put his left forward instead, raised his head and, with a smirk, said:

“Even if I could do that very thing, sir, that is, pretend, sir, and since it is not at all hard for an experienced man to do it, then even so I would be fully within my rights to use the means to save my life from death; for while I am lying ill, even if Agrafena Alexandrovna came to his father, he couldn’t ask a sick man: ‘Why didn’t you tell me?’ He would be ashamed himself.”

“Oh, damn it!” Ivan Fyodorovich flared up suddenly, his face twisted with spite. “Why are you always so frightened for your life? All these threats of my brother Dmitri’s are only hot words and nothing more. He won’t kill you; he’ll kill, but not you!”
“He’ll kill me like a fly, sir, and me first of all, sir. And what I fear even more is that I’ll be counted his accomplice when he does something mad to his father.”
“Why would they count you an accomplice?”
“They’ll count me an accomplice because I told him those very signals in great secrecy, sir.”
“What signals? Told whom? Damn you, speak more plainly!”

“I must confess completely,” Smerdyakov drawled with pedantic calm, “that there is a secret here between me and Fyodor Pavlovich. As you are pleased to know yourself (if only you are pleased to know it), for several days now, as soon as night comes, or even evening, he locks himself in from inside at once. Lately you have taken to going back upstairs early every time, and yesterday you didn’t go out anywhere at all, sir, and so perhaps you don’t know how carefully he has begun locking himself in for the night. And even if Grigory Vasilyevich himself came, he would only open to him once he was sure of his voice, sir. But Grigory Vasilyevich doesn’t come, sir, because now I alone wait on him in the rooms, sir; he arranged it so himself from the very moment he started this business with Agrafena Alexandrovna. And for the night I too now go away, by his order, and sleep in the lodge, on condition that I don’t sleep till midnight but keep watch, get up and go round the yard, and wait for Agrafena Alexandrovna to come, sir, since for several days now he has been waiting for her like a madman. This is how he reasons, sir: she is afraid of him, he says, of Dmitri Fyodorovich (he calls him Mitka, sir), and so she will come to me late at night by the back way; and you, he says, watch for her till midnight and later. And if she comes, you run up to the door and knock on my door, or on the window from the garden, with your hand: the first two times softly, like this, one-two, and then at once three times quicker, knock-knock-knock. Then, he says, I shall understand at once that it is she who has come, and I shall open the door to you quietly. Another signal he told me in case something urgent happens: first two quick knocks, knock-knock, and then, after waiting, one more, much harder. Then he will understand that something sudden has happened and that I very much need to see him, and he will open to me too, and I will go in and report. All in case Agrafena Alexandrovna may not come herself but send some message; besides that, Dmitri Fyodorovich may come too, so I am to let him know that he is near. He is very much afraid of Dmitri Fyodorovich, so that even if Agrafena Alexandrovna had already come and they had locked themselves in together, and Dmitri Fyodorovich turned up somewhere near in the meantime, then too I am bound to report it to him at once by knocking three times; so that the first signal, of five knocks, means ‘Agrafena Alexandrovna has come’, and the second signal, of three knocks, means ‘very much needed’. He taught me himself several times by example and explained it. And since in the whole universe only he and I know about these signals, sir, he will open without the least doubt and without calling out (he is very much afraid to call out aloud). And now those very signals have become known to Dmitri Fyodorovich.”
“How are they known? Did you pass them on? How did you dare pass them on?”

“From that very fear, sir. And how could I have dared keep silent before him, sir? Dmitri Fyodorovich kept pressing me every day: ‘You are deceiving me, you are hiding something from me! I’ll break both your legs!’ So I told him those very secret signals, so that at least he would see my servility and so be sure that I am not deceiving him but reporting everything to him in every way.”
“If you think he will use those signals and try to get in, then don’t let him in.”
“And when I am lying in a fit myself, sir, how will I not let him in, sir, even if I could dare not to let him in, sir, knowing how desperate he is, sir?”
“Oh, damn it! Why are you so sure the falling sickness will come, damn you? Are you laughing at me or not?”
“How could I dare laugh at you, and is this any time for laughing, with such fear? I have a feeling there will be a fit; I have such a presentiment; it will come from fright alone, sir.”
“Oh, damn! If you are lying ill, then Grigory will keep watch. Warn Grigory beforehand; he won’t let him in.”

“I wouldn’t dare tell Grigory Vasilyevich about the signals on any account without the master’s orders, sir. And as for Grigory Vasilyevich hearing him and not letting him in, he has just fallen ill today since yesterday, and Marfa Ignatyevna means to treat him tomorrow. They agreed on it earlier. And this treatment of theirs is very curious, sir: Marfa Ignatyevna knows a certain infusion and always keeps it, a strong one, on some herb; she has a secret, sir. And she treats Grigory Vasilyevich with this secret medicine about three times a year, sir, when his lower back gives out completely, as if he had a paralysis, sir, about three times a year, sir. Then she takes a towel, sir, soaks it in this infusion, and Marfa Ignatyevna rubs his whole back for half an hour, sir, till it is dry, sir; it even goes quite red and swollen, sir; and then what is left in the bottle she gives him to drink, sir, with a certain prayer, sir; not all of it, though, because on this rare occasion she keeps a small part for herself, sir, and drinks it too. And both of them, I tell you, being non-drinkers, drop down on the spot, sir, and sleep soundly for a very long time, sir; and when Grigory Vasilyevich wakes up he is nearly always well after it, sir, and when Marfa Ignatyevna wakes up she always has a headache after it, sir. So if tomorrow Marfa Ignatyevna carries out her intention, sir, they are hardly likely to hear anything, sir, or to keep Dmitri Fyodorovich out, sir. They will be asleep, sir.”

“What nonsense! And all this coincides at once as if on purpose: you have a fit, and those two are senseless!” Ivan Fyodorovich shouted. “Aren’t you yourself trying to arrange it so that it coincides?” broke from him suddenly, and he knitted his brows menacingly.

“How could I arrange it so, sir… and why arrange it, when everything here depends on Dmitri Fyodorovich alone, sir, and on his thoughts alone, sir… If he wants to do something, he will do it, sir; and if not, I am not going to bring him on purpose to push him in on his father.”

“And why should he go to his father’s, and secretly at that, if, as you say yourself, Agrafena Alexandrovna won’t come at all?” Ivan Fyodorovich went on, turning pale with spite. “You say so yourself, and all the time I have been living here I have been sure that the old man is only imagining things and that the creature will not come to him. Why then should Dmitri burst in on the old man if she doesn’t come? Speak! I want to know your thoughts.”

“You know yourself why he will come; what do my thoughts matter? He will come out of sheer spite, or out of his suspiciousness, if I happen to be ill, say; he will have his doubts and go impatiently to search the rooms, as he did yesterday: hasn’t she slipped in to him somehow quietly? He also knows perfectly well that Fyodor Pavlovich has a big envelope ready, with three thousand sealed in it, under three seals, sir, tied with a ribbon and inscribed in his own hand: ‘To my angel Grushenka, if she will come’, and then, three days later, he added: ‘and to my little chick’. So that’s what is doubtful, sir.”

“Rubbish!” Ivan Fyodorovich shouted, almost in a frenzy. “Dmitri won’t go to rob money, and kill his father in the bargain. He might have killed him yesterday over Grushenka, like a frantic, spiteful fool, but he won’t go robbing!”

“He needs money very badly now, sir, needs it to the last extremity, Ivan Fyodorovich. You don’t even know how badly,” Smerdyakov explained extremely calmly and with remarkable distinctness. “Besides, he considers those very three thousand, sir, as good as his own, and explained it to me so himself: ‘My father,’ he says, ‘still owes me exactly three thousand.’ And on top of all that, consider some plain truth too, Ivan Fyodorovich, sir: it is almost certainly so, I must say, sir, that Agrafena Alexandrovna, if only she wants to, will certainly make him marry her, the master himself, that is, Fyodor Pavlovich, sir, if only she wants to; and maybe she will want to, sir. I only say that she won’t come, but maybe she will want even more than that, sir, that is, to become a lady outright. I know myself that her merchant Samsonov told her quite frankly that it would be no stupid thing to do, and laughed as he said it. And she is no fool herself, sir. She won’t go and marry a beggar like Dmitri Fyodorovich, sir. So, taking that, consider for yourself, Ivan Fyodorovich, that then neither Dmitri Fyodorovich, nor even you, sir, nor your brother Alexei Fyodorovich would get anything at all after your father’s death, not a rouble, sir, because Agrafena Alexandrovna would marry him precisely to have everything made over to her and to transfer whatever capital there is to herself, sir. But if your father died now, while there is nothing of that yet, sir, each of you would get a sure forty thousand at once, sir, even Dmitri Fyodorovich, whom he hates so, sir, since he has not made a will, sir… Dmitri Fyodorovich knows all this perfectly well…”
Something seemed to twist and quiver in Ivan Fyodorovich’s face. He suddenly flushed.

“Then why,” he suddenly interrupted Smerdyakov, “after all this, do you advise me to go to Chermashnya? What did you mean by it? I go away, and this is what will happen here.” Ivan Fyodorovich was breathing with difficulty.
“Quite right, sir,” Smerdyakov said quietly and reasonably, watching Ivan Fyodorovich intently all the same.
“What do you mean, quite right?” Ivan Fyodorovich asked again, restraining himself with an effort, his eyes flashing menacingly.

“I spoke out of pity for you. In your place, if it were me, I’d throw it all up on the spot… rather than sit by such a business, sir,” answered Smerdyakov, looking with the most open air at Ivan Fyodorovich’s flashing eyes. Both were silent.

“You seem to be a great idiot and, of course… a terrible scoundrel!” Ivan Fyodorovich suddenly got up from the bench. Then he wanted to go straight through the gate, but suddenly stopped and turned to Smerdyakov. Something strange happened: Ivan Fyodorovich suddenly, as if in a spasm, bit his lip, clenched his fists, and in another instant, of course, would have thrown himself on Smerdyakov. Smerdyakov at least noticed it at that same instant, started, and jerked his whole body back. But the instant passed safely for Smerdyakov, and Ivan Fyodorovich, in silence but as if in some bewilderment, turned in at the gate.

“I am leaving for Moscow tomorrow, if you want to know: early tomorrow morning, and that’s all!” he suddenly said spitefully, distinctly and loudly, wondering at himself afterwards why he had needed to say it to Smerdyakov.

“That is the very best thing, sir,” Smerdyakov caught it up, as if he had been waiting for it, “except perhaps that they may trouble you from here by telegraph in Moscow, sir, in some such event, sir.”

Ivan Fyodorovich stopped again and again turned quickly to Smerdyakov. But something seemed to have happened to Smerdyakov too. All his familiarity and nonchalance had dropped away in an instant; his whole face expressed extraordinary attention and expectation, but timid and fawning now: “Won’t you say something more, won’t you add anything?”, so one could read in his intent gaze, fastened on Ivan Fyodorovich.
“And wouldn’t they send for me from Chermashnya too… in some such event?” Ivan Fyodorovich suddenly yelled, raising his voice terribly for no known reason.
“From Chermashnya too, sir… they would trouble you, sir…” Smerdyakov muttered almost in a whisper, as if at a loss, but still looking intently, intently, straight into Ivan Fyodorovich’s eyes.
“Only Moscow is further and Chermashnya nearer; so is it the fare you are sorry about, insisting on Chermashnya, or are you sorry for me, that I should go a long way round?”

“Quite right, sir…” Smerdyakov muttered in a voice that now broke, smiling vilely and again making himself convulsively ready to jump back in time. But Ivan Fyodorovich suddenly, to Smerdyakov’s surprise, laughed and went quickly through the gate, still laughing. Anyone who had looked at his face would surely have concluded that he did not laugh at all because he felt so merry. And he himself could never have explained what was happening to him at that moment. He moved and walked as if in a spasm.
## Chapter VII · “It Is Worth Talking to a Clever Man”

And he walked as he talked, too. Meeting Fyodor Pavlovich in the hall as soon as he came in, he suddenly shouted at him, waving his arms: “I am going up to my room, not to you, goodbye,” and went past, even trying not to look at his father. It may very well be that the old man was too hateful to him at that moment, but so unceremonious a display of hostility was unexpected even for Fyodor Pavlovich. And the old man evidently did want to tell him something quickly, and had come out into the hall on purpose to meet him; hearing such a civility, he stopped in silence and, with a mocking look, followed his son with his eyes up the stairs to the attic storey until he was out of sight.
“What’s the matter with him?” he quickly asked Smerdyakov, who had come in after Ivan Fyodorovich.
“He is angry about something, sir; who can make him out?” the other muttered evasively.
“The devil take him! Let him be angry! Bring the samovar and clear off yourself, quick. Is there anything new?”

Then began questions of exactly the kind Smerdyakov had just been complaining of to Ivan Fyodorovich, that is, all about the expected visitor, and we will leave them out here. Half an hour later the house was locked, and the crazed old man was pacing alone about the rooms, in tremulous expectation that at any moment the five agreed knocks would sound, now and then looking out of the dark windows and seeing nothing in them but the night.

It was already very late, and Ivan Fyodorovich was still not asleep but thinking. He went to bed late that night, at about two o’clock. But we will not relate the whole course of his thoughts; nor is it time for us to enter that soul: that soul will have its turn. And even if we tried to relate something, it would be very hard to do, because there were no thoughts, but something very indefinite and, above all, far too agitated. He felt himself that he had lost every thread. He was tormented too by various strange and almost wholly unexpected desires. For instance, after midnight he suddenly felt an urgent, unbearable wish to go downstairs, unlock the door, go to the lodge and beat Smerdyakov; but if you had asked him why, he could not definitely have stated a single reason precisely, except perhaps that the servant had become hateful to him as the most grievous offender that could be found in the world. On the other hand, more than once that night his soul was seized by some inexplicable and humiliating timidity, from which, he felt it, he even seemed suddenly to lose his physical strength. His head ached and swam. Something hateful gnawed at his soul, as if he were going to take revenge on someone. He hated even Alyosha, remembering their conversation earlier; at moments he hated himself very much too. Of Katerina Ivanovna he almost forgot to think, and he wondered at that a great deal afterwards, all the more since he remembered firmly that only yesterday morning, when he had boasted so grandly at Katerina Ivanovna’s that he would leave for Moscow tomorrow, he had whispered to himself at once in his soul: “That’s nonsense, you won’t go, and it won’t be as easy for you to tear yourself away as you brag now.” Recalling this night long afterwards, Ivan Fyodorovich remembered with particular disgust how he would suddenly get up from the sofa and quietly, as though terribly afraid of being watched, open the door, go out onto the stairs and listen down into the lower rooms to Fyodor Pavlovich stirring and pacing there below. He listened for a long time, five minutes at a stretch, with some strange curiosity, holding his breath, his heart pounding; and why he did all this, why he listened, of course he did not know himself. All his life afterwards he called this “act” “vile”, and all his life, deep within himself, in the secret places of his soul, he considered it the basest act of his whole life. For Fyodor Pavlovich himself he felt no hatred at all in those minutes, but was only curious, for some reason, with all his might: how he was walking down there, what he must be doing down there in his rooms now; he guessed and pictured how down there he must be looking out of the dark windows and suddenly stopping in the middle of the room and waiting, waiting: wasn’t someone knocking? Ivan Fyodorovich went out onto the stairs for this occupation two or three times. When everything was quiet and Fyodor Pavlovich had gone to bed, at about two o’clock, Ivan Fyodorovich too lay down, with a firm wish to fall asleep as quickly as possible, since he felt terribly worn out. And indeed he suddenly fell sound asleep and slept without dreams, but woke early, at about seven, when it was already light. Opening his eyes, to his amazement he suddenly felt in himself a surge of some extraordinary energy; he jumped up quickly and dressed quickly, then pulled out his trunk and at once, hurriedly, began to pack it. His linen had all come back from the laundress only yesterday morning. Ivan Fyodorovich even smiled at the thought that everything had fallen out so well, that there was nothing to delay a sudden departure. And the departure really was sudden. Although Ivan Fyodorovich had said yesterday (to Katerina Ivanovna, to Alyosha and then to Smerdyakov) that he would leave tomorrow, yet going to bed last night he remembered very well that at that moment he had not been thinking of leaving; at least he had had no idea that on waking in the morning his first impulse would be to rush to pack his trunk. At last the trunk and bag were ready. It was already about nine when Marfa Ignatyevna came up to him with her usual daily question: “Where will you be pleased to take your tea, here or will you come down?” Ivan Fyodorovich came down looking almost cheerful, though there was something sprawling and hurried in him, in his words and gestures. Greeting his father affably and even asking particularly after his health, he did not wait, however, for his father to finish answering, but announced at once that in an hour he was leaving for Moscow, for good, and asked him to send for horses. The old man heard the news without the least surprise, most improperly forgetting to grieve over his son’s departure; instead he suddenly became extremely busy, remembering, as luck would have it, an urgent business of his own.

“Oh, you! What a fellow! You didn’t tell me yesterday… well, never mind, we’ll settle it now. Do me a great kindness, my own dear father, drive round by Chermashnya. From Volovya station you only have to turn left, only twelve versts or so, and there is Chermashnya.”
“Forgive me, I can’t: it is eighty versts to the railway, and the train leaves the station for Moscow at seven in the evening; there is only just time to catch it.”

“You’ll catch it tomorrow, or the day after, but today turn off to Chermashnya. What does it cost you to set your father’s mind at rest? If I hadn’t business here, I’d have flown there myself long ago, because the thing there is urgent and out of the ordinary, but just now my time here is not my own… You see, there’s that wood of mine there, in two lots, at Begichevo and at Dyachkino, on the waste land. The Maslovs, father and son, merchants, offer only eight thousand for the timber, and only last year a buyer turned up who offered twelve, but he wasn’t from these parts, that’s the point. Because now there is no market among the local people: the Maslovs, father and son, are bullying everyone, men worth a hundred thousand; what they put down, you have to take, and none of the local people dares compete with them. And the priest at Ilyinskoye suddenly wrote to me here last Thursday that Gorstkin has come, another petty merchant; I know him; only the precious thing is that he isn’t local but from Pogrebovo, so he isn’t afraid of the Maslovs, because he isn’t local. ‘I’ll give eleven thousand for the wood,’ he says, do you hear? And he will only be here, the priest writes, for another week. So if you went and came to terms with him…”
“Then write to the priest; he will come to terms with him.”

“He doesn’t know how, that’s the thing. This priest doesn’t know how to look. He’s a golden man; I’d hand him twenty thousand this minute to keep for me without a receipt; but he can’t see a thing, as if he weren’t a man at all; a crow could cheat him. And he’s a learned man, imagine that. This Gorstkin looks like a peasant, in a blue coat, only by character he is a perfect scoundrel; that is the trouble for all of us: he lies, that’s the point. Sometimes he lies so that you can only wonder why he does it. Two years ago he lied that his wife had died and that he had married another, and none of it was true, imagine: his wife never died at all; she is alive now and beats him once every three days. So now too one has to find out: is he lying or telling the truth that he wants to buy and give eleven thousand?”
“But I can’t do anything there either; I haven’t the eye for it.”

“Wait, wait, you’ll do too, because I’ll tell you all his signs, Gorstkin’s; I have had dealings with him for a long time. You see: you must look at his beard. He has a nasty, thin little reddish beard. If his beard shakes while he talks and gets angry, then it’s all right, he’s telling the truth, he means business; but if he strokes his beard with his left hand and chuckles, well, that means he wants to cheat, he is up to tricks. Never look him in the eyes; you can’t make out anything from his eyes; deep water, a rogue; look at his beard. I’ll give you a note to him, and you show it. He is Gorstkin, only he isn’t Gorstkin, he’s Lyagavy, the Setter; but don’t tell him he’s Lyagavy, he’ll take offence. If you come to terms with him and see that it’s all right, write to me at once. Just write this: ‘He isn’t lying.’ Hold out for eleven; you may come down one thousand, no more. Think: eight and eleven, that’s three thousand difference. It’s just as if I had found those three thousand; it isn’t every day you get a buyer, and I need the money desperately. Let me know it is serious, and then I’ll fly over from here myself and finish it; I’ll snatch the time somehow. But why should I gallop off there now, if the priest has made it all up? Well, will you go or not?”
“Oh, I haven’t time, spare me.”

“Ah, oblige your father, I’ll remember it! You have no heart, any of you, that’s what it is! What is a day or two to you? Where are you going now, to Venice? Your Venice won’t fall to pieces in two days. I’d send Alyoshka, but what use is Alyoshka in such matters? I ask you only because you are a clever man, don’t I see it? You don’t deal in timber, but you have an eye. All that is needed is to see whether the man is speaking seriously or not. I tell you, look at his beard: if his little beard shakes, he means it.”
“So you yourself are pushing me off to that damned Chermashnya, eh?” cried Ivan Fyodorovich, with a spiteful smile.
Fyodor Pavlovich did not make out the spite, or did not want to, but caught at the smile:
“So you’ll go, you’ll go? I’ll scribble you the note this minute.”
“I don’t know whether I shall go; I don’t know; I’ll decide on the way.”

“Why on the way? Decide now. My dear, decide! If you come to terms, write me two lines, give them to the priest, and he will send me your note in a flash. And after that I won’t keep you; off you go to Venice. The priest will take you back to Volovya station with his own horses…”

The old man was simply delighted; he scribbled the note; they sent for the horses; snacks and brandy were served. When the old man was glad he always began to grow expansive, but this time he seemed to hold himself in. About Dmitri Fyodorovich, for instance, he did not utter a single word. And he was not touched at all by the parting. He even seemed not to find anything to talk about, and Ivan Fyodorovich noticed it very much: “I have bored him, though,” he thought to himself. Only when he was seeing his son off from the porch did the old man seem a little flustered and make to kiss him. But Ivan Fyodorovich quickly held out his hand to be shaken, evidently warding off the kisses. The old man understood at once and instantly checked himself.
“Well, God be with you, God be with you!” he kept repeating from the porch. “You’ll come again some time in your life, won’t you? Well, do come; I’ll always be glad. Well, Christ be with you!”
Ivan Fyodorovich climbed into the carriage.
“Goodbye, Ivan, don’t abuse me too much!” his father called for the last time.

All the household came out to see him off: Smerdyakov, Marfa and Grigory. Ivan Fyodorovich gave each of them ten roubles. When he had already settled into the carriage, Smerdyakov skipped up to straighten the rug.

“You see… I am going to Chermashnya…” somehow broke from Ivan Fyodorovich suddenly; again, as yesterday, it slipped out by itself, and with a sort of nervous little laugh besides. He remembered it for a long time afterwards.
“So it is true what people say, that it is worth talking to a clever man,” Smerdyakov answered firmly, with a penetrating look at Ivan Fyodorovich.

The carriage moved off and raced away. The traveller’s soul was troubled, but he looked eagerly round him at the fields, the hills, the trees, at a flock of geese flying high over him across the clear sky. And suddenly he felt so good. He tried to talk to the driver, and something the peasant answered interested him terribly; but a minute later he realised that it had all gone past his ears and that, to tell the truth, he had not understood the peasant’s answer. He fell silent; it was good enough as it was: the air pure, fresh, coolish, the sky clear. The images of Alyosha and Katerina Ivanovna flashed through his mind; but he smiled quietly and quietly blew on the dear phantoms, and they flew away: “Their time will come,” he thought. They covered the stage quickly, changed horses and raced on to Volovya. “Why is it worth talking to a clever man? What did he mean by that?” It suddenly took his breath away. “And why did I tell him I was going to Chermashnya?” They galloped up to Volovya station. Ivan Fyodorovich got out of the carriage, and the drivers crowded round him. They bargained for Chermashnya, twelve versts by country road, with private horses. He told them to harness. He went into the station house, looked round, glanced at the stationmaster’s wife, and suddenly went back out onto the porch.
“I don’t need Chermashnya. Shan’t I be late for the railway at seven, lads?”
“We’ll just make it. Shall we harness, then?”
“Harness at once. Will any of you be in town tomorrow?”
“To be sure; Mitry here will be.”
“Can you do me a service, Mitry? Go to my father, Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov, and tell him I didn’t go to Chermashnya. Can you or not?”
“Why not? We’ll go; we have known Fyodor Pavlovich a long time.”
“And here is something for your tea, because he probably won’t give you anything…” Ivan Fyodorovich laughed gaily.
“And that he won’t, true enough,” Mitry laughed too. “Thank you, sir, we’ll do it without fail…”

At seven in the evening Ivan Fyodorovich got into the train and flew off to Moscow. “Away with everything that was; I have done with the old world for ever, and let there be no news or echo from it; into a new world, to new places, and no looking back!” But instead of rapture, such darkness suddenly descended on his soul, and such sorrow ached in his heart, as he had never felt before in all his life. He was thinking all night; the train flew on, and only at dawn, already coming into Moscow, did he suddenly seem to come to himself.
“I am a scoundrel!” he whispered to himself.

And Fyodor Pavlovich, having seen his son off, remained very pleased. For two whole hours he felt almost happy and sipped his brandy. But suddenly something happened in the house that was most annoying and unpleasant for everyone and at once threw Fyodor Pavlovich into great confusion: Smerdyakov went to the cellar for something and fell down from the top step. It was lucky that Marfa Ignatyevna happened to be in the yard at the time and heard it in time. She did not see the fall, but she heard the scream, a peculiar, strange scream, but one long familiar to her: the scream of an epileptic falling in a fit. Whether the fit had come on him at the moment he was going down the steps, so that he must of course have tumbled straight down unconscious, or whether, on the contrary, the fit of Smerdyakov, a known epileptic, came from the fall and the shock, could not be made out; but they found him already at the bottom of the cellar, in convulsions and spasms, thrashing about and foaming at the mouth. At first they thought he must have broken something, an arm or a leg, and hurt himself badly; but “the Lord preserved him”, as Marfa Ignatyevna put it: nothing of the kind had happened; only it was hard to get him out and carry him up from the cellar into God’s daylight. But they asked the neighbours for help and managed it somehow. Fyodor Pavlovich himself was present at the whole ceremony, and helped too, evidently frightened and as if at a loss. The sick man, however, did not come to: the fits stopped for a while, but then began again, and everyone concluded that the same thing would happen as last year, when he had also fallen from the attic by accident. They remembered that ice had been put on the crown of his head then. Some ice was still to be found in the cellar, and Marfa Ignatyevna saw to it; and towards evening Fyodor Pavlovich sent for Doctor Herzenstube, who came at once. Having examined the sick man carefully (he was the most careful and attentive doctor in the whole province, an elderly and most respectable little old man), he concluded that the fit was an extraordinary one and “might threaten danger”; that for the moment he, Herzenstube, did not yet understand it all, but that tomorrow morning, if the present remedies did not help, he would decide on others. The sick man was put to bed in the lodge, in a little room next to Grigory and Marfa Ignatyevna’s quarters. After that Fyodor Pavlovich suffered nothing but misfortune upon misfortune all day: Marfa Ignatyevna cooked the dinner, and the soup, compared with Smerdyakov’s cooking, came out “like dishwater”, and the chicken was so overdone that it was impossible to chew it. To her master’s bitter, though just, reproaches, Marfa Ignatyevna retorted that the chicken had been very old to begin with, and that she herself had never trained as a cook. Towards evening came another worry: Fyodor Pavlovich was told that Grigory, who had been unwell since the day before yesterday, had now taken almost completely to his bed; his lower back had given out. Fyodor Pavlovich finished his tea as early as possible and locked himself in the house alone. He was in a state of terrible, anxious expectation. The fact was that that very evening he was expecting Grushenka’s arrival almost for certain; at least he had received from Smerdyakov, early in the morning, almost an assurance that “she has promised to come without fail, sir.” The restless old man’s heart beat anxiously; he paced his empty rooms and listened. He had to keep his ears open: Dmitri Fyodorovich might be on the watch for her somewhere, and as soon as she knocked at the window (Smerdyakov had assured Fyodor Pavlovich two days before that he had told her where and how to knock), he must open the door as quickly as possible and on no account keep her waiting a second in the passage, lest, God forbid, she should take fright and run away. It was a fretful time for Fyodor Pavlovich, but never had his heart bathed in sweeter hope: it could be said almost for certain that this time she would come without fail!…
## Book Six: The Russian Monk · Chapter I · Elder Zosima and His Visitors

When Alyosha, with anxiety and pain in his heart, went into the elder’s cell, he stopped almost in amazement. Instead of a dying man, perhaps already unconscious, as he had feared to find him, he suddenly saw him sitting in his armchair, his face worn with weakness but bright and cheerful, surrounded by visitors and holding a quiet, radiant conversation with them. He had, however, got up from his bed no more than a quarter of an hour before Alyosha came. The visitors had gathered in his cell earlier and waited for him to wake, on Father Paisy’s firm assurance that “the teacher will certainly rise, to talk once more with those dear to his heart, as he himself declared and promised this morning.” Father Paisy believed firmly in this promise, as in every word of the dying elder, so firmly that if he had seen him completely unconscious and even no longer breathing, but had his promise that he would rise once more and take leave of him, he would perhaps not have believed even death itself, but would have gone on expecting the dying man to come to and fulfil what he had promised. That morning, as he lay down to sleep, Elder Zosima had told him positively: “I shall not die before I have once more drunk my fill of talk with you, beloved of my heart, looked on your dear faces and poured out my soul to you once more.” Those who had gathered for what was probably the elder’s last conversation were his most devoted friends of many years. There were four of them: the hieromonks Father Iosif and Father Paisy; the hieromonk Father Mikhail, head of the hermitage, a man not yet very old, far from so learned, of humble origin, but firm in spirit, of unshakeable and simple faith, stern in appearance but deeply tender of heart, though he evidently hid his tenderness to the point of a kind of shame. The fourth visitor was a quite old, simple little monk of the poorest peasant origin, Brother Anfim, hardly able to read and write, silent and quiet, who rarely spoke to anyone, the humblest among the most humble, with the look of a man forever frightened by something great and terrible beyond the reach of his mind. Elder Zosima loved this trembling man very much and all his life treated him with extraordinary respect, though perhaps he had spoken fewer words to him than to anyone in his whole life, despite having once spent many years travelling with him, the two of them alone, all over holy Russia. That was very long ago, some forty years before, when Elder Zosima first began his monastic labours in a poor, little-known monastery in Kostroma, and soon after went with Father Anfim on his wanderings to collect donations for their poor little Kostroma monastery. Everyone, host and visitors, was in the elder’s second room, where his bed stood, a room that, as was said before, was very cramped, so that all four (besides Porfiry the novice, who remained standing) could barely fit round the elder’s armchair on chairs brought in from the first room. It was already getting dark; the room was lit by the icon lamps and wax candles before the icons. Seeing Alyosha, who was embarrassed on coming in and stopped in the doorway, the elder smiled at him joyfully and held out his hand.
“Greetings, my quiet one, greetings, my dear; here you are. I knew you would come.”
Alyosha went up to him, bowed down before him to the ground and wept. Something was bursting from his heart; his soul trembled; he wanted to sob.

“What is this? Wait before you mourn me,” the elder smiled, laying his right hand on his head. “You see, I am sitting and talking; perhaps I shall live another twenty years, as that kind, dear woman from Vyshegorye wished me yesterday, with little Lizaveta in her arms. Remember, Lord, the mother and the little girl Lizaveta!” (He crossed himself.) “Porfiry, did you take her gift where I told you?”

He was remembering the sixty kopecks given yesterday by the cheerful pilgrim woman to be passed on “to one poorer than I am”. Such offerings are made as penances, laid on oneself voluntarily for some reason, and always from money earned by one’s own labour. The elder had sent Porfiry the evening before to a townswoman of ours who had recently been burnt out, a widow with children who had gone begging after the fire. Porfiry hastened to report that it was done and that he had given it, as he had been told, “from an unknown benefactress”.
“Stand up, my dear,” the elder went on to Alyosha, “let me look at you. Have you been to your family? Have you seen your brother?”

It seemed strange to Alyosha that he asked so firmly and precisely about only one of the brothers. But which? So it was perhaps for that brother’s sake that he had sent him away both yesterday and today.
“I have seen one of my brothers,” Alyosha answered.
“I mean the one from yesterday, the eldest, to whom I bowed down to the ground.”
“Him I only saw yesterday; today I could not find him anywhere,” said Alyosha.

“Make haste and find him; go again tomorrow, and make haste; leave everything and make haste. Perhaps you will still be in time to prevent something terrible. Yesterday I bowed down to his great future suffering.”

He suddenly fell silent and seemed to be thinking. The words were strange. Father Iosif, who had witnessed the elder’s bow to the ground the day before, exchanged a glance with Father Paisy. Alyosha could not bear it.
“Father and teacher,” he said in extreme agitation, “your words are too obscure… What suffering awaits him?”

“Do not be curious. Something terrible appeared to me yesterday… as if his whole destiny were expressed in his look yesterday. There was a look he gave… so that my heart was instantly horrified at what this man is preparing for himself. Once or twice in my life I have seen the same expression on certain faces… as if it pictured the whole destiny of those people, and their destiny, alas, came true. I sent you to him, Alexei, because I thought your brotherly face would help him. But all is from the Lord, and all our destinies. ‘Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.’ Remember that. And you, Alexei, I have blessed many times in my thoughts in the course of my life for your face; know that,” the elder said with a quiet smile. “This is what I think of you: you will go forth from these walls, and in the world you will live as a monk. You will have many opponents, but even your enemies will love you. Life will bring you many misfortunes, but through them you will be happy, and you will bless life and make others bless it, which matters most of all. Well, that is what you are like. My fathers and teachers,” he turned to his visitors with a tender smile, “never until this day have I said, even to him, why the face of this youth was so dear to my soul. Only now will I say it: his face was to me as a reminder and a prophecy. At the dawn of my days, when I was still a little child, I had an elder brother who died as a youth, before my eyes, only seventeen years old. And afterwards, passing through my life, I became convinced little by little that this brother of mine had been in my destiny as a sign and a calling from above; for had he not appeared in my life, had he not been at all, never perhaps, so I think, would I have taken the monastic habit and entered on this precious path. That first appearance was in my childhood, and now, at the end of my road, a repetition of it, as it were, has appeared before my eyes. It is wonderful, fathers and teachers, that, not being so like him in face, only a little, Alexei seemed to me so like him in spirit that many times I took him as if he were that youth, my brother, come to me mysteriously at the end of my road for a kind of remembrance and insight, so that I even wondered at myself and at so strange a dream of mine. Do you hear this, Porfiry?” he turned to the novice who waited on him. “Many times I have seen on your face as it were a grief that I love Alexei more than you. Now you know why it was so; but I love you too, know that, and many times I have grieved that you were grieved. And to you, dear visitors, I want to tell about this youth, my brother, for there has been no appearance in my life more precious, more prophetic and moving than this. My heart is moved, and I behold my whole life at this moment as if I were living it all again…”

Here I must remark that this last conversation of the elder with the visitors who came to him on the last day of his life has been preserved partly in writing. Alexei Fyodorovich Karamazov wrote it down from memory some time after the elder’s death. But whether it was entirely the conversation of that evening, or whether in his notes he added to it from earlier conversations with his teacher, I cannot decide. Besides, the elder’s whole speech in these notes runs on as if without a break, as though he were setting out his life in the form of a story addressed to his friends, whereas without doubt, from what was told afterwards, it happened in reality somewhat differently, for the conversation that evening was general, and though the visitors interrupted their host little, they did speak for themselves, joining in the conversation, perhaps even telling and relating something of their own; besides, there could be no such continuity in the account, for the elder sometimes gasped for breath, lost his voice, and even lay down on his bed to rest, though he did not fall asleep, and the visitors did not leave their places. Once or twice the conversation was interrupted by reading from the Gospel; Father Paisy read. It is remarkable too that none of them, however, supposed that he would die that very night, all the more since on this last evening of his life, after his deep sleep during the day, he seemed suddenly to have found a new strength in himself, which sustained him through the whole of this long conversation with his friends. It was like a last tenderness that sustained in him an incredible animation, but only for a short time, for his life broke off suddenly… But of that later. For now I want to say that I have preferred, without setting out all the details of the conversation, to confine myself to the elder’s story as Alexei Fyodorovich Karamazov’s manuscript gives it. It will be shorter and not so tiring, though of course, I repeat, Alyosha took much from earlier conversations too and put it together.

## Chapter II · From the Life of the Hieroschemamonk Elder Zosima, Departed in God, Compiled from His Own Words by Alexei Fyodorovich Karamazov · Biographical Notes · (a) Of Elder Zosima’s Young Brother

Beloved fathers and teachers, I was born in a distant northern province, in the town of V., to a father of the gentry, but not of note and not of high rank. He died when I was only two years old, and I do not remember him at all. He left my mother a small wooden house and some capital, not large, but enough to live on with her children without want. There were only two of us children: I, Zinovy, and my elder brother, Markel. He was about eight years older than I, of a hot and irritable temper, but kind, not given to mockery, and strangely silent, especially at home, with me, with our mother and with the servants. He did well at the high school but did not get on with his schoolfellows, though he did not quarrel with them either; so at least our mother remembered him. Half a year before his death, when he had turned seventeen, he took to visiting a solitary man in our town, a political exile of sorts, banished from Moscow to our town for freethinking. This exile was no small scholar and a distinguished philosopher at the university. For some reason he took a liking to Markel and began to receive him. The youth spent whole evenings with him, all through the winter, until the exile was called back to government service in Petersburg at his own request, for he had patrons. Great Lent began, and Markel would not fast; he swore and laughed at it: “It’s all nonsense,” he said, “and there is no God at all,” so that he horrified our mother and the servants, and me too, little as I was; for though I was only nine, hearing those words I was very frightened too. Our servants were all serfs, four of them, all bought in the name of a landowner we knew. I remember too how of these four my mother sold one, the cook Afimya, lame and elderly, for sixty paper roubles, and hired a free woman in her place. And then in the sixth week of Lent my brother suddenly grew worse. He had always been unwell, weak in the chest, of a frail constitution and inclined to consumption; he was tall, but thin and sickly, and very handsome in face. He had caught cold, perhaps; but the doctor came and soon whispered to our mother that it was galloping consumption and that he would not live through the spring. Mother began to weep and to beg my brother, cautiously (more so as not to frighten him), to fast and take the holy sacrament, for he was still on his feet then. Hearing this, he grew angry and abused the church of God; but he began to think: he guessed at once that he was dangerously ill, and that this was why his mother was sending him to fast and take communion while he still had strength. Besides, he knew himself that he had long been unwell, and a year before had said once at table to my mother and me, coolly: “I am not long for this world among you; perhaps I shan’t live a year”; and it was as if he had prophesied it. Three days passed, and Holy Week came.
