And on the Tuesday morning my brother began to prepare for communion. “I am doing this really for you, mother, to please you and set your mind at rest,” he told her. Mother wept for joy, and for grief too: “His end must be near, if there is such a change in him all of a sudden.” But he did not go to church for long; he took to his bed, so that he made his confession and received communion at home. The days became bright, clear and fragrant; Easter was late that year. All night long, I remember, he would cough and sleep badly, and in the morning he would always dress and try to sit in the soft armchair. That is how I shall remember him: sitting quiet and meek, smiling, ill himself, but his face cheerful and joyful. He was changed altogether in his soul, such a wonderful change had suddenly begun in him! The old nurse would come into his room: “Let me light the lamp before the icon in your room too, my dear.” Before, he would not allow it; he even blew it out. “Light it, dear, light it; I was a monster to forbid you before. You pray to God lighting the lamp, and I pray rejoicing at you. So we pray to the one God.” These words seemed strange to us, and our mother would go to her room and weep and weep, only wiping her eyes and putting on a cheerful look when she went in to him. “Mother, don’t cry, my dear,” he would say, “I have a long time yet to live, a long time to make merry with you, and life, life is merry and joyful!” “Ah, my dear, what merriment is there for you, when you burn in fever all night and cough so that your chest is nearly torn apart?” “Mother,” he answered her, “don’t cry; life is paradise, and we are all in paradise, but we don’t want to know it, and if we wanted to know it, tomorrow there would be paradise in the whole world.” And everyone wondered at his words, he said it so strangely and so decidedly; they were moved and wept. Acquaintances would come to see us: “My dear ones,” he would say, “dear ones, what have I done to deserve your love, why do you love such a one as me, and how is it I didn’t know it before, didn’t value it?” To the servants coming in he would say every minute: “My dear ones, my precious ones, why do you wait on me, and am I worth being waited on? If God had mercy and let me live, I would wait on you myself, for everyone should serve one another.” Our mother, listening, shook her head: “My dear, it is your illness that makes you talk like that.” “Mother, my joy,” he said, “there must be masters and servants, but let me too be the servant of my servants, just as they are to me. And I will tell you something else, mother: every one of us is guilty before everyone in everything, and I more than all.” Our mother even smiled at that; she wept and smiled: “Well, how are you guilty before everyone more than all? There are murderers and robbers, and what sins have you had time to commit, that you accuse yourself more than all?” “Mother, my own heart’s blood,” he said (he had begun to use such tender, unexpected words then), “my dear heart’s blood, my joy, know that truly each of us is guilty before everyone, for everyone and for everything. I don’t know how to explain it to you, but I feel it is so, so that it torments me. And how did we live, and get angry, and know nothing then?” So he would rise from sleep, every day more and more moved and joyful and all trembling with love. The doctor would come (an old German, Eisenschmidt, used to come): “Well, doctor, shall I live another day in the world?” he would joke with him. “Not one day, many days you will live,” the doctor would answer, “and months and years too.” “What years, what months!” he would exclaim. “Why count the days? One day is enough for a man to know all happiness. My dear ones, why do we quarrel, boast to each other, remember each other’s wrongs? Let us go straight into the garden and walk and play, love and praise and kiss each other, and bless our life.” “Your son is not long for this world,” the doctor said to our mother as she saw him off to the porch; “his illness is making him lose his mind.” The windows of his room looked out on the garden, and our garden was shady, with old trees; the spring buds were swelling on the trees, the early birds had come; they chattered and sang at his windows. And suddenly, looking at them and admiring them, he began to beg their forgiveness too: “Birds of God, joyful birds, forgive me too, for I have sinned against you as well.” None of us could understand that then, but he wept for joy: “Yes,” he said, “there was such glory of God all round me: birds, trees, meadows, the heavens; I alone lived in shame, I alone dishonoured everything and never noticed the beauty and the glory at all.” “You take too many sins on yourself,” our mother would weep. “Mother, my joy, I am weeping from gladness, not from grief; I want to be guilty before them myself; only I can’t explain it to you, for I don’t even know how to love them. Let me be guilty before everyone; then everyone will forgive me too, and that is paradise. Am I not in paradise now?”

And there was much more that I cannot remember or write down. I remember that once I went in to him alone, when no one else was with him. It was evening, clear; the sun was setting and lit up the whole room with a slanting ray. He beckoned to me when he saw me; I went up to him; he took me by the shoulders with both hands and looked into my face tenderly, lovingly; he said nothing, only looked at me so for a minute. “Well,” he said, “go now, play, live for me!” I went out then and went to play. And many times afterwards in my life I remembered with tears how he told me to live for him. He said many more such wonderful and beautiful words, though we did not understand them then. He died in the third week after Easter, conscious, and though he had stopped speaking, he did not change until his very last hour: he looked joyfully, there was gladness in his eyes; he looked for us, smiled at us, called us. Even in the town there was much talk of his death. All this shook me then, but not too much, though I cried a great deal when they buried him. I was young, a child; but everything stayed indelibly in my heart; the feeling lay hidden. In its time it was all to rise and answer. And so it did.
## (b) Of Holy Scripture in the Life of Father Zosima

We were left alone then, my mother and I. Good acquaintances soon advised her: you have only one son left, and you are not poor, you have capital; so why not, like others, send your son to Petersburg? By keeping him here you may be depriving him of a distinguished future. And they persuaded my mother to take me to Petersburg, to the Cadet Corps, so that afterwards I could enter the Imperial Guard. My mother hesitated a long time: how could she part with her last son? But she made up her mind, though not without many tears, thinking to further my happiness. She took me to Petersburg and placed me there, and after that I never saw her again; for three years later she died herself, having grieved and trembled for us both all those three years. From my parents’ house I brought away only precious memories, for there are no memories more precious to a man than those of his earliest childhood in his parents’ house, and that is almost always so, if there is even a little love and harmony in the family. Indeed, precious memories may be kept even from the worst family, if only your own soul is able to seek what is precious. Among my memories of home I count also my memories of sacred history, which, child as I was, I was very eager to know in my parents’ house. I had a book then, a sacred history with beautiful pictures, called One Hundred and Four Sacred Stories from the Old and New Testaments, and I learned to read from it. I have it here on my shelf now; I keep it as a precious remembrance. But even before I learned to read, I remember how a certain spiritual insight visited me for the first time, when I was eight years old. My mother took me alone (I don’t remember where my brother was then) to the Lord’s temple, to the liturgy on the Monday of Holy Week. It was a clear day, and, remembering it now, I seem to see again how the incense rose from the censer and slowly went up, and from above, through a narrow little window in the dome, God’s rays poured down on us in the church, and, rising to them in waves, the incense seemed to melt into them. I looked with tender feeling, and for the first time in my life I consciously received into my soul the first seed of the word of God. A youth came out into the middle of the church with a great book, so big that it seemed to me then he could hardly carry it, and laid it on the lectern, opened it and began to read; and suddenly then, for the first time, I understood something; for the first time in my life I understood what is read in God’s church. There was a man in the land of Uz, upright and God-fearing, and he had so much wealth, so many camels, so many sheep and asses, and his children made merry, and he loved them very much and prayed to God for them: perhaps they had sinned in their merrymaking. And now the devil goes up to God together with the sons of God and says to the Lord that he has gone to and fro in all the earth and under the earth. “And hast thou seen my servant Job?” God asks him. And God boasted to the devil, pointing to his great and holy servant. And the devil smiled at God’s words: “Give him over to me, and thou wilt see that thy servant will murmur and curse thy name.” And God gave over his righteous one, whom he loved so, to the devil, and the devil struck down his children and his cattle and scattered his wealth, all at once, as with the thunder of God; and Job rent his garments and threw himself on the ground and cried out: “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return to the earth; the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord from this time forth and for evermore!” Fathers and teachers, forgive my tears now, for all my childhood seems to rise before me again, and I breathe now as I breathed then with my little eight-year-old breast, and I feel, as then, wonder and confusion and joy. And the camels took hold of my imagination so then, and Satan, who talks so with God, and God, who gave his servant over to destruction, and his servant crying out: “Blessed be thy name, though thou punishest me”; and then the quiet, sweet singing in the church: “Let my prayer be set forth”, and again the incense from the priest’s censer and the kneeling prayer! Since then (I took it up only yesterday) I cannot read that most holy story without tears. And how much there is in it that is great, secret, unimaginable! Afterwards I heard the words of the mockers and blasphemers, proud words: how could the Lord give up the most beloved of his saints to be the devil’s sport, take his children from him, strike him himself with sickness and sores so that he scraped the pus from his wounds with a potsherd, and what for? Only to boast before Satan: “See what my saint can endure for my sake!” But the greatness of it lies just in this, that it is a mystery: that the passing face of the earth and eternal truth touched each other here. Before earthly justice the act of eternal justice is accomplished. Here the Creator, as in the first days of creation, ending each day with praise, “That which I have made is good,” looks on Job and again boasts of his creation. And Job, praising the Lord, serves not only him but will serve his whole creation from generation to generation and for ever and ever, for that was what he was destined for. Lord, what a book this is, and what lessons! What a book this holy scripture is, what a miracle and what a power are given with it to man! It is like a sculpture of the world and of man and of human characters, and everything is named and shown for ever and ever. And how many mysteries resolved and revealed: God restores Job again, gives him wealth again; many years pass again, and now he has new children, different ones, and he loves them. Lord, “but how could he love these new ones, it would seem, when those first ones are no more, when he has lost them? Remembering them, how could he be fully happy, as before, with the new ones, however dear the new ones might be?” But he can, he can: old grief, by the great mystery of human life, passes little by little into quiet, tender joy; instead of the young, seething blood comes a meek, serene old age. I bless the rising of the sun each day, and my heart sings to it as before, but now I love its setting more, its long slanting rays, and with them quiet, meek, tender memories, dear images from all my long and blessed life; and over all, God’s truth, moving, reconciling, all-forgiving! My life is ending; I know it and hear it; but I feel, in each day left to me, how my earthly life is already touching a new, infinite, unknown life that is coming close, at the foretaste of which my soul trembles with rapture, my mind shines and my heart weeps with joy… Friends and teachers, I have heard more than once, and in these last days it has become still more audible, how our priests of God, and above all the village priests, complain tearfully and everywhere of their small stipend and of their humiliation, and declare outright, even in print (I have read it myself), that they can no longer, it seems, expound the scriptures to the people because their stipend is so small, and if Lutherans and heretics come and begin to lure the flock away, then let them, for our stipend is small. Lord! I think: God grant them more of this stipend so precious to them (for their complaint is just too); but truly I say: if anyone is to blame for this, half of it is we ourselves! For suppose he has no time, suppose he says rightly that he is weighed down all the time with work and services; still, it is not all the time; surely he has even one hour in the whole week to remember God. And the work does not go on all the year round. Let him gather at his house once a week, in an evening hour, at first only the children; the fathers will hear of it, and the fathers will begin to come too. And there is no need to build mansions for this work; simply take them into your cottage; don’t be afraid, they won’t foul your cottage; you are gathering them for one hour only. Let him open this book for them and begin to read, without wise words and without conceit, without setting himself above them, but tenderly and meekly, himself rejoicing that he is reading to them and that they are listening and understand him, himself loving these words; let him only stop now and then to explain some word a simple man does not understand. Do not worry, they will understand everything; the Orthodox heart will understand everything! Read to them of Abraham and Sarah, of Isaac and Rebecca, of how Jacob went to Laban and wrestled in his dream with the Lord and said, “How dreadful is this place,” and you will strike the pious mind of the simple man. Read to them, and to the children especially, of how the brothers sold into slavery their own brother, the dear boy Joseph, the dreamer and great prophet, and told their father that a wild beast had torn his son, showing him his bloodstained coat. Read how afterwards the brothers came to Egypt for corn, and Joseph, now a great courtier, unrecognised by them, tormented them, accused them, kept back their brother Benjamin, and all out of love: “I love you, and loving you I torment you.” For all his life he had remembered unceasingly how they sold him somewhere out there in the hot steppe, by a well, to merchants, and how he, wringing his hands, had wept and begged his brothers not to sell him as a slave into a strange land; and now, seeing them after so many years, he loved them again beyond measure, but he tormented and tortured them, loving them all the while. At last he goes away from them, unable himself to bear the torment of his heart, throws himself on his bed and weeps; then he wipes his face and comes out radiant and bright and declares to them: “Brothers, I am Joseph your brother!” Let him read further of how old Jacob rejoiced on learning that his dear boy was still alive, and set out for Egypt, leaving even his homeland, and died in a strange land, uttering for ever and ever in his testament the greatest word, which had lain mysteriously in his meek and timid heart all his life: that from his line, from Judah, would come the great hope of the world, its reconciler and saviour! Fathers and teachers, forgive me and do not be angry that like a little child I talk of what you have long known and could teach me a hundred times more skilfully and beautifully. I say it only from rapture; and forgive my tears, for I love this book! Let him weep too, the priest of God, and he will see that the hearts of those who listen to him are shaken in answer. Only a little seed is needed, a tiny one: let him cast it into the soul of a simple man, and it will not die; it will live in his soul all his life, hidden in him amid the darkness, amid the stench of his sins, like a point of light, like a great reminder. And there is no need, no need to explain much and teach much; he will understand everything simply. Do you think the simple man will not understand? Try reading him next the touching and tender story of the beautiful Esther and the haughty Vashti; or the wonderful tale of the prophet Jonah in the belly of the whale. Do not forget the parables of the Lord either, chiefly from the Gospel of Luke (that is what I did), and then from the Acts of the Apostles the conversion of Saul (that without fail, without fail!), and finally from the Lives of the Saints, if only the life of Alexis, the man of God, and of the greatest of the great, the joyful sufferer, the beholder of God and bearer of Christ, our mother Mary of Egypt; and you will pierce his heart with these simple tales, and all in only one hour a week, in spite of your small stipend, just one little hour. And he will see for himself that our people are merciful and grateful; they will repay him a hundredfold; remembering the priest’s zeal and his tender words, they will help him in his fields of their own accord, help him in his house too, and repay him with more respect than before; and there his stipend will have grown already. The thing is so simple-hearted that sometimes we are even afraid to say it, for people will laugh at you; and yet how true it is! He who does not believe in God will not believe in God’s people either. But he who has come to believe in God’s people will see his holiness too, even if he did not believe in it at all before. Only the people and their coming spiritual power will convert our atheists, who have torn themselves away from their native soil. And what is the word of Christ without an example? The people perish without the word of God, for their soul thirsts for the word and for every beautiful impression. In my youth, long ago, nearly forty years since, Father Anfim and I went all over Russia collecting alms for the monastery, and once we spent the night on the bank of a great navigable river with some fishermen, and with us sat a comely youth, a peasant, eighteen years old to look at; he was hurrying to his place, to haul a merchant’s barge by towrope the next day. And I saw him looking before him tenderly and serenely. The night was bright, still, warm, a July night; the river was wide, mist rose from it and refreshed us; now and then a fish splashed; the birds had fallen silent; everything was still and beautiful; everything was praying to God. And only we two were not asleep, I and this youth, and we got to talking of the beauty of God’s world and its great mystery. Every blade of grass, every little beetle, the ant, the golden bee, all of them know their path to the point of wonder; without reason they bear witness to the mystery of God; they themselves accomplish it unceasingly; and I saw that the dear youth’s heart was kindled. He told me that he loved the forest and the forest birds; he was a bird-catcher; he understood every whistle of theirs and knew how to lure every bird. “I know nothing better than being in the forest,” he said, “though everything is good.” “Truly,” I answered him, “everything is good and glorious, because everything is truth. Look,” I said to him, “at the horse, a great animal that stands near to man, or at the ox that feeds him and works for him, downcast and thoughtful; look at their faces: what meekness, what attachment to man, who often beats him without mercy, what gentleness, what trustfulness and what beauty in his face. It is touching even to know that there is no sin on him, for everything is perfect; everything except man is sinless, and Christ is with them even before us.” “Can it be,” the youth asks, “that Christ is with them too?” “How could it be otherwise?” I tell him. “For the Word is for all; all creation and every creature, every little leaf, is striving towards the Word, sings glory to God, weeps to Christ, unknown to itself; it accomplishes this by the mystery of its sinless life. Look,” I tell him, “there in the forest wanders the fearsome bear, terrible and fierce, and not guilty of anything in it.” And I told him how once a bear came to a great saint who was working out his salvation in the forest in a little cell, and the great saint was moved with tenderness for him, went out to him fearlessly and gave him a piece of bread: “Go,” he said, “Christ be with you,” and the fierce beast went away obediently and meekly, without doing harm. And the youth was moved that it went away without doing harm, and that Christ was with it too. “Ah,” he said, “how good that is, how good and wonderful everything of God’s is!” He sat thinking, quietly and sweetly. I saw that he had understood. And he fell asleep beside me with a light, sinless sleep. Lord, bless youth! And I prayed for him myself as I lay down to sleep. Lord, send peace and light to thy people!
## Book Six, Chapter II, continued · (c) Recollections of Elder Zosima’s Youth and Young Manhood in the World · The Duel

I was a long time in Petersburg, in the Cadet Corps, nearly eight years, and with my new education I stifled many of my childhood impressions, though I forgot nothing. Instead I took on so many new habits and even opinions that I was transformed into a creature almost savage, cruel and absurd. Together with the French language I acquired a polish of courtesy and worldly manners; and the soldiers who served us in the Corps we all regarded as perfect cattle, and so did I. I perhaps more than anyone, for of all my comrades I was the most impressionable. When we came out as officers we were ready to shed our blood for the insulted honour of our regiment, but as for real honour, hardly any of us even knew what it was, and if he had found out, he would have been the first to laugh at it. We were all but proud of our drunkenness, our debauchery and our swagger. I will not say we were bad; all those young men were good, but they behaved badly, and I worst of all. The main thing was that I had come into my own capital, and so I threw myself into living for my pleasure, with all the impetuousness of youth, without restraint, under full sail. But here is the wonder of it: I read books then too, and even with great pleasure; the Bible alone I almost never opened at that time, yet I never parted with it either, but carried it everywhere with me: truly I was keeping that book, without knowing it, “for the day and the hour, the month and the year”. After serving in this way for about four years, I found myself at last in the town of K., where our regiment was stationed at the time. The town’s society was varied, numerous and merry, hospitable and rich, and I was well received everywhere, for I was cheerful by nature and besides was reputed to be not poor, which counts for no little in the world. And then something happened that was the beginning of everything. I became attached to a young and beautiful girl, intelligent and worthy, of a bright and noble character, the daughter of respectable parents. They were people of consequence, with wealth, influence and power, and they received me kindly and warmly. And it seemed to me that the girl was disposed towards me in her heart, and my heart was set aflame by the fancy. Afterwards I grasped for myself and fully realised that perhaps I did not love her with such force at all, but only honoured her mind and lofty character, as I could not fail to do. Self-love, however, prevented me from offering her my hand at the time: it seemed hard and frightening to part with the temptations of a dissolute, free bachelor’s life at so young an age, and with money too. I did, however, drop hints. At any rate, I put off every decisive step for a little while. And then suddenly I was sent on duty to another district for two months. I come back two months later and suddenly learn that the girl is already married, to a rich landowner from near the town, a man older than I but still young, who had connections in the capital and in the best society, which I had not, a very amiable man and, besides, educated, while I had no education at all. I was so struck by this unexpected event that my mind was even clouded. The main point was that, as I learned at the same time, this young landowner had long been her suitor, and I myself had met him many times in their house but noticed nothing, blinded by my own merits. But that was just what offended me most: how was it that almost everyone knew, and I alone knew nothing? And I suddenly felt an unbearable spite. With my face burning I began to recall how many times I had almost declared my love to her, and since she had not stopped me or warned me, it followed, I concluded, that she had been laughing at me. Later, of course, I realised and remembered that she had not been laughing at all; on the contrary, she herself had playfully broken off such conversations and started others in their place; but at the time I could not see it and burned for revenge. I remember with surprise that this revenge and my anger were extremely heavy and repugnant to me myself, because, having an easy temper, I could not stay angry with anyone for long, and so I kindled myself artificially, as it were, and became at last monstrous and absurd. I waited my time, and once, in a large company, I managed suddenly to insult my “rival”, as though over a quite unrelated matter, by laughing at an opinion of his about an event of importance at the time (it was in the year twenty-six), and laughed, people said, wittily and cleverly. Then I forced an explanation from him and behaved so rudely in it that he accepted my challenge, despite the enormous difference between us, for I was younger, of no importance and of low rank. I learned for certain afterwards that he accepted my challenge also from a feeling of jealousy towards me: he had been a little jealous of me before, over his wife, then still his betrothed; and now he thought that if she learned he had put up with an insult from me and had not dared to call me out, she might involuntarily despise him and her love might waver. I soon found a second, a comrade, a lieutenant of our regiment. Though duels were cruelly punished in those days, there was even a kind of fashion for them among the military, so savagely do prejudices sometimes grow and take root. It was the end of June, and our meeting was to be the next day, outside the town, at seven in the morning; and truly something fateful happened to me then. Coming home in the evening, ferocious and monstrous, I got angry with my orderly Afanasy and struck him twice in the face with all my strength, so that his face was covered with blood. He had not been with me long, and it had happened before that I struck him, but never with such bestial cruelty. And would you believe it, my dear ones, forty years have passed since then, and I still remember it with shame and torment. I went to bed, slept about three hours, and got up when the day was already beginning. I rose suddenly, did not want to sleep any more, went to the window and opened it (my window looked onto a garden); I see the sun rising; it is warm and beautiful; the birds have begun to sing. What is it, I think, that I feel in my soul, something shameful and base? Is it because I am going to shed blood? No, I think, it seems not that. Is it because I am afraid of death, afraid of being killed? No, not that at all, not that at all… And suddenly I guessed at once what it was: it was that I had beaten Afanasy the evening before! Everything suddenly came back to me as if it were happening again: he stands before me, and I strike him with all my force straight in the face, and he holds his hands at his sides, his head straight, his eyes staring as if on parade; he flinches at every blow and does not even dare raise his hands to shield himself. And a man has been brought to that, and a man is beating a man! What a crime! It was as if a sharp needle had gone right through my soul. I stand as if out of my mind, and the sun is shining, the little leaves are rejoicing and glittering, and the birds, the birds are praising God… I covered my face with both hands, fell on the bed and sobbed aloud. And then I remembered my brother Markel and his words to the servants before his death: “My dear ones, my precious ones, why do you wait on me, why do you love me, and am I worth being waited on?” “Yes, am I worth it?” suddenly leapt into my head. Indeed, what am I worth, that another man, just like me, the image and likeness of God, should serve me? That question pierced my mind then for the first time in my life. “Mother, my own heart’s blood, truly each is guilty before all for all, only people don’t know it, and if they knew it, there would be paradise at once!” “Lord, can that too be untrue?” I weep and think. “Truly, perhaps I am more guilty than all for all, and worse than all men in the world!” And suddenly the whole truth stood before me in all its light: what am I going to do? I am going to kill a good, intelligent, noble man, guilty of nothing towards me, and by that I shall deprive his wife of happiness for ever, torment her and kill her. I lay like that on the bed, face down in the pillow, and did not notice at all how the time went by. Suddenly my comrade the lieutenant comes in for me, with the pistols: “Ah,” he says, “good, you are up already; it’s time, let’s go.” I started rushing about and lost my head completely; still, we went out to get into the carriage. “Wait here a moment,” I say to him, “I’ll run back in a second, I’ve forgotten my purse.” And I ran back alone into the flat, straight to Afanasy’s little room: “Afanasy,” I say, “yesterday I struck you twice in the face; forgive me.” He started as if frightened and stared at me, and I see that it is not enough, not enough, and suddenly, just as I was, in my epaulettes, I threw myself at his feet with my forehead to the ground: “Forgive me!” I say. At that he was utterly dumbfounded: “Your honour, master, sir, how can you… am I worth…” and suddenly he began to cry himself, just as I had earlier; he covered his face with both hands, turned to the window and shook all over with tears; and I ran out to my comrade, leapt into the carriage and shouted, “Drive on!” “Have you ever seen a conqueror?” I shout to him. “There he is before you!” There is such rapture in me; I laugh, I talk, talk all the way; I no longer remember what I said. He looks at me: “Well, brother, you are a fine fellow; I can see you’ll do credit to the uniform.” So we arrived at the place, and they were already there, waiting for us. They placed us twelve paces apart; his was the first shot. I stand before him cheerful, face to face, without blinking an eye, looking at him lovingly; I know what I shall do. He fired, and the shot only grazed my cheek a little and caught my ear. “Thank God,” I shout, “no man has been killed!” And I seized my own pistol, turned round and flung it up and away into the wood: “That’s the place for you!” I shout. I turned to my adversary: “My dear sir,” I say, “forgive me, a foolish young man, for having offended you through my own fault and now making you fire at me. I am ten times worse than you, and perhaps more than that. Tell that to the person whom you honour above all in the world.” I had no sooner said it than all three of them began shouting. “Upon my word,” said my adversary, even getting angry, “if you did not want to fight, why did you trouble me?” “Yesterday,” I say to him, “I was still a fool, and today I have grown wiser,” I answer him cheerfully. “I believe you about yesterday,” he says, “but about today it is hard to judge from your opinion.” “Bravo,” I cry to him, clapping my hands, “I agree with you in that too; I deserved it!” “Will you fire, my dear sir, or not?” “I will not,” I say, “and you, if you like, may fire again, only it would be better for you not to.” The seconds shout too, mine especially: “How can you disgrace the regiment like this, asking forgiveness at the barrier; if only I had known!” Then I stood before them all and was no longer laughing: “Gentlemen,” I say, “is it really so astonishing in our time to meet a man who would repent of his own foolishness and own publicly to what he is guilty of?” “But not at the barrier,” my second shouts again. “That’s just it,” I answer them. “That is just what is astonishing, for I ought to have owned my fault as soon as we arrived here, even before his shot, and not led him into a great and mortal sin; but we have arranged ourselves in the world so monstrously,” I say, “that to act so was almost impossible, for only after I had stood his shot at twelve paces could my words mean anything to him now; whereas if I had said them before the shot, as soon as we arrived, they would simply have said: a coward, frightened of the pistol, no use listening to him. Gentlemen,” I suddenly cried from my whole heart, “look round at the gifts of God: the clear sky, the pure air, the tender grass, the birds; nature is beautiful and sinless, and we, only we, are godless and foolish and do not understand that life is paradise, for we have only to want to understand, and at once it will come in all its beauty, and we shall embrace one another and weep…” I wanted to go on, but I could not; my breath was taken away, so sweetly, so youthfully, and there was such happiness in my heart as I had never felt in all my life. “All this is very sensible and pious,” says my adversary, “and at any rate you are an original man.” “Laugh,” I laugh back at him, “but afterwards you will praise me yourself.” “Why, I am ready to praise you now,” he says. “Allow me, I will hold out my hand to you, for it seems you really are a sincere man.” “No,” I say, “not now; but later, when I have become better and earned your respect, then hold it out, and you will do well.” We went back home; my second swore all the way, and I kept kissing him. My comrades heard of it at once and gathered that same day to judge me: “He has soiled the uniform,” they said, “let him send in his papers.” There were defenders too: “He did stand the shot, though,” they said. “Yes, but he was afraid of more shots and asked forgiveness at the barrier.” “But if he had been afraid of the shots,” the defenders objected, “he would have fired his own pistol first before asking forgiveness, and he threw it into the wood still loaded. No, something else has happened here, something original.” I listen, looking at them cheerfully. “My dearest friends and comrades,” I say, “don’t worry about my sending in my papers, because I have done it already; I sent them in this very day at the office, in the morning; and when I get my discharge I shall go straight into a monastery; that is why I am sending in my papers.” As soon as I said it, every one of them burst out laughing: “You should have told us from the start! Well, now everything is explained; one can’t judge a monk.” They laughed and would not stop, and not mockingly at all, but kindly, merrily; all of them suddenly loved me, even my fiercest accusers, and all that month afterwards, until my discharge came through, they all but carried me in their arms: “Ah, you monk,” they would say. And each of them had a kind word for me; they began to try to talk me out of it, even to pity me: “What are you doing to yourself?” “No,” they would say, “he is brave, our man; he stood the shot and could have fired his own pistol; it’s that he had a dream the night before that he should become a monk; that’s why.” Almost exactly the same happened in the town’s society. Before, they had not taken much notice of me, only received me warmly; and now suddenly they all vied with one another to get to know me and invite me: they laughed at me themselves, and yet they loved me. I will note here that although everyone was talking openly about our duel at the time, the authorities hushed the matter up, for my adversary was a close relative of our general, and since the affair had ended without blood, as a kind of joke, and I had, after all, sent in my papers, they did indeed turn it into a joke. And then I began to speak aloud and without fear, in spite of their laughter, because their laughter was not spiteful but kind. All these conversations took place mostly in the evenings, in the company of ladies; the women liked to listen to me more then, and made the men listen too. “But how can it be that I am guilty for everyone?” each of them would laugh in my face. “Can I be guilty for you, for instance?” “How could you know it,” I answer them, “when the whole world has long since gone off on another road and we take a downright lie for the truth and demand the same lie from others? Here, for once in my life, I went and acted sincerely, and what happened? I became a kind of holy fool for you all: though you have come to love me, you still laugh at me,” I say. “But how could we not love you as you are?” the hostess laughs at me aloud, and there was a large gathering at her house. Suddenly I see, rising from among the ladies, that very young woman over whom I had issued the challenge and whom I had so recently meant for my bride; and I had not even noticed that she had come to the party. She rose, came up to me and held out her hand: “Allow me,” she says, “to tell you that I am the first not to laugh at you, but, on the contrary, I thank you with tears and declare my respect for you for what you did then.” Her husband came up then too, and then suddenly everyone came crowding round me and almost kissed me. I felt so joyful; but most of all I suddenly noticed then a certain gentleman, a man already elderly, who was also coming up to me, whom I knew by name, though I had never been acquainted with him and until that evening had never even exchanged a word with him.
## (d) The Mysterious Visitor

He had been in government service in our town for a long time and held a prominent position; he was a man respected by all, rich, famous for his charity; he had given a considerable sum to the almshouse and the orphanage and, besides, had done many good deeds in secret, without publicity, all of which came out after his death. He was about fifty, with an almost stern look, and spoke little; he had been married no more than ten years, to a wife who was still young, and had three small children by her. Well, the next evening I was sitting at home, when suddenly my door opens and this very gentleman comes in.

I must note that I was no longer living in my old lodgings by then; as soon as I sent in my papers I had moved to others, renting from an old woman, a civil servant’s widow, with her servant; and I had moved to these lodgings only because on the very day I came back from the duel I had sent Afanasy back to his company, for I was ashamed to look him in the eyes after what I had done to him: so inclined is an unprepared man of the world to be ashamed even of some of his most righteous deeds.

“I have been listening to you,” says the gentleman who has come in, “for several days in various houses, with great curiosity, and I wished at last to make your personal acquaintance, so as to talk with you in more detail. Can you do me, my dear sir, so great a service?” “I can,” I say, “with the greatest pleasure, and shall count it a special honour.” I say this to him, but I was almost frightened, so much did he strike me from the first moment. For though people listened to me and were curious, no one had yet approached me with such a serious and stern inner look. And this man had even come to my lodgings himself. He sat down. “I see,” he goes on, “a great strength of character in you, for you were not afraid to serve the truth in a matter where you risked bearing the general contempt of everyone for your truth.” “Perhaps you are praising me much too highly,” I say to him. “No, not too highly,” he answers me. “Believe me, to do such a thing is much harder than you think. It is really just that,” he goes on, “that struck me, and that is why I have come to you. Describe to me, if you are not repelled by my perhaps indecent curiosity, what exactly you felt at the moment when you decided to ask forgiveness at the duel, if you remember. Don’t think my question frivolous; on the contrary, in asking it I have a secret purpose of my own, which I shall probably explain to you later, if it pleases God to bring us closer.”

All the time he was saying this I looked him straight in the face, and suddenly I felt the strongest trust in him, and besides that an extraordinary curiosity on my part too, for I felt that there was some special secret of his own in his soul.

“You ask what exactly I felt at the moment when I asked my adversary’s forgiveness,” I answer him, “but I had better tell you from the very beginning what I have not told others yet,” and I told him everything that had happened between me and Afanasy, and how I had bowed down to the ground before him. “From this you can see for yourself,” I concluded, “that during the duel it was already easier for me, for I had begun at home, and once I had set out on that road, all the rest went not only without difficulty but even joyfully and gaily.”

He heard me out and looked at me so kindly: “All this,” he says, “is extremely interesting; I shall come to you again and again.” And from then on he began coming to me almost every evening. And we would have become great friends if he had told me about himself too. But about himself he said hardly a word; he kept asking me about myself. In spite of that I came to love him very much and trusted him completely with all my feelings, for I thought: what are his secrets to me? I can see without them that he is a righteous man. Besides, he was so serious a man and so much older than I, and yet he came to me, a youth, and did not disdain me. And I learned much that was useful from him, for he was a man of high intelligence. “That life is paradise,” he says to me suddenly, “I have been thinking about that for a long time,” and suddenly he added: “It is all I think about.” He looks at me and smiles. “I am more convinced of it than you are,” he says; “later you will learn why.” I listen to this and think to myself: “He surely wants to reveal something to me.” “Paradise,” he says, “lies hidden in each of us; here it is hidden in me now, and, if I want, it will come for me tomorrow in reality, and for the rest of my life.” I look at him: he speaks with tender feeling and looks at me mysteriously, as if questioning me. “And as for every man being guilty for all and for everything, besides his own sins,” he continues, “you judged that quite rightly, and it is wonderful how you were able all at once to grasp the thought so fully. And it is truly so: when people understand this thought, the kingdom of heaven will come for them, no longer in dreams but in reality.” “But when,” I exclaimed to him with sorrow, “will that come true, and will it ever come true? Is it not only a dream?” “There, you don’t believe,” he says. “You preach and you don’t believe yourself. Know then that this dream, as you call it, will come true without doubt; believe that; but not now, for every action has its law. It is a matter of the soul, a psychological matter. To remake the world anew, people must themselves turn psychologically onto another road. Until you have really become a brother to everyone, brotherhood will not come. People will never, by any science or any advantage, manage to share out their property and their rights without offence. Everything will be too little for each, and they will all murmur, envy and destroy one another. You ask when it will come true. It will come true, but first the period of human isolation must come to an end.” “What isolation?” I ask him. “Why, the isolation that reigns everywhere now, and especially in our age; but it has not yet run its full course, and its time has not yet come. For everyone now strives to set his own person apart as far as possible, wants to experience the fullness of life in himself alone; and yet all his efforts lead, instead of to the fullness of life, only to complete suicide, for instead of the full definition of their being they fall into complete isolation. For in our age all have split into units; each withdraws into his hole; each keeps away from the other, hides himself and hides what he has, and ends by pushing himself away from people and pushing people away from himself. He piles up riches in isolation and thinks: how strong I am now and how secure; and the madman does not know that the more he piles up, the deeper he sinks into a suicidal impotence. For he has grown used to relying on himself alone and has split off from the whole as a unit; he has taught his soul not to believe in the help of others, in people and in mankind, and only trembles lest his money and the rights he has acquired be lost. Everywhere now the mind of man begins, mockingly, not to understand that the true security of the person lies not in his own isolated effort but in the common wholeness of mankind. But it will surely come to pass that this terrible isolation too will come to an end, and all will understand at once how unnaturally they have separated from one another. Such will be the spirit of the time, and they will wonder that they sat so long in darkness and did not see the light. And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in the heavens… But until then one must still guard the banner, and now and then a man must, if only alone, suddenly set an example and draw his soul out of isolation to the great work of brotherly communion, even if in the guise of a holy fool. So that the great idea does not die…”

In such fiery and rapturous conversations our evenings passed one after another. I even gave up society and began appearing much more rarely as a guest, besides which the fashion for me began to pass. I say this not in reproach, for they went on loving me and treating me cheerfully; but that fashion is no small queen in the world must, all the same, be admitted. My mysterious visitor I came at last to regard with admiration, for besides delighting in his mind I began to feel that he was nursing some plan within him and preparing for a great, perhaps heroic deed. Perhaps he liked it too that I did not outwardly show curiosity about his secret, nor question him about it either directly or by hints. But I noticed at last that he himself seemed to be beginning to long to reveal something to me. At least this became very evident about a month after he began visiting me. “Do you know,” he asked me once, “that the town is very curious about us both and wonders that I come to you so often? But let them, for soon everything will be explained.” Sometimes an extraordinary agitation would suddenly come over him, and almost always in such cases he would get up and go. Sometimes he would look at me for a long time, piercingly as it were, and I would think: “He is going to say something now,” but he would suddenly break off and begin to talk of something familiar and ordinary. He began to complain often of headaches too. And then once, quite unexpectedly, after he had been talking long and fervently, I saw him suddenly turn pale; his face was quite distorted, and he stared at me point-blank.
“What is the matter with you?” I say. “Aren’t you feeling unwell?”
He had, in fact, been complaining of a headache.
“I… do you know… I… killed a man.”
He said it and smiled, and he was as white as chalk. “Why is he smiling?” the thought suddenly pierced my heart before I had grasped anything. I turned pale myself.
“What are you saying?” I cry to him.
“You see,” he answers me, still with a pale smile, “how dearly it has cost me to say the first word. Now I have said it, and I seem to have set out on the road. I shall go on.”

For a long time I did not believe him, and I did not believe him all at once, but only after he had come to me for three days and told me everything in detail. I thought him mad, but ended by being convinced at last, plainly, with very great sorrow and amazement. He had committed a great and terrible crime fourteen years before, against a rich lady, young and beautiful, a widowed landowner who kept a house of her own in our town for her visits. Feeling a great love for her, he had declared his love and begun to urge her to marry him. But she had already given her heart to another, a distinguished military man of high rank, who was away on campaign at the time and whom she was expecting back soon. She refused his offer and asked him not to visit her. Having stopped visiting, he, knowing the arrangement of her house, made his way into it one night from the garden over the roof, with extraordinary audacity, risking discovery. But, as very often happens, crimes committed with extraordinary audacity succeed more often than others. Entering the attic of the house by a dormer window, he went down to her into the living rooms by the little attic stairs, knowing that the door at the bottom of the stairs, through the servants’ carelessness, was not always locked. He counted on this carelessness this time too, and was right. Having made his way into the living rooms, he went in the dark into her bedroom, where an icon lamp was burning. And, as if on purpose, both her maids had quietly gone out without leave to a name-day party in the same street. The rest of the servants, men and women, were asleep in the servants’ quarters and the kitchen on the ground floor. At the sight of the sleeping woman passion flared up in him, and then a vengeful, jealous fury seized his heart, and, beside himself, as if drunk, he went up and plunged a knife straight into her heart, so that she did not even cry out. Then, with a hellish and most criminal calculation, he arranged things so that the servants would be suspected: he did not scruple to take her purse; with keys he took from under her pillow he opened her chest of drawers and took some things from it, exactly as an ignorant servant would have done, that is, he left the securities and took only the money, took a few of the larger gold things, and passed over little things ten times more precious. He took something else besides, as a keepsake, but of that later. Having done this terrible deed, he left the way he had come. Neither on the next day, when the alarm was raised, nor ever afterwards in his whole life, did it enter anyone’s head to suspect the real criminal! And no one knew of his love for her, for he had always been of a silent and uncommunicative character and had no friend to whom he confided his soul. He was regarded simply as an acquaintance of the murdered woman, and not even a very close one, for in the last two weeks he had not visited her. Suspicion fell at once on her serf Pyotr, and all the circumstances came together to confirm the suspicion, for this servant knew, and the dead woman had not concealed it, that she meant to send him for a soldier, as part of the recruits due from her peasants, since he was a single man and of bad conduct besides. He had been heard threatening in a tavern, drunk and furious, to kill her. Two days before her death he had run away and was living somewhere in the town in unknown places. The day after the murder he was found on the road at the edge of the town, dead drunk, with a knife in his pocket, and his right palm, for some reason, stained with blood. He insisted that the blood was from his nose, but no one believed him. The maids confessed that they had been at the party and that the front door had stayed unlocked until they came back. And there were many more signs of the same kind besides, on account of which the innocent servant was seized. He was arrested and the trial began, but exactly a week later the prisoner fell ill with a fever and died in the hospital without regaining consciousness. With that the case ended; it was left to the will of God, and everyone, the judges, the authorities and the whole of society, remained convinced that the crime had been committed by none other than the dead servant. And after that the punishment began.

The mysterious visitor, now my friend, told me that at first he did not suffer pangs of conscience at all. He suffered for a long time, but not from that, only from regret that he had killed the woman he loved, that she was no more, that in killing her he had killed his love, while the fire of passion was still in his blood. But of the innocent blood shed, of the murder of a human being, he hardly thought then at all. The thought that his victim might have become another man’s wife seemed impossible to him, and so for a long time he was convinced in his conscience that he could not have acted otherwise. At first the servant’s arrest weighed on him somewhat, but the prisoner’s quick illness and then his death set his mind at rest, for the man had died, to all appearances (so he reasoned then), not of the arrest or of fright but of a chill caught precisely in the days when he was on the run, when, dead drunk, he had lain a whole night on the damp ground. The stolen things and money troubled him little, for (he reasoned in the same way) the theft had been done not for gain but to turn suspicion elsewhere. The sum stolen was insignificant, and he soon gave all of it, and even much more, to the almshouse being founded in our town. He did this on purpose to set his conscience at rest about the theft, and, remarkably, for a time, and even a long time, he really was at rest; he told me so himself. He threw himself then into great activity in his service; he asked for a troublesome and difficult commission himself, which occupied him for about two years, and, being of a strong character, he almost forgot what had happened; and when he did remember it, he tried not to think of it at all. He threw himself into charity too; he set up and gave much in our town, and made his name in the capitals as well, being elected a member of charitable societies in Moscow and Petersburg. But all the same he began at last to brood, with a torment beyond his strength. Then a beautiful and sensible girl took his fancy, and he soon married her, dreaming that by marriage he would drive away his solitary anguish, and that, entering on a new road and zealously doing his duty by his wife and children, he would get away from his old memories altogether. But exactly the opposite of that expectation happened. Even in the first month of the marriage a constant thought began to trouble him: “Here my wife loves me; but what if she knew?” When she became pregnant with their first child and told him so, he was suddenly troubled: “I am giving life, and I have taken life.” Children came: “How dare I love them, teach them and bring them up? How shall I speak to them of virtue? I have shed blood.” The children were growing up beautifully; he wanted to caress them: “But I cannot look at their innocent, bright faces; I am unworthy of it.” At last the blood of his murdered victim began to haunt him menacingly and bitterly, her ruined young life, the blood crying out for vengeance. He began to have terrible dreams. But, being firm of heart, he bore the torment for a long time: “I shall redeem everything by this secret torment of mine.” But that hope too was in vain: the further it went, the stronger the suffering became. In society they came to respect him for his charitable work, though everyone was afraid of his stern and gloomy character; but the more they respected him, the more unbearable it became for him. He confessed to me that he had thought of killing himself. But instead another dream began to haunt him, a dream he thought at first impossible and mad, but which at last fastened itself to his heart so that it could not be torn away. This was his dream: to rise up, go out before the people and announce to everyone that he had killed a human being. For about three years he went about with this dream; it haunted him in various forms. At last he believed with all his heart that by declaring his crime he would heal his soul without doubt and be at peace once for all. But having believed it, he felt horror in his heart, for how was he to do it? And suddenly this incident of my duel happened. “Looking at you, I have now made up my mind.” I look at him.
“And can it be,” I exclaimed to him, throwing up my hands, “that so small an incident could give birth to such a resolve in you?”
“My resolve has been three years being born,” he answers me, “and your incident only gave it a push. Looking at you, I reproached myself and envied you,” he said to me, even with sternness.
“But they won’t believe you,” I observed to him. “Fourteen years have passed.”
“I have proofs, great ones. I shall present them.”
And I wept then and kissed him.

“Decide one thing for me, one thing!” he said to me (as though everything now depended on me). “My wife, my children! My wife may die of grief, and my children, though they will not lose their rank and property, will be a convict’s children, and for ever. And the memory, the memory of me I shall leave in their hearts!”
I am silent.
“And to part with them, to leave them for ever? For it is for ever, for ever!”
I sit, whispering a prayer to myself in silence. At last I got up; I was frightened.
“Well?” he looks at me.
“Go,” I say, “and declare it to people. Everything will pass; only the truth will remain. The children will understand, when they grow up, how much magnanimity there was in your great resolve.”

He left me then as though he had really made up his mind. Yet for more than two weeks after that he came to me every evening without a break, still preparing himself, still unable to bring himself to it. He wore my heart out. Now he would come in firm and say with tender feeling:

“I know that paradise will come for me; it will come the moment I declare it. For fourteen years I have been in hell. I want to suffer. I shall take my suffering and begin to live. You can go through the world on a lie, but you cannot come back. Now I dare not love not only my neighbour but even my own children. Lord, perhaps the children will understand what my suffering has cost me, and will not condemn me! God is not in might but in truth.”
“Everyone will understand your great deed,” I say to him. “If not now, they will understand later, for you have served the truth, the higher truth, not of this earth…”
And he would leave me as if comforted, and the next day he would suddenly come again, spiteful and pale, and say mockingly:

“Every time I come in, you look at me with such curiosity: ‘So he hasn’t declared it again?’ Wait, don’t despise me too much. It isn’t as easy to do as you think. Perhaps I won’t do it at all. You won’t go and inform on me then, eh?”
And I, so far from looking at him with foolish curiosity, was afraid even to glance at him. I was worn out to the point of illness, and my soul was full of tears. I even lost my sleep at night.

“I have just come from my wife,” he goes on. “Do you understand what a wife is? When I was leaving, the children called out to me: ‘Goodbye, papa, come back soon and read Children’s Reading with us.’ No, you don’t understand this! Another man’s trouble doesn’t teach you sense.”
His eyes flashed, his lips twitched. Suddenly he struck the table with his fist so that the things on it jumped. Such a gentle man; it was the first time it had happened to him.

“But is it necessary?” he cried. “Is it needed? No one was convicted, no one was sent to penal servitude because of me; the servant died of illness. And for the blood I shed I have been punished with torments. And they won’t believe me at all; they won’t believe any of my proofs. Must I declare it, must I? For the blood I shed I am ready to go on suffering all my life, only so as not to strike down my wife and children. Will it be just to ruin them along with me? Aren’t we mistaken? Where is the truth here? And will people know this truth, value it, respect it?”

“Lord!” I think to myself. “He is thinking of people’s respect at such a moment!” And I felt so sorry for him then that I think I would have shared his lot myself if only to ease it for him. I see that he is as if in a frenzy. I was horrified, understanding now not with my mind alone but with my living soul what such a resolve costs.
“Decide my fate!” he cried again.

“Go and declare it,” I whispered to him. My voice failed me, but I whispered it firmly. Then I took the Gospel from the table, the Russian translation, and showed him John, chapter twelve, verse twenty-four:
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.” I had read that verse just before he came.
He read it.
“True,” he says, but smiled bitterly. “Yes, in these books,” he says after a pause, “you come across horrors. It’s easy to shove them under people’s noses. And who wrote them? Can it have been men?”
“The Holy Spirit wrote them,” I say.

“It’s easy for you to chatter,” he smiled again, but almost with hatred now. I took the book again, opened it at another place and showed him Hebrews, chapter ten, verse thirty-one. He read: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.”
He read it and flung the book aside. He was trembling all over.

“A fearful verse,” he says. “No denying it, you have picked one.” He got up from his chair. “Well,” he says, “goodbye; perhaps I won’t come again… we shall meet in paradise. So for fourteen years I have already ‘fallen into the hands of the living God’; that is what these fourteen years are called, it seems. Tomorrow I shall ask those hands to let me go…”

I wanted to embrace and kiss him, but I did not dare: his face was so twisted and his look was so heavy. He went out. “Lord,” I thought, “where has the man gone?” I threw myself on my knees then before the icon and wept for him to the most holy Mother of God, the swift intercessor and helper. Half an hour passed as I stood in tears at prayer, and it was already late at night, about twelve. Suddenly I see the door open, and he comes in again. I was amazed.
“Where have you been?” I ask him.
“I,” he says, “I think I forgot something… my handkerchief, I think… Well, even if I didn’t forget anything, let me sit down…”

He sat down on a chair. I stand over him. “Sit down too,” he says. I sat down. We sat for about two minutes; he looked at me intently and suddenly smiled (I remembered that); then he got up, embraced me tightly and kissed me…
“Remember,” he says, “how I came to you the second time. Do you hear, remember it!”
It was the first time he had called me “thou”. And he went out. “Tomorrow,” I thought.

And so it came to pass. I did not know that evening that the next day happened to be his birthday. I had not gone out anywhere in the last days, and so I could not have learned it from anyone. On that day every year there was a great gathering at his house; the whole town came. They came now too. And then, after dinner, he comes out into the middle of the room with a paper in his hands, a formal report to his superiors. And since his superiors were right there, he read the paper aloud then and there to all who were gathered, and in it was a full description of the whole crime in every detail. “I cast myself out from among men as a monster; God has visited me,” he concluded the paper. “I want to suffer!” Then and there he brought out and laid on the table everything by which he thought to prove his crime and which he had kept for fourteen years: the murdered woman’s gold things, which he had taken to turn suspicion from himself; her locket and cross, taken from her neck (in the locket, a portrait of her betrothed); her notebook; and lastly two letters: her betrothed’s letter to her announcing his speedy arrival, and her answer to that letter, which she had begun and not finished and left on the table to send to the post the next day. He had taken both letters with him. Why? Why had he kept them afterwards for fourteen years instead of destroying them as evidence? And what happened? Everyone was amazed and horrified, and no one wanted to believe it, though everyone listened with extraordinary curiosity, but as to a sick man; and a few days later it was decided and settled in every house that the unhappy man had gone out of his mind. The authorities and the court could not but take the matter up, but they too held back: though the things and letters presented did make them think, it was decided there too that even if these documents proved genuine, a final conviction could not be pronounced on the strength of these documents alone. Besides, he might have had all the things from her herself, as her acquaintance and in trust. I heard, however, that the genuineness of the things was later verified through many acquaintances and relatives of the murdered woman and that there was no doubt about it. But again this case was not destined to be concluded. About five days later everyone learned that the sufferer had fallen ill and that his life was feared for. What illness he fell ill with I cannot explain; they said it was a disorder of the heart; but it became known that a council of doctors, at his wife’s insistence, had examined his mental state too and concluded that there was already madness. I gave nothing away, though people rushed to question me; but when I wanted to visit him, I was kept away for a long time, chiefly by his wife. “It was you,” she tells me, “who upset him. He was gloomy before, and in the last year everyone noticed an extraordinary agitation in him and strange behaviour, and then you ruined him; it was you who talked him into it; he never left your rooms for a whole month.” And what happened? Not only his wife, but everyone in the town fell upon me and blamed me: “It’s all your doing,” they said. I keep silent, and in my soul I am glad, for I have beheld the unmistakable mercy of God to a man who rose up against himself and punished himself. And I could not believe in his madness. At last they let me in to him too; he had demanded it insistently himself, to take leave of me. I went in and saw at once that not only his days but his hours were numbered. He was weak and yellow, his hands trembling, he was gasping for breath, but he looked tender and joyful.
“It is accomplished!” he said to me. “I have long been longing to see you; why didn’t you come?”
I did not tell him that I had not been allowed in to him.

“God has had pity on me and is calling me to himself. I know I am dying, but I feel joy and peace for the first time after so many years. I felt paradise in my soul at once, as soon as I had done what had to be done. Now I dare to love my children and kiss them. They don’t believe me, and no one has believed me, neither my wife nor my judges; and my children will never believe it. I see God’s mercy to my children in that. I shall die, and my name will be unstained for them. And now I feel God near; my heart rejoices as in paradise… I have done my duty…”
He cannot speak; he gasps for breath; he presses my hand warmly and looks at me with fire. But we did not talk long; his wife kept looking in on us. But he did manage to whisper to me:
“And do you remember how I came back to you that second time, at midnight? And told you to remember it? Do you know why I came in? I came to kill you!”
I simply shuddered.

“I went out from you then into the darkness, wandered about the streets and fought with myself. And suddenly I hated you so that my heart could hardly bear it. ‘Now,’ I thought, ‘he alone has bound me, and he is my judge; I can no longer refuse tomorrow’s punishment, for he knows everything.’ And not that I was afraid you would inform (there was not a thought of that), but I thought: ‘How shall I look at him if I don’t declare myself?’ And even if you had been at the ends of the earth, but alive, it would have been all the same: the thought was unbearable that you were alive and knew everything and were judging me. I hated you as if you were the cause of everything and to blame for everything. I came back to you then; I remember there was a dagger lying on your table. I sat down and asked you to sit down, and for a whole minute I was thinking. If I had killed you, I should have been ruined for that murder all the same, even if I had not declared my former crime. But I did not think of that at all, and did not want to think of it at that moment. I only hated you and wanted with all my strength to take revenge on you for everything. But my Lord overcame the devil in my heart. Know, though, that you were never nearer to death.”

A week later he died. The whole town followed his coffin to the grave. The archpriest gave a heartfelt address. They mourned the terrible illness that had cut short his days. But the whole town rose against me when they had buried him, and they even stopped receiving me. True, some, few at first, and then more and more, began to believe in the truth of his confession, and began visiting me a great deal and questioning me with great curiosity and joy: for man loves the fall of the righteous and his disgrace. But I fell silent and soon left the town altogether, and five months later I was found worthy by the Lord God to set out on the firm and goodly path, blessing the unseen finger that had so plainly shown me this path. And the much-suffering servant of God Mikhail I remember in my prayers every day to this day.
## Book Six, Chapter III · From the Talks and Teachings of Elder Zosima · (e) Something of the Russian Monk and His Possible Significance

Fathers and teachers, what is a monk? In the enlightened world this word is spoken nowadays by some with mockery, and by some even as a term of abuse. And the further it goes, the more so. True, oh true, there are many parasites in the monastic life too, gluttons, voluptuaries and insolent vagabonds. Educated people of the world point to this: “You are idlers and useless members of society,” they say; “you live on other people’s labour; you are shameless beggars.” And yet how many in the monastic life are humble and meek, thirsting for solitude and for fervent prayer in silence. These are pointed to less, and even passed over in silence altogether; and how surprised people would be if I said that from these meek ones, who thirst for solitary prayer, the salvation of the Russian land will come forth perhaps once more! For truly they are made ready in silence “for the day and the hour, the month and the year”. Meanwhile, in their solitude, they keep the image of Christ beautiful and undistorted, in the purity of God’s truth, from the most ancient fathers, apostles and martyrs, and when the time comes they will reveal it to the shaken truth of the world. That is a great thought. This star will shine forth from the East.

That is what I think of the monk; and is it false, is it arrogant? Look at the worldly, and at the whole world that exalts itself above the people of God: has not the image of God and his truth been distorted in it? They have science; but in science there is only what is subject to the senses. The spiritual world, the higher half of man’s being, is rejected altogether, driven out with a kind of triumph, even with hatred. The world has proclaimed freedom, especially of late, and what do we see in this freedom of theirs? Nothing but slavery and suicide! For the world says: “You have needs, so satisfy them, for you have the same rights as the most distinguished and the richest. Do not be afraid to satisfy them; multiply them even.” That is the world’s teaching today. In that they see freedom. And what comes of this right to multiply needs? Among the rich, isolation and spiritual suicide; among the poor, envy and murder; for they have been given the rights, but not yet shown the means of satisfying the needs. They assure us that the more the world goes on, the more it is united, that it is forming itself into a brotherly communion, because it shortens distances and sends thoughts through the air. Alas, do not believe in such a union of people. Taking freedom to mean the multiplying and the speedy satisfaction of needs, they distort their own nature, for they breed in themselves many senseless and foolish desires, habits and the most absurd inventions. They live only for envy of one another, for the pleasures of the flesh and for vanity. To have dinners, carriages, horses, rank and slavish servants is now thought such a necessity that people sacrifice even life, honour and love of mankind to satisfy it, and even kill themselves if they cannot satisfy it. Among those who are not rich we see the same; and among the poor the unsatisfied needs and the envy are drowned for the present in drink. But soon, instead of wine, they will drink their fill of blood; that is where they are being led. I ask you: is such a man free? I knew one “fighter for an idea” who told me himself that when they deprived him of tobacco in prison he was so tormented by the deprivation that he very nearly went and betrayed his “idea” just to be given some tobacco. And this sort of man says: “I am going to fight for mankind.” Well, how far will such a man go, and what is he capable of? A quick deed, perhaps, but he will not endure long. And no wonder that instead of freedom they have fallen into slavery, and instead of serving brotherly love and human unity they have fallen, on the contrary, into separation and isolation, as my mysterious visitor and teacher told me in my youth. And so in the world the idea of serving mankind, of the brotherhood and wholeness of people, is dying out more and more, and indeed this idea is now met even with mockery; for how is a man to give up his habits, where is this slave to go, if he is so used to satisfying the countless needs he has invented for himself? He is in isolation, and what is the whole to him? And they have reached the point where they have piled up more things, but there is less joy.

The monastic way is a different matter. People even laugh at obedience, fasting and prayer, and yet in them alone lies the way to real, true freedom: I cut away from myself superfluous and unnecessary needs, I humble my proud and self-loving will and scourge it with obedience, and by this, with God’s help, I attain freedom of spirit, and with it spiritual gladness! Which of them is more capable of raising up a great idea and going to serve it: the isolated rich man, or this man freed from the tyranny of things and habits? The monk is reproached for his solitude: “You have shut yourself away to save yourself within the monastery walls, and you have forgotten brotherly service to mankind.” But we shall see who will be more zealous in brotherly love. For the isolation is not with us but with them, only they do not see it. From us, from of old, came men who acted for the people; why should there not be such men now? The same humble and meek men of fasting and silence will rise up and go to the great work. The salvation of Russia is from the people. And the Russian monastery has from of old been with the people. If the people are in isolation, then we too are in isolation. The people believe as we do, and an unbelieving man of action will do nothing in Russia, even if he is sincere at heart and a genius in mind. Remember this. The people will meet the atheist and overcome him, and Russia will become one and Orthodox. Take care of the people, then, and guard their heart. Bring them up in quietness. That is your monastic labour, for this people is a God-bearer.
## (f) Something of Masters and Servants, and Whether It Is Possible for Masters and Servants to Become Brothers in Spirit

God knows there is sin among the people too. And the flame of corruption is spreading visibly, hourly; it comes from above. Isolation is coming upon the people too: kulaks and bloodsuckers of the commune are appearing; already the merchant wants more and more honours, strives to show himself educated without having the least education, and to this end basely scorns ancient custom and is even ashamed of the faith of his fathers. He visits princes, though he is only a spoilt peasant himself. The people are festering with drink and cannot give it up. And how much cruelty there is to their families, to their wives, even to their children; all from drink. I have seen in factories children even ten years old: sickly, stunted, bent and already depraved. A stifling room, a clattering machine, work all God’s day, depraved words and drink, drink; and is that what the soul of so small a child needs? He needs sunshine, children’s games, a bright example everywhere, and at least a drop of love for him. Let there be no more of this, monks; let there be no torturing of children; rise up and preach it quickly, quickly. But God will save Russia, for though the simple man is corrupt and can no longer deny himself his foul sin, yet he knows that his foul sin is cursed by God and that he does wrong in sinning. So our people still believe unwearyingly in righteousness; they acknowledge God; they weep with tender feeling. It is not so with the upper classes. They, following science, want to arrange things justly by their reason alone, but without Christ now, unlike before, and they have already proclaimed that there is no crime, no sin. And that is right, by their way of thinking: for if you have no God, what crime can there be? In Europe the people are already rising against the rich by force, and the people’s leaders everywhere are leading them to blood and teaching them that their wrath is just. But “cursed be their anger, for it was fierce.” And the Lord will save Russia, as he has saved her many times before. Salvation will come from the people, from their faith and their humility. Fathers and teachers, guard the people’s faith; and this is no dream. All my life I have been struck by the true and seemly dignity of our great people; I have seen it myself; I can bear witness myself; I have seen it and wondered at it; I have seen it in spite of the stench of sins and the beggarly look of our people. They are not servile, and this after two centuries of slavery. They are free in look and bearing, but without any insolence. And they are not vindictive and not envious. “You are noble, you are rich, you are clever and gifted; very well, God bless you. I honour you, but I know that I too am a man.
