By honouring you without envy I show you my human dignity.” Truly, if they do not say this (for they do not yet know how to say it), that is how they act; I have seen it myself, I have experienced it myself; and would you believe it, the poorer and lower our Russian man is, the more this seemly truth is to be seen in him; for the rich among them, the kulaks and bloodsuckers, are already corrupted in great numbers, and much, much of that has come from our own negligence and lack of care! But God will save his people, for Russia is great in her humility. I dream of seeing our future, and I seem to see it clearly already: for it will come to pass that even the most corrupt of our rich men will end by being ashamed of his riches before the poor, and the poor man, seeing this humility, will understand and give way to him with joy, and will answer his seemly shame with kindness. Believe that it will end so: things are going that way. Equality is only in man’s spiritual dignity, and this will be understood only among us. If there were brothers, there would be brotherhood; but before there is brotherhood they will never share things out. We keep the image of Christ, and it will shine forth like a precious diamond to the whole world… So be it, so be it!

Fathers and teachers, a touching thing happened to me once. In my wanderings I met, in the provincial town of K., my former orderly Afanasy; eight years had passed since I had parted from him. He caught sight of me by chance in the market, recognised me, ran up to me, and, God, how glad he was! He simply flew at me: “Father, master, is it you? Can I really be seeing you?” He took me home with him. He had left the service by then, married, and already had two baby children. He and his wife made their living by petty trade in the market, from a stall. His little room was poor but clean and joyful. He sat me down, put on the samovar, sent for his wife, as if I had made a holiday for him by turning up there. He brought the children to me: “Bless them, Father.” “Is it for me to bless them?” I answer him. “I am a simple, humble monk. I will pray to God for them; and for you, Afanasy Pavlovich, I pray to God always, every day, from that very day, for everything came from you,” I tell him. And I explained it to him as best I could. And what of the man? He looks at me and still cannot picture to himself that I, his former master, an officer, am now before him in such a guise and such clothes: he even began to cry. “Why are you crying?” I say to him. “You unforgettable man, rather rejoice in your soul for me, my dear, for my path is joyful and bright.” He did not say much, but kept sighing and shaking his head at me tenderly. “Where is your fortune, then?” he asks. I answer him: “I gave it to the monastery, and we live in common.” After tea I began to take leave of them, and suddenly he brought me out a half-rouble, an offering for the monastery; and another half-rouble, I see, he is hurriedly pushing into my hand: “That is for you,” he says, “a wanderer, a traveller; it may be of use to you, Father.” I accepted his half-rouble, bowed to him and to his wife, and went away gladdened, and thought on the way: “Here we both are now, he at home and I on the road, sighing, no doubt, and smiling joyfully in the gladness of our hearts, nodding our heads and remembering how God brought us to meet.” And I never saw him again after that. I was his master and he my servant; and now, when we had kissed each other lovingly and in spiritual tenderness, a great human union had come about between us. I have thought about this a great deal, and now I think this: is it so inconceivable that this great and simple-hearted union might in its time come about everywhere among our Russian people? I believe that it will, and that the time is near.

And about servants I will add the following. As a youth I used to be very angry with servants: “The cook served it too hot; my orderly didn’t brush my clothes.” But then the thought of my dear brother, which I had heard from him in my childhood, suddenly lit me up: “Am I worth it, am I worth it at all, that another should serve me, and that I should order him about because of his poverty and ignorance?” And I wondered then how late the simplest thoughts, plain to the eye, appear in our minds. It is impossible to be without servants in the world, but act so that your servant is freer in spirit than if he were not a servant. And why can I not be a servant to my servant, and in such a way that he even sees it, and without any pride on my part or any disbelief on his? Why should my servant not be like my own kin, so that I take him at last into my family and rejoice in it? Even now this can be done, and it will serve as the foundation for the future, already magnificent, union of men, when a man will not seek servants for himself and will not want to turn people like himself into servants, as now, but, on the contrary, will want with all his strength to become himself the servant of all, according to the Gospel. And is it a dream, that in the end man will find his joys only in deeds of enlightenment and mercy, and not in cruel joys, as now, in gluttony, fornication, vanity, boasting and the envious lording of one over another? I believe firmly that it is not, and that the time is near. They laugh and ask: when will this time come, and does it look as if it will come? But I think that with Christ we shall bring about this great thing. And how many ideas have there been on earth, in human history, which were unthinkable even ten years before and which suddenly appeared when their mysterious time had come, and swept over the whole earth? So it will be with us, and our people will shine forth to the world, and all people will say: “The stone which the builders rejected is become the head of the corner.” And the mockers themselves should be asked: if ours is a dream, then when will you put up your building and arrange things justly by your reason alone, without Christ? If they themselves declare that they, on the contrary, are moving towards union, truly only the most simple-hearted of them believe it, so that one may even wonder at such simple-heartedness. Truly they have more of dreamy fancy than we. They mean to arrange things justly, but, having rejected Christ, they will end by drenching the world in blood, for blood calls for blood, and he who draws the sword shall perish by the sword. And were it not for Christ’s promise, they would destroy one another even to the last two men on earth. And even those last two would not manage, in their pride, to restrain each other, so that the last would destroy the last but one and then himself. And it would come to pass, were it not for Christ’s promise that for the sake of the meek and humble this thing shall be cut short. In those days, still in my officer’s uniform, after my duel, I began to speak about servants in society, and everyone, I remember, wondered at me: “What,” they said, “are we to sit our servant on the sofa and bring him tea?” And I answered them then: “Why not, if only sometimes?” Everyone laughed then. Their question was frivolous, and my answer unclear; but I think there was some truth in it too.
## (g) Of Prayer, of Love, and of Contact with Other Worlds

Young man, do not forget prayer. Every time you pray, if your prayer is sincere, a new feeling will flash through it, and with it a new thought you did not know before, which will give you fresh courage; and you will understand that prayer is an education. Remember this too: every day, and whenever you can, repeat to yourself: “Lord, have mercy on all who have stood before thee this day.” For at every hour and every moment thousands of people leave their life on this earth, and their souls stand before the Lord; and how many of them have parted from the earth in isolation, unknown to anyone, in sadness and anguish that no one will grieve for them or even know of them at all, whether they lived or not. And there, perhaps from the other end of the earth, your prayer for his rest will rise up to the Lord, though you did not know him at all, nor he you. How moving it is for his soul, standing in fear before the Lord, to feel at that moment that there is someone praying for him too, that there is still a human being left on earth who loves him. And God will look more mercifully on you both, for if you have pitied him so much, how much more will he pity him, he who is infinitely more merciful and loving than you. And he will forgive him for your sake.

Brothers, do not be afraid of men’s sin; love man even in his sin, for that is already a likeness of divine love and is the height of love on earth. Love all God’s creation, the whole of it and every grain of sand. Love every leaf, every ray of God’s light. Love the animals, love the plants, love everything. If you love everything, you will perceive the mystery of God in things. Once you perceive it, you will begin to understand it more and more every day, unwearyingly. And you will come at last to love the whole world with an all-embracing, universal love. Love the animals: God has given them the beginnings of thought and an untroubled joy. Do not trouble it, do not torment them, do not take away their joy, do not go against God’s thought. Man, do not exalt yourself above the animals: they are sinless, and you, with your greatness, defile the earth by appearing on it and leave the trail of your defilement behind you; alas, almost every one of us! Love children especially, for they too are sinless, like the angels, and live to soften our hearts, to purify our hearts, and as a kind of guidance for us. Woe to him who offends a child. Father Anfim taught me to love children: dear, silent man that he was on our wanderings, he would buy them little gingerbreads and sweets with the coppers we were given, and hand them out; he could not pass children without his soul being stirred; such was the man.

Before some thought you will stand bewildered, especially at the sight of men’s sin, and you will ask yourself: “Shall I take it by force, or by humble love?” Always decide: “I will take it by humble love.” If you decide so once for all, you may be able to conquer the whole world. Loving humility is a terrible force, the strongest of all, and there is nothing like it. Every day and hour, every minute, walk round yourself and watch yourself, so that your image may be seemly. You pass by a little child; you pass by spiteful, with a foul word, with an angry soul; perhaps you did not even notice the child, but he saw you, and your image, unlovely and ungodly, may remain in his defenceless little heart. You did not know it, but perhaps by that you have already sown a bad seed in him, and it may grow, and all because you did not take care before the child, because you did not nurture in yourself a careful, active love. Brothers, love is a teacher, but one must know how to acquire it, for it is acquired with difficulty, it is bought dearly, by long work and over a long time; for one must love not only for a chance moment but for all time. Anyone can love by chance; even a villain can love. My young brother asked the birds to forgive him: it seems senseless, but it is the truth, for everything is like an ocean; everything flows and touches; touch it in one place and it echoes at the other end of the world. Let it be madness to ask the birds’ forgiveness; still, it would be easier for the birds, and for the child, and for every animal around you, if you yourself were more seemly than you are now, if only by one drop. Everything is like an ocean, I tell you. Then you would pray to the birds too, tormented by an all-embracing love, as if in some rapture, and pray that they too should forgive you your sin. Treasure this rapture, however senseless it may seem to people.

My friends, ask God for gladness. Be glad as children, as the birds of heaven. And let not men’s sin trouble you in your work; do not be afraid that it will wear your work away and not let it be done. Do not say: “Sin is strong, wickedness is strong, the foul surroundings are strong, and we are alone and powerless; the foul surroundings will wear us down and not let the good work be done.” Flee from this despondency, children! There is only one salvation for you: take yourself and make yourself answerable for all men’s sin. Friend, that is indeed the truth, for as soon as you make yourself sincerely answerable for everything and for everyone, you will see at once that it really is so, and that you are guilty for all and for everything. But throwing your own laziness and your own powerlessness onto others, you will end by sharing in Satan’s pride and murmuring against God. Of Satan’s pride I think this: it is hard for us on earth even to comprehend it, and so how easy it is to fall into error and share in it, and while thinking that we are doing something great and beautiful. Indeed, many of the strongest feelings and movements of our nature we cannot comprehend while we are on earth. Do not be led astray by that either, and do not think that it can serve to justify you in anything, for the eternal judge will ask of you what you could comprehend, not what you could not; you will be convinced of that yourself, for then you will see everything rightly and will no longer argue. On earth, indeed, we seem to wander, and if the precious image of Christ were not before us, we should perish and go utterly astray, like the human race before the flood. Much on earth is hidden from us, but in return we have been given a secret, hidden sense of our living bond with another world, a higher and heavenly world; and the roots of our thoughts and feelings are not here but in other worlds. That is why the philosophers say that the essence of things cannot be comprehended on earth. God took seeds from other worlds and sowed them on this earth and grew his garden, and everything that could come up came up; but what has grown lives and is alive only through the feeling of its contact with mysterious other worlds. If that feeling grows weak or is destroyed in you, then what has grown in you dies too. Then you will become indifferent to life and even come to hate it. That is what I think.
## (h) Can One Be the Judge of One’s Fellow Men? Of Faith to the End

Remember especially that you cannot be anyone’s judge. For there can be no judge of a criminal on earth until the judge himself knows that he too is just such a criminal as the one standing before him, and that he perhaps is more to blame than anyone for the crime of the one before him. When he understands that, then he will be able to be a judge. However mad it may seem, it is the truth. For if I myself were righteous, perhaps there would be no criminal standing before me. If you can take upon yourself the crime of the criminal who stands before you and whom your heart is judging, then take it at once and suffer for him yourself, and let him go without reproach. And even if the law itself has made you his judge, act in that spirit then too, as far as you possibly can, for he will go away and condemn himself more bitterly than your judgement would. And if he goes away unfeeling after your kiss, laughing at you, do not be led astray by that either: it means his time has not yet come, but it will come in its time; and if it does not come, no matter: if not he, then another in his place will understand, and suffer, and condemn and accuse himself, and justice will be fulfilled. Believe this, believe it without doubt, for in this very thing lies all the hope and all the faith of the saints.

Work unceasingly. If you remember in the night, as you lie down to sleep, “I have not done what I ought to have done,” get up at once and do it. If the people around you are spiteful and unfeeling and will not listen to you, fall down before them and beg their forgiveness, for truly you too are to blame that they do not want to listen to you. And if you can no longer speak with the embittered, serve them in silence and in lowliness, never losing hope. And if everyone abandons you and even drives you out by force, then, left alone, fall on the earth and kiss it, water it with your tears, and the earth will bear fruit from your tears, even though no one has seen or heard you in your solitude. Believe to the end, even if it should happen that everyone on earth were led astray and you alone remained faithful: offer your sacrifice even then, and praise God, you who alone remain. And if two of you such come together, there is already the whole world, a world of living love; embrace each other in tenderness and praise the Lord: for, if only in the two of you, his truth has been fulfilled.

If you yourself sin and are sorrowful even unto death for your sins, or for your sudden sin, then rejoice for another, rejoice for the righteous one, rejoice that if you have sinned, he is righteous and has not sinned.

But if the wickedness of men rouses in you an indignation and a grief that cannot be overcome, even to the point of wanting revenge on the wicked, then fear that feeling most of all; go at once and seek torments for yourself, as if you yourself were guilty of that wickedness of men. Take those torments and endure them, and your heart will be appeased, and you will understand that you too are guilty, for you might have shone a light for the wicked, even as the one sinless man, and you did not. If you had shone, your light would have lit the way for others too, and he who did the wicked deed would perhaps not have done it in your light. And even if you did shine but see that people are not saved even by your light, then remain firm and do not doubt the power of the heavenly light; believe that if they have not been saved now, they will be saved later. And if they are not saved later, their sons will be saved, for your light will not die, even though you have died. The righteous man departs, but his light remains. People are always saved after the death of him who saves them. The human race does not accept its prophets and kills them, but people love their martyrs and honour those whom they have tortured to death. And you are working for the whole, acting for the future. Never seek a reward, for great is your reward on this earth without it: your spiritual joy, which only the righteous find. Do not fear the great or the mighty, but be wise and always seemly. Know the measure, know the times; learn this. And when you are alone, pray. Love to throw yourself down on the earth and kiss it. Kiss the earth and love it unceasingly, insatiably; love all men, love everything; seek this rapture and ecstasy. Water the earth with the tears of your joy and love those tears of yours. And do not be ashamed of this ecstasy; treasure it, for it is a gift of God, a great one, and it is not given to many, but to the chosen.
## (i) Of Hell and Hellfire: A Mystical Reflection

Fathers and teachers, I ask myself: “What is hell?” And I reason thus: “The suffering of being no longer able to love.” Once, in infinite existence, unmeasured by time or space, a certain spiritual being was given, through his appearance on earth, the ability to say to himself: “I am, and I love.” Once, only once, he was given a moment of active, living love, and for that earthly life was given him, and with it times and seasons; and what then? This fortunate being rejected the priceless gift, did not value it, did not love it, looked at it mockingly and remained unfeeling. Such a one, having already left the earth, sees Abraham’s bosom and talks with Abraham, as we are shown in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, and beholds paradise, and can go up to the Lord; but he is tormented precisely by this, that he will go up to the Lord, he who did not love, and come into contact with those who loved, he who scorned their love. For he sees clearly and says to himself: “Now I have knowledge, and though I have come to thirst to love, there will be no great deed in my love now, nor any sacrifice, for earthly life is over, and Abraham will not come with even a drop of living water (that is, with the gift of earthly life again, the former, active life) to cool the flame of thirst for spiritual love with which I burn now, having scorned it on earth; life is no more, and there shall be time no longer! Even if I would gladly give my life for others, I cannot now, for the life that could have been offered as a sacrifice to love has passed, and now there is a gulf between that life and this existence.” They speak of a material fire in hell. I do not search into that mystery, and I fear it; but I think that if there were a material fire, they would truly be glad of it, for, so I fancy, in material torment the still more terrible spiritual torment would be forgotten for a moment at least. And it is impossible to take that spiritual torment from them, for the torment is not outside them but within. And if it were possible to take it away, then, I think, they would be made even more bitterly unhappy by it. For though the righteous in paradise might forgive them, beholding their torments, and call them to themselves, loving them infinitely, by that very thing they would only multiply their torments, for they would rouse in them still more strongly the flame of thirst for an answering, active and grateful love which is no longer possible. In the timidity of my heart I think, however, that the very awareness of this impossibility would at last serve to relieve them, for, accepting the love of the righteous with no possibility of repaying it, in this submission and in the act of this humility they will find at last a kind of likeness of that active love which they scorned on earth, and a kind of action resembling it… I am sorry, my brothers and friends, that I cannot say this clearly. But woe to those who have destroyed themselves on earth, woe to the suicides! I think there can be none more unhappy than they. It is a sin, they tell us, to pray to God for them, and the church outwardly seems to reject them; but I think in the secret of my soul that one may pray for them too. Christ will not be angry at love. For such as these I have prayed inwardly all my life, I confess it to you, fathers and teachers, and I pray for them every day now.

Oh, there are some who remain proud and fierce even in hell, in spite of their certain knowledge and their contemplation of irrefutable truth; there are terrible ones who have given themselves wholly to Satan and his proud spirit. For them hell is voluntary and insatiable; they are martyrs of their own will. For they have cursed themselves, cursing God and life. They feed on their own spiteful pride, as if a starving man in the desert began to suck the blood out of his own body. But they are insatiable for ever and ever, and they reject forgiveness; they curse God who calls them. They cannot behold the living God without hatred, and they demand that there be no God of life, that God destroy himself and all his creation. And they will burn in the fire of their own wrath for ever, and thirst for death and non-existence. But they will not receive death.

Here Alexei Fyodorovich Karamazov’s manuscript ends. I repeat: it is incomplete and fragmentary. The biographical notes, for instance, cover only the elder’s early youth. And from his teachings and opinions, things said evidently at different times and from different promptings have been brought together as if into a single whole. What the elder actually said in these last hours of his life is not exactly determined; only an idea is given of the spirit and character of this conversation too, if one compares it with what Alexei Fyodorovich’s manuscript gives from his earlier teachings. The elder’s death came truly quite unexpectedly. For though all who had gathered round him on that last evening understood perfectly that his death was near, still it was impossible to imagine that it would come so suddenly; on the contrary, his friends, as I have already remarked, seeing him that night so cheerful, as it seemed, and so talkative, were even convinced that there had been a marked improvement in his health, if only for a short time. Even five minutes before his death, as they told afterwards with surprise, nothing could yet be foreseen. He suddenly felt, it seemed, a very sharp pain in his chest, turned pale and pressed his hands tightly to his heart. Everyone rose from their places then and rushed to him; but he, though suffering, still looking at them with a smile, quietly sank from his armchair to the floor and knelt, then bowed his face to the ground, stretched out his arms, and, as if in joyful rapture, kissing the earth and praying (as he himself had taught), quietly and joyfully gave up his soul to God. The news of his death spread at once through the hermitage and reached the monastery. Those closest to the newly departed, and those whose office it was, began to prepare his body according to the ancient rite, and all the brethren gathered in the cathedral church. And even before dawn, as rumour had it afterwards, the news of the newly departed reached the town. By morning almost the whole town was talking of the event, and a multitude of townspeople streamed to the monastery. But of this we shall speak in the next book; for now we will only add in advance that before the day was out something happened so unexpected for everyone, and, by the impression it made in the monastery and in the town, so strange, disturbing and confusing, that even now, after so many years, the most vivid memory is preserved in our town of that day, so disturbing for many…
## Part Three · Book Seven: Alyosha · Chapter I · The Odour of Corruption

The body of the departed hieroschemamonk Father Zosima was prepared for burial according to the established rite. Dead monks and schemamonks, as is well known, are not washed. “When any of the monks departs unto the Lord” (it is said in the great Book of Rites), “the appointed monk” (that is, the one designated for this) “wipeth his body with warm water, first making with the sponge” (that is, a Greek sponge) “a cross on the forehead of the departed, on the breast, on the hands and on the feet and on the knees, and nothing more.” All this Father Paisy performed himself over the departed. After the wiping he dressed him in the monastic habit and wrapped him in the mantle, cutting it a little for this, according to the rule, so as to wrap it crosswise. On his head he put the cowl with the eight-pointed cross. The cowl was left open, and the face of the departed was covered with a black veil. In his hands they laid an icon of the Saviour. In this form, towards morning, they moved him into the coffin (which had been made ready long before). The coffin they decided to leave in the cell (in the first, large room, the very one in which the late elder had received the brethren and laymen) all day. Since the departed was by rank a hieroschemamonk, hieromonks and hierodeacons had to read over him not the Psalter but the Gospel. Father Iosif began the reading, immediately after the requiem; and Father Paisy, who wished himself to read afterwards all day and all night, was for the time being very busy and anxious, together with the head of the hermitage. For something extraordinary began suddenly to show itself, more and more as time went on, both among the monastery brethren and among the laymen who came in crowds from the monastery guesthouses and from the town: some unheard-of and even “unseemly” agitation and impatient expectation. Both the head of the hermitage and Father Paisy did all they could to calm those so fussily excited. When it was full day, people began arriving from the town, some even bringing their sick with them, especially children, as if they had been waiting on purpose for this moment, evidently hoping for an immediate power of healing, which, by their faith, could not be slow to show itself. And only now did it become clear to what degree everyone among us had grown used to regarding the late elder, even in his lifetime, as an undoubted and great saint. And those arriving were by no means only of the common people. This great expectation of the believers, shown so hastily and so nakedly, and even impatiently, almost as a demand, seemed to Father Paisy an undoubted temptation; and though he had foreseen it long before, in reality it went beyond his expectations. Meeting excited monks, Father Paisy even began to rebuke them: “Such an immediate expectation of something great,” he said, “is a frivolity possible only among people of the world, and unseemly for us.” But they paid him little heed, and Father Paisy noticed it with uneasiness, even though he himself (if everything is to be remembered truthfully), though indignant at the too impatient expectations and finding frivolity and vanity in them, secretly, within himself, in the depths of his soul, was expecting almost the same as these excited ones, as he could not help admitting to himself. Nevertheless certain encounters were particularly unpleasant to him and roused great doubts in him from a kind of foreboding. In the crowd that thronged the dead man’s cell he noticed with an inward disgust (for which he immediately reproached himself) the presence, for instance, of Rakitin, or of the distant visitor, the monk from Obdorsk, who was still staying at the monastery; and both of them Father Paisy suddenly, for some reason, considered suspicious, though they were not the only ones who could be noticed in this sense. The monk from Obdorsk stood out as the most fussy of all the excited ones; he could be seen everywhere, in all places: everywhere he was asking questions, everywhere listening, everywhere whispering with a peculiar, mysterious air. And his face had the most impatient expression, as if he were already irritated that what had been expected so long had not happened. As for Rakitin, he, as it turned out later, had come to the hermitage so early on a special commission from Madame Khokhlakova. This kind but weak-willed woman, who could not be admitted to the hermitage herself, had no sooner woken and heard of the death than she was seized with so violent a curiosity that she at once dispatched Rakitin to the hermitage in her place, with instructions to observe everything and immediately report to her in writing, about every half-hour, everything that happened. She considered Rakitin the most pious and believing of young men, so well did he know how to get on with everyone and present himself to each as that person wished, if only he saw the least advantage to himself in it. The day was clear and bright, and many of the pilgrims who had come crowded round the graves of the hermitage, which were most closely packed round the church, though they were also scattered all over the hermitage. Going round the hermitage, Father Paisy suddenly remembered Alyosha, and that he had not seen him for a long time, almost since the night. And no sooner had he remembered him than he caught sight of him in the farthest corner of the hermitage, by the wall, sitting on the gravestone of a monk who had died long ago and was famous for his ascetic labours. He was sitting with his back to the hermitage, facing the wall, as if hiding behind the monument. Coming right up, Father Paisy saw that he had covered his face with both hands and, though without a sound, was weeping bitterly, his whole body shaking with sobs. Father Paisy stood over him for a while.

“Enough, my dear son, enough, my friend,” he said at last with feeling. “What is it? Rejoice and do not weep. Or don’t you know that this day is the greatest of his days? Only think where he is now, at this moment!”
Alyosha glanced up at him, uncovering his face, swollen with tears like a little child’s, but at once, without a word, turned away and covered it again with both hands.

“But perhaps it is right,” Father Paisy said thoughtfully. “Weep, perhaps; Christ has sent you these tears. ‘Your tender little tears are only a rest for your soul and will serve to gladden your dear heart,’” he added to himself, moving away from Alyosha and thinking of him lovingly. He moved away quickly, though, for he felt that, looking at him, he might weep himself. Meanwhile time went on; the monastery services and requiems for the departed continued in order. Father Paisy again took Father Iosif’s place at the coffin and again took over the reading of the Gospel from him. But it was not yet three in the afternoon when something happened that I mentioned at the end of the last book, something so unexpected by anyone among us and so contrary to the general hope that, I repeat, the detailed and frivolous story of this occurrence is remembered with extraordinary vividness to this day in our town and in all the country round. Here I will add once more from myself personally: it is almost repugnant to me to recall this frivolous and scandalous event, in essence a most trivial and natural one, and I would of course have left it out of my story altogether, had it not influenced in the strongest and most definite way the soul and heart of the chief, though future, hero of my story, Alyosha, making as it were a crisis and turning point in his soul, which shook but also strengthened his mind finally, for his whole life and towards a definite goal.

And so to the story. Before dawn, when they had laid the elder’s body, prepared for burial, in the coffin and carried it into the first room, the former reception room, a question arose among those at the coffin: should the windows in the room be opened? But this question, put by someone in passing, briefly, remained unanswered and almost unnoticed; only a few of those present noticed it, and then to themselves, in this sense only: that to expect corruption and an odour of corruption from the body of such a departed man was an utter absurdity, deserving even pity (if not a smile) for the little faith and frivolity of the one who had asked the question. For they were expecting the exact opposite. And then, soon after midday, something began which at first those who came in and went out received only in silence and to themselves, each with an evident fear of telling anyone the thought that was beginning in him; but by three in the afternoon it had shown itself so clearly and undeniably that the news of it flew instantly all over the hermitage and to all the pilgrims visiting it, at once reached the monastery too and threw everyone in the monastery into amazement, and finally, in the shortest time, reached the town and stirred up everyone there, believers and unbelievers. The unbelievers rejoiced; and as for the believers, some of them rejoiced even more than the unbelievers themselves, for “men love the fall of the righteous and his disgrace,” as the late elder himself had said in one of his teachings. The fact was that from the coffin there began to come, little by little, but more and more noticeably as time went on, an odour of corruption, which by three in the afternoon had become all too evident and was gradually growing stronger. And never for a long time, nor could anyone remember it in all the past life of our monastery, had there been such a scandal, coarsely unbridled, and in any other case even impossible, as broke out immediately after this event even among the monks themselves. Afterwards, even after many years, some sensible monks of ours, recalling that whole day in detail, wondered and were horrified at how the scandal could have reached such a pitch then. For before this too it had happened that monks of very righteous life died, whose righteousness was plain to all, God-fearing elders, and yet from their humble coffins too there came an odour of corruption, appearing naturally, as with all the dead; but that had caused no scandal, nor even the slightest agitation. Of course there were some among us, departed long ago, whose memory was still vividly kept in the monastery, and whose remains, according to tradition, had shown no corruption, which had a moving and mysterious effect on the brethren and was kept in their memory as something seemly and miraculous, and as a promise of still greater glory from their tombs in the future, if only by God’s will the time should come for it. Among these the memory was especially kept of the elder Iov, who lived to a hundred and five, a famous ascetic, a great faster and keeper of silence, who died long ago, back in the second decade of this century, and whose grave was shown with special and extraordinary reverence to all pilgrims arriving for the first time, with mysterious hints at certain great hopes. (It was the very grave on which Father Paisy had found Alyosha sitting that morning.) Besides this elder, departed long ago, a similar memory was alive of the great father hieroschemamonk, the elder Varsonofy, who had died comparatively recently, the very one from whom Father Zosima had received the eldership, and whom in his lifetime all the pilgrims who came to the monastery regarded simply as a holy fool. Of both of these it was preserved in tradition that they lay in their coffins as if alive and were buried quite incorrupt, and that even their faces seemed to grow bright in the coffin. And some even insisted that a fragrance could be plainly felt from their bodies. But despite even such impressive memories, it would still be hard to explain the direct cause by which so frivolous, absurd and spiteful a scene could take place at Elder Zosima’s coffin. For my own part, I suppose that many other things came together at the same time, many different causes acting together. Among them, for instance, was that same inveterate hostility to the eldership as a pernicious innovation, which still lay deeply hidden in the minds of many monks in the monastery. And then, of course, and chiefly, there was envy of the dead man’s holiness, so firmly established in his lifetime that it seemed forbidden even to object to it. For though the late elder had drawn many to himself, and not so much by miracles as by love, and had raised up round himself a whole world, as it were, of those who loved him, nevertheless, and even all the more, by that very thing he had bred envious ones too, and after them bitter enemies, open and secret, and not only among the monks but even among laymen. He had done no one any harm, for instance; but there it was: “Why do they think him so holy?” And that one question alone, repeated little by little, bred at last a whole abyss of the most insatiable spite. That is why I think that many, hearing of the odour of corruption from his body, and so soon too (for not even a day had passed since his death), were immeasurably glad; just as among those devoted to the elder and who had honoured him until then there were at once some who were almost insulted and personally offended by this event. And the thing went on by degrees as follows.

As soon as the corruption began to show itself, one could tell from the mere look of the monks who came into the dead man’s cell why they were coming. One comes in, stands a little, and goes out to confirm the news quickly to the others waiting outside in a crowd. Some of those waiting shook their heads sorrowfully, but others no longer even wanted to hide their joy, which shone plainly in their spiteful eyes. And no one reproached them any more, no one raised a kindly voice, which was even strange, for those devoted to the late elder were still the majority in the monastery; but evidently the Lord himself allowed the minority to get the upper hand for a time on this occasion. Soon laymen too began appearing in the cell, as spies of the same kind, mostly from among the educated visitors. Few of the common people came in, though many of them crowded at the gates of the hermitage. It is certain that precisely after three o’clock the influx of lay visitors greatly increased, and precisely because of the scandalous news. People who would perhaps not have come at all that day and had not meant to come now came on purpose, among them some persons of considerable rank. Outward decorum, however, was not yet broken, and Father Paisy, firmly and distinctly, with a stern face, went on reading the Gospel aloud, as though not noticing what was happening, though he had long since noticed something extraordinary. But now voices began to reach him too, very quiet at first, but gradually growing firmer and bolder. “So God’s judgement is not as man’s!” Father Paisy suddenly heard. The first to say this was a layman, an official from the town, a man already elderly and, as far as was known of him, very devout; but in saying it aloud he only repeated what the monks had long been repeating in each other’s ears. They had long since said this hopeless word, and worst of all was that with almost every minute a kind of triumph showed itself and grew in that word. Soon, however, even decorum itself began to be broken, and it was as if everyone felt that they now even had some right to break it. “And why should this have happened?” some of the monks said, at first as if with regret. “He had a small body, dry, his skin grown to his bones; where could the odour come from?” “It means God wanted to show us on purpose,” others hastily added, and their opinion was accepted at once and without dispute; for again they pointed out that even if there were bound to be an odour naturally, as from any departed sinner, still it would have come later, not with such obvious haste, after a day and a night at least, whereas “this one has forestalled nature”; therefore it was none other than God and his deliberate finger. He wanted to show something. This judgement struck irresistibly. The meek Father Iosif, the hieromonk and librarian, a favourite of the deceased, began objecting to some of the slanderers that “it is not so everywhere”, and that the incorruptibility of the bodies of the righteous is not a dogma of Orthodoxy but only an opinion, and that in the most Orthodox lands, on Athos for instance, they are not so troubled by an odour of corruption, and that there bodily incorruptibility is not considered the chief sign of the glorification of the saved, but the colour of their bones, when their bodies have lain many years in the earth and even decayed in it: “and if the bones are found yellow as wax, that is the chief sign that the Lord has glorified the righteous departed; but if they are found not yellow but black, it means the Lord has not deemed him worthy of such glory; that is how it is on Athos, a great place, where from of old Orthodoxy has been kept inviolate and in the brightest purity,” Father Iosif concluded. But the humble father’s words passed without effect and even provoked a mocking rebuff: “That is all learning and innovations; no need to listen,” the monks decided among themselves. “We keep to the old ways; there are all sorts of innovations coming out now; are we to copy them all?” others added. “We have had no fewer holy fathers than they. They sit there under the Turk and have forgotten everything. Their Orthodoxy has long been muddied, and they haven’t even any bells,” the most mocking ones put in. Father Iosif went away in sorrow, all the more since he himself had stated his opinion not very firmly, as if he had little faith in it himself. But he foresaw with dismay that something very unseemly was beginning and that even disobedience itself was raising its head. Little by little, after Father Iosif, all the sensible voices fell silent too. And somehow it came about that all who had loved the late elder and accepted the institution of the eldership with tender obedience were suddenly terribly frightened of something and, meeting one another, only glanced timidly into each other’s faces. And the enemies of the eldership, as an innovation, proudly raised their heads. “From the late elder Varsonofy there was not only no odour, but a fragrance came from him,” they reminded people gloatingly; “but he did not earn it by being an elder, but because he was righteous himself.” And after this, censures and even outright accusations began to pour down on the newly departed elder: “He taught wrongly; he taught that life is a great joy and not tearful humility,” said some of the most muddle-headed. “He believed in the modern way; he didn’t recognise material fire in hell,” added others still more muddle-headed. “He wasn’t strict about fasting; he allowed himself sweets; he ate cherry jam with his tea; he was very fond of it; ladies used to send it to him. Is it for a schemamonk to be drinking tea?” could be heard from some of the envious ones. “He sat in pride,” the most gloating recalled cruelly. “He thought himself a saint; people fell on their knees before him, and he accepted it as his due.” “He abused the sacrament of confession,” the fiercest opponents of the eldership added in a spiteful whisper, and these were even some of the oldest monks, most severe in their devotions, true fasters and keepers of silence, who had kept silent in the dead man’s lifetime but now suddenly opened their mouths, which was terrible indeed, for their words had a strong effect on the young monks who were not yet settled. The visitor from Obdorsk, the little monk from St Sylvester’s, listened hard to all this, sighing deeply and nodding his head: “No, it seems Father Ferapont judged rightly yesterday,” he thought to himself. And just then Father Ferapont appeared, as if he had come out precisely to make the shock worse.

I have mentioned already that he rarely came out of his wooden cell at the apiary, and even stayed away from church for long periods, and that he was allowed this as a supposed holy fool, without being bound by the rule common to all. But to tell the whole truth, all this was allowed him even from a kind of necessity. For it seemed somehow even shameful to burden with the common rule, against his will, so great a faster and keeper of silence, who prayed day and night (he even fell asleep on his knees), if he did not want to submit himself. “He is holier than all of us and does harder things than the rule requires,” the monks would have said then, “and if he doesn’t come to church, it means he knows himself when to come; he has his own rule.” It was for the sake of this likely murmuring and scandal that Father Ferapont was left in peace. Father Ferapont, as everyone knew, disliked Elder Zosima extremely; and now even to him, in his little cell, the news suddenly came that “God’s judgement is not as man’s, it seems, and that he has even forestalled nature.” It must be supposed that one of the first to run and tell him the news was the visitor from Obdorsk, who had visited him the day before and had left him in horror. I mentioned too that Father Paisy, standing firm and unshaken and reading over the coffin, though he could not hear or see what was happening outside the cell, foresaw unerringly in his heart all the main things, for he knew his surroundings through and through. He was not troubled, but awaited without fear all that might still happen, following with a piercing eye the coming outcome of the agitation, which already presented itself to his mind’s eye. Suddenly an extraordinary noise in the passage, plainly breaking decorum now, struck his ear. The door was flung wide open, and on the threshold appeared Father Ferapont. Behind him, as could be seen and even clearly made out from the cell, many monks who had come with him were crowding at the foot of the steps, and laymen among them. Those who had come with him, however, did not go in or climb the steps, but stopped and waited for what Father Ferapont would say and do next, for they felt, even with a certain fear, in spite of all their boldness, that he had not come for nothing. Stopping on the threshold, Father Ferapont raised his arms, and from under his right arm peeped the sharp, curious little eyes of the visitor from Obdorsk, the only one who had not been able to restrain himself and had run up the steps after Father Ferapont out of his great curiosity. The rest of them, on the contrary, as soon as the door was flung open with a noise, drew back still further in sudden fear. Raising his hands on high, Father Ferapont suddenly howled:

“Casting out I cast out!” And at once, turning to all four sides in turn, he began making the sign of the cross with his hand at the walls and all four corners of the cell. Those who had come with him understood this action of Father Ferapont’s at once, for they knew he always did so wherever he went in, and that he would not sit down or say a word until he had driven out the unclean spirit.

“Satan, begone! Satan, begone!” he repeated with each cross. “Casting out I cast out!” he howled again. He was in his coarse cassock, belted with a rope. From under his hempen shirt his bare chest, overgrown with grey hair, showed. His feet were quite bare. As soon as he began to wave his arms, the cruel chains he wore under his cassock began to shake and clank. Father Paisy broke off his reading, stepped forward and stood before him, waiting.
“Why have you come, honoured father? Why do you break decorum? Why do you trouble the humble flock?” he said at last, looking at him sternly.

“Why hast thou come? What dost thou ask? How dost thou believe?” Father Ferapont shouted, playing the holy fool. “I have hastened here to drive out your guests, the foul devils. I’m looking to see how many you have stored up without me. I want to sweep them out with a birch broom.”
“You drive out the unclean one, and perhaps you serve him yourself,” Father Paisy went on fearlessly. “And who can say of himself, ‘I am holy’? Can you, father?”

“I am foul, not holy. I won’t sit in an armchair and want to be bowed down to like an idol!” thundered Father Ferapont. “Nowadays folk are destroying the holy faith. The dead man, your saint,” he turned to the crowd, pointing his finger at the coffin, “rejected devils. He gave purges against devils. So they have bred here among you like spiders in the corners. And now he stinks himself. In this we see a great sign from the Lord.”

And this really had happened once in Father Zosima’s lifetime. One of the monks began to dream of the unclean spirit, and at last to see it when awake. When he disclosed this in the greatest fear to the elder, the elder advised him to pray unceasingly and to fast more strictly. But when even this did not help, he advised him, while not giving up fasting and prayer, to take a certain medicine. Many were scandalised by this at the time and talked about it among themselves, shaking their heads, and Father Ferapont most of all, to whom certain slanderers had hastened at once to report this “extraordinary” order of the elder’s in so special a case.

“Begone, father!” said Father Paisy commandingly. “It is not men who judge, but God. Perhaps we see here a ‘sign’ that neither you nor I nor anyone has the power to understand. Begone, father, and do not trouble the flock!” he repeated insistently.

“He didn’t keep the fasts according to the rule of his schema; that’s why the sign has come. That is plain, and it is a sin to hide it!” the fanatic would not calm down, carried away by a zeal that went beyond reason. “He was tempted by sweets; ladies brought them to him in their pockets; he sweetened himself with tea; he made offerings to his belly, filling it with sweet things, and his mind with proud thoughts… And so he has suffered shame…”

“Your words are frivolous, father!” Father Paisy too raised his voice. “I marvel at your fasting and your austerity, but your words are frivolous, as if a young man in the world had spoken, fickle and green. Begone, father, I command you!” Father Paisy thundered in conclusion.

“I’ll go!” said Father Ferapont, as if somewhat taken aback, but not giving up his spite. “You learned men! With your great reason you have exalted yourselves above my nothingness. I came here hardly able to read and write, and here I have forgotten what I did know; the Lord God himself has protected little me from your wisdom…”

Father Paisy stood over him and waited firmly. Father Ferapont was silent for a while, and suddenly, growing mournful and putting his right palm to his cheek, he said in a sing-song voice, looking at the coffin of the departed elder:

“Tomorrow they will sing ‘Helper and Protector’ over him, a glorious canon, but over me, when I peg out, only ‘What earthly joy’, a little hymn,” he said tearfully and ruefully. (At the carrying out of the body of a monk or schemamonk, from the cell to the church and after the funeral service from the church to the cemetery, the hymn “What earthly joy…” is sung. If the departed was a hieroschemamonk, the canon “Helper and Protector…” is sung. Author’s note.) “You have grown proud and puffed up; this place is desolate!” he suddenly howled like a madman, and, with a wave of his hand, quickly turned and quickly went down the steps. The crowd waiting below swayed; some went after him at once, but some lingered, for the cell was still open, and Father Paisy, who had come out onto the steps after Father Ferapont, stood watching. But the old man, once roused, had not finished yet. Having gone some twenty paces, he suddenly turned towards the setting sun, raised both arms above him, and, as if someone had cut his legs from under him, crashed to the ground with a great cry:

“My Lord has conquered! Christ has conquered the setting sun!” he shouted frantically, raising his arms to the sun, and, falling face down on the ground, he sobbed aloud like a little child, shaking all over with his tears and stretching out his arms on the ground. At that everyone rushed to him; there were exclamations, answering sobs… A kind of frenzy took hold of them all.
“Here is one who is holy! Here is one who is righteous!” the cries rang out, no longer fearfully. “Here is one who should be an elder,” others added, now spitefully.

“He won’t be an elder… He’ll refuse it himself… He won’t serve the cursed innovation… He won’t copy their foolery,” other voices at once took up; and how far this would have gone it is hard even to imagine, but just at that moment the bell rang for the service. Everyone suddenly began crossing themselves. Father Ferapont got up too and, protecting himself with the sign of the cross, went to his cell without looking back, still exclaiming, but now something quite incoherent. A few, a small number, began to stream after him, but most began to disperse, hurrying to the service. Father Paisy handed the reading over to Father Iosif and went down. The frenzied cries of the fanatics could not shake him, but his heart suddenly grew sad and anguished about something in particular, and he felt it. He stopped and suddenly asked himself: “Why is this sadness of mine so great as to make me lose heart?” And with surprise he understood at once that this sudden sadness of his came, it seemed, from a very small and particular cause: in the crowd that had just been thronging at the entrance to the cell he had noticed Alyosha too among the other excited ones, and he remembered that on seeing him he had at once felt a kind of pain in his heart. “Can this young man mean so much in my heart now?” he suddenly asked himself in surprise. At that moment Alyosha happened to be passing him, as if hurrying somewhere, but not towards the church. Their eyes met. Alyosha quickly looked away and dropped his eyes to the ground, and from the young man’s look alone Father Paisy guessed what a powerful change was taking place in him at this moment.
“Have you too been led astray?” Father Paisy suddenly exclaimed. “Can you too be with those of little faith?” he added sorrowfully.

Alyosha stopped and looked somehow vaguely at Father Paisy, but again quickly looked away and again dropped his eyes to the ground. He stood sideways and did not turn his face to the one who questioned him. Father Paisy watched attentively.
“Where are you hurrying to? They are ringing for the service,” he asked again, but again Alyosha gave no answer.
“Or are you leaving the hermitage? How can you, without asking leave, without a blessing?”

Alyosha suddenly gave a crooked smile, raised his eyes strangely, very strangely, to the father who was questioning him, to the one to whom his former guide, the former master of his heart and mind, his beloved elder, had entrusted him as he was dying; and suddenly, still without answering, he waved his hand, as if not caring even about respectfulness, and with quick steps went towards the gate, out of the hermitage.
“You will come back!” whispered Father Paisy, looking after him with sorrowful surprise.
## Book Seven, Chapter II · Such a Moment

Father Paisy was not mistaken, of course, when he decided that his “dear boy” would come back again, and perhaps he even saw (not entirely, but still with insight) into the true meaning of Alyosha’s state of mind. Nevertheless I confess frankly that it would be very hard for me myself now to convey clearly the exact meaning of this strange and indefinite moment in the life of the hero of my story, so much loved by me and still so young. To Father Paisy’s sorrowful question, aimed at Alyosha, “Can you too be with those of little faith?” I could of course answer firmly for Alyosha: “No, he is not with those of little faith.” More than that: here it was even quite the opposite: all his confusion came precisely from his having believed much. But the confusion was there all the same; it did happen, and it was so tormenting that even afterwards, long afterwards, Alyosha considered that sorrowful day one of the most painful and fateful days of his life. If I am asked straight out, “Can all this anguish and such alarm really have arisen in him only because the body of his elder, instead of at once beginning to work cures, had on the contrary undergone an early corruption?”, I will answer without beating about the bush: “Yes, that is really how it was.” I would only ask the reader not to be in too much of a hurry to laugh at the pure heart of my young man. For my part, not only do I not intend to ask forgiveness for him, or to excuse and justify his simple faith by his youth, for instance, or by his small progress in the studies he had followed before, and so on, and so on, but I shall do the very opposite and declare firmly that I feel a sincere respect for the nature of his heart. No doubt another young man, who takes in the impressions of the heart cautiously, who already knows how to love not hotly but only warmly, with a mind that is sound but, for his age, much too reasonable (and therefore cheap), such a young man, I say, would have escaped what happened to mine; but in some cases, truly, it is more honourable to give way to some passion, unreasonable though it may be, yet arising from a great love, than not to give way to it at all. And all the more in youth, for a young man who is too constantly reasonable is not to be relied upon and is worth little: that is my opinion! “But,” sensible people will exclaim here perhaps, “not every young man can believe in such a superstition, and your young man is no example for the rest.” To this I will answer again: yes, my young man believed, believed sacredly and unshakeably, but all the same I do not ask forgiveness for him.

You see, though I declared above (and perhaps too hastily) that I would not explain, excuse or justify my hero, I see that something must still be made clear for the further understanding of the story. This is what I will say: it was not miracles exactly. It was not a frivolous expectation of miracles in its impatience. And it was not for the triumph of some convictions that Alyosha needed miracles then (that not at all), nor for some former, preconceived idea that was to triumph quickly over another; oh no, not at all. Here, in all this, before everything, in the first place, there stood before him a face, and only a face: the face of his beloved elder, the face of that righteous man whom he revered to the point of worship. That was just it: all the love for “all and everything” that lay hidden in his young and pure heart had at that time, and all through the year before it, been concentrated at moments, and perhaps even wrongly, on one being above all, at least in the strongest impulses of his heart: on his beloved elder, now departed. True, this being had stood before him so long as an undisputed ideal that all his young strength and all its striving could not but be directed exclusively towards this ideal, and at moments even to the point of forgetting “all and everything”. (He remembered afterwards himself that on that heavy day he had quite forgotten his brother Dmitri, about whom he had been so concerned and anxious the day before; forgotten too to take Ilyushechka’s father the two hundred roubles, which he had so ardently meant to do the day before as well.) But again it was not miracles he needed, but only “a higher justice”, which, as he believed, had been violated, and by which his heart had been so cruelly and suddenly wounded. And what does it matter that this “justice”, in Alyosha’s expectations, by the very course of things took the form of miracles expected at once from the remains of his adored former guide? Why, everyone in the monastery thought and expected the same, even those before whose intelligence Alyosha bowed, Father Paisy himself, for instance; and so Alyosha, not troubling himself with any doubts, clothed his dreams too in the same form in which everyone clothed theirs. Besides, it had long since been so arranged in his heart, through a whole year of his monastic life, and his heart had acquired the habit of expecting in this way. But it was justice he thirsted for, justice, and not miracles only! And now the one who ought, by his hopes, to have been exalted above all in the whole world, that very one, instead of the glory due to him, was suddenly cast down and disgraced! What for? Who had judged? Who could have judged so? These were the questions that at once tormented his inexperienced and virginal heart. He could not endure without offence, even without an anger of the heart, that the most righteous of the righteous should be given up to such mocking and spiteful derision by a crowd so frivolous and so far beneath him. Well, let there have been no miracles at all, let nothing wonderful have appeared and the immediate expectation not have been fulfilled; but why should dishonour appear, why should disgrace be permitted, why this hasty corruption that “forestalled nature”, as the spiteful monks said? Why this “sign”, which they now drew with such triumph, together with Father Ferapont, and why did they believe that they had even been given the right to draw it? Where was providence and its finger? Why had it hidden its finger “at the very moment it was needed” (thought Alyosha), as if it had itself wanted to submit to the blind, dumb, pitiless laws of nature?

That was why Alyosha’s heart was bleeding; and of course, as I have said, above all there stood a face, the one he loved more than anything in the world, and that same face “disgraced”, that same face “dishonoured”! This murmuring of my young man may have been frivolous and unreasonable; but again, I repeat for the third time (and I agree beforehand that perhaps this too is frivolous), I am glad that my young man turned out not to be so reasonable at such a moment, for reason will always come in time to a man who is no fool; but if there is no love in a young man’s heart at so exceptional a moment, when will it come? I will not, however, keep silent on this occasion about a certain strange thing that appeared, if only for an instant, in Alyosha’s mind at this fateful and confusing moment. This new thing that showed itself and flashed by consisted of a certain tormenting impression from his conversation of the day before with his brother Ivan, which Alyosha kept recalling unceasingly now. Precisely now. Oh, not that anything among the basic, elemental beliefs of his soul, so to speak, had been shaken. He loved his God and believed in him unshakeably, though he had suddenly murmured against him. But all the same, some vague but tormenting and evil impression from recalling the conversation of the day before with his brother Ivan suddenly stirred in his soul again now and more and more begged to come up to its surface. When it was already getting very dark, Rakitin, passing through the pine wood from the hermitage to the monastery, suddenly noticed Alyosha lying under a tree, face to the ground, motionless, as if asleep. He went up and called to him.

“You here, Alexei? Can you really have…” he began in surprise, but stopped without finishing. He had meant to say: “Can you really have come to this?” Alyosha did not look at him, but from a certain movement he made Rakitin guessed at once that he heard and understood him.
“But what is the matter with you?” he went on in surprise, but the surprise was already beginning to give way on his face to a smile that took on a more and more mocking expression.
“Listen, I have been looking for you for over two hours. You suddenly vanished from over there. What are you doing here? What sanctimonious nonsense is this? At least look at me…”

Alyosha raised his head, sat up and leaned his back against the tree. He was not crying, but his face expressed suffering, and irritation showed in his eyes. He was not looking at Rakitin, however, but somewhere to the side.
“You know, your face has quite changed. None of that famous meekness of yours. Are you angry with someone, or what? Has someone hurt you?”
“Leave me alone!” Alyosha said suddenly, still not looking at him, and waved his hand wearily.

“Oho, so that’s how we are! Shouting at people just like other mortals. And this from one of the angels! Well, Alyoshka, you have surprised me, do you know that? I say it sincerely. I haven’t been surprised by anything here for a long time. I did take you for an educated man, though…”
Alyosha looked at him at last, but somehow absently, as if he still hardly understood him.
“Can it really be just because your old man has begun to stink? Did you seriously believe he would start working miracles?” Rakitin exclaimed, passing again into the most sincere amazement.
“I believed, I believe, and I want to believe, and I will believe; what more do you want!” Alyosha shouted irritably.

“Nothing at all, my dear. Ugh, the devil, even a schoolboy of thirteen doesn’t believe that nowadays. But still, the devil… So now you are angry with your God, you have rebelled: passed over for promotion, as it were, not given a decoration for the holiday! Oh, you people!”
Alyosha looked at Rakitin long, with his eyes somehow narrowed, and something suddenly flashed in his eyes… but not anger at Rakitin.
“I am not rebelling against my God; I simply ‘do not accept his world’,” Alyosha suddenly smiled crookedly.
“What do you mean, you don’t accept his world?” Rakitin thought a little over his answer. “What gibberish is that?”
Alyosha did not answer.
“Well, enough of nonsense; now to business: have you eaten today?”
“I don’t remember… I think I have.”

“You need something to keep you going, to judge by your face. It makes one feel sorry to look at you. You didn’t sleep last night either; I heard you had a meeting there. And then all this fuss and mess… I expect you have chewed only a scrap of the holy bread. I have some sausage in my pocket; I brought it from town on my way here just in case; only you won’t eat sausage…”
“Give me the sausage.”

“Hey! So that’s how it is! So it’s a regular revolt, barricades! Well, brother, that is not to be sneezed at. Let’s go to my place… I could do with a drop of vodka myself now, I’m dead tired. I don’t suppose you’ll go so far as vodka… or will you?”
“Give me vodka too.”
“Well I never! This is a wonder, brother!” Rakitin looked at him wildly. “Well, one way or another, vodka or sausage, this is a fine, dashing business and not to be missed; come on!”
Alyosha got up from the ground in silence and went after Rakitin.
“If your brother Vanechka could see this, how amazed he would be! By the way, your brother Ivan Fyodorovich went off to Moscow this morning, did you know?”

“I know,” Alyosha said listlessly, and suddenly the image of his brother Dmitri flashed through his mind, but only flashed; and though it reminded him of something, some urgent business that could not be put off another minute, some debt, a terrible obligation, yet this memory too made no impression on him, did not reach his heart, and in the same instant flew out of his memory and was forgotten. But Alyosha remembered it long afterwards.

“Your brother Vanechka once declared that I was ‘a talentless liberal windbag’. And you too, once, couldn’t restrain yourself and let me understand that I was ‘dishonourable’… So be it! Now let’s have a look at your talent and honour” (Rakitin finished this to himself, in a whisper). “Ugh, listen!” he began again aloud. “Let’s go round the monastery and take the path straight into town… Hm. I ought to call in at Khokhlakova’s, by the way. Imagine: I wrote to her about everything that had happened, and, just think, she answers me at once with a note in pencil (that lady is terribly fond of writing notes), that ‘she never expected such conduct from so venerable an elder as Father Zosima!’ That’s just what she wrote: ‘conduct’! She’s angry too; oh, you people, all of you! Wait!” he suddenly shouted again, stopped all at once and, holding Alyosha by the shoulder, stopped him too.

“You know, Alyoshka,” he looked searchingly into his eyes, entirely under the impression of a sudden new thought that had just lit him up, and though he was laughing outwardly, he was evidently afraid to say this sudden new thought aloud, so little could he yet believe in the mood, strange to him and wholly unexpected, in which he now saw Alyosha. “Alyoshka, do you know where it would be best of all for us to go now?” he brought out at last, timidly and ingratiatingly.
“It doesn’t matter… wherever you like.”
“Let’s go to Grushenka’s, eh? Will you come?” Rakitin brought out at last, trembling all over with timid expectation.
“Let’s go to Grushenka’s,” Alyosha answered calmly and at once, and this was so unexpected for Rakitin, that is, such a quick and calm agreement, that he almost jumped back.

“W-well!… There!” he began to shout in amazement, but suddenly, taking Alyosha firmly by the arm, he quickly drew him along the path, still terribly afraid that his resolve would vanish. They walked in silence; Rakitin was even afraid to speak.

“And how glad she will be, how glad…” he began to mutter, but fell silent again. And it was not at all for Grushenka’s gladness that he was drawing Alyosha to her; he was a serious man and undertook nothing without an aim profitable to himself. His aim now was twofold: in the first place, vengeful, that is, to see “the disgrace of the righteous” and Alyosha’s probable “fall from saint to sinner”, which he was already gloating over in advance; and in the second place he had in view here a certain material aim, very profitable to him, of which more will be said below.
“So such a moment has come,” he thought to himself, gleefully and spitefully. “Well then, we’ll catch it by the scruff of the neck, this moment, for it suits us very well.”
## Chapter III · An Onion

Grushenka lived in the busiest part of the town, near Cathedral Square, in the house of the merchant’s widow Morozova, from whom she rented a small wooden lodge in the yard. Morozova’s house was large, of stone, two storeys high, old and very unattractive to look at; the owner herself lived in it in seclusion, an old woman, with her two nieces, also rather elderly spinsters. She had no need to let her lodge in the yard, but everyone knew that she had taken in Grushenka as a lodger (some four years before) solely to oblige her relative, the merchant Samsonov, Grushenka’s open protector. It was said that the jealous old man, in placing his “favourite” with Morozova, had at first had in mind the old woman’s sharp eye, to watch over the new lodger’s conduct. But the sharp eye very soon proved unnecessary, and it ended with Morozova rarely even meeting Grushenka and, towards the end, not troubling her with any supervision at all. True, four years had passed since the old man had brought to this house from the provincial capital a girl of eighteen, timid, shy, slender, thin, pensive and sad, and much water had flowed since then. The story of this girl, however, was little known in our town, and in a muddled way; nothing more was learned of late either, even when a great many people had begun to take an interest in the “raving beauty” that Agrafena Alexandrovna had turned into in four years. There were only rumours that, when still a girl of seventeen, she had been deceived by someone, an officer supposedly, and then at once abandoned by him. The officer, it was said, had gone away and married somewhere afterwards, and Grushenka had been left in disgrace and poverty. It was said, however, that though Grushenka had indeed been taken by her old man out of poverty, she came of an honest family and was of clerical origin somehow, the daughter of some supernumerary deacon or something of the kind. And in four years the sensitive, injured and pitiful little orphan had become a rosy, full-bodied Russian beauty, a woman of a bold and decided character, proud and insolent, who understood money, acquisitive, stingy and cautious, who, by fair means or foul, had already managed, so they said, to scrape together a little capital of her own. Everyone was convinced of one thing only: that Grushenka was hard of access, and that, apart from the old man, her protector, there had not been a single man in all those four years who could boast of her favour. This was a firm fact, because not a few eager men had come forward to win that favour, especially in the last two years. But all the attempts came to nothing, and some of the suitors were even forced to retreat with a comic and shameful ending, thanks to the firm and mocking rebuff of the strong-willed young person. It was known too that the young person, especially in the last year, had gone in for what is called “business”, and that in this direction she proved to have extraordinary abilities, so that in the end many called her a regular Jewess. Not that she lent money at interest; but it was known, for instance, that in company with Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov she had for a time really been buying up promissory notes for next to nothing, ten kopecks to the rouble, and afterwards realised on some of those notes a rouble for every ten kopecks. The sick Samsonov, who in the last year had lost the use of his swollen legs, a widower, the tyrant of his grown-up sons, a man worth a great many hundreds of thousands, stingy and implacable, had nevertheless fallen under the strong influence of his protégée, whom at first he had kept in an iron grip and on short commons, “on Lenten oil”, as the wags said then. But Grushenka had managed to emancipate herself, while inspiring him with a boundless trust in her faithfulness to him. This old man, a great man of business (long dead now), was also of a remarkable character, above all stingy and hard as flint; and though Grushenka had so struck him that he could not live without her (in the last two years, for instance, that was really so), still he did not settle any large, considerable capital on her, and even if she had threatened to leave him altogether, he would have remained implacable. But he did settle a small capital on her, and when this became known it too was a matter of general surprise. “You are no fool of a woman yourself,” he told her, settling some eight thousand on her; “go and manage it yourself; but know that, apart from your yearly allowance as before, until my death you will get nothing more from me, and in my will I shan’t leave you anything more either.” And so he kept his word: he died and left everything to his sons, whom all his life he had kept by him on the same footing as servants, with their wives and children, and he did not even mention Grushenka in his will at all. All this became known later. But he helped Grushenka a good deal with advice on how to manage “her own capital” and pointed out “deals” to her. When Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov, who had first got involved with Grushenka over some chance piece of “business”, ended, quite unexpectedly for himself, by falling madly in love with her and as it were losing his wits, old Samsonov, who by then had one foot in the grave, laughed at him heartily. It is remarkable that throughout their acquaintance Grushenka was completely, and even heartily, frank with her old man, and with him, it seems, alone of all men in the world. Most recently, when Dmitri Fyodorovich too had suddenly appeared with his love, the old man stopped laughing. On the contrary, he once gave Grushenka serious and stern advice: “If you must choose between the two, father or son, choose the old man, but on condition that the old scoundrel marries you without fail and settles at least some capital on you first. And have nothing to do with the captain; no good will come of it.” These were the very words of the old voluptuary to Grushenka, who already felt his death near and did in fact die five months after giving this advice. I will note too, in passing, that though many in our town even then knew of the absurd and monstrous rivalry of the Karamazovs, father and son, of which Grushenka was the object, few people then understood the real meaning of her attitude to both of them, to the old man and to the son. Even both of Grushenka’s maids (after the catastrophe that broke later, of which more is to come) testified afterwards in court that Agrafena Alexandrovna received Dmitri Fyodorovich only out of fear, because, it was said, “he threatened to kill her”. She had two maids: a very old cook, from her parents’ family, sick and almost deaf, and her granddaughter, a lively young girl of about twenty, Grushenka’s housemaid. Grushenka lived very thriftily and in surroundings by no means rich. In her lodge there were only three rooms, furnished by the landlady with ancient mahogany furniture in the style of the twenties. When Rakitin and Alyosha came in it was already quite dusk, but the rooms were not yet lit. Grushenka herself was lying in her drawing room on her big clumsy sofa with a back of imitation mahogany, hard and covered with leather that had long since worn thin and into holes. Under her head were two white down pillows from her bed. She lay on her back, stretched out motionless, both hands behind her head. She was dressed up as if expecting someone, in a black silk dress and a light lace cap on her head, which suited her very well; over her shoulders a lace kerchief was thrown, fastened with a massive gold brooch. She really was expecting someone; she lay as if in anguish and impatience, her face somewhat pale, her lips and eyes burning, impatiently tapping the arm of the sofa with the tip of her right foot. As soon as Rakitin and Alyosha appeared there was a small commotion: one could hear from the hall how Grushenka jumped up quickly from the sofa and suddenly cried out in fright: “Who is there?” But the maid met the visitors and at once called back to her mistress:
“It isn’t him, ma’am, it’s others; these are all right.”

“What’s the matter with her?” Rakitin muttered, leading Alyosha by the hand into the drawing room. Grushenka was standing by the sofa as if still frightened.
