A thick lock of her dark-brown plait had suddenly slipped out from under her cap and fallen onto her right shoulder, but she did not notice it or put it right until she had looked closely at her visitors and recognised them.
“Ah, it’s you, Rakitka? You quite frightened me. Who is that with you? Who have you brought? Lord, look who he has brought!” she exclaimed, making out Alyosha.
“Have some candles brought, then!” said Rakitin with the free and easy air of a most intimate acquaintance, someone close who even has the right to give orders in the house.

“Candles… of course, candles… Fenya, bring him a candle… Well, you have found a time to bring him!” she exclaimed again, nodding at Alyosha, and, turning to the mirror, she quickly began to put her plait back in place with both hands. She seemed to be displeased.
“Haven’t I pleased you?” asked Rakitin, almost offended in an instant.

“You frightened me, Rakitka, that’s what,” Grushenka turned with a smile to Alyosha. “Don’t be afraid of me, Alyosha, my dear; I’m awfully glad to see you, my unexpected guest. But you frightened me, Rakitka: I thought Mitya was breaking in. You see, I fooled him earlier and made him give me his word of honour to believe me, and I lied to him. I told him I was going to Kuzma Kuzmich, my old man, for the whole evening and would be counting money with him till night. I go to him every week for the whole evening to settle accounts. We lock ourselves in: he clicks away on the abacus and I sit and write in the books; he trusts no one but me. Mitya believed I was there, and I have locked myself in at home; I’m sitting here waiting for a certain message. How did Fenya let you in? Fenya, Fenya! Run to the gate, open it and look round, see if the captain isn’t somewhere about. Perhaps he’s hiding and spying; I’m frightened to death!”
“There’s no one, Agrafena Alexandrovna; I looked round just now, and I keep going and peeping through the crack every minute; I’m all of a tremble myself.”

“Are the shutters closed, Fenya? And the curtain should be drawn, there!” She drew the heavy curtains herself. “Or he’ll fly straight at the light. I’m afraid of Mitya, your brother, today, Alyosha.” Grushenka spoke loudly, anxious, yet also as if in a kind of rapture.
“Why are you so afraid of Mitenka today?” Rakitin inquired. “You don’t seem timid with him as a rule; he dances to your tune.”

“I tell you, I’m waiting for a message, a golden little message, so that I don’t need Mitenka at all now. And he didn’t believe me, I can feel it, that I was going to Kuzma Kuzmich. I expect he is sitting there now, at Fyodor Pavlovich’s, in the garden at the back, watching for me. And if he has settled down there, he won’t come here, so much the better! I did really run to Kuzma Kuzmich’s; Mitya saw me there himself; I said I’d sit there till midnight and that he must come at midnight without fail to see me home. He went away, and I sat with the old man for ten minutes and then came back here; oh, I was frightened; I ran so as not to meet him.”
“And what are you dressed up for? Look at the curious cap you’re wearing!”

“And how curious you are yourself, Rakitin! I tell you, I’m waiting for a certain little message. When it comes, I’ll jump up and fly away, and that’s the last you’ll see of me. That’s why I’m dressed up, to be ready.”
“And where will you fly to?”
“Curiosity killed the cat.”
“Look at that. All joy… I’ve never seen you like this before. Got up as if for a ball,” Rakitin looked her over.
“Much you know about balls.”
“And you know a lot?”

“I’ve seen a ball. Two years ago Kuzma Kuzmich married off his son, and I watched from the gallery. But why should I be talking to you, Rakitka, when there is such a prince standing here? There’s a guest for you! Alyosha, my dear, I look at you and don’t believe it; Lord, how did you come to be here with me? To tell you the truth, I never expected it, never dreamed of it, and I never believed before that you could come. Though it isn’t the moment for it now, I’m awfully glad to see you! Sit on the sofa, here, like that, my bright young moon. Really, I can’t seem to take it in yet… Oh, Rakitka, if only you had brought him yesterday or the day before!… Well, I’m glad as it is. Perhaps it’s better that it’s now, at such a moment, and not the day before yesterday…”

She sat down briskly beside Alyosha on the sofa, right next to him, and looked at him with decided admiration. And she really was glad; she was not lying when she said so. Her eyes were burning, her lips were laughing, but good-naturedly, merrily. Alyosha had not expected such a kind expression on her face… He had met her little until yesterday and had formed a terrifying idea of her, and yesterday he had been so dreadfully shaken by her spiteful and treacherous outburst against Katerina Ivanovna that he was very surprised now to see in her suddenly quite another and unexpected being. And crushed though he was by his own grief, his eyes rested on her involuntarily with attention. All her manners too seemed to have changed completely for the better since yesterday: there was almost none of yesterday’s mawkishness in her speech, none of those pampered and affected movements… everything was simple, artless; her movements were quick, direct, trusting; but she was very excited.
“Lord, what things are coming to pass today, really,” she prattled again. “And why I am so glad to see you, Alyosha, I don’t know myself. Ask me, and I don’t know.”
“Oh, so you don’t know what you’re glad about?” Rakitin smirked. “Before, you kept pestering me for some reason: bring him, bring him; you had some aim.”

“Before, I had another aim, but now that has passed; it isn’t the moment. I’m going to treat you both, that’s what. I’ve grown kind now, Rakitka. And sit down yourself, Rakitka; why are you standing? Or have you sat down already? Trust Rakitushka not to forget himself. There he is now, Alyosha, sitting opposite us and taking offence: why didn’t I ask him to sit down before you? Oh, my Rakitka is touchy, touchy!” Grushenka laughed. “Don’t be cross, Rakitka; today I’m kind. But why are you sitting so sad, Alyoshechka? Are you afraid of me?” She peered into his eyes with merry mockery.
“He is in grief. He wasn’t promoted,” Rakitin boomed.
“Promoted to what?”
“His elder has begun to stink.”

“What do you mean, begun to stink? You are grinding out some nonsense; you want to say something nasty. Be quiet, you fool. Will you let me sit on your knee, Alyosha, like this!” And suddenly in an instant she sprang up and jumped, laughing, onto his knee, like a coaxing kitten, her right arm tenderly round his neck. “I’ll cheer you up, my pious boy! No, really, will you let me sit on your knee? You won’t be angry? Tell me to, and I’ll jump down.”

Alyosha was silent. He sat afraid to move; he heard her words, “Tell me to, and I’ll jump down,” but he did not answer, as if he had frozen. But what was in him was not what, for instance, Rakitin, watching greedily from his place, might have expected or imagined in him now. The great grief of his soul swallowed up all the sensations that might have been born in his heart, and if he could have given himself a full account at that moment, he would have guessed himself that he was now in the strongest armour against every seduction and temptation. Nevertheless, in spite of all the vague unaccountability of his state of mind and of all the grief that oppressed him, he could not help wondering at a new and strange sensation being born in his heart. This woman, this “terrible” woman, not only did not frighten him now with the old fear, the fear that used to rise in him at any thought of a woman, if such a thought flashed through his soul; on the contrary, this woman, whom he had feared more than anyone, sitting on his knee and embracing him, now suddenly roused in him a quite different, unexpected and peculiar feeling, a feeling of some extraordinary, immense and most pure-hearted curiosity about her, and all this without any fear, without the slightest trace of his former horror: that was the main thing, and it involuntarily surprised him.
“That’s enough of your nonsense,” Rakitin shouted. “You had better bring the champagne; you owe it, you know you do!”

“True, I do. You see, Alyosha, I promised him champagne on top of everything if he brought you. Out with the champagne, and I’ll drink too! Fenya, Fenya, bring us champagne, the bottle Mitya left; run, quick. Stingy as I am, I’ll bring out a bottle, not for you, Rakitka, you’re a toadstool, but he’s a prince! And though it isn’t that my soul is full of now, so be it, I’ll drink with you; I feel like a spree!”

“But what is this moment of yours, and what sort of ‘message’ is it, may one ask, or is it a secret?” Rakitin put in again with curiosity, trying with all his might to look as if he paid no attention to the flicks that kept flying at him.

“Oh, it’s no secret, and you know it yourself,” Grushenka said suddenly with a worried look, turning her head to Rakitin and leaning away a little from Alyosha, though still sitting on his knee with her arm round his neck. “The officer is coming, Rakitin, my officer is coming!”
“I heard he was coming; but is he so near already?”
“He is at Mokroye now; he’ll send a courier from there; he wrote so himself; I got a letter today. I’m sitting and waiting for the courier.”
“Well, well! Why at Mokroye?”
“It’s a long story, and you have heard enough.”
“So what about Mitenka now? Oh, oh! Does he know or not?”

“Know what! He knows nothing at all! If he found out, he’d kill me. But I’m not afraid of that at all now; I’m not afraid of his knife now. Be quiet, Rakitka, don’t remind me of Dmitri Fyodorovich: he has crushed my heart to pieces. And I don’t want to think about any of that at this moment. I can think of Alyoshechka; I’m looking at Alyoshechka… Smile at me, my dear, cheer up, smile at my foolishness, at my joy… Why, he smiled, he smiled! Look how kindly he looks. You know, Alyosha, I kept thinking you were angry with me for the day before yesterday, for that young lady. I was a dog, that’s what… Only it is good all the same that it happened so. It was bad and it was good,” Grushenka suddenly smiled thoughtfully, and a sort of cruel little line flashed in her smile. “Mitya said she screamed, ‘She ought to be flogged!’ I offended her terribly then. She invited me, wanted to conquer me, to seduce me with her chocolate… No, it’s good that it happened so,” she smiled again. “Only I keep being afraid that you are angry…”
“Why, it’s true,” Rakitin suddenly put in with serious surprise. “She really is afraid of you, Alyosha, a little chick like you.”

“To you, Rakitka, he is a chick, that’s what… because you have no conscience, that’s what! I, you see, I love him with my soul, that’s what! Do you believe, Alyosha, that I love you with all my soul?”
“Oh, you shameless woman! She is declaring her love to you, Alexei!”
“And why not? I do love him.”
“And the officer? And the golden little message from Mokroye?”
“That is one thing, and this is another.”
“That’s a woman’s way of looking at it!”

“Don’t make me angry, Rakitka,” Grushenka caught him up hotly. “That is one thing, and this is another. I love Alyosha differently. It’s true, Alyosha, I had a sly idea about you before. But then I’m low, I’m violent; and yet at another moment, Alyosha, I used to look at you as at my conscience. I kept thinking: ‘How a man like that must despise a nasty woman like me now.’ I thought it the day before yesterday too, as I ran here from the young lady’s. I noticed you like that long ago, Alyosha, and Mitya knows; I told him. Now Mitya understands. Would you believe it, sometimes, really, Alyosha, I look at you and feel ashamed, ashamed of my whole self… And how I came to think of you, and since when, I don’t know and don’t remember…”
Fenya came in and set a tray on the table, with an uncorked bottle on it and three glasses already poured.

“The champagne has come!” Rakitin shouted. “You are excited, Agrafena Alexandrovna, and beside yourself. One glass, and you’ll be off dancing. Ugh, they couldn’t even do that properly,” he added, looking at the champagne. “The old woman poured it out in the kitchen, and they have brought the bottle without a cork, and it’s warm. Well, let’s have it as it is.”
He went to the table, took a glass, drank it at a gulp and poured himself another.

“One doesn’t often come across champagne,” he said, licking his lips. “Come on, Alyosha, take a glass, show what you’re made of. What shall we drink to? The gates of paradise? Take a glass, Grusha, and you drink to the gates of paradise too.”
“What gates of paradise?”
She took a glass. Alyosha took his, drank a sip and put the glass back.
“No, better not!” he smiled quietly.
“And you boasted!” cried Rakitin.
“Well, if so, I won’t either,” Grushenka caught up. “I don’t want to anyway. Drink the whole bottle by yourself, Rakitka. If Alyosha drinks, then I’ll drink.”

“Here comes the calf-love!” Rakitin teased. “And she’s sitting on his knee herself! He has his grief, let’s say, but what have you got? He has rebelled against his God; he was ready to gobble sausage…”
“How so?”
“His elder died today, Elder Zosima, the saint.”

“So Elder Zosima has died!” Grushenka exclaimed. “Lord, and I didn’t know it!” She crossed herself devoutly. “Lord, what am I doing, sitting on his knee now!” She started up suddenly as if in fright, slipped off his knee in an instant and moved to the sofa. Alyosha gave her a long, surprised look, and something seemed to light up in his face.

“Rakitin,” he said suddenly, loudly and firmly, “don’t taunt me with having rebelled against my God. I don’t want to bear you any spite, so be kinder yourself. I have lost such a treasure as you have never had, and you cannot judge me now. Look at her instead: did you see how she spared me? I came here to find a wicked soul; I was drawn to it myself, because I was base and wicked; and I have found a true sister, I have found a treasure, a loving soul… She spared me just now… Agrafena Alexandrovna, I am speaking of you. You have restored my soul just now.”
Alyosha’s lips trembled and his breath caught. He stopped.
“As if she had saved you!” Rakitin laughed spitefully. “And she wanted to swallow you up, do you know that?”

“Stop, Rakitka!” Grushenka suddenly jumped up. “Be quiet, both of you. Now I’ll say everything. You, Alyosha, be quiet, because such words of yours make me ashamed, because I am wicked and not good; that’s what I am. And you, Rakitka, be quiet because you are lying. I did have such a vile idea, that I wanted to swallow him up; but now you are lying; now it isn’t that at all… and don’t let me hear another word from you, Rakitka!” Grushenka said all this with extraordinary agitation.
“Look at them both raving!” hissed Rakitin, staring at them both in amazement. “Like madmen; as if I’d landed in a lunatic asylum. They’ve both gone soft; they’ll start crying in a minute!”
“And I will start crying, I will!” said Grushenka. “He called me his sister, and I shall never forget that! Only this, Rakitka: wicked as I am, I did give an onion.”
“What onion? Ugh, the devil, they really have gone mad!”

Rakitin wondered at their rapture and grew angry and offended, though he might have realised that everything had come together for both of them that could shake their souls as happens not often in life. But Rakitin, who could understand very sensitively everything that concerned himself, was very coarse in understanding the feelings and sensations of his neighbours, partly from his youthful inexperience and partly from his great egoism.

“You see, Alyoshechka,” Grushenka suddenly laughed nervously, turning to him, “I boasted to Rakitka that I gave an onion, but I won’t boast to you; I’ll tell it to you with another aim. It’s only a fable, but it’s a good fable; I heard it when I was still a child from my Matryona, who is my cook now. This is how it goes: ‘Once upon a time there was a woman, as wicked as wicked could be, and she died. And not a single good deed was left behind her. The devils seized her and threw her into the lake of fire. And her guardian angel stood and thought: what good deed of hers can I remember to tell God? He remembered and said to God: she once pulled up an onion in her garden and gave it to a beggar woman. And God answered him: take that very onion, then, hold it out to her in the lake, let her catch hold of it and be pulled, and if you pull her out of the lake, let her go to paradise; but if the onion breaks, then the woman must stay where she is now. The angel ran to the woman and held out the onion to her: here, woman, catch hold and be pulled. And he began to pull her carefully and had almost pulled her out, when the other sinners in the lake, seeing her being pulled out, all began catching hold of her, so as to be pulled out with her. But the woman was as wicked as wicked could be, and she began kicking them with her feet: “It’s me that’s being pulled, not you; it’s my onion, not yours.” As soon as she said that, the onion broke. And the woman fell into the lake and is burning to this day. And the angel wept and went away.’ That’s the fable, Alyosha; I learned it by heart, because I am that very woman, as wicked as can be. I boasted to Rakitka that I gave an onion, but to you I’ll say it differently: in my whole life I have given only one onion or so; that is all the good deed there is in me. And don’t praise me after that, Alyosha; don’t think me good. I’m wicked, as wicked as can be, and if you praise me you’ll put me to shame. Oh, I may as well confess everything. Listen, Alyosha: I wanted so much to lure you here, and I pestered Rakitka so, that I promised him twenty-five roubles if he brought you to me. Wait, Rakitka, wait!” She went with quick steps to the table, opened a drawer, took out a purse, and from it a twenty-five-rouble note.
“What nonsense! What nonsense!” exclaimed the disconcerted Rakitin.
“Take what I owe you, Rakitka; I don’t suppose you’ll refuse; you asked for it yourself.” And she flung the note at him.
“As if I would refuse,” Rakitin boomed, evidently embarrassed but covering his shame with a swagger. “It will come in very handy; fools exist for the profit of the clever man.”
“And now be quiet, Rakitka; everything I’m going to say now is not for your ears. Sit in the corner there and be quiet; you don’t love us, so be quiet.”

“And why should I love you?” Rakitin snapped, no longer hiding his spite. He had stuffed the twenty-five-rouble note into his pocket, and he was decidedly ashamed in front of Alyosha. He had reckoned on getting his payment afterwards, so that Alyosha would not even know, and now he was furious from shame. Until this moment he had found it very politic not to contradict Grushenka much, in spite of all her flicks, for it was clear that she had some power over him. But now he too lost his temper:
“People love for some reason; and what have you two done for me?”
“Love for no reason, the way Alyosha loves.”
“And how does he love you, and what has he shown you that you make such a fuss of him?”
Grushenka was standing in the middle of the room; she spoke with heat, and hysterical notes could be heard in her voice.

“Be quiet, Rakitka, you understand nothing about us! And don’t you dare speak to me so familiarly in future; I won’t allow it; where did you get such boldness, I’d like to know! Sit in the corner and be quiet, like my footman. And now, Alyosha, I’ll tell you the whole pure truth, you alone, so that you see what a creature I am! I’m saying it to you, not to Rakitka. I wanted to ruin you, Alyosha; that is the great truth; I had quite made up my mind to it; I wanted it so much that I bribed Rakitka with money to bring you. And what made me want it so? You, Alyosha, knew nothing; you turned away from me; when you passed me you dropped your eyes; and I had looked at you a hundred times before this; I began asking everyone about you. Your face stayed in my heart: ‘He despises me,’ I thought; ‘he won’t even want to look at me.’ And such a feeling took hold of me in the end that I wonder at myself: why am I afraid of such a boy? I’ll swallow him whole and laugh. I was quite furious. Would you believe it: no one here dares to say or think that he could come to Agrafena Alexandrovna for that bad business; I have only the old man; I am bound to him and sold to him, Satan married us; but of the others, no one. But looking at you, I made up my mind: I’ll swallow him. I’ll swallow him and laugh. You see what a wicked dog I am, whom you called your sister! And now this man who wronged me has come, and I’m sitting here waiting for a message. And do you know what this man who wronged me was to me? Five years ago, when Kuzma brought me here, I used to sit hiding from people, so that they shouldn’t see or hear me, thin, silly; I would sit and sob; I didn’t sleep for nights on end; I kept thinking: ‘And where is he now, the man who wronged me? Laughing at me with another woman, I expect; and oh, if only I could see him, meet him some time, I’d pay him back, I’d pay him back!’ At night in the dark I would sob into my pillow and think it all over; I tore my heart on purpose, I fed it with spite: ‘Oh, I’ll pay him back, I’ll pay him back!’ That’s how I would cry out in the dark. And when I suddenly remembered that I could do nothing to him, while he was laughing at me now, or perhaps had forgotten me altogether and didn’t remember, I would throw myself from the bed onto the floor, flood myself with helpless tears and shake and shake till dawn. In the morning I’d get up angrier than a dog, ready to swallow the whole world. Then, what do you think? I began to save up capital; I grew pitiless; I grew stout; I grew wiser, you think, eh? Well, I didn’t; no one sees it or knows it in the whole universe, but when the darkness of night comes down, I lie there sometimes just as I did as a girl five years ago, grinding my teeth and crying all night: ‘Oh, I’ll pay him back, I’ll pay him back,’ I think! Did you hear all that? Well, then, how do you understand me now? A month ago, suddenly, this very letter comes to me: he is coming, he has been left a widower, he wants to see me. It took my breath away, Lord, and suddenly I thought: and if he comes and whistles to me, calls me, I’ll crawl to him like a little beaten dog, guilty! I think this and don’t believe myself: ‘Am I vile or not? Shall I run to him or not?’ And such anger at myself has come over me all this month, worse even than five years ago. Do you see now, Alyosha, how violent I am, how furious? I’ve told you the whole truth! I played with Mitya so as not to run to the other one. Be quiet, Rakitka, it’s not for you to judge me; it wasn’t you I was telling. Before you came I was lying here waiting, thinking, deciding my whole fate, and you will never know what was in my heart. No, Alyosha, tell your young lady not to be angry about the day before yesterday!… And no one in the whole world knows what it is like for me now, and no one can know… Because perhaps I’ll take a knife with me there today; I haven’t decided yet…”

And having uttered this “pitiful” word, Grushenka suddenly broke down; she did not finish, but covered her face with her hands, threw herself on the sofa among the pillows and sobbed like a little child. Alyosha got up and went over to Rakitin.
“Misha,” he said, “don’t be angry. She has hurt you, but don’t be angry. Did you hear her just now? One can’t demand so much of a human soul; one must be more merciful…”

Alyosha said this in an irresistible impulse of his heart. He needed to speak out, and he turned to Rakitin. If Rakitin had not been there he would have begun exclaiming to himself. But Rakitin gave him a mocking look, and Alyosha suddenly stopped.
“That’s your elder they loaded you with earlier, and now you’ve fired your elder off at me, Alyoshenka, little man of God,” Rakitin said with a hateful smile.

“Don’t laugh, Rakitin, don’t smirk, don’t talk of the dead man: he is higher than anyone who has ever lived on earth!” Alyosha cried with tears in his voice. “I didn’t stand up to speak to you as a judge, but as the lowest of the accused myself. What am I before her? I came here to be ruined, and I said, ‘Let it be, let it be!’, and that from my faint-heartedness; and she, after five years of torment, as soon as someone came and spoke a sincere word to her, has forgiven everything, forgotten everything, and is weeping! The man who wronged her has come back, he is calling her, and she forgives him everything and hurries to him in joy, and she won’t take a knife, she won’t! No, I am not like that. I don’t know whether you are like that, Misha, but I am not! I have had this lesson today, just now… She is higher than we are in love… Had you heard from her before what she has told us now? No, you hadn’t; if you had, you would have understood everything long ago… and the other one, who was insulted the day before yesterday, let her forgive her too! And she will forgive, if she learns… and she will learn… This soul is not yet reconciled; one must spare it… there may be a treasure in this soul…”
Alyosha fell silent because his breath failed him. Rakitin, in spite of all his spite, was looking at him in surprise. He had never expected such a tirade from the quiet Alyosha.
“Here’s a lawyer for you! Have you fallen in love with her or what? Agrafena Alexandrovna, our faster really has fallen in love with you; you have conquered!” he shouted with an insolent laugh.
Grushenka raised her head from the pillow and looked at Alyosha with a tender smile that lit up her face, somehow swollen all at once from her recent tears.

“Leave him alone, Alyosha, my cherub; you see what he is like; you’ve found someone to talk to. Mikhail Osipovich,” she turned to Rakitin, “I meant to ask your forgiveness for abusing you, but now I don’t want to again. Alyosha, come to me, sit here,” she beckoned him with a joyful smile, “like that, sit here; tell me” (she took his hand and peered smiling into his face), “tell me: do I love that man or not? The man who wronged me, do I love him or not? Before you came I was lying here in the dark, questioning my heart over and over: do I love him or not? Decide it for me, Alyosha; the time has come; whatever you decide, so it shall be. Shall I forgive him or not?”
“But you have forgiven him already,” Alyosha said, smiling.

“And so I have,” Grushenka said thoughtfully. “What a vile heart! To my vile heart!” She suddenly snatched a glass from the table, drank it at one gulp, raised it and flung it on the floor. The glass broke with a ring. A sort of cruel little line flashed in her smile.

“And yet perhaps I haven’t forgiven him yet,” she said somehow menacingly, dropping her eyes to the ground, as if talking to herself alone. “Perhaps my heart is only getting ready to forgive. I’ll struggle with my heart yet. You see, Alyosha, I have grown terribly fond of my five years’ tears… Perhaps I have only grown fond of my wrong, and not of him at all!”
“Well, I shouldn’t like to be in his skin!” hissed Rakitin.
“And you won’t be, Rakitka; you will never be in his skin. You shall make my shoes, Rakitka; that’s the job I’ll use you for; and a woman like me you will never see… And perhaps he won’t either…”
“He won’t? Then what have you dressed up for?” Rakitin teased venomously.

“Don’t reproach me with my dress, Rakitka; you don’t know my whole heart yet! If I like, I’ll tear my finery off; I’ll tear it off this minute, this very minute,” she cried ringingly. “You don’t know what this finery is for, Rakitka! Perhaps I’ll go out to him and say: ‘Have you ever seen me like this?’ For he left me a thin, consumptive cry-baby of seventeen. And I’ll sit down beside him and charm him and set him on fire: ‘Have you seen what I’m like now?’ I’ll say. ‘Well then, stay as you are, my dear sir: so near and yet so far!’ That’s perhaps what this finery is for, Rakitka,” Grushenka finished with a spiteful little laugh. “I’m violent, Alyosha, furious. I’ll tear off my finery, I’ll disfigure myself, my beauty; I’ll burn my face and cut it with a knife, and go begging. If I like, I won’t go anywhere now, to anyone; if I like, tomorrow I’ll send Kuzma back everything he has given me, and all his money, and go out as a day labourer for the rest of my life!… You think I won’t do it, Rakitka, won’t dare to do it? I will, I will; I can do it this minute; only don’t provoke me… and as for that one, I’ll drive him away, I’ll show him a fig, he won’t see me!”
She cried out the last words hysterically, but again she broke down, covered her face with her hands, threw herself on the pillow and again shook with sobs. Rakitin got up.
“It’s time,” he said. “It’s late; they won’t let us into the monastery.”
Grushenka simply leapt up.

“Can you really want to go, Alyosha?” she exclaimed in sorrowful amazement. “But what are you doing to me now? You have roused me all, torn me apart, and now there is this night again, and I am to be alone again!”
“He’s not going to spend the night with you, is he? Though if he wants to, let him! I’ll go alone!” Rakitin jeered caustically.
“Be quiet, you wicked soul,” Grushenka shouted at him furiously. “You have never said such words to me as he came to say to me.”
“What did he say to you, then?” Rakitin grumbled irritably.

“I don’t know, I don’t know, I don’t know at all what he said to me; it spoke to my heart; he turned my heart over… He was the first, the only one, to pity me, that’s what! Why didn’t you come before, my cherub?” She suddenly fell on her knees before him as if in a frenzy. “All my life I have been waiting for someone like you; I knew someone like that would come and forgive me. I believed that someone would love me too, nasty as I am, not only for my shame!…”
“What have I done for you?” Alyosha answered with a tender smile, bending over her and gently taking her hands. “I gave you an onion, one very little onion, only that, only that!…”

And having said it, he began to cry himself. At that moment there was suddenly a noise in the passage; someone had come into the hall. Grushenka leapt up as if in terrible fright. Fenya ran into the room with noise and shouting.

“Mistress, my dear, mistress, the courier has galloped up!” she cried gaily and out of breath. “A carriage from Mokroye for you, Timofei the driver with a troika; they are changing the horses this minute… A letter, a letter, mistress, here is a letter!”

The letter was in her hand, and all the time she was shouting she waved it in the air. Grushenka snatched the letter from her and held it to the candle. It was only a note, a few lines; she read it in an instant.
“He has called!” she cried, quite pale, her face twisted with a painful smile. “He has whistled! Crawl, little dog!”
But only for one instant did she stand as if irresolute; suddenly the blood rushed to her head and flooded her cheeks with fire.

“I’m going!” she suddenly exclaimed. “My five years! Goodbye! Goodbye, Alyosha, my fate is decided… Go, go, go away from me now, all of you, so that I don’t see you again!… Grushenka has flown off into a new life… Don’t remember me unkindly, you either, Rakitka. Perhaps I am going to my death! Ugh! As if I were drunk!”
She suddenly left them and ran into her bedroom.
“Well, she has no time for us now!” Rakitin grumbled. “Let’s go, or perhaps that woman’s screaming will start again; I’m sick of these tearful screams…”

Alyosha let himself be led out mechanically. In the yard stood the carriage; they were unharnessing the horses, walking about with a lantern, bustling. A fresh troika was being led in through the open gate. But no sooner had Alyosha and Rakitin come down from the porch than the window of Grushenka’s bedroom suddenly opened, and she called after Alyosha in a ringing voice:

“Alyoshechka, give my greetings to your brother Mitenka, and tell him not to remember me, his evil one, unkindly. And tell him too, in my words: ‘Grushenka has gone to a scoundrel, and not to you, a noble man!’ And tell him too that Grushenka loved him for one little hour, only one little hour she loved him, so let him remember that little hour all his life from now on; tell him Grushenka bids him so for all his life!…”
She finished in a voice full of sobs. The window slammed shut.
“Hm, hm!” Rakitin mumbled, laughing. “She has cut brother Mitenka’s throat and tells him to remember it all his life too. What carnivorousness!”

Alyosha made no answer, as if he had not heard; he walked fast beside Rakitin, as if in a terrible hurry; he was as if in a trance, walking mechanically. Something suddenly stung Rakitin, as if someone had touched his fresh wound with a finger. This was not at all what he had expected earlier, when he brought Grushenka and Alyosha together; something quite different had happened from what he had very much wanted.

“He is a Pole, that officer of hers,” he began again, restraining himself, “and he isn’t an officer at all now; he served as a customs official in Siberia, somewhere there on the Chinese border; some puny little Pole, I expect. He lost his job, they say. Now he has heard that Grushenka has got hold of some capital, so he has come back; that’s all the miracle.”
Again Alyosha seemed not to hear. Rakitin could not contain himself:

“Well, have you converted the sinner?” he laughed spitefully at Alyosha. “Turned the harlot to the path of truth? Cast out seven devils, eh? So here they are, our miracles we were waiting for this morning; they have come to pass!”
“Stop it, Rakitin,” Alyosha answered, with suffering in his soul.
“So now you ‘despise’ me for those twenty-five roubles this evening? Sold a true friend, you think. But you are not Christ, and I am not Judas.”
“Oh, Rakitin, I assure you I had forgotten about it,” Alyosha exclaimed. “You reminded me yourself just now…”
But Rakitin was now thoroughly furious.
“The devil take you all, every one of you!” he suddenly yelled. “And why the devil did I get mixed up with you? I don’t want to know you from now on. Go on alone; there’s your road!”
And he turned sharply into another street, leaving Alyosha alone in the darkness. Alyosha went out of the town and across the fields towards the monastery.
## Book Seven, Chapter IV · Cana of Galilee

It was already very late by monastery hours when Alyosha came back to the hermitage; the gatekeeper let him in by a special way. It had already struck nine, the hour of general rest and quiet after a day so troubling for everyone. Alyosha timidly opened the door and went into the elder’s cell, where his coffin now stood. Apart from Father Paisy, who was reading the Gospel over the coffin alone, and the young novice Porfiry, who, worn out by last night’s conversation and today’s commotion, was asleep on the floor in the other room with his sound young sleep, there was no one in the cell. Father Paisy, though he heard Alyosha come in, did not even look his way. Alyosha turned to the right of the door, into the corner, knelt down and began to pray. His soul was overflowing, but somehow vaguely, and no one sensation stood out too strongly; on the contrary, one pushed out another in a kind of quiet, even rotation. But there was sweetness in his heart, and, strangely, Alyosha was not surprised at it. Again he saw before him this coffin, this dead man so precious to him, covered all round; but there was no weeping, aching, tormenting pity in his soul as there had been that morning. Coming in just now, he had fallen down before the coffin as before a holy thing; but joy, joy was shining in his mind and in his heart. One window of the cell was open; the air was fresh and coolish. “So the odour has grown stronger, if they decided to open the window,” thought Alyosha. But even this thought of the odour of corruption, which only a little while ago had seemed to him so terrible and inglorious, did not stir in him now his earlier anguish and his earlier indignation. He began quietly to pray, but soon felt himself that he was praying almost mechanically. Fragments of thought flashed through his soul, flared up like little stars and went out again at once, giving way to others; but something whole, firm and soothing reigned in his soul, and he was aware of it himself. At times he would begin a prayer fervently; he so wanted to give thanks and to love… But having begun the prayer, he would suddenly pass to something else, fall to thinking, and forget both the prayer and what had interrupted it. He began to listen to what Father Paisy was reading, but, being very tired, little by little he began to doze…
“And the third day there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee,” Father Paisy was reading, “and the mother of Jesus was there: and both Jesus was called, and his disciples, to the marriage.”

“A marriage? What is that… a marriage…” rushed like a whirlwind through Alyosha’s mind. “She has happiness too… she has gone to a feast… No, she didn’t take a knife, she didn’t take a knife… It was only a ‘pitiful’ word… Well… pitiful words must be forgiven, without fail. Pitiful words comfort the soul… without them grief would be too heavy for people. Rakitin went off into a side street. As long as Rakitin thinks about his grievances he will always go off into a side street… But the road… the road is wide, straight, bright, crystal, and the sun is at the end of it… Eh?… What are they reading?”
“…And when they wanted wine, the mother of Jesus saith unto him, They have no wine…” Alyosha heard.

“Ah yes, I missed that, and I didn’t want to miss it; I love this passage: it is Cana of Galilee, the first miracle… Ah, that miracle, ah, that dear miracle! It was not grief but men’s joy that Christ visited when he worked his first miracle; he helped men’s joy… ‘He who loves men loves their joy too…’ The dead man used to repeat that every minute; it was one of his chief thoughts… One can’t live without joy, says Mitya… Yes, Mitya… Everything that is true and beautiful is always full of all-forgiveness; that again was what he said…”
“…Jesus saith unto her, Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come. His mother saith unto the servants, Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.”

“Do it… Joy, the joy of some poor, very poor people… Of course they were poor, if there wasn’t even enough wine for a wedding… The historians write that round the lake of Gennesaret and in all those parts the poorest population imaginable was settled then… And another great heart, of another great being who was there too, his mother, knew that he had come down then not only for his great and terrible deed, but that his heart was open to the simple, artless merrymaking of some dark, dark and unsophisticated creatures who had kindly invited him to their poor wedding. ‘Mine hour is not yet come,’ he says with a quiet smile (he surely smiled at her gently)… Indeed, was it to multiply wine at poor weddings that he came down to earth? And yet he went and did it at her request… Ah, he is reading again.”

“…Jesus saith unto them, Fill the waterpots with water. And they filled them up to the brim. And he saith unto them, Draw out now, and bear unto the governor of the feast. And they bare it. When the ruler of the feast had tasted the water that was made wine, and knew not whence it was: (but the servants which drew the water knew;) the governor of the feast called the bridegroom, and saith unto him, Every man at the beginning doth set forth good wine; and when men have well drunk, then that which is worse: but thou hast kept the good wine until now.”

“But what is this, what is this? Why is the room growing wider… Ah yes… of course, it is the marriage, the wedding… yes, of course. Here are the guests, here are the young couple sitting, and the merry crowd, and… where is the wise governor of the feast? But who is this? Who? The room has grown wider again… Who is that getting up there from the great table? What… Is he here too? But he is in the coffin… But he is here too… he has got up, he has seen me, he is coming this way… Lord!…”

Yes, he came up to him, to him, the dry little old man with fine wrinkles on his face, joyful and laughing quietly. There was no coffin now, and he was in the same clothes in which he had sat with them yesterday when the visitors had gathered round him. His face was all uncovered; his eyes were shining. How is this? So he too is at the feast, he too has been called to the marriage in Cana of Galilee…
“I too, my dear, I too am called; called and bidden,” a quiet voice sounds above him. “Why have you hidden yourself here, so that you can’t be seen?… Come and join us too.”
His voice, the voice of Elder Zosima… And how could it not be he, if he is calling? The elder raised Alyosha with his hand; Alyosha rose from his knees.

“We are making merry,” the dry little old man goes on. “We are drinking new wine, the wine of a new, great joy. Do you see how many guests there are? Here are the bridegroom and the bride, here is the wise governor of the feast, tasting the new wine. Why do you wonder at me? I gave an onion, and so I am here. And many here gave only an onion, only one little onion… What are our deeds? And you, my quiet one, you too, my gentle boy, you too were able today to give an onion to a hungry woman. Begin, my dear, begin, my gentle one, your work!… And do you see our Sun, do you see him?”
“I am afraid… I dare not look…” whispered Alyosha.

“Do not be afraid of him. He is terrible in his greatness before us, awful in his height, but infinitely merciful; out of love he has become like us and makes merry with us; he turns water into wine so that the guests’ joy may not be cut short; he is waiting for new guests, he is calling new ones unceasingly, and now for ever and ever. See, they are bringing the new wine; do you see, they are bringing the vessels…”
Something was burning in Alyosha’s heart; something suddenly filled it till it hurt; tears of rapture were breaking from his soul… He stretched out his arms, cried out and woke…

Again the coffin, the open window, and the quiet, solemn, distinct reading of the Gospel. But Alyosha was no longer listening to what was being read. Strange: he had fallen asleep on his knees, and now he was standing on his feet; and suddenly, as if torn from his place, with three firm, quick steps he went right up to the coffin. He even brushed Father Paisy with his shoulder and did not notice it. Father Paisy raised his eyes to him from the book for a moment, but at once looked away again, understanding that something strange had happened to the young man. For half a minute Alyosha looked at the coffin, at the dead man lying there covered, motionless, stretched out in the coffin, with the icon on his breast and the cowl with the eight-pointed cross on his head. Only just now he had heard his voice, and that voice was still ringing in his ears. He was still listening; he was still expecting sounds… But suddenly, turning sharply, he went out of the cell.

He did not stop even on the steps, but went quickly down. His soul, full of rapture, thirsted for freedom, space, breadth. Above him the dome of heaven, full of quiet shining stars, was spread out wide and boundless. From the zenith to the horizon the still faint Milky Way ran double. The fresh night, still to the point of motionlessness, lay over the earth. The white towers and golden domes of the cathedral gleamed against the sapphire sky. The splendid autumn flowers in the beds round the house had fallen asleep till morning. The silence of the earth seemed to merge with the silence of the heavens; the mystery of the earth touched the mystery of the stars… Alyosha stood and looked, and suddenly, as if cut down, threw himself on the earth.

He did not know why he embraced it; he did not try to understand why he so irresistibly longed to kiss it, to kiss all of it; but he kissed it, weeping, sobbing and watering it with his tears, and vowed in ecstasy to love it, to love it for ever and ever. “Water the earth with the tears of your joy and love those tears of yours…” rang in his soul. What was he weeping over? Oh, in his rapture he was weeping even over those stars that shone on him from the abyss, and “he was not ashamed of this ecstasy”. It was as if threads from all those countless worlds of God had come together at once in his soul, and it was trembling all over, “in contact with other worlds”. He wanted to forgive everyone and for everything, and to beg forgiveness, oh! not for himself, but for all, for everything and for everyone; “and others are begging for me,” rang again in his soul. But with every moment he felt plainly, almost tangibly, how something firm and unshakeable, like that vault of heaven, was entering his soul. A sort of idea, as it were, was taking possession of his mind, and now for his whole life and for ever and ever. He had fallen on the earth a weak youth, and he rose up a fighter, steadfast for the rest of his life; and he knew and felt it suddenly, in that same moment of his rapture. And never, never in all his life afterwards could Alyosha forget that moment. “Someone visited my soul in that hour,” he would say afterwards, with firm faith in his words…
Three days later he left the monastery, which was in keeping too with the word of his late elder, who had bidden him “to sojourn in the world”.
## Book Eight: Mitya · Chapter I · Kuzma Samsonov

Meanwhile Dmitri Fyodorovich, to whom Grushenka, flying off into a new life, had “bidden” Alyosha pass on her last greeting, and whom she had told to remember for ever her little hour of love, was at that moment, knowing nothing of what had happened to her, also in terrible confusion and bustle. For the last two days he had been in such an unimaginable state that he really might have fallen ill with brain fever, as he said himself afterwards. Alyosha had not been able to find him the morning before, and his brother Ivan had not been able to arrange to meet him at the tavern that same day. The people who owned the little flat where he lodged had hidden his tracks on his orders. And during those two days he had literally been rushing about in all directions, “struggling with his fate and saving himself”, as he put it afterwards, and had even flown out of town for a few hours on a certain urgent business, although he was terribly afraid to go away and leave Grushenka even for a minute without an eye on her. All this came out later in the most detailed and documented form, but for now we will set down, in terms of fact, only what is most necessary from the story of those two terrible days in his life that preceded the dreadful catastrophe which broke so suddenly over his fate.

Grushenka, though she did love him truly and sincerely for her little hour, it is true, also at the same time tormented him at times really cruelly and mercilessly. The main thing was that he could make out nothing of her intentions; nor was there any possibility of coaxing it out of her by kindness or by force: she would never have given in, but would only have grown angry and turned away from him altogether; he understood that clearly then. He suspected then, quite rightly, that she herself was in some kind of struggle, in some extraordinary indecision, that she was making up her mind to something and still could not make it up; and so, not without reason, he supposed with a sinking heart that at moments she must simply hate him and his passion. Perhaps it was so; but what exactly Grushenka was pining over he still did not understand. For him the whole question that tormented him came down to two terms only: “Either he, Mitya, or Fyodor Pavlovich.” Here, by the way, one firm fact must be noted: he was entirely convinced that Fyodor Pavlovich would certainly offer Grushenka lawful marriage (if he had not already), and did not believe for a minute that the old voluptuary hoped to get off with only three thousand. Mitya concluded this, knowing Grushenka and her character. That was why it could seem to him at times that all Grushenka’s torment and all her indecision arose simply from her not knowing which of them to choose and which would be more profitable to her. As for the speedy return of the “officer”, that is, of the fateful man in Grushenka’s life whose arrival she was awaiting with such agitation and fear, strange to say, in those days he did not even think of thinking about it. True, in the very last days Grushenka had kept very silent with him about it. Yet he knew perfectly well from her own lips about the letter she had received a month before from her former seducer; he knew in part the contents of the letter too. Then, in a spiteful moment, Grushenka had shown him the letter; but, to her surprise, he attached almost no value to it. And it would be very hard to explain why: perhaps simply because, crushed himself by all the ugliness and horror of his struggle with his own father for this woman, he could not imagine anything more terrible and dangerous for himself, at least at that time. As for a suitor who suddenly sprang up from somewhere after five years’ disappearance, he simply did not believe in him, and especially not that he would come soon. Besides, in that very first letter from the “officer”, which had been shown to Mitenka, the arrival of this new rival was spoken of very vaguely: the letter was very cloudy, very high-flown and filled only with sentiment. It should be noted that on that occasion Grushenka hid from him the last lines of the letter, in which the return was spoken of somewhat more definitely. Besides, Mitenka remembered afterwards that at that moment he had caught on Grushenka’s own face a kind of involuntary and proud contempt for this missive from Siberia. After that Grushenka told Mitenka nothing more about any further communications with this new rival. And so, little by little, he even forgot about the officer altogether. He thought only that whatever might come of it, and however things turned out, the final clash with Fyodor Pavlovich that was approaching was too near and must be settled before everything else. With a sinking soul he waited every minute for Grushenka’s decision and kept believing that it would come suddenly, as if by inspiration. Suddenly she would say to him: “Take me, I am yours for ever,” and everything would be over: he would seize her and carry her off to the ends of the earth at once. Oh, he would carry her off at once, as far, as far as possible, if not to the ends of the earth, then somewhere to the ends of Russia; he would marry her there and settle with her incognito, so that no one would know about them at all, neither here nor there nor anywhere. Then, oh, then a completely new life would begin at once! Of this other, renewed and now “virtuous” life (“virtuous without fail, without fail”) he dreamed every minute, frantically. He thirsted for this resurrection and renewal. The vile pit in which he had got stuck by his own will weighed on him too heavily, and he, like very many in such cases, believed most of all in a change of place: if only not these people, if only not these circumstances, if only he could fly away from this cursed place, and everything would be reborn and go on in a new way! That was what he believed in and what he longed for.

But this was only in the case of the first, happy solution of the question. There was another solution too; another, but now terrible, outcome presented itself. Suddenly she would say to him: “Go away; I have just settled things with Fyodor Pavlovich and am marrying him, and I don’t need you.” And then… but then… Mitya, however, did not know what would happen then; he did not know until the very last hour; in this one must acquit him. He had no definite intentions; no crime was premeditated. He only watched, spied and tormented himself, but still prepared himself only for the first, happy outcome of his fate. He even drove away every other thought. But here a quite different torment began; a quite new and extraneous, but also fateful and insoluble, circumstance arose.

Namely: in case she said to him, “I am yours, take me away,” how was he to take her away? Where were his means, his money? Just at this time all his income from Fyodor Pavlovich’s handouts, which had never been interrupted through so many years, had run dry. Of course Grushenka had money, but in this respect a terrible pride suddenly showed itself in Mitya: he wanted to take her away himself and begin a new life with her on his own means, not on hers; he could not even imagine taking her money from her, and suffered from the thought to the point of tormented disgust. I do not enlarge on this fact here or analyse it, but only note it: such was the cast of his soul at that moment. All this may have arisen indirectly, and as if even unconsciously, from the secret torments of his conscience over Katerina Ivanovna’s money, which he had appropriated like a thief: “I am a scoundrel to the one, and I shall at once turn out a scoundrel to the other again,” he thought then, as he confessed himself afterwards; “and if Grushenka finds out, she won’t want such a scoundrel herself.” And so, where was he to get the means, where was he to get this fateful money? Otherwise everything would be lost and nothing would come off, “and solely because the money ran short, oh, shame!”

I run ahead: the point is that perhaps he did know where to get this money; he knew, perhaps, even where it lay. I will say nothing more about it this time, for everything will be explained later; but this was where his chief trouble lay, and I will state it, though vaguely: in order to take these means lying somewhere, in order to have the right to take them, he must first return the three thousand to Katerina Ivanovna; otherwise, “I am a pickpocket, I am a scoundrel, and I don’t want to begin a new life as a scoundrel,” Mitya decided; and so he decided to turn the whole world upside down, if necessary, but without fail to give these three thousand back to Katerina Ivanovna at all costs and before everything else. The final process of this decision took place in him, so to speak, in the very last hours of his life, namely after his last meeting with Alyosha, two days before, in the evening, on the road, after Grushenka had insulted Katerina Ivanovna and Mitya, hearing the story of it from Alyosha, had confessed that he was a scoundrel and told him to tell Katerina Ivanovna so, “if it could ease her in any way”. That same night, having parted from his brother, he felt in his frenzy that it would be better even “to kill and rob someone, but pay back the debt to Katya”. “Better that I should be a murderer and a thief before the man I killed and robbed, and before all people, and go to Siberia, than that Katya should have the right to say that I betrayed her and stole money from her and ran off with Grushenka on her money to begin a virtuous life! That I cannot do!” So Mitya declared, grinding his teeth, and at times he really could imagine that he would end with brain fever. But meanwhile he struggled…

Strange to say: it would seem that with such a decision nothing but despair was left to him, for where was he suddenly to get such money, and a beggar like him at that? And yet to the end, all that time, he went on hoping that he would get these three thousand, that they would come, would fly to him somehow of themselves, even from the sky. But that is just how it is with those who, like Dmitri Fyodorovich, all their lives know only how to spend and squander money that came to them by inheritance for nothing, and have no idea how money is earned. The most fantastic whirlwind rose in his head as soon as he had parted from Alyosha two days before, and confused all his thoughts. And so it came about that he began with the wildest of enterprises. Indeed, perhaps it is precisely in such situations that to such people the most impossible and fantastic enterprises present themselves first as the most possible. He suddenly decided to go to the merchant Samsonov, Grushenka’s protector, and propose a certain “plan” to him, and get from him on this “plan” the whole sum he needed at one stroke; of the commercial side of his plan he had not the least doubt; he doubted only how Samsonov himself would look on his escapade, if he chose to look at it not only from the commercial side. Though Mitya knew this merchant by sight, he was not acquainted with him and had never even once spoken to him. But for some reason a conviction had formed in him, long since, that this old debauchee, who now had one foot in the grave, might not at all object at this moment if Grushenka were to arrange her life honestly somehow and marry “a reliable man”. And that not only would he not object, but he wished it himself, and, given the chance, would help it on himself. Whether from some rumours or from some words of Grushenka’s, he had also concluded that the old man might prefer him to Fyodor Pavlovich for Grushenka. Perhaps to many readers of our story this reckoning on such help, and the intention of taking his bride, so to speak, from the hands of her protector, will seem much too coarse and unscrupulous on Dmitri Fyodorovich’s part. I can only remark that to Mitya Grushenka’s past seemed already finally past. He looked at that past with infinite compassion and decided with all the fire of his passion that as soon as Grushenka told him she loved him and would marry him, a completely new Grushenka would begin at once, and with her a completely new Dmitri Fyodorovich, without any vices now, only with virtues: they would both forgive each other and begin their life in a completely new way. As for Kuzma Samsonov, he regarded him, in this former, collapsed past of Grushenka’s, as a fateful man in her life, whom, however, she had never loved, and who, this was the main thing, had also “passed”, had come to an end, so that he no longer existed at all now. Besides, Mitya could not even regard him as a man now, for it was known to everyone in the town that he was only a sick ruin, who kept up relations with Grushenka, so to speak, only as a father, and not at all on the old footing, and that it had been so for a long time, for almost a year now. In any case there was a great deal of simple-heartedness in this on Mitya’s part, for with all his vices he was a very simple-hearted man. In consequence of this simple-heartedness he was, among other things, seriously convinced that old Kuzma, preparing to depart into the next world, felt a sincere repentance for his past with Grushenka, and that she had now no protector and friend more devoted than this already harmless old man.

On the very next day after his conversation with Alyosha in the field, after which Mitya hardly slept all night, he appeared at Samsonov’s house at about ten in the morning and asked to be announced. The house was old, gloomy, very spacious, of two storeys, with outbuildings and a lodge. On the ground floor lived Samsonov’s two married sons with their families, his aged sister and one unmarried daughter. In the lodge lived his two clerks, one of whom also had a large family. Both the children and the clerks were crowded into their quarters, but the upper floor of the house was occupied by the old man alone, and he would not let even his daughter live there with him, though she looked after him and, at fixed hours and at his unfixed summons, had to run up to him from below every time in spite of her long-standing breathlessness. This “upstairs” consisted of a great many large state rooms, furnished in the old merchant style, with long, dreary rows of clumsy mahogany armchairs and chairs along the walls, with crystal chandeliers in covers and gloomy mirrors between the windows. All these rooms stood quite empty and uninhabited, because the sick old man huddled in one room only, his remote little bedroom, where he was waited on by an old servant woman with her hair tied in a kerchief and by a “lad” who sat on the bench in the hall. Because of his swollen legs the old man could hardly walk at all any more and only rarely got up from his leather armchair, and the old woman, holding him under the arms, would walk him once or twice round the room. He was stern and taciturn even with this old woman. When the arrival of “the captain” was announced to him, he at once ordered that he be refused. But Mitya insisted and had himself announced again. Kuzma Kuzmich questioned the lad in detail: what did he look like, was he drunk? Was he making a row? And received the answer that “he is sober, but won’t go away.” The old man again ordered him refused. Then Mitya, who had foreseen all this and had brought paper and pencil with him on purpose for the occasion, wrote one line clearly on a scrap of paper: “On a most urgent matter closely concerning Agrafena Alexandrovna,” and sent it to the old man. After thinking a little, the old man told the lad to show the visitor into the hall, and sent the old woman downstairs with an order to his younger son to come up to him at once. This younger son, a man over six feet tall and of enormous strength, who shaved his face and dressed in the German fashion (Samsonov himself went about in a kaftan and with a beard), appeared at once and without a word. They all trembled before their father. The father summoned this fine fellow not exactly from fear of the captain (he was of a very far from timid character), but just in case, more so as to have a witness. Accompanied by his son, who took his arm, and the lad, he sailed at last into the hall. One must suppose that he felt a certain rather strong curiosity. This hall, in which Mitya was waiting, was a huge, gloomy room that crushed the soul with dreariness, two storeys high, with a gallery, with walls painted “in imitation marble” and three enormous crystal chandeliers in covers. Mitya was sitting on a little chair by the entrance door, waiting for his fate in nervous impatience. When the old man appeared at the opposite entrance, some seventy feet from Mitya’s chair, Mitya suddenly jumped up and went to meet him with his firm, military, yard-long strides. Mitya was decently dressed, in a buttoned frock coat, with a round hat in his hands and black gloves, exactly as he had been three days before at the monastery, at the elder’s, at the family meeting with Fyodor Pavlovich and his brothers. The old man waited for him standing, gravely and sternly, and Mitya felt at once that while he was approaching, the old man had taken him all in. Mitya was struck too by Kuzma Kuzmich’s face, which had swollen extremely of late: his lower lip, thick enough before, now looked like a kind of hanging pancake. Gravely and silently he bowed to his visitor, pointed him to an armchair by the sofa, and himself, slowly, leaning on his son’s arm and groaning painfully, began to settle himself on the sofa opposite Mitya, so that Mitya, seeing his painful efforts, at once felt in his heart remorse and a delicate shame at his present insignificance before so important a person whom he had troubled.
“What do you want of me, sir?” said the old man, having settled at last, slowly, distinctly, sternly but politely.

Mitya started, was about to jump up, but sat down again. Then he at once began to speak loudly, rapidly, nervously, with gestures and in a decided frenzy. It was plain that the man had reached the limit, was ruined and was looking for a last way out, and if that failed, then he might as well go and drown himself. Old Samsonov probably understood all this in an instant, though his face remained unchanged and cold as an idol’s.

“The most honourable Kuzma Kuzmich has probably heard more than once of my quarrels with my father, Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov, who robbed me of my inheritance from my own mother… since the whole town is already chattering about it… for here everyone chatters about what they shouldn’t… And besides, it may have reached you from Grushenka… excuse me: from Agrafena Alexandrovna… from the highly respected Agrafena Alexandrovna, whom I so deeply honour…” So Mitya began, and broke off at the very first word. But we will not give his whole speech word for word, but only a summary. The point, as it were, was this: he, Mitya, three months before, had expressly consulted (he said precisely “expressly”, and not “on purpose”) a lawyer in the provincial capital, “a famous lawyer, Kuzma Kuzmich, Pavel Pavlovich Korneplodov; you have probably heard of him? A vast forehead, almost a statesman’s mind… he knows you too… spoke of you in the highest terms…” Mitya broke off a second time. But his breaks did not stop him; he leapt over them at once and rushed on further and further. This same Korneplodov, it seemed, having questioned him in detail and examined the documents Mitya could show him (about the documents Mitya expressed himself vaguely and in particular haste at this point), had given the opinion that as regards the village of Chermashnya, which should, as it were, have belonged to him, Mitya, through his mother, a suit could indeed be brought and the old reprobate staggered by it… “because not all doors are locked, and justice knows where to squeeze through.” In a word, one could hope even, it seemed, for some six thousand more from Fyodor Pavlovich, seven even, since Chermashnya was worth no less than twenty-five thousand, that is, surely twenty-eight, “thirty, thirty, Kuzma Kuzmich, and, imagine, I haven’t got even seventeen out of that cruel man!…” So I, Mitya, had dropped the matter then, for I don’t know how to deal with the law; and on coming here I was struck dumb by a counter-claim (here Mitya got confused again and again leapt over it abruptly): so wouldn’t you, most honourable Kuzma Kuzmich, like to take over all my rights against this monster, and give me only three thousand yourself?… You can’t lose in any case; I swear it on my honour, my honour; quite the contrary, you may make six or seven thousand instead of three… And the main thing is to finish it “today even”. “I’d sign it over to you at a notary’s, or however it is done… In a word, I am ready for anything; I will hand over all the documents you require, sign everything… and we could draw up the paper at once, and if it were possible, if only it were possible, this very morning… You would give me those three thousand… for who is a capitalist to compare with you in this little town?… and by that you would save me from… in a word, you would save my poor head for a most noble deed, a most lofty deed, one may say… for I cherish the noblest feelings for a certain person whom you know only too well and over whom you watch like a father. I would not have come otherwise, if it were not like a father. And, if you like, three heads have knocked together here, for fate is a monster, Kuzma Kuzmich! Realism, Kuzma Kuzmich, realism! And since you have long had to be left out of it, there remain two heads, as I put it, clumsily perhaps, but I am not a literary man. That is, one head is mine and the other is that monster’s. So choose: either me or the monster. Everything is in your hands now: three destinies and two lots… Forgive me, I have got muddled, but you understand… I see by your honourable eyes that you have understood… And if you haven’t, then into the water today, so there!”

Mitya broke off his absurd speech with this “so there”, and, jumping up from his seat, waited for an answer to his foolish proposal. With the last phrase he had suddenly and hopelessly felt that it had all burst, and above all that he had reeled off a terrible heap of nonsense. “Strange: while I was coming here everything seemed fine, and now it is nonsense!” suddenly flashed through his hopeless head. All the time he was talking the old man sat motionless, following him with an icy expression in his eyes. Having kept him waiting a minute, however, Kuzma Kuzmich pronounced at last in the most decided and comfortless tone:
“Excuse me, sir, we don’t go in for such deals.”
Mitya suddenly felt his legs giving way under him.
“What am I to do now, Kuzma Kuzmich?” he muttered with a pale smile. “I am done for now, don’t you think?”
“Excuse me, sir…”
Mitya still stood and still stared motionless, point-blank, and suddenly noticed that something had moved in the old man’s face. He started.
“You see, sir, such deals are not in our line,” the old man said slowly. “There’d be lawsuits, lawyers, a regular misery! But if you like, there is a man here; you apply to him…”
“My God, who is it?… You are bringing me back to life, Kuzma Kuzmich,” Mitya suddenly began to babble.

“He isn’t from these parts, this man, and he isn’t here now either. He is of peasant stock; he deals in timber; his nickname is Lyagavy, the Setter. He has been bargaining with Fyodor Pavlovich for a year now over that wood of yours at Chermashnya, but they can’t agree on the price; perhaps you have heard. Now he has just come again and is staying with the priest at Ilyinskoye, twelve versts or so from Volovya station, in the village of Ilyinskoye. He wrote here to me too about this very matter, that is, about the wood; he asked my advice. Fyodor Pavlovich wants to go and see him himself. So if you were to get in before Fyodor Pavlovich and propose to Lyagavy just what you have told me, perhaps he might…”

“A brilliant idea!” Mitya broke in rapturously. “He is the very man; it is just right for him! He is bargaining, they are asking too much of him, and here is a deed to the very property, ha-ha-ha!” And Mitya suddenly burst out laughing with his short wooden laugh, quite unexpectedly, so that even Samsonov’s head gave a jerk.
“How can I thank you, Kuzma Kuzmich?” Mitya was boiling over.
“Not at all, sir,” Samsonov bowed his head.
“But you don’t know, you have saved me; oh, a presentiment drew me to you… So, to this priest!”
“No need for thanks, sir.”
“I hurry, I fly. I have taxed your health. I shall never forget it; it is a Russian who tells you so, Kuzma Kuzmich, a R-Russian!”
“Ve-ery well.”

Mitya was about to seize the old man’s hand and shake it, but something spiteful flashed in the old man’s eyes. Mitya drew back his hand, but at once reproached himself for his suspiciousness. “He is tired…” flashed through his mind.

“For her! For her, Kuzma Kuzmich! You understand that it is for her!” he suddenly bellowed through the whole hall, bowed, turned sharply and, with the same quick, yard-long strides, without looking back, made for the door. He was trembling with rapture. “Everything was being lost, and now my guardian angel has saved me,” rushed through his mind. “And if such a man of business as this old man (a most honourable old man, and what a bearing!) has pointed out this way, then… then of course the way is won. I must fly at once. I’ll be back before night, I’ll be back at night, but the thing is won. Can the old man have been laughing at me?” So Mitya exclaimed as he strode to his lodgings; and of course it could not present itself to his mind otherwise: that is, either it was sound advice (from such a man of business), given with knowledge of the matter, with knowledge of this Lyagavy (a strange name!), or… or the old man had been laughing at him! Alas, the latter thought was the only right one. Afterwards, long afterwards, when the whole catastrophe had already happened, old Samsonov himself confessed, laughing, that he had made a fool of “the captain” then. He was a spiteful, cold and mocking man, with morbid antipathies besides. Whether it was the captain’s rapturous look, or the foolish conviction of this “spendthrift and wastrel” that he, Samsonov, could fall for such wild nonsense as his “plan”, or a jealous feeling about Grushenka, in whose name “this scapegrace” had come to him with some wild nonsense for money, I do not know what exactly moved the old man then; but at the moment when Mitya stood before him, feeling his legs giving way, and exclaiming senselessly that he was done for, at that moment the old man looked at him with infinite spite and thought of making a fool of him. When Mitya had gone, Kuzma Kuzmich, pale with spite, turned to his son and told him to see to it that this ragamuffin never set foot there again, not to let him into the yard even, or else…

He did not finish what he threatened, but even his son, who had often seen him in a rage, trembled with fear. For a whole hour afterwards the old man was even shaking all over with spite, and by evening he fell ill and sent for the “doctor”.
## Chapter II · Lyagavy

And so he had to “gallop”, and still he had not a kopeck for horses; that is, he had two twenty-kopeck pieces, and that was all, all that was left of so many years of former prosperity! But he had at home an old silver watch, which had long since stopped going. He seized it and took it to a Jewish watchmaker who had his little shop in the market. The man gave him six roubles for it. “I didn’t even expect that!” cried the delighted Mitya (he still went on being delighted); he seized his six roubles and ran home. At home he made up the sum by borrowing three roubles from his landlords, who gave them to him with pleasure, though they were giving him their last money, so much did they love him. Mitya in his rapturous state told them there and then that his fate was being decided, and told them, in a terrible hurry of course, almost the whole of his “plan” that he had just put to Samsonov, then Samsonov’s decision, his future hopes, and so on, and so on. His landlords had been let into many of his secrets before this, and that was why they looked on him as one of their own, not at all a proud gentleman. Having thus put together nine roubles, Mitya sent for post-horses to Volovya station. But in this way the fact was remembered and noted that “on the eve of a certain event, at midday, Mitya had not a kopeck, and that, to get money, he sold his watch and borrowed three roubles from his landlords, and all before witnesses.”
I note this fact in advance; it will be explained later why I do so.

Galloping to Volovya station, Mitya, though he was radiant with a joyful presentiment that at last he would finish and untangle “all these affairs”, was nevertheless trembling with fear too: what would become of Grushenka now in his absence? What if this very day she made up her mind at last to go to Fyodor Pavlovich? That was why he had left without telling her and had told his landlords on no account to reveal where he had gone if anyone came from anywhere to ask for him. “Without fail, without fail, I must be back this evening,” he kept repeating, jolting in the cart, “and perhaps drag this Lyagavy here too… to execute the deed…” So Mitya dreamed with a sinking soul; but alas, his dreams were not at all destined to be fulfilled according to his “plan”.

In the first place, he was late, having set off from Volovya station by the country road. The country road turned out to be not twelve versts but eighteen. In the second place, he did not find the Ilyinskoye priest at home; he had gone off to a neighbouring village. By the time Mitya had tracked him down there, having driven to the neighbouring village with the same horses, now worn out, it was almost night. The priest, a timid and kindly-looking little man, explained to him at once that this Lyagavy, though he had stayed with him at first, was now at Sukhoi Posyolok, spending the night in the forester’s cottage there, because he was bargaining for timber there too. At Mitya’s insistent entreaties to take him to Lyagavy at once and “thereby, so to speak, save him”, the priest, though he hesitated at first, agreed to show him the way to Sukhoi Posyolok, evidently feeling curious; but, unluckily, he advised going “on foot”, since it was only a verst or so “and a little more”. Mitya of course agreed and strode off with his yard-long strides, so that the poor priest almost had to run after him. He was not yet old and a very cautious little man. Mitya at once began talking to him too about his plans, hotly, nervously demanded advice about Lyagavy, and talked all the way. The priest listened attentively but advised little. To Mitya’s questions he answered evasively: “I don’t know, oh, I don’t know; how should I know?” and so on. When Mitya began to speak of his quarrels with his father over the inheritance, the priest was even frightened, because he stood in some relation of dependence on Fyodor Pavlovich. He asked with surprise, however, why he called this trading peasant Gorstkin “Lyagavy”, and obligingly explained to Mitya that though he really was Lyagavy, he was not Lyagavy, because he took terrible offence at the name, and that one must be sure to call him Gorstkin, “or you will get nowhere with him; he won’t even listen,” the priest concluded. Mitya was somewhat and hastily surprised and explained that Samsonov himself had called him so. On hearing of this circumstance the priest at once dropped the subject, though he would have done well to explain to Dmitri Fyodorovich there and then his own guess: that if Samsonov himself had sent him to this peasant as to “Lyagavy”, had he not done so for some reason as a joke, and was there not something wrong about it? But Mitya had no time to stop “over such trifles”. He hurried, he strode on, and only on reaching Sukhoi Posyolok did he realise that they had walked not one verst, nor one and a half, but surely three; this vexed him, but he put up with it. They went into the cottage. The forester, an acquaintance of the priest, lived in one half of the cottage, and in the other, the clean half, across the passage, Gorstkin had installed himself. They went into this clean half and lit a tallow candle. The room was heated terribly hot. On the pine table stood a samovar that had gone out, with a tray of cups, an empty bottle of rum, a not quite empty quart bottle of vodka and the remains of a wheaten loaf. The newcomer himself lay stretched out on the bench, with his coat bundled under his head instead of a pillow, snoring heavily. Mitya stood perplexed. “Of course I must wake him: my business is too important; I hurried so; I am in a hurry to get back today,” Mitya began to fret; but the priest and the forester stood silent, not giving their opinion. Mitya went up and began to wake him himself; he set about it energetically, but the sleeper did not wake. “He is drunk,” Mitya decided, “but what am I to do, Lord, what am I to do!” And suddenly, in terrible impatience, he began pulling the sleeper by the arms and legs, rocking him by the head, lifting him up and sitting him on the bench; and still, after very prolonged efforts, all he achieved was that the man began to mumble absurdly and to swear, roundly though indistinctly.
“No, you had better wait,” the priest said at last, “for he is plainly in no condition.”
“He has been drinking all day,” said the forester.
“God!” Mitya kept crying. “If only you knew how necessary it is for me and what despair I am in now!”
“No, you had better wait till morning,” the priest repeated.

“Till morning? Have mercy, it’s impossible!” And in despair he was about to rush at the drunkard again to wake him, but at once gave it up, understanding how useless his efforts were. The priest was silent; the sleepy forester was gloomy.

“What terrible tragedies realism contrives with people!” Mitya said in complete despair. The sweat was pouring down his face. Taking advantage of the moment, the priest very reasonably explained that even if they did manage to wake the sleeper, being drunk he would still be incapable of any conversation, “and your business is important, so you had better leave it till morning…” Mitya spread out his hands and agreed.
