“I’ll stay here with the candle, father, and catch the moment. When he wakes, then I’ll begin… I’ll pay you for the candle,” he turned to the forester, “and for the lodging too; you will remember Dmitri Karamazov. Only I don’t know what to do with you now, father: where will you sleep?”
“No, I’ll go home, sir. I’ll ride on his mare,” he pointed to the forester. “And so goodbye, sir; I wish you every success.”

So it was settled. The priest set off on the mare, glad to have got away at last, but still shaking his head in perplexity and wondering whether he ought not to inform his benefactor Fyodor Pavlovich of this curious incident tomorrow in good time, “or else, who knows, he’ll find out, be angry, and stop his favours.” The forester scratched himself and went in silence to his own half of the cottage, and Mitya sat down on the bench to catch the moment, as he put it. A deep anguish lay over his soul like a heavy fog. A deep, terrible anguish! He sat and thought, but could think nothing through. The candle was burning down; a cricket began to chirp; in the overheated room it was becoming unbearably stuffy. Suddenly he pictured the garden, the passage behind the garden; in his father’s house a door is mysteriously opening, and Grushenka is running in through the door… He jumped up from the bench.

“A tragedy!” he said, grinding his teeth, went mechanically up to the sleeper and began to look at his face. He was a lean peasant, still not old, with a very long face, light-brown curls and a long, thin, reddish beard, in a cotton shirt and a black waistcoat, from the pocket of which peeped the chain of a silver watch. Mitya examined this physiognomy with terrible hatred, and for some reason he particularly hated the fact that the man had curls. The main thing that was unbearably humiliating was that here he was, Mitya, standing over him with his urgent business, having sacrificed so much, given up so much, utterly worn out, while this parasite, “on whom my whole fate depends now, snores as if nothing had happened, as if he came from another planet.” “Oh, the irony of fate!” Mitya exclaimed, and suddenly, losing his head completely, rushed again to wake the drunken peasant. He tried to wake him with a kind of fury, tugged at him, pushed him, even beat him; but after struggling for five minutes and again achieving nothing, he went back in helpless despair to his bench and sat down.

“Stupid, stupid!” Mitya exclaimed. “And… how dishonourable it all is!” he suddenly added for some reason. His head began to ache terribly. “Shall I give it up? Go away altogether?” flashed through his mind. “No, till morning. I’ll stay on purpose, on purpose! Why did I come, then? And there is nothing to go away in; how could I get away from here now? Oh, the senselessness of it!”

His head, however, ached more and more. He sat motionless and no longer remembered how he began to doze, and suddenly he fell asleep sitting up. It seems he slept for two hours or more. He came to himself from an unbearable headache, unbearable enough to make him scream. His temples were throbbing, the crown of his head ached; coming to, he could not for a long time recover himself completely and grasp what had happened to him. At last he realised that the overheated room was full of fumes from the stove, and that he might have died. And the drunken peasant still lay snoring; the candle had guttered and was about to go out. Mitya shouted and rushed, staggering, across the passage into the forester’s room. The forester soon woke, but on hearing that there were fumes in the other room, though he went to see to it, he took the fact with strange indifference, which surprised Mitya and offended him.
“But he is dead, he is dead, and then… what then?” Mitya cried in a frenzy before him.

They opened the doors, opened the window, opened the flue; Mitya dragged a bucket of water in from the passage, first wetted his own head, and then, finding some rag, dipped it in the water and put it on Lyagavy’s head. The forester went on treating the whole event even somehow contemptuously, and, having opened the window, said gloomily, “It’ll do like this,” and went back to sleep, leaving Mitya a lighted iron lantern. Mitya fussed over the fume-stupefied drunkard for half an hour, wetting his head again and again, and seriously meant not to sleep all night; but, worn out, he sat down somehow for a minute to get his breath, and instantly closed his eyes; then at once, unconsciously, he stretched out on the bench and fell asleep like the dead.

He woke terribly late. It was already about nine in the morning. The sun was shining brightly through the two little windows of the cottage. The curly-haired peasant of the night before was sitting on the bench, already dressed in his coat. Before him stood a new samovar and a new quart bottle. The old one of the night before had been finished, and the new one was more than half empty. Mitya jumped up and in an instant realised that the cursed peasant was drunk again, deeply and irretrievably drunk. He stared at him for a minute, his eyes starting out. And the peasant looked at him silently and slyly, with a kind of insulting calm, even with a kind of contemptuous haughtiness, as it seemed to Mitya. He rushed to him.
“Allow me, you see… I… you have probably heard from the forester here in the other room: I am Lieutenant Dmitri Karamazov, son of old Karamazov, whose wood you are bargaining for…”
“That’s a lie!” the peasant suddenly rapped out, firmly and calmly.
“What do you mean, a lie? You know Fyodor Pavlovich?”
“I don’t know any Fyodor Pavlovich of yours,” the peasant said, somehow moving his tongue heavily.
“The wood, the wood; you are bargaining with him for it; wake up, come to your senses. Father Pavel of Ilyinskoye brought me here… You wrote to Samsonov, and he sent me to you…” Mitya was gasping.
“That’s a l-lie!” Lyagavy rapped out again.
Mitya’s legs went cold.
“Have mercy, this is no joke! Perhaps you are tipsy. But you can speak, after all, understand… otherwise… otherwise I understand nothing!”
“You’re a painter!”
“Have mercy, I am Karamazov, Dmitri Karamazov; I have a proposal for you… a profitable proposal… a very profitable one… precisely about the wood.”
The peasant was stroking his beard importantly.
“No, you took on a contract and turned out a scoundrel. You’re a scoundrel!”
“I assure you, you are mistaken!” Mitya wrung his hands in despair. The peasant kept stroking his beard and suddenly screwed up his eyes slyly.
“No, you show me this: you show me a law that allows people to play dirty tricks, do you hear! You’re a scoundrel, do you understand?”

Mitya stepped back gloomily, and suddenly it was as if “something struck him on the forehead”, as he put it himself afterwards. In an instant a kind of illumination came over his mind: “a light was kindled, and I understood everything.” He stood dumbfounded, wondering how he, an intelligent man after all, could have fallen for such foolishness, rushed headlong into such an adventure and kept it up for almost a whole day and night, fussing over this Lyagavy, wetting his head… “Well, the man is drunk, drunk as a lord, and he’ll go on drinking for another week; what is there to wait for? And what if Samsonov sent me here on purpose? And what if she… Oh God, what have I done!…”

The peasant sat looking at him and chuckling. Had it been any other time, Mitya might have killed this fool in his rage; but now he himself had grown as weak as a child. He went quietly to the bench, took his overcoat, put it on in silence and went out of the room. In the forester’s half he found no one; there was nobody there. He took fifty kopecks in small change out of his pocket and put it on the table, for the night’s lodging, for the candle and for the trouble. Coming out of the cottage, he saw that all round there was only forest and nothing more. He went at random, not even remembering which way to turn from the cottage, to the right or to the left; last night, hurrying here with the priest, he had not noticed the road. There was no thought of revenge on anyone in his soul, not even on Samsonov. He strode along the narrow forest track senselessly, at a loss, with a “lost idea”, and not caring at all where he was going. A child he met could have knocked him down, so weak had he suddenly become in soul and body. Somehow, however, he made his way out of the forest: suddenly reaped, bare fields stretched before him, boundless. “What despair, what death all round!” he repeated, striding on and on.

He was saved by travellers: a driver was taking an old merchant along the country road. When they came abreast, Mitya asked the way, and it turned out that they too were going to Volovya. They struck a bargain and took Mitya along. About three hours later they arrived. At Volovya station Mitya at once ordered post-horses to the town, and suddenly realised that he was impossibly hungry. While the horses were being harnessed they cooked him some fried eggs. He ate them all in a moment, ate the whole big hunk of bread, ate some sausage they found and drank three glasses of vodka. Fortified, he cheered up, and his soul grew bright again. He flew along the road, urged the driver on, and suddenly made a new and now “infallible” plan for getting “this cursed money” that very day before evening. “And to think, only to think, that a man’s fate is being ruined for the sake of these miserable three thousand!” he exclaimed contemptuously. “I shall settle it today!” And had it not been for the incessant thought of Grushenka, and whether something had happened to her, he might perhaps have become quite cheerful again. But the thought of her pierced his soul every minute like a sharp knife. At last they arrived, and Mitya at once ran to Grushenka.
## Book Eleven, Chapter III · A Little Demon

Going in to Lise, he found her half lying in her old chair, the one in which she had been wheeled about when she could not yet walk. She did not move to meet him, but her keen, sharp eyes fastened on him. Her eyes were somewhat feverish, her face a pale yellow. Alyosha was amazed at how she had changed in three days; she had even grown thin. She did not hold out her hand to him. He touched her thin, long little fingers himself, which lay motionless on her dress, then sat down opposite her in silence.
“I know you are in a hurry to get to the prison,” Lise said sharply, “and mama has kept you two hours; she has just told you about me and about Yulia.”
“How do you know?” asked Alyosha.
“I was eavesdropping. Why are you staring at me? I want to eavesdrop, so I eavesdrop; there is nothing wrong in that. I don’t ask forgiveness.”
“Are you upset about something?”

“On the contrary, I’m very glad. I was just thinking it over again, for the thirtieth time: how good it is that I refused you and won’t be your wife. You are no good as a husband: I’d marry you, and suddenly give you a note to take to the man I’d fallen in love with after you, and you would take it and be sure to deliver it, and bring back an answer too. And you’ll be forty, and you’ll still be carrying notes like that for me.”
She suddenly laughed.
“There is something spiteful in you and at the same time something simple-hearted,” Alyosha smiled at her.

“The simple-hearted thing is that I’m not ashamed before you. Not only am I not ashamed, I don’t want to be ashamed, precisely before you, precisely of you. Alyosha, why don’t I respect you? I love you very much, but I don’t respect you. If I respected you, I wouldn’t talk without shame, would I?”
“No.”
“And do you believe that I’m not ashamed before you?”
“No, I don’t.”
Lise laughed nervously again; she was talking fast, rapidly.
“I sent your brother Dmitri Fyodorovich some sweets in prison. Alyosha, do you know how sweet you are? I shall love you terribly for having let me not love you so quickly.”
“Why did you send for me today, Lise?”
“I wanted to tell you a wish of mine. I want someone to torment me, marry me and then torment me, deceive me, go away and leave me. I don’t want to be happy!”
“You have come to love disorder?”

“Ah, I want disorder. I keep wanting to set fire to the house. I imagine how I’ll go up and set fire to it quietly; it must be quietly. They’ll be putting it out, and it will be burning. And I’ll know and say nothing. Ah, what nonsense! And how dull it is!”
She waved her little hand in disgust.
“You live in luxury,” Alyosha said quietly.
“Is it better to be poor, then?”
“It is better.”

“That is what your dead monk told you. It isn’t true. Let me be rich and everyone else poor; I’ll eat sweets and drink cream and give none to anyone. Ah, don’t speak, don’t say anything,” she waved her hand, though Alyosha had not opened his mouth. “You’ve told me all that before; I know it all by heart. It’s dull. If I am poor I’ll kill someone; and if I’m rich, perhaps I’ll kill someone too; why sit about! Do you know, I want to reap, to reap rye. I’ll marry you, and you become a peasant, a real peasant; we’ll have a little foal; would you like that? Do you know Kalganov?”
“I do.”

“He keeps walking about dreaming. He says: why live for real? It’s better to dream. One can dream the merriest things, but living is dull. And yet he’ll be married soon; he has already declared his love to me too. Can you spin a top?”
“I can.”
“Well, he’s like a top: wind him up and set him spinning and whip him, whip him, whip him with a little whip. I’ll marry him and keep him spinning all my life. Aren’t you ashamed to sit with me?”
“No.”
“You are terribly angry that I’m not talking about holy things. I don’t want to be holy. What will they do in the next world for the very greatest sin? You must know exactly.”
“God will judge,” said Alyosha, looking at her intently.
“That’s just what I want. I’d come, and they’d judge me, and I’d suddenly laugh in all their faces. I terribly want to set fire to the house, Alyosha, our house; you still don’t believe me?”
“Why not? There are even children, about twelve years old, who very much want to set fire to something, and they do. It is a sort of illness.”
“That’s not true, not true; there may be children like that, but that isn’t what I mean.”
“You take evil for good: it is a passing crisis; perhaps your former illness is to blame for it.”
“So you do despise me! I simply don’t want to do good; I want to do evil, and there is no illness in it at all.”
“Why do evil?”

“So that nothing should be left anywhere. Ah, how good it would be if nothing were left! Do you know, Alyosha, I sometimes think of doing a terrible lot of evil and everything nasty, and I’ll go on doing it quietly for a long time, and suddenly everyone will find out. Everyone will crowd round me and point their fingers at me, and I’ll look at them all. That is very pleasant. Why is it so pleasant, Alyosha?”
“It just is. A need to crush something good, or, as you said, to set fire to something. That happens too.”
“I didn’t just say it; I shall do it.”
“I believe you.”
“Ah, how I love you for saying ‘I believe you’. And you aren’t lying at all, at all. But perhaps you think I’m saying all this on purpose, to tease you?”
“No, I don’t think so… though perhaps there is a little of that need too.”
“There is a little. I shall never lie to you,” she said, with a sort of little fire flashing in her eyes.

What struck Alyosha most of all was her seriousness: there was not a shadow of laughter or playfulness in her face now, though before, gaiety and playfulness had never left her even in her most “serious” moments.
“There are moments when people love crime,” Alyosha said thoughtfully.

“Yes, yes! You have said my thought; they love it, everyone loves it, and always, not just at ‘moments’. You know, it’s as if everyone once agreed to lie about it, and everyone has lied ever since. Everyone says they hate what is bad, and in themselves they all love it.”
“Are you still reading bad books?”
“I am. Mama reads them and hides them under her pillow, and I steal them.”
“Aren’t you ashamed to destroy yourself?”

“I want to destroy myself. There is a boy here who lay under the rails while the train went over him. Lucky boy! Listen, your brother is being tried now for killing his father, and everyone loves it that he killed his father.”
“Loves it that he killed his father?”
“They love it, everyone loves it! Everyone says it’s terrible, but in themselves they love it terribly. I am the first to love it.”
“There is some truth in what you say about everyone,” Alyosha said quietly.

“Oh, what thoughts you have!” Lise squealed in rapture. “And from a monk! You wouldn’t believe how I respect you, Alyosha, for never lying. Ah, I’ll tell you a funny dream of mine. I sometimes dream of devils. It is night, and I am in my room with a candle, and suddenly there are devils everywhere, in all the corners and under the table, and they open the doors, and there is a crowd of them behind the doors, and they want to come in and seize me. And they come nearer, they are seizing me already. And suddenly I cross myself, and they all draw back; they are afraid; only they don’t go away altogether, but stand at the doors and in the corners, waiting. And suddenly I terribly want to begin abusing God aloud, and so I begin abusing him, and they all come crowding at me again, they are so glad, and they are seizing me again, and suddenly I cross myself again, and they all draw back. It is terribly jolly; it takes my breath away.”
“I have had that very dream too,” Alyosha said suddenly.
“Really?” Lise cried out in surprise. “Listen, Alyosha, don’t laugh; this is terribly important: can two different people really have the same dream?”
“They can, I suppose.”

“Alyosha, I tell you, it is terribly important,” Lise went on in an excessive surprise. “It isn’t the dream that is important, but that you could have had the very same dream as I. You never lie to me; don’t lie now either: is it true? You aren’t laughing?”
“It is true.”
Lise was terribly struck by something and was silent for half a minute.
“Alyosha, come and see me, come and see me more often,” she said suddenly in an imploring voice.
“I shall always, all my life, come and see you,” Alyosha answered firmly.

“I tell it only to you,” Lise began again. “I tell it only to myself, and to you as well. To you alone in the whole world. And I tell it to you more willingly than to myself. And I am not ashamed before you at all. Alyosha, why am I not ashamed before you at all, not at all? Alyosha, is it true that the Jews steal children at Passover and kill them?”
“I don’t know.”

“I have a book here; I read about some trial somewhere, and that a Jew first cut off all the fingers on both hands of a little boy of four, and then crucified him on the wall, nailed him up with nails and crucified him; and then at the trial he said that the boy died quickly, in four hours. Quickly, indeed! He said the boy moaned, kept moaning, and he stood there admiring him. That is good!”
“Good?”
“Good. I sometimes imagine that I crucified him myself. He hangs there moaning, and I sit down opposite him and eat pineapple compote. I am very fond of pineapple compote. Are you?”
Alyosha was silent and looked at her. Her pale yellow face suddenly became distorted; her eyes were burning.

“You know, when I read about that Jew, I shook in tears all night. I imagined how the little child cried and moaned (four-year-old boys do understand, after all), and all the while this thought about the compote wouldn’t leave me. In the morning I sent a letter to a certain person, asking him to come and see me without fail. He came, and I suddenly told him about the boy and the compote, told him everything, everything, and said that ‘it was good’. He suddenly laughed and said that it really was good. Then he got up and went away. He only stayed five minutes. Did he despise me, did he despise me? Tell me, tell me, Alyosha, did he despise me or not?” She sat up straight on the couch, her eyes flashing.
“Tell me,” Alyosha said in agitation, “did you send for him yourself, this person?”
“I did.”
“You sent him a letter?”
“A letter.”
“Simply to ask about this, about the child?”
“No, not about that at all, not at all. But as soon as he came in, I asked him about that at once. He answered, laughed, got up and went away.”
“That person treated you honestly,” Alyosha said quietly.
“And did he despise me? Did he laugh at me?”
“No, because perhaps he believes in the pineapple compote himself. He is very ill now too, Lise.”
“Yes, he believes in it!” Lise’s eyes flashed.
“He doesn’t despise anyone,” Alyosha went on. “He only doesn’t believe anyone. And if he doesn’t believe, then of course he despises too.”
“So me too? Me?”
“You too.”
“That’s good,” Lise somehow ground out. “When he went out and laughed, I felt that it is good to be despised. And the boy with his fingers cut off is good, and being despised is good…”
And she laughed somehow spitefully and feverishly in Alyosha’s face.

“You know, Alyosha, you know, I should like… Alyosha, save me!” She suddenly jumped up from the couch, rushed to him and clasped him tightly in her arms. “Save me,” she almost moaned. “Would I tell anyone in the world what I have told you? And I was telling the truth, the truth, the truth! I shall kill myself, because everything is loathsome to me! I don’t want to live, because everything is loathsome to me! Everything is loathsome to me, everything is loathsome! Alyosha, why don’t you love me at all, not at all?” she finished in a frenzy.
“But I do love you!” Alyosha answered warmly.
“And will you weep for me? Will you?”
“I will.”
“Not because I wouldn’t be your wife, but just weep for me, just weep?”
“I will.”

“Thank you! I only need your tears. And let all the rest punish me and crush me under their feet, all, all, without exception! Because I don’t love anyone. Do you hear, no-o-one! On the contrary, I hate them! Go, Alyosha; it’s time for you to go to your brother!” She suddenly tore herself away from him.
“But how can I leave you like this?” Alyosha said, almost in alarm.
“Go to your brother; they’ll lock the prison; go, here is your hat! Kiss Mitya for me; go, go!”

And she almost pushed Alyosha out of the door by force. He was looking at her in sorrowful perplexity, when suddenly he felt a letter in his right hand, a little letter, folded tight and sealed. He glanced at it and instantly read the address: To Ivan Fyodorovich Karamazov. He looked quickly at Lise. Her face had become almost menacing.
“Give it to him, be sure to give it to him!” she ordered in a frenzy, trembling all over. “Today, at once! Or I’ll poison myself! That’s why I sent for you!”

And she quickly slammed the door. The latch clicked. Alyosha put the letter in his pocket and went straight to the stairs, without going in to Madame Khokhlakova, forgetting about her even. And Lise, as soon as Alyosha had gone, at once unfastened the latch, opened the door a tiny crack, put her finger in the crack and, slamming the door, crushed it with all her might. About ten seconds later, freeing her hand, she walked quietly, slowly, to her chair, sat down, holding herself quite straight, and began to look intently at her blackened little finger and at the blood that had been squeezed out from under the nail. Her lips were trembling, and she whispered quickly, quickly to herself:
“Vile, vile, vile, vile!”
## Chapter IV · A Hymn and a Secret

It was already quite late (and how long is a November day?) when Alyosha rang at the prison gate. It was even beginning to get dark. But Alyosha knew he would be let in to Mitya without hindrance. All this is the same in our little town as everywhere. At first, of course, after the whole preliminary investigation was over, access to Mitya for visits from relatives and certain other persons was still surrounded with some necessary formalities; but afterwards the formalities, not that they were relaxed, but for certain persons at least who came to see Mitya, certain exceptions somehow established themselves of their own accord. So much so that sometimes even visits to the prisoner in the room set aside for them took place almost tête-à-tête. There were very few such persons, however: only Grushenka, Alyosha and Rakitin. But Grushenka was very much in the good graces of the police captain Mikhail Makarovich himself. The old man had on his conscience his shouting at her at Mokroye. Later, having learned the whole truth, he had completely changed his opinion of her. And, strange to say, though he was firmly convinced of Mitya’s crime, since his imprisonment he had somehow come to look on him more and more gently: “A man with a good soul perhaps, and he has come to grief like a Swede at Poltava, from drink and disorder!” The former horror had given way in his heart to a kind of pity. As for Alyosha, the police captain was very fond of him and had known him a long time; and Rakitin, who had later taken to visiting the prisoner very often, was one of the most intimate acquaintances of “the police captain’s young ladies”, as he called them, and was always hanging about their house. He also gave lessons in the house of the prison governor, a good-natured old man, though a sound old officer. And Alyosha again was a special and long-standing acquaintance of the governor too, who loved to talk with him about “wisdom” in general. Ivan Fyodorovich, for instance, the governor did not so much respect as fear, above all his opinions, though he was a great philosopher himself, “having worked it out with his own wits”, of course. But for Alyosha he had a kind of invincible liking. In the last year the old man had just taken up the apocryphal gospels and was constantly telling his young friend his impressions of them. Before, he had even visited him at the monastery and talked with him and the hieromonks for hours on end. In a word, even if Alyosha was late for the prison, he had only to go to the governor and it was always arranged. Besides, everyone in the prison, down to the last warder, had grown used to Alyosha. The guard, of course, made no difficulties, so long as the authorities gave permission. When he was called, Mitya always came down from his cell to the place appointed for visits. Coming into the room, Alyosha ran straight into Rakitin, who was just leaving Mitya. They were both talking loudly. Mitya, seeing him out, was laughing heartily at something, and Rakitin seemed to be grumbling. Rakitin, especially of late, did not like meeting Alyosha; he hardly spoke to him and even bowed to him with an effort. Seeing Alyosha come in now, he frowned particularly and looked away, as if entirely absorbed in buttoning his big warm overcoat with its fur collar. Then he at once began looking for his umbrella.
“Mustn’t forget anything of my own,” he muttered, simply to say something.
“Mind you don’t forget anything of other people’s!” Mitya joked, and at once roared with laughter at his own joke. Rakitin flared up instantly.
“Recommend that to your Karamazovs, your brood of serf-owners, not to Rakitin!” he suddenly shouted, shaking with rage.

“What’s the matter with you? I was joking!” Mitya cried out. “Ugh, the devil! They are all like that,” he turned to Alyosha, nodding at the quickly retreating Rakitin. “There he sat laughing and cheerful all the time, and suddenly he boils over! He didn’t even nod to you; have you quarrelled altogether, or what? Why are you so late? I wasn’t just waiting for you, I was thirsting for you all morning. Well, never mind! We’ll make up for it.”
“Why has he taken to coming to you so often? Have you made friends with him, or what?” asked Alyosha, nodding too at the door through which Rakitin had gone.

“Made friends with Mikhail? No, not exactly. He’s a pig, what else! He thinks I am… a scoundrel. And they don’t understand a joke either; that’s the main thing about them. They’ll never understand a joke. And their souls are dry, flat and dry, just as I was when I drove up to the prison and looked at the prison walls. But a clever man, clever. Well, Alexei, my head is lost now!”
He sat down on the bench and sat Alyosha down beside him.
“Yes, the trial is tomorrow. Can you really have no hope at all, brother?” Alyosha said with a timid feeling.

“What do you mean?” Mitya looked at him somehow vaguely. “Ah, you mean the trial! Oh, the devil! We have talked of nothing but trifles all this time, nothing but this trial, and I have said nothing to you about the most important thing. Yes, the trial is tomorrow, only it wasn’t the trial I meant when I said my head is lost. My head isn’t lost, but what was sitting in my head is lost. Why are you looking at me with such criticism in your face?”
“What do you mean, Mitya?”
“Ideas, ideas, that’s what! Ethics. What is ethics?”
“Ethics?” Alyosha was surprised.
“Yes, is it a science or something?”
“Yes, there is such a science… only… I confess I can’t explain to you what science it is.”

“Rakitin knows. Rakitin knows a lot, the devil take him! He won’t become a monk. He is planning to go to Petersburg. There, he says, he’ll go into the critical department, but with a noble tendency. Well, he may be of use and make a career. Ugh, they are masters at careers! The devil take ethics! I am lost, Alexei, I am, you man of God! I love you more than anyone. My heart trembles for you, that’s what. Who was that Karl Bernard?”
“Karl Bernard?” Alyosha was surprised again.
“No, not Karl; wait, I’m wrong: Claude Bernard. What is that? Chemistry or something?”
“It must be a scientist,” Alyosha answered, “only, I confess, I can’t tell you much about him either. I have only heard that he is a scientist, but what kind, I don’t know.”

“Well, the devil take him; I don’t know either,” Mitya swore. “Some scoundrel, most likely; they are all scoundrels. But Rakitin will get on; Rakitin will squeeze through a crack; he is a Bernard too. Ugh, these Bernards! There are lots of them now!”
“But what is the matter with you?” Alyosha asked insistently.

“He wants to write an article about me, about my case, and begin his part in literature with it; that’s why he comes; he explained it himself. He wants it to have a tendency: ‘he couldn’t help killing, he was eaten up by his environment’, and so on; he explained it to me. It will have a tinge of socialism, he says. Well, the devil take him; a tinge, then, a tinge; it’s all the same to me. He doesn’t like brother Ivan; he hates him; and he isn’t fond of you either. Well, and I don’t drive him away, because he is a clever man. He gives himself airs, though. I told him just now: ‘The Karamazovs are not scoundrels but philosophers, because all real Russian people are philosophers, and you, though you have studied, are not a philosopher; you are a lout.’ He laughs, so spitefully. And I said to him: de thoughtibus non est disputandum. Good joke? At least I’ve gone in for the classics too,” Mitya suddenly roared with laughter.
“Why are you lost? You said so just now,” Alyosha broke in.
“Why am I lost? Hm! In fact… if you take the whole thing, I am sorry for God, that’s why!”
“Sorry for God?”

“Imagine: it’s there in the nerves, in the head, that is, there in the brain, these nerves (the devil take them!)… there are sort of little tails, the nerves have little tails, and as soon as they start quivering there… that is, you see, I look at something with my eyes, like this, and they quiver, those little tails… and when they quiver, an image appears, and not at once, but some instant, a second, passes, and there appears a sort of moment, that is, not a moment, the devil take the moment, but an image, that is, an object or an event, well, the devil take it; and that is why I contemplate, and then think… because of the little tails, and not at all because I have a soul and am some sort of image and likeness; all that is nonsense. Mikhail explained this to me only yesterday, brother, and it was as if I’d been scalded. It is magnificent, Alyosha, this science! A new man is coming; that I do understand… And yet I am sorry for God!”
“Well, that is good too,” said Alyosha.

“That I’m sorry for God? Chemistry, brother, chemistry! There’s no help for it, your reverence; move up a little; chemistry is coming! But Rakitin doesn’t love God; ugh, how he doesn’t love him! That is the sorest spot with all of them! But they hide it. They lie. They pretend. ‘Well, will you put that forward in the critical department?’ I ask. ‘Well, they won’t let me do it openly,’ he says, and laughs. ‘But then what becomes of man?’ I ask. ‘Without God and without a future life? So now everything is permitted, one can do anything?’ ‘Didn’t you know?’ he says. He laughs. ‘For a clever man,’ he says, ‘everything is permitted; a clever man knows how to catch crayfish; but you,’ he says, ‘you killed and got caught, and you are rotting in prison!’ He says that to me! A natural pig! I used to throw such fellows out, but now I listen. He says a lot that is sensible, too. And he writes cleverly. About a week ago he began reading me an article; I copied out three lines on purpose then; wait, here they are.”
Mitya hurriedly took a scrap of paper from his waistcoat pocket and read:
“‘In order to resolve this question it is necessary, first of all, to set one’s personality in opposition to one’s reality.’ Do you understand it or not?”
“No, I don’t,” said Alyosha.
He was looking at Mitya with curiosity and listening to him.

“I don’t understand it either. Dark and obscure, but clever. ‘Everyone writes like that now,’ he says, ‘because such is the environment…’ They are afraid of the environment. He writes verses too, the scoundrel; he has sung of Khokhlakova’s foot, ha-ha-ha!”
“I have heard,” said Alyosha.
“You have? And have you heard the verses?”
“No.”

“I have them; here, I’ll read them. You don’t know; I haven’t told you; there is a whole story here. The rogue! Three weeks ago he took it into his head to tease me: ‘There you are,’ he says, ‘you have landed yourself like a fool over three thousand, but I’ll grab a hundred and fifty thousand; I’ll marry a little widow and buy a stone house in Petersburg.’ And he told me he was courting Khokhlakova, and she wasn’t clever even when she was young, and at forty she has quite lost her wits. ‘But she is very sentimental,’ he says, ‘and that’s how I shall finish her off. I’ll marry her, take her to Petersburg, and there I’ll start publishing a newspaper.’ And there was such nasty, lustful slobber on his lips, not slobber over Khokhlakova but over those hundred and fifty thousand. And he convinced me, convinced me; he kept coming to me every day: she is giving way, he says. He was beaming with joy. And then suddenly he was turned out: Pyotr Ilyich Perkhotin got the upper hand, good man! I could have kissed that fool of a woman for turning him out! It was while he was coming to see me that he made up these verses. ‘It’s the first time I have soiled my hands,’ he says, ‘writing verses, for seduction, that is, for a useful purpose. Once I have got the capital from the fool of a woman, I can be of civic use.’ They have a civic justification for every vileness! ‘And all the same,’ he says, ‘I’ve written better than your Pushkin, because even into a comic verse I have managed to slip civic grief.’ What he says about Pushkin, I understand. Well, if he really was a gifted man, and only described feet! And how proud he was of his little verses! The vanity of them, the vanity! ‘On the Recovery of the Ailing Foot of My Beloved’: that’s the title he thought up. A playful fellow!

> Oh, the little foot, the sweet,
> Swollen up, poor little feet!
> Doctors come to treat it, bind it,
> Bandage it, and maim, and wind it.
> But it’s not for feet I languish;
> Leave the feet to Pushkin’s singing:
> For the little head’s my anguish,
> Where ideas won’t start ringing.
> Once it understood a little;
> Then the foot got in its way!
> Let the foot be cured, the little,
> So the head may think one day.
A pig, a pure pig, but the scoundrel has made it playful! And he really has slipped in the ‘civic’ stuff. And how angry he was when they turned him out. He ground his teeth!”
“He has taken his revenge already,” said Alyosha. “He has written a piece about Khokhlakova for the paper.”
And Alyosha told him hastily about the correspondence in the newspaper Rumours.

“It’s he, it’s he!” Mitya confirmed, frowning. “It’s he! Those correspondences… I know… I mean, how many base things have been written already, about Grusha, for instance!… And about the other one too, about Katya… Hm!”
He walked up and down the room with a worried look.

“Brother, I can’t stay long,” Alyosha said after a pause. “Tomorrow is a terrible, great day for you: God’s judgement will be passed on you… and I wonder at you: you walk about, and instead of talking business you talk of God knows what.”

“No, don’t wonder,” Mitya broke in hotly. “What, am I to talk about that stinking dog? About the murderer? We have talked enough about that, you and I. I don’t want to talk any more about the stinking one, the son of Stinking Lizaveta! God will kill him, you’ll see; say no more!”
He came up to Alyosha in agitation and suddenly kissed him. His eyes were burning.

“Rakitin won’t understand this,” he began, as if in a kind of rapture, “but you, you will understand everything. That’s why I was thirsting for you. You see, for a long time I have wanted to say a great deal to you here, within these peeling walls, but I kept silent about the most important thing: the time seemed not to have come yet. Now I have waited till the last moment to pour out my soul to you. Brother, these last two months I have felt a new man in myself; a new man has risen in me! He was shut up inside me, but he would never have appeared if it hadn’t been for this thunderbolt. It’s terrifying! And what do I care if I spend twenty years in the mines hammering out ore? I am not afraid of that at all; it is something else I am afraid of now: that the man who has risen in me may leave me! One can find there too, in the mines, under the earth, next to oneself, in another convict and murderer, a human heart, and become close to him, because there too one can live and love and suffer! One can bring back to life and raise up the frozen heart in that convict; one can tend him for years and at last bring up from the den into the light a lofty soul, a suffering consciousness, give new life to an angel, raise up a hero! And there are many of them, hundreds, and we are all to blame for them! Why did I dream of that ‘babe’ at such a moment? ‘Why is the babe poor?’ That was a prophecy to me at that moment! I shall go for the ‘babe’. Because we are all to blame for all. For all the ‘babes’, because there are little children and big children. All are ‘babes’. I shall go for all, because someone must go for all. I didn’t kill my father, but I must go. I accept it! All this came to me here… here within these peeling walls. And there are many of them, hundreds of them there, underground, with hammers in their hands. Oh yes, we shall be in chains and there will be no freedom; but then, in our great grief, we shall rise again into joy, without which man cannot live, nor God exist, for God gives joy; it is his privilege, his great privilege… Lord, let man melt away in prayer! How shall I be there underground without God? Rakitin is lying: if they drive God from the earth, we shall meet him under the earth! A convict cannot be without God; it is even more impossible than for one who is not a convict! And then we, the men underground, will sing from the bowels of the earth a tragic hymn to God, in whom there is joy! Hail to God and his joy! I love him!”
Mitya was almost gasping as he uttered his wild speech. He had turned pale, his lips were quivering, tears were rolling from his eyes.

“No, life is full; there is life even underground!” he began again. “You won’t believe, Alexei, how I want to live now, what a thirst to exist and to be conscious has been born in me precisely within these peeling walls! Rakitin doesn’t understand it; all he wants is to build a house and let out flats; but I was waiting for you. And what is suffering? I am not afraid of it, even if it were beyond counting. I am not afraid now; I was afraid before. You know, perhaps I won’t even answer at the trial… And it seems there is so much strength in me now that I can overcome everything, all sufferings, only to say and to tell myself every minute: I am! In a thousand torments, I am; I writhe on the rack, but I am! I sit on a pillar, but I exist; I see the sun; and if I don’t see the sun, I know it is there. And to know that the sun is there, that is already the whole of life. Alyosha, my cherub, all sorts of philosophies are killing me, the devil take them! Brother Ivan…”
“What about brother Ivan?” Alyosha tried to interrupt, but Mitya did not hear.

“You see, I never had any of these doubts before, but it was all lying hidden in me. Perhaps it was precisely because unknown ideas were raging in me that I drank and fought and raged. I fought to quench them in myself, to subdue them, to crush them. Brother Ivan isn’t Rakitin; he hides an idea. Brother Ivan is a sphinx and keeps silent, always silent. But God torments me. That alone torments me. What if he doesn’t exist? What if Rakitin is right, that it is an artificial idea in mankind? Then, if he doesn’t exist, man is the chief of the earth, of the universe. Magnificent! Only how is he going to be virtuous without God? That’s the question! I keep coming back to it. For whom will man love then? To whom will he be grateful, to whom will he sing the hymn? Rakitin laughs. Rakitin says one can love mankind without God. Well, only a snivelling little toadstool could assert that; I can’t understand it. Life is easy for Rakitin. ‘You,’ he said to me today, ‘you had better bother about extending the civil rights of man, or at least about keeping the price of beef from going up; that way you will show your love for mankind more simply and directly than with philosophies.’ And I came out with this to him: ‘And you,’ I said, ‘without God, you’ll put up the price of beef yourself, if you get the chance, and make a rouble on every kopeck.’ He was angry. For what is virtue? Answer me that, Alexei. I have one virtue, and a Chinaman has another; so it is a relative thing. Or isn’t it? Or isn’t it relative? A treacherous question! You won’t laugh if I tell you I haven’t slept for two nights over it. The only thing I wonder at now is how people live there and think nothing about it. Vanity! Ivan has no God. He has an idea. It isn’t on my scale. But he keeps silent. I think he is a freemason. I asked him; he keeps silent. I wanted to drink a little water from his spring; he keeps silent. Only once he said one little word.”
“What did he say?” Alyosha caught it up hastily.

“I said to him: so then everything is permitted, if that is so? He frowned: ‘Fyodor Pavlovich, our papa, was a pig,’ he said, ‘but his thinking was right.’ That is what he came out with. That is all he said. That goes further than Rakitin.”
“Yes,” Alyosha confirmed bitterly. “When was he with you?”

“Of that later; now something else. I have told you almost nothing about Ivan so far. I have put it off till the end. When this business of mine here is over and they have pronounced the sentence, then I’ll tell you something, I’ll tell you everything. There is a terrible matter here… And you shall be my judge in this matter. But don’t begin on it now; mum’s the word for now. There you are talking about tomorrow, about the trial, and would you believe it, I know nothing.”
“Have you talked with this lawyer?”

“What of the lawyer! I told him everything. A soft rogue from the capital. A Bernard! Only he doesn’t believe me a broken farthing’s worth. He believes I killed him, imagine; I can see it. ‘Then why have you come to defend me?’ I ask him. I spit on them. They have sent for a doctor too; they want to make me out a madman. I won’t allow it! Katerina Ivanovna wants to do ‘her duty’ to the end. With an effort!” Mitya smiled bitterly. “A cat! A cruel heart! And she knows what I said about her then at Mokroye, that she is a woman ‘of great wrath’! They passed it on. Yes, the evidence has multiplied like the sand of the sea! Grigory sticks to his story. Grigory is honest, but a fool. Many people are honest because they are fools. That is a thought of Rakitin’s. Grigory is my enemy. Some people it pays better to have among one’s enemies than one’s friends. I say that of Katerina Ivanovna. I am afraid, oh, I am afraid she will tell at the trial about her bow to the ground after the four thousand five hundred! She will pay me back to the end, to the last farthing. I don’t want her sacrifice! They will put me to shame at the trial! I’ll bear it somehow. Go to her, Alyosha, ask her not to tell that at the trial. Or is it impossible? Oh, the devil, it’s all the same; I’ll bear it! And I don’t pity her. She wants it herself. The thief deserves his torment. I shall make my speech, Alexei.” He smiled bitterly again. “Only… only Grusha, Grusha, Lord! Why should she take such torment on herself now?” he suddenly exclaimed with tears. “Grusha is killing me; the thought of her is killing me, killing me! She was here with me earlier…”
“She told me. She was very much hurt by you today.”
“I know. The devil take my character. I was jealous! As I let her go I repented and kissed her. I didn’t ask her forgiveness.”
“Why didn’t you?” exclaimed Alyosha.
Mitya suddenly laughed almost gaily.

“God preserve you, my dear boy, from ever asking forgiveness of a woman you love for something you have done wrong! Of one you love especially, especially, however much you are to blame before her! Because a woman, brother, is the devil knows what; I at least know something about them! Well, try confessing your fault to her, ‘I am to blame, forgive me, excuse me’: then the hail of reproaches begins! She will never forgive you straight and simply, but will humble you to a rag, read you a lecture on things that never even happened, take everything, forget nothing, add her own, and only then will she forgive you. And that is the best, the best of them! She will scrape up the last scrapings and pile them all on your head; such a flaying spirit, I tell you, sits in them, in every one of them, in these angels without whom we can’t live! You see, my dear, I will say it frankly and simply: every decent man ought to be under the heel of some woman or other. That is my conviction; not a conviction, a feeling. A man ought to be magnanimous, and it won’t soil a man. It won’t soil even a hero; it won’t soil Caesar! But still, don’t ask forgiveness, never and for nothing. Remember the rule: it was given you by your brother Mitya, who was ruined by women. No, I had better earn Grusha’s forgiveness some other way, without asking. I revere her, Alexei, I revere her! Only she doesn’t see it; no, she thinks there is never enough love. And she torments me, torments me with love. What was before! Before, it was only her infernal curves that tormented me, but now I have taken her whole soul into my soul, and through her I have become a man myself! Will they marry us? Otherwise I shall die of jealousy. I dream of something or other every day… What did she say to you about me?”
Alyosha repeated all that Grushenka had said earlier. Mitya listened to it in detail, asked about much of it again, and was satisfied.

“So she isn’t angry that I’m jealous!” he exclaimed. “A real woman! ‘I have a cruel heart myself.’ Ugh, I love them like that, cruel ones, though I can’t bear being made jealous, can’t bear it! We shall fight. But love, I shall love her endlessly. Will they marry us? Do they marry convicts? That’s the question. And I can’t live without her…”
Mitya walked about the room frowning. It was growing almost dark in the room. He suddenly became terribly worried.

“So there is a secret, she says, a secret? That the three of us are plotting against her, and ‘Katka’ is mixed up in it? No, my dear Grushenka, that isn’t it. You have made a mistake there, your silly little woman’s mistake! Alyosha, my dear, oh, come what may! I will tell you our secret!”

He looked round in all directions, came quickly right up to Alyosha, who was standing in front of him, and began to whisper to him with a mysterious air, though in reality no one could hear them: the old warder was dozing on a bench in the corner, and not a word could reach the soldiers on guard.

“I will tell you our whole secret!” Mitya whispered hurriedly. “I meant to tell you later, because how could I decide on anything without you? You are everything to me. Though I say that Ivan is above us, you are my cherub. Only your decision will decide it. Perhaps it is you who are the higher man, and not Ivan. You see, it is a matter of conscience, a matter of the highest conscience, a secret so important that I can’t manage it myself and have put it all off until you. And yet it is too early to decide now, for we must wait for the verdict: when the verdict comes, then you will decide my fate. Don’t decide now; I’ll tell you now, you’ll hear, but don’t decide. Stand and keep silent. I won’t tell you everything. I’ll only tell you the idea, without details, and you keep silent. Not a question, not a movement; agreed? And yet, Lord, what shall I do with your eyes? I am afraid your eyes will tell me the decision, even if you are silent. Ugh, I am afraid! Alyosha, listen: brother Ivan is proposing that I escape. I won’t tell you the details: everything has been foreseen; everything can be arranged. Keep silent; don’t decide. To America with Grusha. For I can’t live without Grusha! What if they won’t let her come to me there? Do they marry convicts? Brother Ivan says not. And without Grusha what shall I do there underground with a hammer? I shall only smash my head in with that hammer! And on the other hand, what about my conscience? I shall have run away from suffering! There was a sign, and I rejected the sign; there was a path of purification, and I turned about face. Ivan says that in America, ‘with good inclinations’, one can be of more use than underground. Well, and where will our underground hymn be sung? What is America? America is vanity again! And there is a lot of swindling in America too, I expect. I shall have run away from crucifixion! I tell you this, Alexei, because you alone can understand it, and no one else; for the others it is nonsense, raving, all that I told you about the hymn. They’ll say he has gone mad, or is a fool. But I haven’t gone mad, and I am not a fool. Ivan understands about the hymn too, oh, he understands; only he doesn’t answer about it; he keeps silent. He doesn’t believe in the hymn. Don’t speak, don’t speak: I can see how you are looking: you have decided already! Don’t decide; spare me; I can’t live without Grusha; wait for the trial!”
Mitya finished as if in a frenzy. He held Alyosha by the shoulders with both hands and fastened his thirsting, feverish eyes on Alyosha’s eyes.
“Do they marry convicts?” he repeated for the third time, in an imploring voice.
Alyosha listened in extreme surprise and was deeply shaken.
“Tell me one thing,” he said. “Is Ivan very insistent, and who thought of it first?”

“He did, he thought of it; he insists! He never came to see me, and suddenly he came a week ago and began straight away with this. He insists terribly. He doesn’t ask; he orders. He has no doubt that I shall obey, though I turned my whole heart inside out to him, as to you, and talked about the hymn. He told me how he would arrange it; he has collected all the information; but that later. He wants it to the point of hysterics. The main thing is money: ten thousand for the escape, he says, and twenty thousand for America; and with ten thousand, he says, we can arrange a magnificent escape.”
“And he told you on no account to tell me?” Alyosha asked again.
“On no account, to no one, and above all to you: on no account to you! He is afraid, I expect, that you will stand before me like a conscience. Don’t tell him I told you. Oh, don’t tell him!”

“You are right,” Alyosha decided. “It is impossible to decide before the verdict of the court. After the trial you will decide yourself; then you will find the new man in yourself, and he will decide.”
“The new man, or a Bernard; and he’ll decide in Bernard’s way! For it seems I am a contemptible Bernard myself!” Mitya grinned bitterly.
“But can it really be, brother, that you have no hope at all of being acquitted?”
Mitya shrugged his shoulders convulsively and shook his head.

“Alyosha, my dear, it’s time for you to go!” he suddenly became hurried. “The governor has shouted in the yard; he’ll be here in a minute. It’s late for us; it’s irregular. Embrace me quickly, kiss me, make the sign of the cross over me, my dear, make the sign of the cross over me for tomorrow’s cross…”
They embraced and kissed.
“And Ivan,” Mitya said suddenly, “proposed that I escape, and yet he believes I killed him!”
A sad smile was squeezed out on his lips.
“Have you asked him whether he believes it or not?” asked Alyosha.
“No, I haven’t asked him. I wanted to ask, but I couldn’t; I hadn’t the strength. It doesn’t matter; I can see it in his eyes. Well, goodbye!”
They kissed once more, hastily, and Alyosha was just going out when Mitya suddenly called him back again:
“Stand in front of me, like this.”

And again he gripped Alyosha tightly by the shoulders with both hands. His face had suddenly turned quite pale, so that even in the near darkness it was terribly noticeable. His lips were twisted; his eyes were fastened on Alyosha.

“Alyosha, tell me the whole truth, as before the Lord God: do you believe that I killed him, or not? You, you yourself, do you believe it or not? The whole truth, don’t lie!” he shouted at him in a frenzy.
Alyosha seemed to sway all over, and in his heart, he felt it, something sharp seemed to pass through.
“Stop, what are you saying…” he began to murmur as if lost.
“The whole truth, the whole, don’t lie!” Mitya repeated.

“Not for a single minute have I believed that you are the murderer,” suddenly broke in a trembling voice from Alyosha’s breast, and he raised his right hand, as if calling on God to witness his words. Bliss lit up Mitya’s whole face in an instant.

“Thank you!” he brought out slowly, as if letting out a sigh after a faint. “Now you have given me new life… Would you believe it: until now I was afraid to ask you, you, you! Well, go, go! You have given me strength for tomorrow; God bless you! Well, go; love Ivan!” broke from Mitya as his last word.

Alyosha went out all in tears. Such a degree of suspiciousness in Mitya, such a degree of distrust even of him, of Alyosha: all this suddenly opened before Alyosha such an abyss of hopeless grief and despair in his unhappy brother’s soul as he had never suspected before. A deep, infinite compassion suddenly seized and tormented him in an instant. His pierced heart ached terribly. “Love Ivan!” Mitya’s words of a moment ago suddenly came back to him. Indeed he was going to Ivan. He had needed terribly to see Ivan since the morning. Ivan tormented him no less than Mitya, and now, after seeing his brother, more than ever.
## Chapter V · Not You, Not You!

On the way to Ivan he had to pass the house where Katerina Ivanovna lodged. There were lights in the windows. He suddenly stopped and decided to go in. He had not seen Katerina Ivanovna for more than a week. But it occurred to him now that Ivan might be with her at that moment, especially on the eve of such a day. Having rung and gone in onto the stairs, dimly lit by a Chinese lantern, he saw a man coming down from above, in whom, as they came level, he recognised his brother. So he had been at Katerina Ivanovna’s and was leaving.
“Ah, it’s only you,” Ivan Fyodorovich said drily. “Well, goodbye. Are you going to her?”
“Yes.”
“I don’t advise it; she is ‘agitated’, and you will upset her still more.”
“No, no!” a voice suddenly cried from above, from a door that had instantly opened. “Alexei Fyodorovich, have you come from him?”
“Yes, I have been with him.”
“Did he send me any message? Come in, Alyosha, and you, Ivan Fyodorovich, you must come back, you must. Do you hear?”
There was such a commanding note in Katya’s voice that Ivan Fyodorovich, after hesitating for a moment, decided all the same to go up again with Alyosha.
“She was eavesdropping!” he whispered irritably to himself, but Alyosha heard it.
“Allow me to keep my overcoat on,” said Ivan Fyodorovich, going into the drawing room. “I won’t even sit down. I shan’t stay more than a minute.”

“Sit down, Alexei Fyodorovich,” said Katerina Ivanovna, remaining standing herself. She had changed little in this time, but her dark eyes flashed with an ominous fire. Alyosha remembered afterwards that she had seemed to him extraordinarily beautiful at that moment.
“Well, what message did he send?”

“Only one thing,” said Alyosha, looking her straight in the face: “that you should spare yourself and not give evidence at the trial about…” he hesitated a little, “what happened between you… at the very beginning of your acquaintance… in that town…”

“Ah, about the bow to the ground for that money!” she caught him up with a bitter laugh. “Well, is he afraid for himself or for me, eh? He said I should spare… whom? Him or myself? Tell me, Alexei Fyodorovich.”
Alyosha looked at her intently, trying to understand her.
“Both yourself and him,” he said quietly.

“Just so,” she rapped out somehow spitefully, and suddenly flushed. “You don’t know me yet, Alexei Fyodorovich,” she said menacingly, “and I don’t know myself yet either. Perhaps you will want to trample me underfoot after tomorrow’s examination.”
“You will give your evidence honestly,” said Alyosha; “that is all that is needed.”

“A woman is often dishonest,” she ground out. “Only an hour ago I was thinking that I was afraid to touch that monster… as if he were a reptile… and yet no, he is still a human being to me! But did he kill him? Was it he who killed him?” she suddenly exclaimed hysterically, turning quickly to Ivan Fyodorovich. Alyosha understood in an instant that she had already asked Ivan Fyodorovich this very question, perhaps only a minute before he came in, and not for the first time but for the hundredth, and that they had ended in a quarrel.

“I have been to see Smerdyakov… It was you, you who convinced me that he killed his father. It was you alone I believed!” she went on, still addressing Ivan Fyodorovich. He smiled as if with an effort. Alyosha started on hearing that “you”, spoken so familiarly. He could never have suspected such relations between them.

“Well, that’s enough, though,” Ivan cut her short. “I’m going. I’ll come tomorrow.” And turning at once, he went out of the room and straight onto the stairs. Katerina Ivanovna suddenly, with a sort of commanding gesture, seized Alyosha by both hands.

“Go after him! Catch him up! Don’t leave him alone for a minute,” she whispered quickly. “He is out of his mind. Don’t you know he has gone out of his mind? He has a fever, a nervous fever! The doctor told me; go, run after him…”
Alyosha jumped up and rushed after Ivan Fyodorovich. Ivan had not gone fifty paces.
“What do you want?” he suddenly turned to Alyosha, seeing him catching up. “She told you to run after me because I’m mad. I know it by heart,” he added irritably.
“She is mistaken, of course, but she is right that you are ill,” said Alyosha. “I was looking at your face at her house just now; you have a very ill face, very, Ivan!”
Ivan walked on without stopping. Alyosha followed.
“And do you know, Alexei Fyodorovich, how people go mad?” Ivan asked in a suddenly quite quiet voice, no longer irritable at all, in which the most simple-hearted curiosity could suddenly be heard.
“No, I don’t; I suppose there are many different kinds of madness.”
“And can one observe oneself going mad?”
“I think one can’t watch oneself clearly in such a case,” Alyosha answered in surprise. Ivan was silent for half a minute.
“If you want to talk to me about anything, change the subject, please,” he said suddenly.

“Here, before I forget, there is a letter for you,” Alyosha said timidly, and, taking Lise’s letter from his pocket, he held it out to him. They had just come up to a street lamp. Ivan recognised the hand at once.
“Ah, it’s from that little demon!” he laughed spitefully, and, without opening the envelope, he suddenly tore it into several pieces and threw them to the wind. The scraps flew away.
“She isn’t sixteen yet, I believe, and already she is offering herself!” he said contemptuously, striding along the street again.
“What do you mean, offering herself?” exclaimed Alyosha.
“As depraved women offer themselves, of course.”

“What are you saying, Ivan, what are you saying?” Alyosha defended her sorrowfully and hotly. “She is a child; you are insulting a child! She is ill, she is very ill herself; perhaps she too is going out of her mind… I couldn’t help giving you her letter… On the contrary, I wanted to hear something from you… to save her.”
“You have nothing to hear from me. If she is a child, I am not her nurse. Be quiet, Alexei. Don’t go on. I don’t even think about it.”
They were silent again for a minute.
“She will be praying to the Mother of God all night now to show her how to act at the trial tomorrow,” he began again suddenly, sharply and spitefully.
“You… you mean Katerina Ivanovna?”

“Yes. Is she to appear as Mitenka’s saviour or his destroyer? That is what she will be praying for: that light may shine into her soul. She doesn’t know herself yet, you see; she hasn’t had time to prepare. She takes me for a nurse too; she wants me to lull her to sleep!”
“Katerina Ivanovna loves you, brother,” Alyosha said with a sad feeling.
“Perhaps. Only I don’t care for her.”

“She is suffering. Then why do you say such things to her… sometimes… that give her hope?” Alyosha went on with timid reproach. “For I know you have given her hope; forgive me for saying so,” he added.

“I can’t act as I ought here, break it off and tell her straight out!” Ivan said irritably. “I must wait till they pass sentence on the murderer. If I break with her now, she will ruin that scoundrel at the trial tomorrow out of revenge on me, because she hates him and knows she hates him. It is all lies here, lie upon lie! But now, while I haven’t broken with her, she still hopes and won’t ruin that monster, knowing how much I want to get him out of trouble. Oh, when will that cursed verdict come!”
The words “murderer” and “monster” echoed painfully in Alyosha’s heart.
“But how could she ruin our brother?” he asked, thinking over Ivan’s words. “What could she give in evidence that could ruin Mitya outright?”
“You don’t know that yet. She has a document in her hands, in Mitenka’s own hand, that proves mathematically that he killed Fyodor Pavlovich.”
“That can’t be!” exclaimed Alyosha.
“Why can’t it? I have read it myself.”
“There can be no such document!” Alyosha repeated hotly. “There can’t be, because he isn’t the murderer. It wasn’t he who killed father, not he!”
Ivan Fyodorovich suddenly stopped.
“Who is the murderer, then, in your opinion?” he asked, coldly to all appearance, and there was even a sort of haughty note in the tone of the question.
“You know yourself who,” Alyosha said quietly and with deep feeling.
“Who? That fable about that crazy idiot of an epileptic? About Smerdyakov?”
Alyosha suddenly felt that he was trembling all over.
“You know yourself who,” broke from him helplessly. He was gasping.
“But who, who?” Ivan shouted now almost savagely. All his restraint had suddenly vanished.
“I know one thing only,” Alyosha said, still almost in a whisper. “It wasn’t you who killed father.”
“‘Not you’! What do you mean, not you?” Ivan was dumbfounded.
“It wasn’t you who killed father, not you!” Alyosha repeated firmly.
The silence lasted for half a minute.
“Why, I know myself it wasn’t I; are you raving?” said Ivan with a pale, twisted smile. He seemed to fasten his eyes on Alyosha. They were both standing by the lamp again.
“No, Ivan, you have told yourself several times that you are the murderer.”
“When did I say so?… I was in Moscow… When did I say so?” Ivan murmured, quite at a loss.

“You have said it to yourself many times, when you were alone during these two terrible months,” Alyosha went on as before, quietly and distinctly. But he was speaking now as if beside himself, as if not of his own will, obeying some irresistible command. “You have accused yourself and confessed to yourself that the murderer was no one but you. But it wasn’t you who killed him; you are mistaken; you are not the murderer, do you hear me, not you! God has sent me to tell you this.”

Both were silent. The silence lasted a whole long minute. They both stood and kept looking into each other’s eyes. Both were pale. Suddenly Ivan began to tremble all over and gripped Alyosha tightly by the shoulder.
“You have been in my room!” he said in a grating whisper. “You were in my room at night when he came… Confess… you saw him, you saw him?”
“Whom do you mean… Mitya?” Alyosha asked in bewilderment.
“Not him, to the devil with the monster!” Ivan yelled frantically. “Do you know that he comes to me? How did you find out? Tell me!”
“Who is he? I don’t know whom you mean,” Alyosha murmured, frightened now.
“Yes, you do know… otherwise how could you… it can’t be that you don’t know…”
But suddenly he seemed to check himself. He stood as if thinking something over. A strange smile twisted his lips.

“Brother,” Alyosha began again in a trembling voice, “I said that to you because you will believe my word; I know that. I have said that word to you for your whole life: not you! Do you hear, for your whole life. And God has laid it on my soul to say it to you, even if you hate me for ever from this hour…”
But Ivan Fyodorovich had evidently quite regained his self-control.

“Alexei Fyodorovich,” he said with a cold smile, “I can’t stand prophets and epileptics, messengers of God especially; you know that only too well. From this moment I break with you, and, I think, for ever. I beg you to leave me this very minute, at this very crossroads. Besides, your way home is down this lane. And be especially careful not to come to me today! Do you hear?”
He turned and, striding firmly, walked straight on without looking back.
“Brother,” Alyosha called after him, “if anything happens to you today, think of me first of all!…”

But Ivan did not answer. Alyosha stood at the crossroads by the lamp until Ivan had disappeared completely into the darkness. Then he turned and walked slowly home down the lane. Both he and Ivan Fyodorovich lodged separately, in different places: neither of them wanted to live in Fyodor Pavlovich’s empty house. Alyosha rented a furnished room in the family of some townspeople; Ivan Fyodorovich lived rather far from him and occupied a spacious and fairly comfortable apartment in the lodge of a good house belonging to a well-to-do civil servant’s widow. But in the whole lodge he was waited on by only one ancient, completely deaf little old woman, full of rheumatism, who went to bed at six in the evening and got up at six in the morning. Ivan Fyodorovich had become strangely undemanding in these two months and liked very much to be quite alone. He even tidied the room he lived in himself, and rarely even went into the other rooms of his apartment. Reaching the gate of his house and already taking hold of the bell handle, he stopped. He felt that he was still trembling all over with a spiteful trembling. Suddenly he let go of the bell, spat, turned back and walked quickly off again to quite the other, opposite end of the town, about two versts from his lodgings, to a tiny, lopsided log house where Marya Kondratyevna lodged, Fyodor Pavlovich’s former neighbour, who used to come to Fyodor Pavlovich’s kitchen for soup and to whom Smerdyakov had sung his songs and played the guitar in those days. She had sold her former little house and now lived with her mother almost in a peasant hut; and the sick, almost dying Smerdyakov had settled with them ever since Fyodor Pavlovich’s death. It was to him that Ivan Fyodorovich now set off, drawn by a sudden and irresistible consideration.
## Book Eleven, Chapter VI · The First Meeting with Smerdyakov

This was already the third time Ivan Fyodorovich had gone to talk with Smerdyakov since his return from Moscow. The first time after the catastrophe he had seen him and talked with him on the very first day of his arrival; then he had visited him once more two weeks later. But after this second time he had stopped seeing Smerdyakov, so that now it was over a month since he had seen him and he had heard almost nothing of him. Ivan Fyodorovich had come back from Moscow only on the fifth day after his father’s death, so that he did not even find the coffin: the funeral had taken place on the very day before his arrival. The reason for Ivan Fyodorovich’s delay was that Alyosha, not knowing his Moscow address exactly, had turned to Katerina Ivanovna to send the telegram, and she, also not knowing his real address, had telegraphed to her sister and aunt, reckoning that Ivan Fyodorovich would call on them as soon as he reached Moscow. But he called on them only on the fourth day after his arrival, and, reading the telegram, of course flew back to us at once at breakneck speed. Here he met Alyosha first, but, talking with him, he was very surprised that Alyosha would not even suspect Mitya, but pointed straight at Smerdyakov as the murderer, which went against all other opinion in our town. Then, after seeing the police captain and the prosecutor and learning the details of the charge and the arrest, he was still more surprised at Alyosha, and put his opinion down only to his brotherly feeling, roused to the utmost, and to his compassion for Mitya, whom, as Ivan knew, Alyosha loved very much. By the way, let us say just two words once for all about Ivan’s feelings for his brother Dmitri Fyodorovich: he decidedly did not love him, and at the very most felt compassion for him at times, but even that mixed with a great contempt that went as far as disgust. Mitya, his whole person, even his whole figure, was extremely unsympathetic to him. Katerina Ivanovna’s love for him Ivan regarded with indignation. With the accused Mitya, however, he had also had a meeting on the first day of his arrival, and this meeting not only did not weaken his conviction of his guilt but even strengthened it. He found his brother then restless, in a morbid agitation. Mitya was talkative, but scattered and disjointed; he spoke very sharply, accused Smerdyakov and got terribly muddled. Most of all he kept talking about the same three thousand that the dead man had “stolen” from him. “The money was mine, it was mine,” Mitya kept repeating; “even if I had stolen it, I would have been in the right.” He hardly disputed any of the evidence against him, and if he interpreted the facts in his own favour, again it was very confusedly and absurdly, as if in general he did not even wish to justify himself at all before Ivan or anyone; on the contrary, he was angry, proudly disdained the accusations, swore and fumed. At Grigory’s evidence about the open door he only laughed contemptuously and declared that “the devil opened it”. But he could offer no coherent explanation of this fact. In this first meeting he even managed to insult Ivan Fyodorovich, telling him sharply that it was not for those who maintain that “everything is permitted” to suspect and question him. In general he was very unfriendly to Ivan Fyodorovich this time. Immediately after this meeting with Mitya, Ivan Fyodorovich set off to see Smerdyakov.

Already in the train, flying back from Moscow, he had been thinking all the time about Smerdyakov and about his last conversation with him on the evening before his departure. Much troubled him; much seemed suspicious. But in giving his evidence to the examining magistrate, Ivan Fyodorovich had kept silent for the time being about that conversation. He had put everything off until he saw Smerdyakov. Smerdyakov was then in the town hospital. Doctor Herzenstube, and the physician Varvinsky, whom Ivan Fyodorovich met at the hospital, answered Ivan Fyodorovich’s insistent questions firmly that Smerdyakov’s falling sickness was beyond doubt, and were even surprised at the question: “Wasn’t he shamming on the day of the catastrophe?” They gave him to understand that the fit had even been an unusual one, lasting and recurring for several days, so that the patient’s life had been in decided danger, and that only now, after the measures taken, could it be said positively that he would live, though it was very possible (Doctor Herzenstube added) that his reason would remain partly disordered, “if not for life, then for a fairly long time”. To Ivan Fyodorovich’s impatient question, “Then he is mad now?”, they answered that “it isn’t so yet in the full sense, but certain abnormalities are observed.” Ivan Fyodorovich resolved to find out for himself what these abnormalities were. At the hospital he was admitted at once. Smerdyakov was in a separate room, lying on a bed. Next to him was another bed, occupied by an enfeebled townsman, all swollen with dropsy, evidently ready to die tomorrow or the day after; he could be no hindrance to their conversation. Smerdyakov grinned distrustfully on seeing Ivan Fyodorovich, and in the first instant even seemed to quail. So at least it flashed upon Ivan Fyodorovich. But that was only for an instant; for the rest of the time, on the contrary, Smerdyakov almost astonished him with his calm. From the very first glance at him, Ivan Fyodorovich was convinced beyond doubt of his complete and extreme state of illness: he was very weak, spoke slowly, as if moving his tongue with difficulty; he had grown very thin and yellow. Throughout the twenty minutes or so of their meeting he complained of headache and of aching in all his limbs. His dry, gelded face seemed to have grown so small; the hair at his temples was dishevelled, and in place of the little tuft only one thin wisp of hair stuck up. But his left eye, screwed up and as if hinting at something, betrayed the old Smerdyakov. “It is worth talking to a clever man,” Ivan Fyodorovich remembered at once. He sat down at his feet on a stool. Smerdyakov moved his whole body on the bed with suffering, but did not speak first; he was silent, and even looked as if he were not very curious.
“Can you talk to me?” asked Ivan Fyodorovich. “I won’t tire you much.”
“I can very well, sir,” Smerdyakov mumbled in a weak voice. “Have you been back long?” he added condescendingly, as though encouraging an embarrassed visitor.
“Only today… To clear up the mess you have made here.”
Smerdyakov sighed.
“Why do you sigh? You knew, didn’t you?” Ivan Fyodorovich blurted out.
Smerdyakov was solidly silent for a while.
“How could I not know, sir? It was clear beforehand. Only how could anyone know, sir, that they would take it this way?”
“Take what this way? Don’t wriggle! You predicted, didn’t you, that you would have a fit as soon as you went down into the cellar? You pointed straight at the cellar.”
“Have you already said so in your evidence?” Smerdyakov inquired calmly.
Ivan Fyodorovich suddenly grew angry.
“No, I haven’t yet, but I certainly shall. You must explain a great deal to me now, brother, and know, my dear fellow, that I won’t allow myself to be played with!”
“And why should I play such a game, sir, when all my hope is in you, as in the Lord God alone, sir!” said Smerdyakov, still quite calmly, only closing his eyes for a moment.

“In the first place,” Ivan Fyodorovich began, “I know that a fit of the falling sickness can’t be foretold. I have made inquiries; don’t wriggle. The day and the hour can’t be foretold. Then how did you foretell the day and the hour to me, and the cellar too? How could you know beforehand that you would fall into that very cellar in a fit, unless you shammed the fit on purpose?”

“I had to go to the cellar anyway, sir, even several times a day, sir,” Smerdyakov drawled unhurriedly. “In just the same way, a year ago I fell from the attic, sir. It is quite true that a fit can’t be foretold by the day and the hour, but one can always have a presentiment.”
“But you foretold the day and the hour!”
“As regards my falling sickness, sir, you had best inquire of the doctors here whether it was real or not, and I have nothing more to say to you on that subject.”
“And the cellar? How did you know about the cellar beforehand?”

“You do keep on about that cellar! When I went down into that cellar, I was in fear and in doubt; more in fear, because I had lost you and expected protection from no one in the whole world. So I go down into that very cellar and think: ‘Now it will come, now it will strike me; shall I fall or not?’ And from that very doubt the inevitable spasm suddenly seized me in the throat, sir… and down I went. All this, and the whole of our previous conversation, sir, the evening before at the gate, sir, when I told you my fear and about the cellar, sir, I disclosed all of it in detail to Doctor Herzenstube and to the investigator, Nikolai Parfenovich, and they wrote it all down in the record, sir. And the doctor here, Mr Varvinsky, particularly insisted before them all that it came about precisely from brooding, from that very apprehension, that is, ‘shall I fall or not?’ And that was when it caught hold of me. So they wrote down, sir, that it was bound to happen just so, from my fear alone, sir.”
Having said this, Smerdyakov drew a deep breath, as if exhausted.

“So you have already stated that in your evidence?” asked Ivan Fyodorovich, somewhat taken aback. He had meant to frighten him precisely by threatening to tell about their conversation that evening, and it turned out that Smerdyakov had already told everything himself.
“What have I to be afraid of? Let them write down the whole real truth,” Smerdyakov said firmly.
“And you told them everything about our conversation at the gate, word for word?”
“No, not exactly word for word, sir.”
“And did you tell them too that you know how to sham fits, as you boasted to me then?”
“No, I didn’t tell them that either, sir.”
“Tell me now: why did you send me to Chermashnya then?”
“I was afraid you would go to Moscow; Chermashnya is nearer, after all, sir.”
“You lie; you invited me to go away yourself: go away, you said, out of harm’s way!”

“I said that then out of pure friendship for you and my heartfelt devotion, foreseeing trouble in the house, sir, out of pity for you. Only I pitied myself more than you, sir. That is why I said: go away out of harm’s way, so that you would understand that things would go badly at home and would stay to protect your father.”
“Then you should have said it more plainly, you fool!” Ivan Fyodorovich suddenly flared up.

“How could I have said it more plainly then, sir? It was only fear speaking in me, sir, and you might have been angry. Of course I might have feared that Dmitri Fyodorovich would make some scandal and carry off that very money, since he regarded it as good as his own; but who could know it would end in such a murder? I thought he would simply steal the three thousand roubles that lay under the master’s mattress, sir, in an envelope, sir; and he went and killed him, sir. How could you have guessed it either, sir?”
“But if you say yourself that it couldn’t be guessed, how could I have guessed and stayed? What are you muddling?” said Ivan Fyodorovich, thinking it over.
“You might have guessed from my directing you to Chermashnya instead of Moscow, sir.”
