“How could anyone guess from that!”
Smerdyakov seemed very tired and was silent again for a minute.

“You might have guessed from that very thing, sir: that if I was turning you away from Moscow to Chermashnya, then I wanted you to be nearer, because Moscow is far, and Dmitri Fyodorovich, knowing you were not far off, would not be so emboldened. And you could have come back more quickly, in case of need, and protected me too; for I pointed out to you Grigory Vasilyevich’s illness besides, and that I was afraid of a fit. And having explained to you about the knocks by which one could get in to the deceased, and that Dmitri Fyodorovich knew them all through me, I thought you would guess for yourself then that he would certainly do something, and would not only not go to Chermashnya but would stay altogether.”
“He talks very coherently,” thought Ivan Fyodorovich, “though he mumbles; what disorder of the faculties was Herzenstube talking about?”
“You are being cunning with me, damn you!” he exclaimed angrily.
“I confess, I thought then that you had guessed everything,” Smerdyakov parried with the most simple-hearted air.
“If I had guessed, I would have stayed!” cried Ivan Fyodorovich, flaring up again.
“Well, sir, and I thought that, having guessed everything, you were going away as fast as possible only to get out of harm’s way, just to run off somewhere and save yourself from fear, sir.”
“You thought everyone was as much a coward as you?”
“Forgive me, sir, I thought you were like me.”

“Of course I ought to have guessed,” Ivan said in agitation, “and I did suspect something vile on your part… Only you are lying, lying again,” he cried, suddenly remembering. “Do you remember how you came up to the carriage then and said to me: ‘It is worth talking to a clever man’? So you were glad I was going, since you praised me?”
Smerdyakov sighed again and again. A flush seemed to appear on his face.

“If I was glad,” he said, somewhat breathlessly, “it was only that you had agreed to Chermashnya and not Moscow. Because it was nearer, all the same; only I said those very words to you then not in praise, sir, but in reproach. You didn’t make that out, sir.”
“What reproach?”

“Why, that, foreseeing such a misfortune, you were leaving your own father, sir, and didn’t want to protect us, because I could always have been dragged in over those three thousand, as if I had stolen them, sir.”
“Damn you!” Ivan swore again. “Wait: did you tell the investigator and the prosecutor about the signals, about those knocks?”
“I told them everything just as it was, sir.”
Ivan Fyodorovich was surprised to himself again.

“If I thought of anything then,” he began again, “it was only of some vileness on your part. Dmitri might kill, but that he would steal, I didn’t believe then… But from you I expected every vileness. You told me yourself that you knew how to sham fits; why did you tell me that?”

“Out of pure simple-heartedness. And I never in my life shammed a fit on purpose; I only said it to boast before you. Just foolishness, sir. I had grown very fond of you then, and I was quite simple with you.”
“My brother accuses you outright of having killed and stolen.”

“Why, what else is left for him?” Smerdyakov grinned bitterly. “And who will believe him after all that evidence? Grigory Vasilyevich saw the door open, sir; after that, how can he? Well, never mind, God be with him! He is trembling to save himself…”
He was quietly silent for a while, and suddenly, as if reflecting, added:

“You see, sir, there it is again: he wants to put it on me, that it was my doing, sir; I have heard that already, sir. But take just this very thing, that I am a master at shamming fits: would I have told you beforehand that I knew how to sham, if I had really had some design on your father then? If I had planned such a murder, could I have been such a fool as to tell such evidence against myself beforehand, and to his own son, if you please, sir?! Does that sound likely? For that to be possible, sir, why, on the contrary, never, sir. Now, this conversation of ours no one hears but providence itself, sir; and if you were to tell the prosecutor and Nikolai Parfenovich, you could thereby defend me completely, sir: for what sort of villain is that, who is so simple-hearted beforehand? They can very well reason all this out.”

“Listen,” Ivan Fyodorovich got up, struck by Smerdyakov’s last argument, and broke off the conversation. “I don’t suspect you at all, and I even think it absurd to accuse you… On the contrary, I am grateful to you for having set my mind at rest. I am going now, but I shall come again. Goodbye for now; get well. Do you need anything?”
“I am grateful for everything, sir. Marfa Ignatyevna doesn’t forget me, sir, and helps me in everything, if I need anything, out of her old kindness. Good people visit me every day.”
“Goodbye. I won’t say anything, though, about your knowing how to sham… and I advise you not to mention it either,” Ivan said suddenly, for some reason.
“I understand very well, sir. And if you don’t mention that, then I won’t tell, sir, the whole of our conversation that time at the gate either…”

Here it happened that Ivan Fyodorovich suddenly went out, and only when he had gone some ten paces along the corridor did he suddenly feel that there was some insulting meaning in Smerdyakov’s last phrase. He was about to go back, but it only flashed through his mind; and, saying “Nonsense!”, he hurried out of the hospital. The main thing was that he felt he really had been set at rest, and precisely by the circumstance that it was not Smerdyakov who was guilty but his brother Mitya, though it would seem that it should have been the other way round. Why this was so he did not want to examine then; he even felt disgust at digging into his own sensations. He wanted as quickly as possible to forget something, as it were. Then, in the following few days, he became completely convinced of Mitya’s guilt, when he became more closely and thoroughly acquainted with all the overwhelming evidence against him. There was evidence from the most insignificant people, but almost staggering, for instance from Fenya and her mother. About Perkhotin, the tavern, Plotnikov’s shop, the witnesses at Mokroye, there was nothing to be said. Above all, the details were overwhelming. The news of the secret “knocks” struck the investigator and the prosecutor almost as much as Grigory’s evidence about the open door. Grigory’s wife, Marfa Ignatyevna, in answer to Ivan Fyodorovich’s question, told him straight out that Smerdyakov had lain all night behind the partition in their room, “not three steps from our bed”, and that though she herself slept soundly, she woke many times, hearing him moaning there: “He moaned all the time, moaned without stopping.” Talking with Herzenstube and telling him his opinion that Smerdyakov did not seem to him mad at all, only weak, he only drew a thin little smile from the old man. “And do you know what he is particularly busy with now?” he asked Ivan Fyodorovich. “He is learning French words by heart; he has a notebook under his pillow, and somebody has written French words in it in Russian letters, he-he-he!” At last Ivan Fyodorovich gave up all his doubts. Of his brother Dmitri he could no longer even think without loathing. One thing, however, was strange: that Alyosha stubbornly went on insisting that it was not Dmitri who had killed him, but “in all probability” Smerdyakov. Ivan had always felt that Alyosha’s opinion counted for much with him, and so he was very puzzled by him now. It was strange too that Alyosha did not seek conversations with him about Mitya and never began them himself, but only answered Ivan’s questions. Ivan Fyodorovich noticed this very much too. At that time, however, he was very much distracted by a quite unrelated circumstance: on coming back from Moscow, he had in the very first days given himself up wholly and irrevocably to his ardent and insane passion for Katerina Ivanovna. This is not the place to begin on this new passion of Ivan Fyodorovich’s, which was afterwards reflected in his whole life: all this could serve as the canvas for another story, another novel, which I do not know whether I shall ever undertake. But still I cannot keep silent even now about this: when Ivan Fyodorovich, walking at night with Alyosha from Katerina Ivanovna’s, as I have described, said to him, “I don’t care for her,” he was lying terribly at that moment: he loved her madly, though it is true too that at times he hated her so much that he could even have killed her. Many causes came together here. Shattered by the event with Mitya, she had thrown herself at Ivan Fyodorovich, who had come back to her again, as at a kind of saviour. She was hurt, insulted, humiliated in her feelings. And now there appeared again the man who had loved her so before (oh, she knew it only too well), and whose mind and heart she had always set so high above herself. But the severe young woman did not give herself up entirely as a sacrifice, in spite of all the Karamazov unrestraint of her lover’s desires and all his fascination for her. At the same time she tormented herself unceasingly with remorse for having betrayed Mitya, and in the stormy moments of quarrel with Ivan (and there were many of them) she told him so outright. That was what he called, speaking to Alyosha, “lie upon lie”. There was indeed a great deal of lying in it, and that irritated Ivan Fyodorovich most of all… but all this later. In a word, for a time he almost forgot about Smerdyakov. And yet, two weeks after his first visit to him, the same strange thoughts as before began to torment him again. It is enough to say that he began continually to ask himself why, on his last night in Fyodor Pavlovich’s house before his departure, he had gone out quietly onto the stairs, like a thief, and listened to what his father was doing below. Why had he remembered it afterwards with disgust? Why, on the next morning on the road, had he suddenly been seized with such anguish, and, coming into Moscow, said to himself: “I am a scoundrel”? And now it once occurred to him that because of all these tormenting thoughts he was ready, perhaps, to forget even Katerina Ivanovna, so strongly had they suddenly taken hold of him again! Just as he thought this, he met Alyosha in the street. He stopped him at once and suddenly asked him a question:

“Do you remember when Dmitri burst into the house after dinner and beat father, and afterwards I told you in the yard that I reserved ‘the right to wish’? Tell me, did you think then that I wished for father’s death, or not?”
“I did,” Alyosha answered quietly.

“And so it was; there was nothing to guess there. But didn’t it occur to you then too that I was wishing precisely that ‘one reptile should devour the other’, that is, that Dmitri should kill father, and soon too… and that I myself was not averse even to helping it along?”
Alyosha turned slightly pale and looked silently into his brother’s eyes.

“Speak!” exclaimed Ivan. “I want with all my strength to know what you thought then. I need it; the truth, the truth!” He drew a heavy breath, already looking at Alyosha with a kind of spite in advance.
“Forgive me, I thought that too then,” Alyosha whispered, and fell silent, without adding a single “extenuating circumstance”.

“Thank you!” Ivan snapped, and, leaving Alyosha, walked quickly on his way. From then on Alyosha noticed that his brother Ivan began somehow sharply to draw away from him and even seemed to take a dislike to him, so that afterwards he himself stopped going to see him. But at that moment, immediately after that meeting with him, Ivan Fyodorovich, without going home, suddenly set off again to see Smerdyakov.
## Chapter VII · The Second Visit to Smerdyakov

By that time Smerdyakov had already left the hospital. Ivan Fyodorovich knew his new lodgings: that very lopsided little log house of two rooms divided by a passage. In one room lived Marya Kondratyevna with her mother, and in the other, separately, Smerdyakov. God knows on what terms he had settled with them, whether he lived there for nothing or for money. Afterwards it was supposed that he had settled with them as Marya Kondratyevna’s suitor and was living there for nothing for the time being. Both mother and daughter respected him very much and looked on him as a man above them. Having knocked till he was let in, Ivan Fyodorovich went into the passage and, on Marya Kondratyevna’s direction, went straight to the left into the “best room”, occupied by Smerdyakov. In this room there was a tiled stove, and it was heated very hot. The walls were adorned with blue wallpaper, all torn, it is true, and in the cracks under it cockroaches swarmed in terrible numbers, so that there was an incessant rustling. The furniture was paltry: two benches along the two walls and two chairs by the table. The table, though of plain wood, was covered with a cloth with a pink pattern. On each of the two little windows stood a pot of geraniums. In the corner was an icon case. On the table stood a small, much-dented copper samovar and a tray with two cups. But Smerdyakov had already finished his tea, and the samovar had gone out… He himself was sitting at the table on the bench, looking at a notebook and tracing something with a pen. A bottle of ink stood beside him, as well as a low cast-iron candlestick with a stearin candle in it. Ivan Fyodorovich concluded at once from Smerdyakov’s face that he had completely recovered from his illness. His face was fresher, fuller; his tuft was whipped up, the hair at his temples smoothed down. He was sitting in a motley quilted dressing gown, very much worn, however, and considerably frayed. On his nose were spectacles, which Ivan Fyodorovich had never seen him wear before. This most trivial circumstance seemed suddenly to make Ivan Fyodorovich doubly angry: “Such a creature, and in spectacles too!” Smerdyakov slowly raised his head and looked intently through his spectacles at the newcomer; then he quietly took them off and half rose on the bench, but somehow not at all so respectfully, somehow even lazily, simply to observe the barest courtesy without which one can hardly manage. All this flashed upon Ivan in an instant; he took it all in and noticed it at once, and above all Smerdyakov’s look, decidedly spiteful, unfriendly and even haughty: “Why do you come hanging about? We settled everything that time; why have you come again?” Ivan Fyodorovich could hardly restrain himself.
“It’s hot in here,” he said, still standing, and unbuttoned his overcoat.
“Take it off, sir,” Smerdyakov permitted.

Ivan Fyodorovich took off his overcoat and threw it on the bench; with trembling hands he took a chair, quickly drew it up to the table and sat down. Smerdyakov had managed to lower himself onto his bench before him.
“First of all, are we alone?” Ivan Fyodorovich asked sternly and impetuously. “They can’t hear us from in there?”
“No one will hear anything, sir. You saw for yourself: there is the passage.”

“Listen, my dear fellow: what was that you blurted out when I was leaving you at the hospital, that if I kept quiet about your being a master at shamming fits, you wouldn’t tell the investigator everything about our conversation at the gate? What is this ‘everything’? What could you have meant by it? Were you threatening me, or what? Have I entered into some sort of alliance with you, am I afraid of you, or what?”

Ivan Fyodorovich said this in a perfect fury, evidently giving him to understand on purpose that he scorned all beating about the bush and all roundabout approaches, and was playing openly. Smerdyakov’s eyes flashed spitefully, his left eye began to wink, and at once, though with his usual restraint and measure, he gave his answer: “You want it straight; well, here it is straight for you.”

“What I meant then, and why I said it, was that you, knowing beforehand about this murder of your own father, left him as a sacrifice then; and so that people should not conclude anything bad afterwards about your feelings, and perhaps about something else besides: that is what I promised then not to tell the authorities.”

Though Smerdyakov spoke without haste and to all appearance in command of himself, something firm and insistent could now be heard in his voice, something spiteful and insolently defiant. He stared boldly at Ivan Fyodorovich, and for the first minute everything even swam before Ivan’s eyes.
“What? What? Are you in your right mind or not?”
“Perfectly in my right mind, sir.”
“Did I know about the murder then?” Ivan Fyodorovich cried out at last, and struck the table hard with his fist. “What do you mean, ‘about something else besides’? Speak, you scoundrel!”
Smerdyakov was silent and went on looking Ivan Fyodorovich over with the same insolent look.
“Speak, you stinking rogue, what ‘something else besides’?” Ivan yelled.
“By that ‘something else besides’ I meant just now that perhaps you yourself very much wished for your father’s death then.”

Ivan Fyodorovich jumped up and struck him on the shoulder with his fist with all his might, so that he reeled back against the wall. In an instant his whole face was flooded with tears, and, saying, “It is shameful, sir, to strike a weak man!”, he suddenly covered his eyes with his blue-checked cotton handkerchief, thoroughly soiled with blowing his nose, and sank into quiet, tearful weeping. A minute passed.
“Enough! Stop it!” Ivan Fyodorovich said at last commandingly, sitting down on the chair again. “Don’t drive me out of my last patience.”
Smerdyakov took his rag away from his eyes. Every line of his wrinkled face expressed the insult he had just suffered.
“So you thought then, you scoundrel, that I wanted to kill my father together with Dmitri?”
“I didn’t know your thoughts then, sir,” said Smerdyakov in an injured tone, “and that is why I stopped you then, as you were coming in at the gate, to test you on that very point, sir.”
“To test what? What?”
“Why, that very circumstance: did you or did you not want your father to be killed as soon as possible?”
What revolted Ivan Fyodorovich most of all was this insistent, insolent tone, from which Smerdyakov stubbornly refused to depart.
“It was you who killed him!” he suddenly exclaimed.
Smerdyakov smiled contemptuously.
“That it was not I who killed him, you know yourself for certain. And I thought there was no need for a clever man to say anything more about it.”
“But why, why did such a suspicion of me come to you then?”

“As you know already, sir, from fear alone. For I was in such a position then that, shaking with fear, I suspected everyone. I resolved to test you too, sir, for if you too, I thought, want the same as your brother, then that is the end of this whole business, and I shall perish along with it, like a fly.”
“Listen, two weeks ago you didn’t say that.”

“I meant the very same thing in the hospital, talking with you; only I supposed that you would understand without unnecessary words, and didn’t want a straight talk yourself, being the cleverest of men, sir.”
“Just listen to him! But answer, answer, I insist: from what exactly, by what exactly could I have put such a low suspicion of me into your vile soul then?”
“To kill, you yourself could never have done that, sir, and didn’t want to; but to want someone else to kill, that you did want.”
“And how calmly, how calmly he says it! But why should I want it? What the devil should I want it for?”

“What do you mean, what the devil for, sir? And the inheritance, sir?” Smerdyakov caught it up venomously and even somehow vindictively. “Why, after your father’s death each of the three brothers would have come in for nearly forty thousand, and maybe even more, sir; whereas if Fyodor Pavlovich had married that very lady then, sir, Agrafena Alexandrovna, she would have transferred all the capital to herself immediately after the wedding, for she is no fool, sir, so that you three brothers wouldn’t have got even two roubles after your father. And how much was left then before the wedding? A hair’s breadth, sir: that lady had only to do like this to him with her little finger, and he would have run to the church after her at once with his tongue hanging out.”
Ivan Fyodorovich restrained himself with suffering.
“Very well,” he said at last. “You see, I haven’t jumped up, I haven’t beaten you, I haven’t killed you. Go on: so, in your opinion, I meant my brother Dmitri for it; I was counting on him?”

“How could you not count on him, sir? For if he killed him, he would lose all the rights of his rank, his rank and property, and go into exile, sir. So then his share after your father would be left to you and your brother Alexei Fyodorovich, in equal parts, sir; that is, you would each have got not forty but sixty thousand, sir. You were certainly counting on Dmitri Fyodorovich then!”

“What I put up with from you! Listen, you villain: if I had been counting on anyone then, it would surely have been on you, not on Dmitri; and, I swear, I even had a presentiment of some vileness from you… then… I remember my impression!”

“And I too thought then, for one little minute, that you were counting on me too,” Smerdyakov grinned mockingly, “so that by that very thing you gave yourself away to me still more then; for if you had a presentiment about me and at the same time went away, then by that very thing it was just as if you had said to me: you may kill my father, and I won’t hinder you.”
“Scoundrel! That’s how you understood it!”

“And all through that very Chermashnya, sir. Have mercy! You were getting ready to go to Moscow and refused all your father’s requests to go to Chermashnya, sir! And on one foolish word of mine you suddenly agreed, sir! And why should you have agreed to that Chermashnya then? If you went not to Moscow but to Chermashnya, without reason, on one word of mine, then you must have been expecting something from me.”
“No, I swear, no!” Ivan yelled, grinding his teeth.

“How do you mean, no, sir? On the contrary, for such words of mine then, you, your father’s son, ought first of all to have taken me to the police station and had me flogged, sir… or at least boxed my ears on the spot; whereas you, if you please, sir, on the contrary, without being the least bit angry, at once in a friendly way do exactly as my very foolish word says, sir, and go away, which was quite absurd, sir, for you ought to have stayed to guard your father’s life… How could I not conclude something?”
Ivan sat scowling, his two fists pressed convulsively against his knees.

“Yes, it’s a pity I didn’t box your ears,” he smiled bitterly. “I couldn’t have dragged you to the police station then: who would have believed me, and what could I have pointed to? But your ears… ugh, a pity I didn’t think of it; though ear-boxing is forbidden, I would have made pulp of your mug.”
Smerdyakov looked at him almost with relish.

“In the ordinary cases of life,” he said in that self-satisfied, doctrinaire tone in which he had once argued with Grigory Vasilyevich about faith and teased him, standing behind Fyodor Pavlovich’s table, “in the ordinary cases of life ear-boxing is indeed forbidden by law nowadays, and everyone has stopped beating, sir; but in the distinctive cases of life, not only here but all over the world, even in the most complete French republic, they go on beating just the same as in the days of Adam and Eve, sir, and they never will stop, sir; but you didn’t dare even in a distinctive case then, sir.”
“Why are you learning French words?” Ivan nodded at the notebook lying on the table.
“And why shouldn’t I learn them, sir, to further my education, thinking that I too may some day happen to be in those happy parts of Europe?”

“Listen, you monster,” Ivan’s eyes flashed and he shook all over, “I am not afraid of your accusations; say what you like against me; and if I haven’t beaten you to death just now, it is only because I suspect you of this crime and will bring you to trial. I shall expose you yet!”

“In my opinion, you had better keep quiet, sir. For what can you say against me, in my complete innocence, and who will believe you? Only, if you begin, then I will tell everything too, sir; for how could I not defend myself?”
“Do you think I am afraid of you now?”
“Even if they don’t believe all these words of mine that I have been telling you now in court, sir, the public will believe them, sir, and you will be ashamed, sir.”
“So that means again: ‘It is worth talking to a clever man,’ eh?” Ivan ground out.
“You have hit the very point, sir. So be clever, sir.”

Ivan Fyodorovich got up, trembling all over with indignation, put on his overcoat and, without answering Smerdyakov any more, without even looking at him, went quickly out of the room. The fresh evening air refreshed him. The moon was shining brightly in the sky. A terrible nightmare of thoughts and sensations was seething in his soul. “Shall I go and inform against Smerdyakov at once? But inform of what? He is innocent all the same. On the contrary, he will accuse me. Indeed, why did I go to Chermashnya then? Why, why?” Ivan Fyodorovich asked himself. “Yes, of course I was expecting something, and he is right…” And again for the hundredth time he remembered how on the last night at his father’s he had listened to him from the stairs; but he remembered it now with such suffering that he even stopped on the spot as if pierced: “Yes, I was expecting it then; that is true! I wanted, I precisely wanted the murder! Did I want the murder, did I?… I must kill Smerdyakov!… If I don’t dare to kill Smerdyakov now, life is not worth living!…” Ivan Fyodorovich, without going home, went straight then to Katerina Ivanovna and frightened her by his appearance: he was like a madman. He told her his whole conversation with Smerdyakov, every bit of it. He could not calm down, however much she tried to persuade him; he kept walking about the room and talking in a jerky, strange way. At last he sat down, leaned his elbows on the table, propped his head in both hands and uttered a strange aphorism:

“If it wasn’t Dmitri but Smerdyakov who killed him, then of course I am at one with him, for I egged him on. Whether I egged him on I don’t know yet. But if it was he who killed him, and not Dmitri, then of course I am a murderer too.”

Hearing this, Katerina Ivanovna rose silently from her place, went to her writing desk, unlocked a casket that stood on it, took out a piece of paper and laid it before Ivan. This piece of paper was that very document of which Ivan Fyodorovich afterwards told Alyosha as of “mathematical proof” that his brother Dmitri had killed their father. It was a letter written by Mitya when drunk to Katerina Ivanovna, on the very evening when he met Alyosha in the fields on his way back to the monastery, after the scene in Katerina Ivanovna’s house when Grushenka had insulted her. Then, having parted from Alyosha, Mitya had rushed off to Grushenka; it is not known whether he saw her, but by night he found himself at the Metropolis tavern, where he got thoroughly drunk. Drunk, he demanded pen and paper and scrawled a document of great importance against himself. It was a frenzied, wordy and incoherent letter, a “drunken” one precisely. It was like when a drunken man, coming home, begins with extraordinary heat to tell his wife or someone in the household how he has just been insulted, what a scoundrel the man who insulted him is, what a fine man he himself is, on the contrary, and how he will pay that scoundrel out; and all this long, long, incoherent and excited, with fists banging on the table and drunken tears. The paper they gave him in the tavern was a dirty scrap of ordinary writing paper, of poor quality, with some bill written on the back of it. The drunken verbosity evidently had not enough room, and Mitya filled not only all the margins, but even wrote the last lines crosswise over what was already written. The letter ran as follows:

“Fatal Katya! Tomorrow I shall get the money and give you back your three thousand, and farewell, woman of great wrath, but farewell, my love too! Let us make an end! Tomorrow I shall try to get it from everyone, and if I can’t get it from people, I give you my word of honour I shall go to my father and smash his head and take it from under his pillow, if only Ivan has gone. I shall go to penal servitude, but I shall give back the three thousand. And as for you, farewell. I bow down to the ground before you, for I am a scoundrel before you. Forgive me. No, better not forgive me: it will be easier for me and for you! Better penal servitude than your love, for I love another, and today you have come to know her too well; how can you forgive? I shall kill my thief! I shall go away from you all to the East, so as to know no one. Her too, for you are not my only tormentress; she is too. Farewell!

“P.S. I write a curse, and I adore you! I hear it in my breast. A string is left and it rings. Better my heart torn in two! I shall kill myself, but first of all the cur. I shall tear the three thousand from him and fling it to you. Though a scoundrel before you, I am not a thief! Expect the three thousand. It is under the cur’s mattress, a pink ribbon. It is not I who am the thief, but I shall kill my thief. Katya, don’t look contemptuous: Dmitri is not a thief, but a murderer! He has killed his father and ruined himself, so as to stand firm and not have to bear your pride. And not to love you.
“P.P.S. I kiss your feet; farewell!
“P.P.S.S. Katya, pray to God that people will give me the money. Then I shall not be steeped in blood; but if they don’t give it, in blood! Kill me!
“Your slave and enemy, “D. Karamazov.”

When Ivan had read the “document”, he got up convinced. So it was his brother who had killed him, and not Smerdyakov. And if not Smerdyakov, then not he, Ivan, either. In his eyes the letter suddenly took on a mathematical meaning. There could no longer be any doubt for him of Mitya’s guilt. Incidentally, Ivan had never had any suspicion that Mitya might have killed him together with Smerdyakov; nor did it fit the facts. Ivan was completely set at rest. The next morning he remembered Smerdyakov and his jeers only with contempt. A few days later he even wondered how he could have been so tormentingly offended by his suspicions. He resolved to despise him and forget him. So a month passed. He did not ask anyone about Smerdyakov any more, but heard in passing, two or three times, that he was very ill and not in his right mind. “He will end in madness,” the young doctor Varvinsky once said of him, and Ivan remembered it. In the last week of that month Ivan himself began to feel very unwell. He had already been to consult the doctor from Moscow whom Katerina Ivanovna had sent for and who had arrived just before the trial. And just at this time his relations with Katerina Ivanovna became strained to the last degree. They were like two enemies in love with each other. Katerina Ivanovna’s returns to Mitya, momentary but strong, now drove Ivan into perfect frenzy. It is strange that until the very last scene, which we have described at Katerina Ivanovna’s, when Alyosha came to her from Mitya, he, Ivan, had not once heard from her during the whole month any doubts of Mitya’s guilt, in spite of all her “returns” to him, which he hated so. It is remarkable too that, feeling that he hated Mitya more and more every day, he understood at the same time that he hated him not for Katya’s “returns” to him, but precisely for having killed their father! He felt and was fully aware of this himself. Nevertheless, some ten days before the trial he went to Mitya and proposed to him a plan of escape, a plan evidently thought out long before. Here, besides the main cause that moved him to such a step, there was also to blame a certain scratch in his heart that would not heal, from one little word of Smerdyakov’s: that it was supposedly to his, Ivan’s, advantage that his brother should be convicted, because the sum of the inheritance from their father would then rise for him and Alyosha from forty to sixty thousand. He resolved to sacrifice thirty thousand on his own part to arrange Mitya’s escape. Coming back from him that time, he was terribly sad and troubled: he suddenly began to feel that he wanted the escape not only so as to sacrifice thirty thousand to it and heal the scratch, but for some other reason too. “Is it because in my soul I am just such a murderer too?” he began to ask himself. Something remote but burning stung his soul. Above all, all that month his pride had suffered terribly; but of that later… When, after his conversation with Alyosha, he had taken hold of the bell of his lodgings and suddenly decided to go to Smerdyakov, Ivan Fyodorovich was obeying a particular indignation that had suddenly boiled up in his breast. He suddenly remembered how Katerina Ivanovna had just cried out to him in Alyosha’s presence: “It was you, you alone who convinced me that he (that is, Mitya) was the murderer!” Remembering this, Ivan was even dumbfounded: never in his life had he assured her that Mitya was the murderer; on the contrary, he had even suspected himself before her when he came back from Smerdyakov. On the contrary, it was she, she, who had laid the “document” before him then and proved his brother’s guilt! And now suddenly she herself exclaims: “I have been to Smerdyakov myself!” When had she been? Ivan knew nothing of it. So she was not at all so sure of Mitya’s guilt! And what could Smerdyakov have told her? What, what exactly had he told her? A terrible anger blazed up in his heart. He could not understand how half an hour before he could have let those words pass and not shouted out at once. He let go of the bell and set off for Smerdyakov’s. “Perhaps I shall kill him this time,” he thought on the way.
## Book Eleven, Chapter VIII · The Third and Last Meeting with Smerdyakov

He was still only halfway there when a sharp, dry wind rose, like the one early that morning, and a fine, thick, dry snow began to fall. It fell on the ground without sticking to it; the wind whirled it about, and soon there was a regular blizzard. In the part of the town where Smerdyakov lived there are hardly any street lamps. Ivan Fyodorovich strode on in the darkness, not noticing the blizzard, making out the way by instinct. His head ached and his temples throbbed tormentingly. In his wrists, he could feel it, there were spasms. A little before he reached Marya Kondratyevna’s cottage, Ivan Fyodorovich suddenly met a solitary drunk, a little peasant in a patched coat, walking in zigzags, grumbling and swearing, then suddenly breaking off his swearing and beginning a song in a hoarse, drunken voice:

> Oh, Vanka’s gone to Petersburg,
> I won’t wait for him to come!

But he kept breaking off at the second line and swearing at someone again, then suddenly striking up the same song again. Ivan Fyodorovich had long been feeling a terrible hatred for him, before he had even thought about him, and suddenly he became aware of him. At once he felt an irresistible desire to knock the little peasant down with his fist. Just at that moment they came abreast, and the little peasant, swaying heavily, suddenly lurched against Ivan with all his weight. Ivan pushed him off furiously. The little peasant flew back and fell like a log on the frozen ground, gave only one painful moan, “O-oh!”, and was silent. Ivan stepped up to him. He lay on his back, quite motionless, unconscious. “He’ll freeze!” thought Ivan, and strode on again to Smerdyakov’s.

In the passage Marya Kondratyevna, who had run out with a candle in her hand to open the door, whispered to him that Pavel Fyodorovich (that is, Smerdyakov) was very ill, sir; not that he was in bed, sir, but almost as if he were not in his right mind, sir, and he had even told her to take away the tea; he didn’t want to drink it.
“What, is he making a row?” Ivan Fyodorovich asked rudely.
“Oh no, on the contrary, he is quite quiet, sir; only don’t talk with him very long…” Marya Kondratyevna begged.
Ivan Fyodorovich opened the door and stepped into the room.

It was heated as before, but some changes could be noticed in the room: one of the side benches had been taken out, and in its place stood a large old leather sofa of imitation mahogany. A bed had been made up on it, with fairly clean white pillows. On the bed sat Smerdyakov, in the same dressing gown. The table had been moved in front of the sofa, so that the room had become very cramped. On the table lay some thick book in a yellow cover, but Smerdyakov was not reading it; he seemed to be sitting and doing nothing. He met Ivan Fyodorovich with a long, silent look and evidently was not in the least surprised at his coming. His face had changed very much; he had grown very thin and yellow. His eyes were sunken, the lower lids blue.
“Why, you really are ill?” Ivan Fyodorovich stopped. “I won’t keep you long; I won’t even take off my overcoat. Where can one sit down here?”
He went round to the other end of the table, drew a chair up to it and sat down.
“Why do you look at me and say nothing? I have come with only one question, and I swear I won’t leave without an answer: has the young lady, Katerina Ivanovna, been to see you?”
Smerdyakov was silent for a long time, still looking quietly at Ivan as before, but suddenly he waved his hand and turned his face away from him.
“What is it?” exclaimed Ivan.
“Nothing.”
“What do you mean, nothing?”
“Well, she has been; well, and it makes no difference to you. Leave me alone, sir.”
“No, I won’t leave you alone! Tell me, when was she here?”

“Why, I have quite forgotten to remember her,” Smerdyakov smiled contemptuously, and suddenly, turning his face to Ivan again, he stared at him with a sort of frenzied, hateful look, the very look with which he had looked at him at their meeting a month before.
“You seem to be ill yourself; see how you’ve fallen away; you look dreadful,” he said to Ivan.
“Never mind my health; tell me what you are asked.”
“And why have your eyes gone yellow? The whites are quite yellow. Are you tormenting yourself very much, or what?”
He smiled contemptuously, and suddenly laughed outright.
“Listen, I told you I won’t leave without an answer!” Ivan shouted in terrible irritation.
“Why do you keep on at me, sir? Why do you torment me?” Smerdyakov said with suffering.
“Oh, the devil! I have nothing to do with you. Answer the question and I’ll go at once.”
“I have nothing to answer you!” Smerdyakov looked down again.
“I assure you I will make you answer!”

“Why are you always so uneasy?” Smerdyakov suddenly stared at him, not exactly with contempt, but almost with a kind of disgust now. “Is it because the trial begins tomorrow? Why, nothing will happen to you; be sure of that at last! Go home, go to bed and sleep peacefully; don’t be afraid of anything.”
“I don’t understand you… what have I to be afraid of tomorrow?” Ivan said in surprise, and suddenly a kind of fright really did breathe coldly on his soul. Smerdyakov measured him with his eyes.
“You don’t un-der-stand?” he drawled reproachfully. “What a pleasure it must be for a clever man to play such a farce!”

Ivan looked at him in silence. This unexpected tone alone, quite unprecedentedly haughty, in which his former servant now addressed him, was extraordinary. There had been no such tone even the last time.

“I tell you, you have nothing to be afraid of. I shan’t say anything against you; there is no evidence. Look how your hands are shaking. Why are your fingers twitching? Go home; it wasn’t you who killed him.”
Ivan started; he remembered Alyosha.
“I know it wasn’t I…” he began to murmur.
“You kno-ow?” Smerdyakov caught him up again.
Ivan jumped up and seized him by the shoulder.
“Tell me everything, you reptile! Tell me everything!”
Smerdyakov was not in the least frightened. He only riveted his eyes on him with insane hatred.
“Why, it was you who killed him, if that’s how it is,” he whispered to him furiously.
Ivan sank down on the chair, as if he had reasoned something out. He smiled spitefully.
“You mean that business of that time? The same as last time?”
“Last time too you stood before me and understood everything, and you understand now.”
“All I understand is that you are mad.”

“Doesn’t a man ever get tired of it! Here we are sitting face to face; why should we fool each other, it seems, and play a farce? Or do you still want to throw it all on me alone, to my face? You killed him; you are the chief murderer, and I was only your accomplice, your faithful servant Lichard, and I did the deed on your word.”
“Did the deed? Was it you who killed him, then?” Ivan went cold.

Something seemed to shake in his brain, and he began to tremble all over with a fine, cold trembling. At this Smerdyakov himself looked at him in surprise: probably Ivan’s fright had struck him at last by its sincerity.
“Can you really not have known anything?” he murmured distrustfully, smiling crookedly in his face.
Ivan kept looking at him; he seemed to have lost his tongue.

> Oh, Vanka’s gone to Petersburg,
> I won’t wait for him to come,
suddenly rang in his head.
“Do you know what: I am afraid that you are a dream, that you are a phantom sitting before me?” he murmured.
“There is no phantom here, sir, besides the two of us, sir, and a certain third. Without a doubt he is here now, that third one, between the two of us.”
“Who is he? Who is here? Who is the third?” Ivan Fyodorovich said in fright, looking round and hurriedly searching with his eyes for someone in all the corners.
“That third is God, sir, providence itself, sir; it is here now beside us, sir; only don’t look for it; you won’t find it.”
“You lied that you killed him!” Ivan yelled furiously. “You are either mad or teasing me, as you did last time!”

Smerdyakov, as before, not frightened at all, kept watching him searchingly. He still could not overcome his distrust; it still seemed to him that Ivan “knew everything” and was only pretending, so as “to throw it all on him alone, to his face”.

“Wait, sir,” he said at last in a weak voice, and suddenly, drawing his left leg out from under the table, he began to roll up his trouser leg. The leg turned out to be in a long white stocking and shod in a slipper. Without hurrying, Smerdyakov took off his garter and thrust his fingers deep into the stocking. Ivan Fyodorovich looked at him and suddenly began to shake in convulsive fright.

“Madman!” he yelled, and, jumping up quickly, staggered back so that he struck his back against the wall and seemed to stick to the wall, drawn out straight as a thread. He was looking at Smerdyakov in insane horror. Smerdyakov, not in the least disturbed by his fright, was still fumbling in his stocking, as if still trying to catch hold of something in it with his fingers and pull it out. At last he caught hold of it and began to pull. Ivan Fyodorovich saw that it was some papers, or a bundle of papers. Smerdyakov pulled it out and laid it on the table.
“There, sir!” he said quietly.
“What?” Ivan answered, shaking.
“Kindly look, sir,” Smerdyakov said just as quietly.
Ivan stepped up to the table, took hold of the bundle and began to unfold it, but suddenly jerked his fingers away as if from the touch of some loathsome, terrible reptile.

“Your fingers keep trembling, sir, in a spasm,” Smerdyakov remarked, and unhurriedly unfolded the paper himself. Under the wrapping there turned out to be three packets of hundred-rouble rainbow notes.
“It’s all here, sir, all three thousand; you needn’t even count it. Take it, sir,” he invited Ivan, nodding at the money. Ivan sank down on the chair. He was white as a sheet.
“You frightened me… with that stocking…” he said, grinning somehow strangely.
“Can you, can you really not have known till now?” Smerdyakov asked once more.
“No, I didn’t know. I always thought it was Dmitri. Brother! Brother! Ah!” He suddenly clutched his head in both hands. “Listen: did you kill him alone? Without my brother, or with him?”
“Only together with you, sir; I killed him together with you, sir; and Dmitri Fyodorovich is as innocent as can be, sir.”
“All right, all right… About me later. Why do I keep trembling?… I can’t get a word out.”

“You were always bold then, sir; ‘everything is permitted’, you used to say, sir; and now see how frightened you are!” Smerdyakov murmured, wondering. “Won’t you have some lemonade? I’ll order it at once, sir. It can be very refreshing. Only this ought to be covered up first, sir.”

And he nodded at the packets again. He moved to get up and call through the door to Marya Kondratyevna to make some lemonade and bring it; but, looking for something to cover the money with, so that she would not see it, he first took out his handkerchief, and since it again proved to be thoroughly soiled with blowing his nose, he took from the table the one thick yellow book lying on it, which Ivan had noticed when he came in, and weighted the money down with it. The title of the book was The Sayings of Our Holy Father Isaac the Syrian. Ivan Fyodorovich managed to read the title mechanically.
“I don’t want lemonade,” he said. “About me later. Sit down and tell me: how did you do it? Tell me everything…”
“You might at least take off your overcoat, sir, or you’ll be all in a sweat.”
Ivan Fyodorovich, as if only now realising it, tore off his overcoat and threw it, without getting up from the chair, onto the bench.
“Speak, please, speak!”
He seemed to have grown calm. He waited with assurance for Smerdyakov to tell everything now.
“About how it was done, sir?” Smerdyakov sighed. “It was done in the most natural way, sir, from those very words of yours…”

“About my words later,” Ivan interrupted again, but no longer shouting as before, pronouncing his words firmly and as if he had quite mastered himself. “Just tell me in detail how you did it. Everything in order. Don’t forget anything. Details, details above all. I beg you.”
“You went away, and I fell into the cellar then, sir…”
“In a fit, or did you sham?”

“Of course I shammed, sir. I shammed all of it. I went down the steps calmly, sir, to the very bottom, sir, and lay down calmly, sir, and as soon as I lay down, then I began to howl. And I thrashed about until they carried me out.”
“Wait! And all the time, and afterwards, and in the hospital, were you shamming all the time?”

“Not at all, sir. The very next day, in the morning, before the hospital, a real one struck me, and so violent that there hadn’t been one like it for many years. For two days I was completely unconscious.”
“All right, all right. Go on.”

“They laid me on that bed, sir; I knew it would be behind the partition, sir, because every time I was ill Marfa Ignatyevna always put me to bed for the night behind that very partition in her rooms, sir. She was always tender to me, ever since I was born, sir. At night I moaned, sir, only quietly. I kept waiting for Dmitri Fyodorovich.”
“Waiting how? For him to come to you?”

“Why to me? I was waiting for him to come to the house, because I had no doubt at all that he would come that very night; for, having lost me and having no information, he would certainly have to climb into the house himself over the fence, sir, as he knew how, sir, and do something or other.”
“And if he hadn’t come?”
“Then nothing would have happened, sir. I wouldn’t have dared without him.”
“All right, all right… speak more plainly; don’t hurry; above all, don’t leave anything out!”

“I was expecting him to kill Fyodor Pavlovich, sir… that for certain, sir. Because I had prepared him so… in the last days, sir… and above all he had come to know those signals. With his suspiciousness and the fury that had built up in him in those days, he was bound to get into the house itself by means of the signals, sir. That was certain. That is how I was expecting him, sir.”

“Wait,” Ivan interrupted. “If he had killed him, he would have taken the money and carried it off; that is how you must have reasoned, surely? Then what would have been left for you after him? I don’t see.”

“But he would never have found the money, sir. It was only I who told him the money was under the mattress. Only that wasn’t true, sir. Before, it had been in a box; that is how it was, sir. And afterwards I taught Fyodor Pavlovich, since he trusted me alone of all mankind, to move that very envelope with the money to the corner behind the icons, because there nobody at all would guess, especially if he came in a hurry. So that envelope was lying there in his corner behind the icons, sir. And to keep it under the mattress would have been simply absurd; in a box at least it was under lock and key. And now everyone here believes it was under the mattress. A foolish idea, sir. So if Dmitri Fyodorovich had committed that very murder, then, finding nothing, he would either have run away in haste, afraid of every rustle, as always happens with murderers, or he would have been arrested, sir. So then I could always, sir, the next day or even that same night, sir, climb up behind the icons and carry off that very money, sir, and it would all have fallen on Dmitri Fyodorovich. That I could always count on.”
“Well, and if he hadn’t killed him, but only beaten him?”

“If he hadn’t killed him, then of course I wouldn’t have dared to take the money, and it would have come to nothing. But there was this calculation too: that he would beat him senseless, and I would have time to take it then, and afterwards I would report to Fyodor Pavlovich that it was none other than Dmitri Fyodorovich who had beaten him and stolen the money.”
“Wait… I am getting confused. So it was Dmitri who killed him after all, and you only took the money?”

“No, it wasn’t he who killed him, sir. Why, I could tell you even now that he is the murderer… but I don’t want to lie before you now, because… because if you really, as I see myself, didn’t understand anything till now and weren’t pretending before me, so as to throw your obvious guilt on me to my face, still you are guilty of everything, sir; for you knew about the murder, sir, and you charged me to kill, sir, and you yourself, knowing everything, went away. That is why I want to prove it to your face this evening: that the chief murderer in all this is you alone, sir, and I am only not the chief one, though it was I who killed him. And you are the most rightful murderer!”

“Why, why am I a murderer? Oh God!” Ivan could not bear it at last, forgetting that he had put off everything about himself till the end of the conversation. “Is it still that Chermashnya? Wait, tell me: why did you need my consent, if you had already taken Chermashnya for consent? How will you explain that now?”

“Being sure of your consent, I would have known that you would not raise an outcry over those three thousand being lost when you came back, if for some reason the authorities suspected me instead of Dmitri Fyodorovich, or as Dmitri Fyodorovich’s accomplice; on the contrary, you would have protected me from others… And having got the inheritance, you could reward me afterwards too, sometime, for all the rest of my life; because after all you would have got that inheritance through me; whereas if he had married Agrafena Alexandrovna, you would have got nothing but a fig.”
“Ah! So you meant to torment me afterwards too, all my life!” Ivan ground out. “And what if I hadn’t gone away then, but had informed against you?”

“And what could you have informed then? That I was persuading you to go to Chermashnya? Why, that is nonsense, sir. Besides, after our conversation you would either go or stay. If you stayed, then nothing would have happened; I would have known, sir, that you didn’t want this business, and I wouldn’t have undertaken anything. And if you went, that meant you had assured me that you wouldn’t dare inform against me in court and would forgive me those three thousand. And you couldn’t have prosecuted me afterwards at all, because then I would have told everything in court, sir; that is, not that I stole or killed, I wouldn’t have said that, sir, but that you yourself had egged me on to steal and kill, and only I didn’t agree. That is why I needed your consent then, so that you couldn’t corner me with anything, sir; because where is your proof? Whereas I could always corner you, sir, by revealing what a thirst you had for your father’s death; and I give you my word, the public would all have believed it, and you would have been ashamed all your life.”
“So I had it, I had that thirst, did I?” Ivan ground out again.

“You undoubtedly had it, sir, and by your consent you silently allowed me this business then, sir,” Smerdyakov looked firmly at Ivan. He was very weak and spoke quietly and wearily, but something inward and hidden was kindling him; he evidently had some intention. Ivan felt it.
“Go on,” he said to him. “Go on about that night.”

“Well, what next, sir! There I lay, and I heard what seemed like the master crying out. And Grigory Vasilyevich had suddenly got up before that and gone out, and suddenly he yelled, then everything was quiet, darkness. I lay there waiting; my heart was pounding; I couldn’t bear it. At last I got up and went, sir. I see the window on the left into the garden is open at his place; I took another step to the left, sir, to listen whether he was sitting there alive or not, and I hear the master tossing about and groaning; so he is alive, sir. Ah, I think! I went up to the window and called to the master: ‘It’s me,’ I said. And he says to me: ‘He was here, he was here, he ran away!’ That is, Dmitri Fyodorovich had been there, sir. ‘He has killed Grigory!’ ‘Where?’ I whisper to him. ‘There, in the corner,’ he points; he is whispering too. ‘Wait,’ I say. I went to the corner to look, and by the wall I stumbled on Grigory Vasilyevich lying there, all covered in blood, unconscious. So it is true that Dmitri Fyodorovich was here, leapt into my head at once, and at once and there I decided to finish it all off suddenly, sir, since Grigory Vasilyevich, even if he was still alive, lying unconscious, would see nothing for the time being. There was only one risk, sir: that Marfa Ignatyevna might suddenly wake up. I felt it at that moment, only that thirst had taken hold of me entirely, so that it took my breath away. I came back under the window to the master and said: ‘She is here; she has come; Agrafena Alexandrovna has come; she wants to be let in.’ Why, he started all over like a baby: ‘Where is she? Where?’ he groans, and still doesn’t believe it. ‘There,’ I say, ‘she is standing there; open the door!’ He looks at me through the window, and believes and doesn’t believe, and is afraid to open; it’s me he is afraid of now, I think. And it was funny, too: suddenly I thought of tapping out those very signals on the window frame then, that Grushenka had come, right before his eyes: he didn’t seem to believe the words, but as soon as I tapped out the signals he ran at once to open the door. He opened it. I made to go in, but he stood there and wouldn’t let me past with his body. ‘Where is she, where is she?’ He looks at me and trembles. Well, I think, if he is so afraid of me, it’s bad! And then my legs even went weak from fear myself, that he wouldn’t let me into the rooms, or would cry out, or Marfa Ignatyevna would come running, or something else would happen; I don’t remember now; I must have been standing before him pale. I whisper to him: ‘But she is there, there under the window; how is it you didn’t see her?’ ‘Bring her, bring her!’ ‘But she is afraid,’ I say; ‘the shouting frightened her; she has hidden in a bush; go and call her yourself from the study.’ He ran, went to the window and put the candle on the windowsill. ‘Grushenka,’ he cries, ‘Grushenka, are you there?’ He is crying out like that, but he won’t lean out of the window, won’t move away from me, from that very fear, because he had grown very much afraid of me, and so he dared not move away from me. ‘There she is,’ I say (I went up to the window and leaned right out myself); ‘there she is in the bush, laughing at you; do you see?’ Suddenly he believed it; he simply shook all over; he was terribly in love with her, sir; and he leaned right out of the window. Then I seized that very iron paperweight on his table, you remember, sir, it must weigh about three pounds; I swung it and hit him from behind with the corner right on the crown of his head. He didn’t even cry out. He only sank down suddenly, and I hit him a second time and a third. At the third I felt that I had smashed it. He suddenly fell over on his back, face upwards, all covered in blood. I looked myself over: there was no blood on me; it hadn’t spattered; I wiped the paperweight and put it back, went behind the icons, took the money out of the envelope, and threw the envelope on the floor, and that very pink ribbon beside it. I went down into the garden, trembling all over. Straight to that apple tree with the hollow; you know that hollow, and I had had my eye on it for a long time; there was a rag and some paper lying in it already; I had got them ready long before; I wrapped the whole sum in the paper, and then in the rag, and pushed it in deep. So it stayed there for over two weeks, that very sum, sir; I took it out afterwards, after the hospital. I went back to my bed, lay down and thought in fear: ‘Now if Grigory Vasilyevich has been killed outright, then something very bad may come of it; but if he isn’t killed and comes to, then it will turn out very well, because he will be a witness that Dmitri Fyodorovich came, and so it was he who killed him and carried off the money, sir.’ Then from doubt and impatience I began to moan, so as to wake Marfa Ignatyevna as soon as possible. At last she got up and rushed to me, but as soon as she saw that Grigory Vasilyevich was not there, she ran out, and I heard her yell in the garden. Well, then it all went on all night, sir, and I was quite at ease about everything.”

The narrator stopped. Ivan had listened to him all the time in deathly silence, without moving, without taking his eyes off him. Smerdyakov, as he told it, only glanced at him now and then, and looked aside more. Having finished his story, he was evidently agitated himself and was breathing heavily. Sweat appeared on his face. It was impossible to guess, however, whether he felt remorse or what.
“Wait,” Ivan caught him up, thinking. “And the door? If he opened the door only to you, how could Grigory have seen it open before you? For Grigory saw it before you, didn’t he?”

It is remarkable that Ivan asked in the most peaceable voice, even in quite a different tone, as it were, not spiteful at all, so that if anyone had opened their door now and looked at them from the threshold, he would certainly have concluded that they were sitting talking peaceably about some ordinary, though interesting, subject.

“As for that door, and Grigory Vasilyevich supposedly having seen it open, he only fancied it,” Smerdyakov smiled crookedly. “For he isn’t a man, I tell you, sir, but no better than a stubborn gelding: he didn’t see it, but he fancied he saw it, and now you will never shake him, sir. It is just our good luck, yours and mine, that he thought of it, because after that Dmitri Fyodorovich will certainly be convicted completely.”

“Listen,” said Ivan Fyodorovich, as if beginning to lose himself again and struggling to grasp something, “listen… There was a lot more I wanted to ask you, but I have forgotten… I keep forgetting and getting confused… Yes! Tell me just this one thing: why did you open the envelope and leave it there on the floor? Why didn’t you simply carry it off in the envelope?… When you were telling it, it seemed to me that you spoke of that envelope as if that was how it had to be done… but why it had to be so, I can’t understand…”

“I did that for a certain reason, sir. For if a man was knowing and practised, as I am, for instance, who had seen that money himself beforehand and perhaps had wrapped it in that envelope himself and watched with his own eyes how it was sealed and inscribed, then why on earth should such a man, sir, if he were the one who killed him, say, open that envelope after the murder, and in such a hurry too, knowing quite certainly without that that the money was in that envelope for sure, sir? On the contrary, if it were a thief like me, for instance, he would simply have stuffed that envelope into his pocket without opening it at all and made off with it as fast as possible, sir. It is quite different with Dmitri Fyodorovich: he only knew of the envelope by hearsay; he had never seen it himself; and so when he got hold of it, say from under the mattress, he would have opened it there and then as quickly as possible, to make sure the money really was in it. And he would have thrown the envelope down there and then, not having time to think that it would be left behind as evidence against him; because he is an unpractised thief, sir, and had never stolen anything openly before, being a gentleman born, sir; and if he had made up his mind to steal now, it was as if not to steal, but only to come and take back what was his own, since he had announced it to the whole town beforehand and had even boasted aloud before everyone in advance that he would go and take his property from Fyodor Pavlovich. I didn’t exactly say this very idea plainly to the prosecutor at my examination, but on the contrary led him up to it as if by a hint, sir, as though I didn’t understand it myself, and as though he had thought of it himself and I hadn’t prompted him, sir; so that the prosecutor’s mouth even watered at that hint of mine, sir…”
“Can it be, can it be that you thought all this out then and there on the spot?” exclaimed Ivan Fyodorovich, beside himself with amazement. He was again looking at Smerdyakov in fright.
“Have mercy, could anyone think it all up in such a hurry, sir? It was all thought out beforehand.”
“Well… well, then the devil himself was helping you!” Ivan Fyodorovich exclaimed again. “No, you are no fool; you are much cleverer than I thought…”

He got up, evidently meaning to walk about the room. He was in terrible anguish. But since the table blocked the way and one almost had to squeeze between the table and the wall, he only turned round where he stood and sat down again. Perhaps not having been able to walk about suddenly irritated him, so that, almost in his former frenzy, he suddenly yelled:

“Listen, you wretched, contemptible man! Can’t you understand that if I haven’t killed you yet, it is only because I am keeping you to answer at the trial tomorrow? God sees,” Ivan raised his hand on high, “perhaps I too was guilty; perhaps I really had a secret desire that… my father should die; but I swear to you, I was not so guilty as you think, and perhaps I did not egg you on at all. No, no, I did not egg you on! But no matter; I shall give evidence against myself, tomorrow, at the trial; I have decided! I shall tell everything, everything. But we shall appear together, you and I! And whatever you say against me at the trial, whatever evidence you give, I accept it and am not afraid of you; I shall confirm everything myself! But you too must confess before the court! You must, you must; we shall go together! So it shall be!”
Ivan said this solemnly and with energy, and it could be seen from his flashing eyes alone that so it would be.
“You are ill, I see, sir, quite ill, sir. Your eyes are quite yellow, sir,” said Smerdyakov, but without any mockery at all, even as if sympathising.
“We shall go together!” Ivan repeated. “And if you won’t go, I shall confess alone just the same.”
Smerdyakov was silent, as if thinking it over.
“None of this will happen, sir, and you won’t go, sir,” he decided at last, without appeal.
“You don’t understand me!” Ivan exclaimed reproachfully.

“You will be too ashamed, sir, if you confess everything against yourself. And what is more, it will be useless, quite useless, sir; because I shall say straight out that I never told you anything of the kind, sir, and that you are either in some illness (and that is what it looks like, sir), or you are so sorry for your brother that you have sacrificed yourself and made it up against me, since all your life you have regarded me as a midge anyway, and not as a man. Well, and who will believe you, and what single proof have you got?”
“Listen: you showed me that money just now, of course, to convince me.”
Smerdyakov took Isaac the Syrian off the packets and laid it aside.
“Take that money with you, sir, carry it away,” Smerdyakov sighed.
“Of course I’ll take it! But why do you give it to me, if you killed him for it?” Ivan looked at him in great surprise.

“I don’t want it at all, sir,” Smerdyakov said in a trembling voice, waving his hand. “I did have that idea before, sir, that I would begin a life with such money, in Moscow, or better still abroad; I had that dream, sir; and most of all because ‘everything is permitted’. That is what you really taught me, sir, for you used to talk to me a lot about it then: for if there is no infinite God, then there is no virtue either, and no need of it at all then. That was really you. That is how I reasoned it out.”
“You arrived at it with your own wits?” Ivan smiled crookedly.
“Under your guidance, sir.”
“And now, then, you have come to believe in God, since you are giving the money back?”
“No, sir, I haven’t come to believe, sir,” whispered Smerdyakov.
“Then why are you giving it back?”

“Stop it… there’s no point, sir!” Smerdyakov waved his hand again. “You yourself used to say then that everything is permitted; so why are you so alarmed now, sir, you yourself? You even want to go and give evidence against yourself… Only none of that will happen! You won’t go and give evidence!” Smerdyakov decided again firmly and with conviction.
“You’ll see!” said Ivan.

“It can’t be. You are very clever, sir. You love money, I know that, sir; you love respect too, because you are very proud; you love feminine charms excessively; and most of all you love to live in peaceful comfort and not to bow to anyone; that most of all, sir. You won’t want to spoil your life for ever by taking such shame on yourself at the trial. You are like Fyodor Pavlovich, most of all, sir; of all his children you have turned out most like him, with the same soul as he, sir.”

“You are no fool,” said Ivan, as if struck; the blood rushed to his face. “I used to think you were a fool. You are serious now!” he remarked, looking at Smerdyakov somehow in a new way all of a sudden.
“It was your pride that made you think I was a fool. Take the money, sir.”
Ivan took all three packets of notes and stuffed them into his pocket without wrapping them in anything.
“I shall show them at the trial tomorrow,” he said.
“Nobody will believe you there, sir, seeing that you have plenty of money of your own now; you took it out of your cashbox and brought it, sir.”
Ivan got up from his place.
“I repeat to you: if I haven’t killed you, it is only because you are needed for tomorrow; remember that; don’t forget it!”

“Well, kill me, sir. Kill me now,” Smerdyakov said suddenly, strangely, looking strangely at Ivan. “You won’t dare even that, sir,” he added, smiling bitterly. “You won’t dare anything, you who were so bold, sir!”
“Till tomorrow!” Ivan shouted, and moved to go.
“Wait… show them to me once more.”
Ivan took out the notes and showed them to him. Smerdyakov looked at them for about ten seconds.
“Well, go,” he said, waving his hand. “Ivan Fyodorovich!” he suddenly called after him again.
“What do you want?” Ivan turned round, already moving away.
“Goodbye, sir!”
“Till tomorrow!” Ivan shouted again, and went out of the room.

The blizzard was still going on. He took the first steps briskly, but suddenly he seemed to begin to stagger. “It’s something physical,” he thought with a smile. A sort of joy seemed to have descended into his soul now. He felt in himself an infinite firmness: an end to the wavering that had so terribly tormented him all this last time! The decision was taken, “and now it won’t change,” he thought with happiness. At that moment he suddenly stumbled over something and nearly fell. Stopping, he made out at his feet the little peasant he had knocked down, still lying in the same place, unconscious and motionless. The blizzard had already covered almost all his face. Ivan suddenly seized him and dragged him along on himself. Seeing a light in a little house on the right, he went up, knocked on the shutters, and asked the townsman who owned the little house and who answered to help him drag the peasant to the police station, promising to give him three roubles for it then and there. The townsman got ready and came out. I will not describe in detail how Ivan Fyodorovich managed then to achieve his aim and get the peasant settled at the police station, with a view to having him examined by a doctor at once, for which again he gave freely “for expenses”. I will say only that the business took almost a whole hour. But Ivan Fyodorovich remained very pleased. His thoughts were ranging and working. “If my decision for tomorrow had not been taken so firmly,” he suddenly thought with delight, “I wouldn’t have stopped for a whole hour to settle the little peasant, but would have passed him by and only spat at the thought that he would freeze… But how well I can observe myself,” he thought at the same moment with still greater delight, “and they have decided that I am going mad!” On reaching his house he suddenly stopped at a sudden question: “Oughtn’t I to go at once, now, to the prosecutor and tell everything?” He settled the question by turning back towards the house again. “Everything together tomorrow!” he whispered to himself; and, strange to say, almost all his joy, all his satisfaction with himself, passed in a moment. And when he went into his room, something icy suddenly touched his heart, like a memory, or rather a reminder, of something tormenting and loathsome that was in that room precisely now, at this moment, and had been there before too. He sank wearily onto his sofa. The old woman brought him the samovar; he made tea but did not touch it; he sent the old woman away till the morning. He sat on the sofa and felt giddy. He felt that he was ill and powerless. He began to fall asleep, but got up uneasily and walked about the room to drive away sleep. At moments it seemed to him that he was delirious. But it was not his illness that occupied him most; sitting down again, he began now and then to look round, as if looking out for something. So it happened several times. At last his gaze was fixed intently on one point. Ivan smiled, but a flush of anger flooded his face. He sat a long time in his place, his head propped firmly in both hands, and yet looking sideways all the while at the same point, at the sofa that stood against the opposite wall. Evidently something there was irritating him, some object; it troubled him, tormented him.
## Book Eleven, Chapter IX · The Devil. Ivan Fyodorovich’s Nightmare

I am not a doctor, and yet I feel that the moment has come when it is absolutely necessary for me to explain to the reader at least something of the nature of Ivan Fyodorovich’s illness. Running ahead, I will say only one thing: he was now, that evening, precisely on the very eve of brain fever, which at last took complete possession of his organism, long since disordered but stubbornly resisting the disease. Knowing nothing of medicine, I venture to suggest that perhaps by a terrible effort of will he really had managed for a time to put off the illness, dreaming, of course, of overcoming it altogether. He knew he was unwell, but he was loath to be ill at this time, in these approaching fateful moments of his life, when he had to be present, to speak his word boldly and decisively, and himself “to justify himself to himself”. He had, however, once been to the new doctor who had come from Moscow, sent for by Katerina Ivanovna because of a certain fancy of hers which I have already mentioned. The doctor, having listened to him and examined him, concluded that he had even something like a disorder of the brain, and was not in the least surprised by a certain confession which Ivan, with disgust, nevertheless made to him. “Hallucinations in your condition are very possible,” the doctor decided, “though they ought to be verified… In general you must begin serious treatment without losing a minute, or things will go badly.” But Ivan Fyodorovich, on leaving him, did not follow this sensible advice and neglected to go to bed for treatment. “I am walking about, I have strength for the present; if I collapse, that is another matter; then let anyone who likes treat me,” he decided, with a wave of his hand. And so he was sitting now, almost aware himself that he was delirious, and, as I have said, gazing persistently at some object on the sofa by the opposite wall. There, suddenly, someone turned out to be sitting, who had come in God knows how, for he had not been in the room when Ivan Fyodorovich came back from Smerdyakov’s and entered it. It was a gentleman, or, better to say, a Russian gentleman of a certain kind, no longer young, “qui frisait la cinquantaine”, as the French say, close on fifty, with not very much grey in his dark, rather long and still thick hair and in his small pointed beard. He was dressed in a sort of brown jacket, evidently from the best tailor, but already worn, made perhaps two years before and quite out of fashion, so that no well-to-do people of the world had worn such for two years. His linen, his long scarf-like tie, all was as with all smart gentlemen; but the linen, if one looked closer, was rather dirty, and the wide scarf very frayed. The visitor’s checked trousers fitted excellently, but again were too light and somehow too narrow, as they are no longer worn, as was the soft white felt hat which the visitor had brought with him, much out of season. In a word, there was a look of respectability on very slender means. It looked as if the gentleman belonged to the class of former idle landowners who flourished in the days of serfdom; evidently a man who had seen the world and decent society, who had once had connections and had kept them perhaps even to this day, but who, gradually impoverished after a gay life in his youth and the recent abolition of serfdom, had turned into a sort of well-bred hanger-on, going the rounds of good old acquaintances, who received him for his easy, accommodating character, and also in view of his being, after all, a respectable man whom one could even sit at one’s table in anyone’s presence, though of course in a modest place. Such hangers-on, gentlemen of accommodating character, who can tell a story, make up a hand at cards, and decidedly dislike being given any errands if they are thrust on them, are usually solitary, either bachelors or widowers; perhaps they have children, but their children are always being brought up somewhere far away, by some aunts or other, whom the gentleman almost never mentions in decent society, as if a little ashamed of such kinship. He gradually loses the habit of his children altogether, receiving from them now and then letters of congratulation for his name day and for Christmas, and sometimes even answering them. The unexpected visitor’s face was not so much good-natured as, again, accommodating and ready, according to circumstances, for any amiable expression. He had no watch, but he had a tortoiseshell lorgnette on a black ribbon. On the middle finger of his right hand gleamed a massive gold ring with a cheap opal. Ivan Fyodorovich was spitefully silent and did not want to begin talking. The visitor waited, and sat precisely like a hanger-on who has just come down from the room assigned to him to keep his host company at tea, but is meekly silent because his host is busy and thinking frowningly about something; ready, however, for any amiable conversation as soon as the host begins it. Suddenly his face expressed a sort of sudden concern.

“Listen,” he began to Ivan Fyodorovich, “forgive me, it is only to remind you: you went to Smerdyakov’s to find out about Katerina Ivanovna, and you came away without finding out anything about her; you must have forgotten…”

“Ah yes!” broke from Ivan suddenly, and his face darkened with worry. “Yes, I forgot… Still, it’s all the same now; everything till tomorrow,” he muttered to himself. “And you,” he turned irritably to the visitor, “I would have remembered that myself in a moment, because it was precisely that which was tormenting me with anguish! Just because you popped up, am I to believe that you prompted me, and that I didn’t remember it myself?”

“Then don’t believe it,” the gentleman smiled kindly. “What is faith by force? Besides, in matters of faith no proofs help, especially material ones. Thomas believed not because he saw the risen Christ but because he wanted to believe before that. Take the spiritualists, for instance… I am very fond of them… imagine, they suppose they are serving the faith because the devils show them their little horns from the other world. ‘That,’ they say, ‘is proof, material proof, so to speak, that the other world exists.’ The other world and material proofs, tra-la-la! And finally, if the devil is proved, it is still not known whether God is proved. I want to join an idealist society; I’ll be the opposition there: ‘I am a realist, you see, but not a materialist, he-he!’”

“Listen,” Ivan Fyodorovich suddenly got up from the table. “I am as if delirious now… and of course I am delirious… lie as you like; it’s all the same to me! You won’t drive me to frenzy as you did last time. Only I feel ashamed of something… I want to walk about the room… Sometimes I don’t see you and don’t even hear your voice, as last time, but I always guess what you are drivelling, because it is I, I myself who am speaking, and not you! Only I don’t know whether I was asleep last time or saw you awake. I’ll wet a towel with cold water and put it on my head, and perhaps you will evaporate.”
Ivan Fyodorovich went into the corner, took a towel, did as he said, and with the wet towel on his head began walking up and down the room.
“I like it that we have gone straight to saying ‘thou’ to each other,” the visitor began.

“Fool,” laughed Ivan, “do you think I shall say ‘you’ to you? I am cheerful now, only my temple aches… and the crown of my head… only, please, don’t philosophise as you did last time. If you can’t clear off, then tell me something amusing. Gossip; you are a hanger-on, so gossip. What a nightmare to fasten on one! But I am not afraid of you. I shall get the better of you. They won’t take me to a madhouse!”

“C’est charmant (charming): a hanger-on. Why, I am in my true character. What am I on earth but a hanger-on? By the way, I am listening to you and wondering a little: upon my word, you seem to be beginning little by little to take me for something real, and not only for your fancy, as you insisted last time…”

“Not for a single moment do I take you for the real truth,” Ivan cried, even with a sort of fury. “You are a lie, you are my illness, you are a phantom. Only I don’t know how to destroy you, and I see that I must suffer for a time. You are my hallucination. You are the incarnation of myself, but only of one side of me… of my thoughts and feelings, but only the nastiest and stupidest of them. From that side you might even be of interest to me, if only I had time to bother with you…”
