“Allow me, allow me, I’ll catch you out: this evening by the lamp, when you flew at Alyosha and shouted at him: ‘You learned it from him! How did you know he comes to see me?’ You were thinking of me then. So for one little instant you did believe, you did believe that I really exist,” the gentleman laughed softly.
“Yes, that was a weakness of nature… but I couldn’t believe in you. I don’t know whether I was asleep or awake last time. Perhaps I only saw you in a dream then, and not awake at all…”
“And why were you so stern with him this evening, with Alyosha? He is a dear; I am to blame before him for Elder Zosima.”
“Not a word about Alyosha! How dare you, lackey!” Ivan laughed again.
“You swear, and yet you laugh: a good sign. You are much more amiable with me today than last time, though, and I understand why: that great resolution…”
“Not a word about the resolution!” Ivan cried savagely.
“I understand, I understand, c’est noble, c’est charmant (it is noble, it is charming); you are going to defend your brother tomorrow and sacrifice yourself… c’est chevaleresque (it is chivalrous).”
“Be quiet, or I’ll kick you!”

“I shall be partly glad, for then my aim will be achieved: if it comes to kicks, it means you believe in my reality, because one doesn’t kick a phantom. Joking aside: it is all the same to me; swear if you like; but still it is better to be a drop more polite, even with me. Otherwise ‘fool’ and ‘lackey’: what words!”
“Abusing you, I abuse myself!” Ivan laughed again. “You are I, I myself, only with a different mug. You say precisely what I already think… and you are unable to tell me anything new!”
“If I coincide with you in my thoughts, that only does me honour,” the gentleman said with delicacy and dignity.
“Only you take all my nasty thoughts, and above all the stupid ones. You are stupid and vulgar. You are terribly stupid. No, I can’t stand you! What am I to do, what am I to do!” Ivan ground out.

“My friend, all the same I want to be a gentleman and to be received as one,” the visitor began, in a fit of a certain purely hanger-on’s ambition, already yielding and good-natured in advance. “I am poor, but… I won’t say very honest, but… in society it is usually accepted as an axiom that I am a fallen angel. Upon my word, I can’t imagine how I could ever have been an angel. If I ever was, it was so long ago that it is no sin to have forgotten it. Now I value only my reputation as a decent man, and live as best I can, trying to be agreeable. I love people sincerely; oh, I have been much slandered! Here, when I move in with you from time to time, my life goes on like something real, and that is what I like most of all. For I too, like you, suffer from the fantastic, and that is why I love your earthly realism. Here with you everything is outlined; here there is formula, here there is geometry; while with us it is all some sort of indeterminate equations! I walk about here and dream. I love to dream. Besides, on earth I become superstitious; don’t laugh, please: that is just what I like, that I become superstitious. Here I take on all your habits: I have grown fond of going to the public baths, can you imagine that? And I love to steam myself with merchants and priests. My dream is to become incarnate, but once for all, irrevocably, in some fat merchant’s wife weighing two hundred and fifty pounds, and to believe everything she believes. My ideal is to go into a church and light a candle from a pure heart, upon my word. Then there would be an end to my sufferings. I have grown fond of being treated by your doctors too: in the spring there was smallpox about, and I went and was vaccinated at the foundling hospital; if you knew how pleased I was that day: I gave ten roubles for our Slav brothers!… But you aren’t listening. You know, you are very much out of sorts today,” the gentleman paused a little. “I know you went to that doctor yesterday… well, how is your health? What did the doctor tell you?”
“Fool!” Ivan snapped.
“How clever you are, though. Swearing again? I don’t ask out of sympathy, just like that. Don’t answer if you like. Now the rheumatism has started again…”
“Fool,” Ivan repeated again.
“You keep on with your own; but last year I caught such a rheumatism that I still remember it.”
“The devil has rheumatism?”
“Why not, if I become incarnate sometimes? If I become incarnate, I accept the consequences. Satan sum et nihil humanum a me alienum puto (I am Satan, and I count nothing human foreign to me).”
“What, what? Satan sum et nihil humanum… That isn’t stupid, for a devil!”
“Glad to have pleased you at last.”
“But you didn’t get that from me,” Ivan suddenly stopped, as if struck. “That never entered my head; that is strange…”

“C’est du nouveau, n’est-ce pas? (That is something new, isn’t it?) This time I shall act honestly and explain it to you. Listen: in dreams, and especially in nightmares, well, from indigestion or something, a man sometimes sees such artistic dreams, such a complex and real reality, such events, or even a whole world of events, woven together with such a plot, with such unexpected details, from your highest manifestations to the last button on a shirt front, that, I swear to you, Lev Tolstoy could not invent it; and yet such dreams are sometimes seen not by writers at all, but by the most ordinary people, officials, journalists, priests… There is even a whole problem about it: one minister even confessed to me himself that all his best ideas come to him when he is asleep. Well, so it is now. Though I am your hallucination, yet, as in a nightmare, I say original things that have never entered your head till now, so that I am not repeating your thoughts at all; and yet I am only your nightmare and nothing more.”
“You lie. Your aim is precisely to convince me that you exist in yourself and are not my nightmare, and now you yourself confirm that you are a dream.”
“My friend, today I have adopted a special method; I’ll explain it to you later. Wait, where did I stop? Yes, I caught cold then, only not here with you, but still over there…”

“Where over there? Tell me, will you be staying with me long; can’t you go away?” Ivan exclaimed almost in despair. He stopped walking, sat down on the sofa, again leaned his elbows on the table and squeezed his head in both hands. He tore the wet towel off and threw it aside in vexation: evidently it did not help.

“Your nerves are out of order,” the gentleman observed with a free-and-easy, careless, but perfectly friendly air. “You are angry with me even for being able to catch cold, and yet it happened in the most natural way. I was hurrying then to a diplomatic evening at the house of a lady of high Petersburg society who was aiming at ministers. Well, evening dress, white tie, gloves; and yet I was still God knows where, and to reach you on earth I still had to fly through space… of course it is only an instant, but then a ray of light from the sun takes a full eight minutes; and imagine, in evening dress and an open waistcoat. Spirits don’t freeze, but once I had become incarnate… in a word, I was reckless and set off; and in those spaces, you know, in the ether, in ‘the waters which were above the firmament’, why, it is such frost… I mean, what frost? It can’t even be called frost; can you imagine: a hundred and fifty degrees below zero! You know the village girls’ game: in thirty degrees of frost they invite a newcomer to lick an axe; his tongue freezes to it instantly, and the dolt tears the skin off it till it bleeds. And that is only at thirty degrees; but at a hundred and fifty, I think if you merely put your finger to the axe, there would be no finger left, if only… if only there could be an axe there…”

“And can there be an axe there?” Ivan Fyodorovich suddenly interrupted, absently and with disgust. He was resisting with all his might, so as not to believe in his delirium and fall finally into madness.
“An axe?” the visitor asked in surprise.
“Well, yes, what would become of an axe there?” Ivan Fyodorovich suddenly cried with a sort of savage and insistent obstinacy.

“What would become of an axe in space? Quelle idée! (What an idea!) If it landed far enough out, it would begin, I think, to fly round the earth, without knowing why itself, as a satellite. The astronomers would calculate the rising and setting of the axe, Gatsuk would put it in his almanac, and that’s all.”

“You are stupid, terribly stupid!” Ivan said perversely. “Lie more cleverly, or I won’t listen. You want to overcome me with realism, to convince me that you exist; but I don’t want to believe that you exist! I won’t believe it!!”

“But I am not lying; it is all true; unfortunately the truth is almost always unwitty. I see you are decidedly expecting something great of me, and perhaps something beautiful. That is a great pity, for I give only what I can.”
“Don’t philosophise, you ass!”

“What philosophy is there, when my whole right side is paralysed and I groan and moan? I have been to all the doctors: they diagnose splendidly; they will tell you the whole illness on their fingers; but cure it they can’t. There was an enthusiastic little student here: ‘If you do die,’ he says, ‘at least you will know perfectly what illness you died of!’ And again this way of theirs of sending you to specialists: we only diagnose, they say, but go to such and such a specialist, and he will cure you. The old doctor who treated all diseases has quite, quite disappeared, I tell you; now there are only specialists, and they all advertise in the newspapers. If your nose aches, they send you to Paris: there, they say, is a European specialist who treats noses. You go to Paris; he examines your nose: ‘I can only cure your right nostril,’ he says, ‘for I don’t treat left nostrils; that is not my speciality; but after me go to Vienna; there a special specialist will finish curing your left nostril.’ What is one to do? I resorted to folk remedies; a German doctor advised me to rub myself with honey and salt on the top shelf at the baths. I went, solely so as to go to the baths once more: I got myself all smeared, and no good at all. In despair I wrote to Count Mattei in Milan; he sent a book and some drops, God bless him. And imagine: Hoff’s malt extract helped! I bought it by chance, drank a bottle and a half, and I could have danced; it all went as if by magic. I resolved without fail to print a ‘thank you’ to him in the newspapers; my feeling of gratitude spoke up; and imagine, then another story began: not one editorial office would take it! ‘It will be very retrograde,’ they say; ‘no one will believe it; le diable n’existe point (the devil does not exist any more). Publish it anonymously,’ they advise. Well, what sort of ‘thank you’ is it, if it is anonymous? I laugh with the clerks: ‘It is believing in God that is retrograde in our age,’ I say, ‘but I am the devil; one may believe in me.’ ‘We understand,’ they say; ‘who doesn’t believe in the devil? But still it can’t be done; it might harm our tendency. Perhaps as a joke?’ Well, as a joke, I thought, it would be unwitty. So they didn’t print it. And would you believe it, it has even stayed on my heart. My very best feelings, gratitude for instance, are formally forbidden me solely by my social position.”
“Into philosophy again!” Ivan ground out with hatred.

“God preserve me; but one can’t help complaining sometimes. I am a slandered man. Here you keep telling me every minute that I am stupid. That is just like a young man. My friend, intelligence isn’t everything! I have by nature a kind and merry heart; ‘I too write little vaudevilles, you know.’ You seem decidedly to take me for a grey-haired Khlestakov, and yet my fate is much more serious. By some pre-temporal decree, which I have never been able to make out, I have been appointed ‘to deny’, and yet I am sincerely kind and quite incapable of denying. No, go and deny; without denial, they say, there will be no criticism; and what sort of journal is it without a ‘critical department’? Without criticism there would be nothing but ‘hosanna’. But ‘hosanna’ alone is not enough for life; this ‘hosanna’ must pass through the crucible of doubt, and so on, in that vein. I don’t meddle in all that, though; I didn’t create it, and I am not answerable for it. Well, they chose a scapegoat; they made me write in the critical department, and life resulted. We understand this comedy: I, for instance, simply and plainly demand to be annihilated. No, live, they say, because without you there will be nothing. If everything on earth were sensible, nothing would happen. Without you there will be no events, and there must be events. So I serve against my will, so that there may be events, and I do the unreasonable by order. People take this whole comedy for something serious, even with all their undoubted intelligence. That is their tragedy. Well, and they suffer, of course, but… still, they live; they live really, not fantastically; for suffering is life. Without suffering what pleasure would there be in it? Everything would turn into one endless prayer service: it is holy, but a little dull. And I? I suffer, and still I don’t live. I am the x in an indeterminate equation. I am some sort of phantom of life who has lost all ends and beginnings, and has even forgotten at last what to call himself. You laugh… no, you are not laughing; you are angry again. You are for ever angry; all you want is intelligence; but I repeat to you again that I would give all this super-stellar life, all ranks and honours, just to become incarnate in the soul of a two-hundred-and-fifty-pound merchant’s wife and light candles to God.”
“So even you don’t believe in God?” Ivan smiled with hatred.
“How shall I put it to you, if you are serious…”
“Is there a God or not?” Ivan cried again with savage insistence.
“Ah, so you are serious? My dear fellow, upon my word, I don’t know. There, I have said a great word.”
“You don’t know, and yet you see God? No, you are not by yourself; you are I; you are I and nothing more! You are rubbish; you are my fancy!”

“That is, if you like, I share your philosophy; that would be fair. Je pense, donc je suis (I think, therefore I am); that I know for certain; but all the rest around me, all these worlds, God and even Satan himself, all that is not proved for me: whether it exists in itself or is only my emanation, a consistent development of my self, which exists pre-temporally and uniquely… in a word, I break off quickly, because I think you are about to jump up and fight.”
“You had better tell me some anecdote!” Ivan said painfully.

“There is an anecdote, and precisely on our subject; that is, not an anecdote, just a legend. You reproach me with unbelief: ‘you see, and yet you don’t believe’. But, my friend, I am not the only one like that; everyone over there has gone muddled now, and all because of your sciences. While there were still atoms, the five senses, the four elements, well, then everything held together somehow. There were atoms in the ancient world too. But as soon as we learned over there that you had discovered the ‘chemical molecule’ and ‘protoplasm’ and the devil knows what else, we simply put our tails between our legs. A regular hubbub began; above all superstition, gossip; for there is as much gossip with us as with you, even a little more; and finally informing too; for we too have a certain department where certain ‘information’ is received. So, this wild legend, from our Middle Ages, not yours but ours, and no one believes it even among us, except two-hundred-and-fifty-pound merchants’ wives, again not yours but ours. Everything you have, we have too; I am telling you one of our secrets out of friendship, though it is forbidden. The legend is about paradise. There was, they say, a certain thinker and philosopher here on your earth, who ‘rejected everything, laws, conscience, faith’, and above all the future life. He died, thinking he would go straight into darkness and death, and there before him was the future life. He was amazed and indignant: ‘This,’ he said, ‘goes against my convictions.’ And for that he was sentenced… that is, you see, excuse me, I am only passing on what I heard; it is only a legend… he was sentenced, you see, to walk a quadrillion kilometres in darkness (we have gone over to kilometres now, you know), and when he finishes that quadrillion, the gates of paradise will be opened to him and everything forgiven…”
“And what torments have you in the other world, besides the quadrillion?” Ivan interrupted with a strange animation.

“What torments? Ah, don’t ask: before, there was this and that, but nowadays they are mostly moral ones, ‘pangs of conscience’ and all that nonsense. That too came from you, from ‘the softening of your manners’. And who has gained by it? Only the unscrupulous, for what are pangs of conscience to a man who has no conscience at all? Instead, decent people have suffered, who still had some conscience and honour left… There you are: reforms on unprepared soil, and copied from foreign institutions too: nothing but harm! The old fire was better. Well, this man sentenced to the quadrillion stood, looked, and lay down across the road: ‘I don’t want to go; on principle I won’t go!’ Take the soul of a Russian enlightened atheist and mix it with the soul of the prophet Jonah, who sulked in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, and there you have the character of this thinker who lay down on the road.”
“And what did he lie down on there?”
“Well, there must have been something there. You aren’t laughing?”
“Good man!” cried Ivan, still with the same strange animation. He was now listening with a sort of unexpected curiosity. “Well, and is he lying there still?”
“That’s just it: no. He lay there for almost a thousand years, and then got up and went.”

“What an ass!” exclaimed Ivan, laughing nervously, and still as if intently thinking something out. “Isn’t it all the same whether he lies there for ever or walks a quadrillion versts? Why, that is a billion years’ walk, isn’t it?”
“Much more even; only I haven’t a pencil and paper, or one could work it out. But he got there long ago, and that is where the anecdote begins.”
“What, he got there! But where did he get a billion years from?”

“Why, you keep thinking of our present earth! But the present earth may itself have repeated itself a billion times; well, it lived out its time, froze, cracked, crumbled, broke down into its constituent elements; again ‘the waters which were above the firmament’, then a comet again, a sun again, from the sun the earth again; why, this development may have repeated itself an infinite number of times already, and always in exactly the same form, down to the last detail. A most indecent bore…”
“Well, well, what happened when he got there?”

“Why, as soon as they opened paradise to him and he went in, before he had been there two seconds, and that by the watch, by the watch (though his watch, in my opinion, must long since have broken down into its constituent elements in his pocket on the way), before he had been there two seconds he exclaimed that for those two seconds it was worth walking not only a quadrillion, but a quadrillion of quadrillions, and raised to the quadrillionth power! In a word, he sang ‘hosanna’, and overdid it, so that some there, with a nobler cast of mind, at first even refused to shake hands with him: he had jumped over to the conservatives too precipitately, they said. The Russian nature. I repeat: it is a legend. I sell it as I bought it. That is the kind of ideas that are going about among us there about all these subjects.”

“I have caught you!” Ivan cried with an almost childish joy, as if he had finally remembered something. “That anecdote about the quadrillion years, I made it up myself! I was seventeen then, I was at the high school… I made up that anecdote then and told it to a schoolfellow; his name was Korovkin; it was in Moscow… The anecdote is so characteristic that I couldn’t have got it from anywhere. I had forgotten it… but it has come back to me now unconsciously, to me myself; you didn’t tell it! As thousands of things sometimes come back unconsciously, even when one is being taken to execution… it came back to me in a dream. You are that dream! You are a dream and you don’t exist!”
“From the passion with which you reject me,” the gentleman laughed, “I am convinced that you believe in me all the same.”
“Not in the least! I don’t believe in you one hundredth part!”
“But a thousandth part you do. Homoeopathic doses are perhaps the strongest. Admit that you believe, well, to the ten-thousandth part…”
“Not for one minute!” Ivan cried furiously. “Though I should like to believe in you!” he strangely added suddenly.

“Aha! There’s an admission, though! But I am kind; I will help you here too. Listen: it is I who have caught you, not you me! I told you your own anecdote, which you had forgotten, on purpose, so that you would lose your belief in me completely.”
“You lie! The aim of your appearing is to convince me that you exist.”

“Precisely. But hesitation, but uneasiness, but the struggle between belief and unbelief: that is sometimes such torment for a conscientious man like you that it is better to hang oneself. Knowing that you believe in me a tiny bit, I deliberately let in some unbelief once for all by telling you that anecdote. I lead you alternately between belief and unbelief, and I have my own aim in it. A new method, sir: for when you have lost your belief in me completely, you will at once begin assuring me to my face that I am not a dream but really exist; I know you already; and then I shall have achieved my aim. And my aim is a noble one. I shall throw only a tiny seed of faith into you, and from it an oak will grow, and such an oak that you, sitting in the oak, will want to join ‘the desert fathers and the holy women’; for secretly you want that very, very much; you will eat locusts; you will drag yourself off to the wilderness to save your soul!”
“So you, you scoundrel, are working for the salvation of my soul?”
“One must do a good deed sometime. How angry you are, though, I see!”
“Buffoon! And did you ever tempt such ones as that, who eat locusts and pray for seventeen years in the bare wilderness till they are overgrown with moss?”

“My dear fellow, that is all I have ever done. You forget the whole world and worlds, and fasten on to one such, because the diamond is so very precious; one such soul is sometimes worth a whole constellation; we have our own arithmetic. The victory is precious! And some of them, upon my word, are not beneath you in development, though you won’t believe it: they can contemplate such abysses of belief and unbelief at one and the same moment that sometimes, truly, it seems that only one more hair, and the man will go flying ‘head over heels’, as the actor Gorbunov says.”
“Well, and did you go away with a long nose?”

“My friend,” the visitor remarked sententiously, “it is better, after all, to go away with a long nose than sometimes with no nose at all, as an ailing marquis (a specialist must have treated him) said not long ago at confession to his spiritual father, a Jesuit. I was present; simply charming. ‘Give me back my nose!’ he says, and beats his breast. ‘My son,’ the father wriggles, ‘by the inscrutable decrees of providence everything is made good, and a visible misfortune sometimes brings with it an extraordinary, though invisible, advantage. If stern fate has deprived you of your nose, your advantage is that now no one in all your life will dare to say that you were left with a long nose.’ ‘Holy father, that is no consolation!’ cries the desperate man. ‘On the contrary, I would be delighted all my life to be left with a long nose every day, if only it were in its proper place!’ ‘My son,’ sighs the father, ‘one cannot demand all blessings at once, and this is already murmuring against providence, which even here has not forgotten you; for if you cry out, as you cried out just now, that you would gladly be left with a long nose all your life, then even here your wish has already been fulfilled indirectly; for, having lost your nose, you have by that very thing, as it were, been left with a long nose…’”
“Ugh, how stupid!” cried Ivan.

“My friend, I only wanted to make you laugh; but I swear it is real Jesuit casuistry, and I swear it all happened word for word as I have told you. It was a recent case and caused me a lot of trouble. The unhappy young man went home and shot himself that same night; I was with him constantly to the last moment… As for those little Jesuit confession boxes, they are truly my sweetest diversion in the sad moments of life. Here is another case for you, only the other day. A little blonde comes to an old priest, a Norman girl of about twenty. Beauty, figure, nature: it makes your mouth water. She bends down and whispers her sin to the priest through the little hole. ‘What, my daughter, have you fallen again already?’ exclaims the priest. ‘O Sancta Maria (O holy Mary), what do I hear: and not with the same one this time. But how long is this to go on, and how is it you are not ashamed!’ ‘Ah, mon père (ah, my father),’ answers the sinner, all in penitent tears, ‘ça lui fait tant de plaisir, et à moi si peu de peine!’ (‘it gives him so much pleasure, and me so little trouble!’) Well, imagine such an answer! Even I drew back at that: it is the cry of nature itself; it is, if you like, better than innocence itself! I absolved her sin on the spot and turned to go, but I was at once forced to come back: I hear the priest through the little hole making an appointment with her for the evening; and the old man was flint, and he fell in an instant! Nature, the truth of nature, had its way! What, turning up your nose again, angry again? I really don’t know how to please you…”

“Leave me alone; you are knocking in my brain like an inescapable nightmare,” Ivan moaned painfully, powerless before his vision. “I am bored with you, unbearably and tormentingly! I would give a great deal to be able to drive you away!”

“I repeat, moderate your demands; don’t demand ‘everything great and beautiful’ of me, and you will see how amicably we shall get on together,” the gentleman said impressively. “Truly, you are angry with me because I didn’t appear to you in some red glow, ‘thundering and flashing’, with scorched wings, but have presented myself in such a modest form. You are offended, in the first place, in your aesthetic feelings, and in the second, in your pride: how, you think, could such a vulgar devil come to such a great man? No, there is that romantic streak in you, which Belinsky laughed at so long ago. What’s to be done, young man? I thought this evening, as I was getting ready to come to you, of appearing for a joke as a retired actual state councillor who had served in the Caucasus, with the star of the Lion and the Sun on my coat; but I was decidedly afraid, for you would have beaten me just for daring to pin the Lion and the Sun on my coat, and not at least the Pole Star or Sirius. And you keep on that I am stupid. But my God, I have no pretensions to compare with you in intelligence. Mephistopheles, appearing to Faust, testified of himself that he wills evil and does only good. Well, that is as he pleases; I am quite the opposite. I am perhaps the only being in all nature who loves the truth and sincerely desires good. I was there when the Word, who died on the cross, was ascending into heaven, carrying on his bosom the soul of the thief crucified on his right hand; I heard the joyful shrieks of the cherubim singing and crying ‘Hosanna’, and the thunderous cry of rapture of the seraphim, which shook heaven and all creation. And, I swear by all that is holy, I wanted to join the choir and cry with them all: ‘Hosanna!’ It was already escaping, already bursting from my breast… for, you know, I am very sensitive and artistically impressionable. But common sense, oh, the unhappiest trait of my nature, kept me within due bounds even then, and I let the moment pass! For what, I thought at that same moment, what would have come of it after my ‘hosanna’? Everything in the world would have gone out at once, and no events would have happened any more. And so, solely from a sense of duty and because of my social position, I was forced to stifle the good moment in myself and remain with the dirty tricks. Someone takes all the honour of goodness for himself, and only dirty tricks are left as my portion. But I don’t envy the honour of living by sponging; I am not ambitious. Why, of all creatures in the world, am I alone condemned to be cursed by all decent people, and even to be kicked with boots, for, becoming incarnate, I must sometimes accept even such consequences? I know there is a secret in it, but they won’t reveal the secret to me for anything, because then, perhaps, guessing what is what, I would bellow ‘hosanna’, and at once the indispensable minus would vanish, and good sense would begin all over the world, and with it, of course, the end of everything, even of newspapers and journals, for who would subscribe to them then? I know that in the end I shall be reconciled; I too shall walk my quadrillion and learn the secret. But until that happens, I sulk, and against my will I fulfil my destiny: to ruin thousands so that one may be saved. How many souls, for instance, had to be ruined and how many honest reputations disgraced to get just one righteous Job, over whom they caught me out so spitefully in days of old! No, until the secret is revealed, there are two truths for me: one over there, theirs, quite unknown to me as yet, and the other mine. And it is not yet known which will turn out the cleaner… Have you fallen asleep?”

“I should think so,” Ivan moaned spitefully. “Everything that is stupid in my nature, long since lived through, ground over in my mind, thrown away like carrion, you bring me as if it were some novelty!”

“Missed again! And I thought I would even charm you with my literary style: that ‘hosanna’ in heaven, really, I did it rather well, didn’t I? And then this sarcastic tone just now, à la Heine, eh, isn’t that so?”
“No, I was never such a lackey! How could my soul have given birth to such a lackey as you?”

“My friend, I know a most charming and most delightful young Russian gentleman: a young thinker and a great lover of literature and elegant things, author of a poem of great promise entitled ‘The Grand Inquisitor’… It was only him I had in mind!”
“I forbid you to speak of ‘The Grand Inquisitor’,” Ivan exclaimed, crimson all over with shame.
“Well, and ‘The Geological Upheaval’? Do you remember? Now that was a little poem!”
“Be quiet, or I’ll kill you!”

“Kill me, you mean? No, excuse me, I’ll have my say. That is what I came for, to treat myself to this pleasure. Oh, I love the dreams of my ardent young friends, trembling with thirst for life! ‘There are new people,’ you decided last spring, when you were getting ready to come here; ‘they propose to destroy everything and begin with cannibalism. Fools, they didn’t ask me! In my opinion there is no need to destroy anything; one need only destroy the idea of God in mankind; that is where one must set to work! That, that is where one must begin; oh, blind men, who understand nothing! Once mankind has renounced God, every one of them (and I believe that this period, parallel to the geological periods, will come about), then of itself, without cannibalism, the whole former world view will fall, and above all the whole former morality, and everything new will begin. People will unite to take from life all that it can give, but only for happiness and joy in this world alone. Man will be exalted with a spirit of divine, titanic pride, and the man-god will appear. Conquering nature hourly, now without limits, by his will and by science, man will by that very thing hourly feel so lofty a delight that it will replace for him all his former hopes of heavenly delights. Everyone will know that he is wholly mortal, without resurrection, and will accept death proudly and calmly, like a god. Out of pride he will understand that he has no reason to murmur that life is a moment, and he will love his brother without any reward. Love will satisfy only a moment of life, but the very consciousness of its momentariness will strengthen its fire as much as it was formerly dissipated in hopes of a love beyond the grave and infinite…’ and so on, and so on in the same vein. Most charming!”
Ivan was sitting with his hands pressed over his ears, looking at the ground, but he had begun to tremble all over. The voice went on:

“The question now, my young thinker thought, is this: is it possible that such a period will ever come or not? If it comes, everything is decided, and mankind will be settled once for all. But since, in view of man’s inveterate stupidity, it may not be settled even in a thousand years, everyone who already knows the truth even now is permitted to settle himself entirely as he pleases, on the new principles. In that sense ‘everything is permitted’ to him. More than that: even if this period never comes at all, still, since there is no God and no immortality anyway, the new man is permitted to become a man-god, even if he is the only one in the whole world, and of course, in his new rank, to leap over with a light heart every former moral barrier of the former slave-man, if need be. For God there is no law! Where God stands, there is God’s place! Where I stand, there will at once be the first place… ‘everything is permitted’, and that’s that! All this is very charming; only, if one wants to swindle, why, one would think, the sanction of truth as well? But such is our modern Russian little man: he won’t bring himself to swindle without a sanction, so much has he come to love the truth…”

The visitor was talking, evidently carried away by his own eloquence, raising his voice more and more and looking mockingly at his host; but he did not manage to finish: Ivan suddenly seized a glass from the table and flung it with all his might at the orator.

“Ah, mais c’est bête enfin! (Ah, but this is stupid, really!)” exclaimed the latter, jumping up from the sofa and flicking the drops of tea off himself with his fingers. “He remembered Luther’s inkpot! He thinks me a dream himself, and he throws glasses at a dream! That is like a woman! And I suspected that you were only pretending to stop your ears, and you were listening…”
Suddenly there was a firm and insistent knocking at the window frame from the yard. Ivan Fyodorovich jumped up from the sofa.
“Do you hear? You had better open,” cried the visitor. “It is your brother Alyosha with the most unexpected and curious news, I can answer for it!”
“Be quiet, you deceiver; I knew it was Alyosha before you did; I had a presentiment of him; and of course he has not come for nothing; of course he has ‘news’!…” Ivan exclaimed in a frenzy.

“Open, then, open to him. There is a blizzard outside, and he is your brother. Monsieur, sait-il le temps qu’il fait? C’est à ne pas mettre un chien dehors… (Does monsieur know what weather it is? One wouldn’t put a dog out in it…)”

The knocking went on. Ivan wanted to rush to the window; but something seemed suddenly to bind his legs and arms. He strained with all his might as if to break his bonds, but in vain. The knocking at the window grew more and more and louder. At last the bonds suddenly broke, and Ivan Fyodorovich jumped up on the sofa. He looked round wildly. Both candles had almost burned out; the glass he had just thrown at his visitor stood before him on the table; and on the opposite sofa there was no one. The knocking at the window frame, though it went on insistently, was not nearly so loud as it had seemed to him just now in his dream; on the contrary, it was very restrained.
“It was not a dream! No, I swear it was not a dream; it all happened just now!” cried Ivan Fyodorovich, rushed to the window and opened the small pane.
“Alyosha, I told you not to come!” he shouted savagely to his brother. “In two words: what do you want? In two words, do you hear?”
“An hour ago Smerdyakov hanged himself,” Alyosha answered from the yard.
“Come round to the porch; I’ll open the door to you at once,” said Ivan, and went to let Alyosha in.
## Chapter X · “It Was He Who Said That!”

Coming in, Alyosha told Ivan Fyodorovich that a little over an hour before, Marya Kondratyevna had run to his lodgings and announced that Smerdyakov had taken his own life. “I went in to him to clear away the samovar, and there he was hanging on a little nail by the wall.” To Alyosha’s question, “Have you reported it to the proper person?”, she answered that she had not reported it to anyone, but “rushed straight to you first and ran all the way.” She was like a madwoman, Alyosha said, and trembling all over like a leaf. And when Alyosha had run back with her to their cottage, he found Smerdyakov still hanging. On the table lay a note: “I destroy my life of my own will and desire, so as to blame no one.” Alyosha left the note on the table and went straight to the police captain and reported everything to him, “and from there straight to you,” Alyosha concluded, looking intently into Ivan’s face. And all the time he was telling it, he did not take his eyes off him, as if struck by something in the expression of his face.
“Brother,” he suddenly cried, “you must be terribly ill! You are looking at me and seem not to understand what I am saying.”
“It is good that you have come,” Ivan said as if thoughtfully, and as if he had not heard Alyosha’s exclamation at all. “And I knew he had hanged himself.”
“From whom?”
“I don’t know from whom. But I knew. Did I know? Yes, he told me. He was telling me just now…”
Ivan was standing in the middle of the room and still speaking thoughtfully, looking at the ground.
“Who is he?” asked Alyosha, involuntarily looking round.
“He has slipped away.”
Ivan raised his head and smiled quietly.

“He was afraid of you, of you, a dove. You are a ‘pure cherub’. Dmitri calls you a cherub. Cherub… The thunderous cry of rapture of the seraphim! What is a seraph? Perhaps a whole constellation. And perhaps the whole constellation is only some chemical molecule… There is a constellation of the Lion and the Sun; don’t you know it?”

“Brother, sit down!” said Alyosha in alarm. “Sit down on the sofa, for God’s sake. You are delirious; lie back on the pillow, like that. Would you like a wet towel on your head? Perhaps it will make you better?”
“Give me the towel; it’s here on the chair; I threw it here just now.”

“It isn’t here. Don’t worry, I know where it is; here it is,” said Alyosha, finding in another corner of the room, by Ivan’s dressing table, a clean towel, still folded and unused. Ivan looked strangely at the towel; his memory seemed to come back to him in an instant.
“Wait,” he half rose from the sofa. “Just now, an hour ago, I took this very towel from there and wetted it. I put it on my head and threw it here… How is it dry? There was no other.”
“You put this towel on your head?” asked Alyosha.
“Yes, and walked about the room, an hour ago… Why have the candles burned down so? What time is it?”
“Nearly twelve.”

“No, no, no!” Ivan cried suddenly. “It was not a dream! He was here; he was sitting here, there on that sofa. When you knocked at the window I threw a glass at him… this one… Wait, I was asleep before, but this dream is not a dream. It has happened before. I have dreams now, Alyosha… but they are not dreams; they are real: I walk, talk and see… and I am asleep. But he was sitting here, he was here, on that sofa… He is terribly stupid, Alyosha, terribly stupid,” Ivan suddenly laughed and began pacing the room.
“Who is stupid? Whom are you talking about, brother?” Alyosha asked again in anguish.

“The devil! He has taken to coming to me. He has been here twice, almost three times. He teased me by saying I was angry that he was simply a devil and not Satan with scorched wings, in thunder and lightning. But he is not Satan; he lies about that. He is an impostor. He is simply a devil, a paltry, petty devil. He goes to the baths. Undress him and you will surely find a tail, long, smooth, like a Great Dane’s, a yard long, brown… Alyosha, you are chilled; you have been in the snow; will you have some tea? What? Cold? Shall I have it heated? C’est à ne pas mettre un chien dehors…”
Alyosha ran quickly to the washstand, wetted the towel, persuaded Ivan to sit down again and wrapped the wet towel round his head. He sat down beside him.

“What were you telling me this evening about Lise?” Ivan began again. (He was becoming very talkative.) “I like Lise. I said something nasty to you about her. I lied; I like her… I am afraid for Katya tomorrow; that is what I am most afraid of. For the future. Tomorrow she will throw me over and trample me underfoot. She thinks I am ruining Mitya out of jealousy of her! Yes, she thinks that! Well, I am not! Tomorrow the cross, but not the gallows. No, I won’t hang myself. Do you know that I can never take my own life, Alyosha? From baseness, perhaps? I am not a coward. From thirst for life! How did I know that Smerdyakov had hanged himself? Yes, it was he who told me…”
“And you are firmly convinced that someone was sitting here?” asked Alyosha.

“There on that sofa, in the corner. You would have driven him away. Why, you did drive him away: he vanished as you appeared. I love your face, Alyosha. Did you know that I love your face? And he is I, Alyosha, I myself. All that is low in me, all that is vile and contemptible! Yes, I am a ‘romantic’; he noticed that… though it is a slander. He is terribly stupid, but that is how he gets the better of me. He is cunning, animal cunning; he knew how to infuriate me. He kept teasing me that I believed in him, and so he made me listen to him. He fooled me like a little boy. He told me a great deal of truth about myself, though. I should never have said it to myself. You know, Alyosha, you know,” Ivan added terribly seriously and as if confidentially, “I should very much like him really to be he, and not I!”
“He has tormented you,” said Alyosha, looking at his brother with compassion.

“He teased me! And cleverly, you know, cleverly: ‘Conscience! What is conscience? I make it myself. Why do I torment myself, then? From habit. From the universal human habit of seven thousand years. So let us lose the habit, and we shall be gods.’ It was he who said that, it was he who said that!”

“And not you, not you?” Alyosha cried irresistibly, looking clearly at his brother. “Well, let him be; throw him off and forget him! Let him take with him everything that you curse now, and never come again!”

“Yes, but he is malicious. He laughed at me. He was impudent, Alyosha,” Ivan said, shuddering with offence. “But he slandered me; he slandered me in many things. He lied to me about myself to my face. ‘Oh, you are going to perform a great act of virtue; you will declare that you killed your father, that the lackey killed your father at your instigation…’”
“Brother,” Alyosha interrupted, “restrain yourself: it was not you who killed him. That is not true!”

“That is what he says, he, and he knows it: ‘You are going to perform a great act of virtue, and you don’t believe in virtue; that is what angers and torments you; that is why you are so vindictive.’ That is what he told me about myself, and he knows what he is saying…”
“It is you who are saying it, not he!” Alyosha exclaimed sorrowfully. “And you are saying it in illness, in delirium, tormenting yourself!”

“No, he knows what he is saying. ‘You are going out of pride,’ he says; ‘you will stand up and say: “It was I who killed him; why are you writhing with horror? You are lying! I despise your opinion; I despise your horror.”’ That is what he says about me, and suddenly he says: ‘And you know, you want them to praise you: a criminal, a murderer, but what magnanimous feelings he has; he wanted to save his brother, and confessed!’ Now that is a lie, Alyosha!” Ivan suddenly cried, his eyes flashing. “I don’t want the rabble to praise me! He lied, Alyosha, he lied, I swear to you! I threw the glass at him for that, and it smashed against his ugly face.”
“Brother, calm yourself; stop!” Alyosha begged.

“No, he knows how to torment; he is cruel,” Ivan went on, not listening. “I always had a presentiment of why he comes. ‘Granted,’ he says, ‘that you were going out of pride; still there was a hope too that they would convict Smerdyakov and send him to penal servitude, that Mitya would be acquitted, and you would be condemned only morally’ (do you hear, he laughed at that!) ‘and others would even praise you. But now Smerdyakov is dead; he has hanged himself; and who will believe you alone at the trial now? And yet you are going, you are going; you will go all the same; you have decided to go. Why are you going, after this?’ It is terrible, Alyosha; I can’t bear such questions. Who dares to ask me such questions?”

“Brother,” Alyosha interrupted, sinking with fear, but still as if hoping to bring Ivan to reason, “how could he have spoken to you of Smerdyakov’s death before I came, when no one yet knew of it, and there was no time for anyone to find out?”

“He did speak of it,” Ivan said firmly, not admitting any doubt. “It was all he spoke about, if you like. ‘And it would be all very well,’ he says, ‘if you believed in virtue: let them not believe me; I go for the principle of it. But you are a little pig, like Fyodor Pavlovich, and what is virtue to you? Why will you drag yourself there, if your sacrifice will serve no purpose? Because you don’t know yourself why you are going! Oh, you would give a great deal to know yourself why you are going! And have you really decided? You have not decided yet. You will sit up all night deciding whether to go or not. But you will go all the same, and you know you will go; you know yourself that however you decide, the decision no longer depends on you. You will go because you dare not not go. Why you dare not, guess that yourself; there’s a riddle for you!’ He got up and went. You came, and he went. He called me a coward, Alyosha! Le mot de l’énigme (the answer to the riddle) is that I am a coward! ‘It is not for such eagles to soar above the earth!’ He added that, he added that! And Smerdyakov said the same. He must be killed! Katya despises me; I have seen it for a month; and Lise will begin to despise me too! ‘You are going so that they will praise you’: that is a bestial lie! And you despise me too, Alyosha. Now I shall hate you again. And I hate the monster, I hate the monster! I don’t want to save the monster; let him rot in penal servitude! He has started singing a hymn! Oh, tomorrow I shall go, stand before them and spit in all their faces!”

He jumped up in a frenzy, threw off the towel and began pacing the room again. Alyosha remembered his words of a little while ago: “It is as though I were asleep awake… I walk, talk and see, and I am asleep.” It was exactly as if that were happening now. Alyosha did not leave him. The thought flashed through his mind of running for a doctor and bringing him, but he was afraid to leave his brother alone: there was absolutely no one to leave him with. At last Ivan little by little began to lose consciousness entirely. He kept on talking, talking without stopping, but quite incoherently now. He even pronounced his words badly, and suddenly he swayed heavily where he stood. But Alyosha managed to hold him up. Ivan let himself be led to the bed; Alyosha undressed him somehow and put him to bed. He sat over him for another two hours. The sick man slept soundly, without moving, breathing quietly and evenly. Alyosha took a pillow and lay down on the sofa without undressing. As he fell asleep he prayed for Mitya and for Ivan. Ivan’s illness was becoming clear to him: “The torments of a proud decision, a deep conscience!” God, in whom he did not believe, and his truth were overcoming a heart that still did not want to submit. “Yes,” ran through Alyosha’s head as it lay on the pillow, “yes, now that Smerdyakov is dead, no one will believe Ivan’s evidence; but he will go and give it!” Alyosha smiled quietly. “God will conquer!” he thought. “Either he will rise up in the light of truth, or… he will perish in hatred, taking revenge on himself and on everyone for having served what he does not believe in,” Alyosha added bitterly, and prayed for Ivan again.
## Book Twelve, Chapter XIV · The Peasants Stood Their Ground

So Fetyukovich ended, and the rapture of his listeners that broke out this time was irresistible as a storm. It was unthinkable now to restrain it: the women wept; many of the men wept too; even two dignitaries shed tears. The presiding judge gave way and even delayed ringing his bell: “To attack such enthusiasm would have been to attack something sacred,” as our ladies cried afterwards. The orator himself was sincerely moved. And at just such a moment our Ippolit Kirillovich rose once more “to exchange rejoinders”. He was looked at with hatred: “What? What is this? Does he dare to object still?” the ladies began to babble. But even if the ladies of the whole world had babbled, with the prosecutor’s wife herself, Ippolit Kirillovich’s spouse, at their head, it would have been impossible to restrain him at that moment. He was pale; he was shaking with agitation; his first words, his first sentences, were even unintelligible; he was gasping, articulating badly, losing the thread. He soon recovered, however. But of this second speech of his I will quote only a few sentences.

“…We are reproached with having made up novels. But what has the defence given us but novel upon novel? Only the verses were missing. Fyodor Pavlovich, waiting for his mistress, tears open the envelope and throws it on the floor. We are even told what he said on this remarkable occasion. Is that not a poem? And where is the proof that he took out the money; who heard what he said? The feeble-minded idiot Smerdyakov, transformed into some Byronic hero avenging himself on society for his illegitimacy: is that not a poem in the Byronic taste? And the son who broke into his father’s house and killed him, and at the same time did not kill him: that is not even a novel or a poem any more; it is a sphinx setting riddles which it certainly cannot solve itself. If he killed him, he killed him; but how can it be that, having killed him, he did not kill him? Who can understand that? Then we are told that our tribune is a tribune of truth and sound ideas, and from this tribune of ‘sound ideas’ there rings out, with an oath, the axiom that to call the murder of a father parricide is only a prejudice! But if parricide is a prejudice, and if every child is to question his father, ‘Father, why must I love you?’, what will become of us, what will become of the foundations of society, where will the family go? Parricide, you see, is only the ‘bogey’ of a Moscow merchant’s wife. The most precious, the most sacred precepts of the purpose and future of the Russian court are presented perversely and frivolously, merely to gain an end, to gain the acquittal of what cannot be justified. ‘Oh, crush him with mercy,’ cries the defence; and that is all the criminal wants, and tomorrow everyone will see how crushed he is! And is not the defence too modest, in asking only for the acquittal of the accused? Why not demand the founding of a scholarship in the parricide’s name, to immortalise his exploit for posterity and the younger generation? The Gospel and religion are corrected: that, they say, is all mysticism, but ours is the only true Christianity, already tested by the analysis of reason and sound ideas. And so a false likeness of Christ is set up before us! ‘With what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again,’ cries the defence, and in the same breath concludes that Christ commanded us to measure with the measure that is measured to us, and this from the tribune of truth and sound ideas! We glance into the Gospel only on the eve of our speeches, so as to show off our acquaintance with what is, after all, a rather original composition, which may come in handy and serve for a certain effect, as need requires, all as need requires! But Christ bids us precisely not to do so, to beware of doing so, because the wicked world does so; whereas we must forgive and turn the other cheek, and not measure out with the same measure with which our offenders measure to us. That is what our God taught us, and not that to forbid children to kill their fathers is a prejudice. And we will not correct from the chair of truth and sound ideas the Gospel of our God, whom the defence deigns to call only ‘the crucified lover of mankind’, in opposition to all Orthodox Russia, which cries out to him: ‘For thou art our God!…’”

At this point the presiding judge intervened and checked the speaker, who had got carried away, asking him not to exaggerate, to keep within proper bounds, and so on, and so on, as presiding judges usually say on such occasions. And the hall was restless too. The public stirred, even exclaimed in indignation. Fetyukovich did not even reply; he only mounted the platform to say, with his hand on his heart and in an injured voice, a few words full of dignity. He only touched again, lightly and mockingly, on “novels” and “psychology”, and in one place slipped in apropos: “Jupiter, you are angry; therefore you are wrong,” which provoked a numerous approving titter among the public, for Ippolit Kirillovich was not at all like Jupiter. Then, to the charge that he was supposedly allowing the younger generation to kill their fathers, Fetyukovich remarked with profound dignity that he would not even reply. As for “the false likeness of Christ”, and his not having deigned to call Christ God but only “the crucified lover of mankind”, which “is contrary to Orthodoxy and could not have been said from the tribune of truth and sound ideas”, Fetyukovich hinted at “insinuation”, and at the fact that in coming here he had at least counted on this tribune being secure from accusations “dangerous to my person as a citizen and a loyal subject…” But at these words the presiding judge checked him too, and Fetyukovich, bowing, concluded his reply, accompanied by a general approving murmur in the hall. And Ippolit Kirillovich, in the opinion of our ladies, was “crushed for ever”.

Then the accused himself was allowed to speak. Mitya stood up, but said little. He was terribly exhausted both in body and in spirit. The look of independence and strength with which he had appeared in the hall in the morning had almost disappeared. It was as if he had lived through something that day for his whole life, which had taught him and made him understand something very important that he had not understood before. His voice had grown weak; he no longer shouted as he had earlier. In his words there could be heard something new, humbled, defeated and bowed.

“What shall I say, gentlemen of the jury! My judgement has come; I feel the right hand of God upon me. The end of a dissolute man! But as I confess to God, I say to you too: ‘Of my father’s blood, no, I am not guilty!’ For the last time I repeat: ‘It was not I who killed him.’ I was dissolute, but I loved what is good. Every moment I strove to reform, and I lived like a wild beast. Thanks to the prosecutor: he told me much about myself that I did not know; but it is not true that I killed my father; the prosecutor is mistaken! Thanks to the defence too: I wept listening to him; but it is not true that I killed my father, and there was no need even to suppose it! And don’t believe the doctors: I am in my perfect mind; only my soul is heavy. If you spare me, if you let me go, I will pray for you. I will become better; I give my word, I give it before God. And if you condemn me, I will break the sword over my head myself, and having broken it, I will kiss the pieces! But spare me; do not take my God from me; I know myself: I shall murmur! My soul is heavy, gentlemen… spare me!”

He almost fell back into his seat; his voice broke; he could hardly get out the last phrase. Then the court proceeded to put the questions and began asking the parties for their conclusions. But I do not describe the details. At last the jury rose to withdraw for their deliberations. The presiding judge was very tired, and so he gave them a very weak parting word: “Be impartial; do not be influenced by the eloquent words of the defence; but still, weigh everything; remember that a great responsibility lies upon you,” and so on, and so on. The jury withdrew, and the session was adjourned. One could get up, walk about, exchange accumulated impressions, have a snack at the buffet. It was very late, already about one in the morning, but no one went home. Everyone was so tense and wrought up that there was no question of rest. Everyone was waiting with a sinking heart; though, it is true, not everyone’s heart was sinking. The ladies were only in hysterical impatience, but their hearts were calm: “An acquittal is inevitable.” They were all preparing for the effective moment of general enthusiasm. I confess that in the men’s half of the hall too there were a great many convinced of an inevitable acquittal. Some were glad, others frowned, and some simply hung their heads: they did not want an acquittal! Fetyukovich himself was firmly convinced of success. He was surrounded, received congratulations, was fawned upon.

“There are,” he said in one group, as was reported afterwards, “there are these invisible threads binding the defence to the jury. They are tied and felt already during the speech. I felt them; they exist. Our case is won; rest assured.”
“And what will our peasants say now, I wonder?” said a frowning, stout, pockmarked gentleman, a landowner from near the town, coming up to one group of gentlemen who were talking.
“But there aren’t only peasants. There are four officials.”
“Yes, the officials,” said a member of the district council, coming up.
“And do you know Nazaryev, Prokhor Ivanovich, that merchant with the medal, the juryman?”
“What of him?”
“A man of brains.”
“But he never says anything.”
“He doesn’t, and so much the better. It’s not for a Petersburg man to teach him; he could teach the whole of Petersburg himself. Twelve children, think of it!”
“But really, can they possibly not acquit him?” one of our young officials was crying in another group.
“They’ll acquit him for certain,” said a decided voice.

“It would be shameful, disgraceful not to acquit him!” the official exclaimed. “Suppose he did kill him; but there are fathers and fathers! And then, he was in such a frenzy… He really may only have swung the pestle, and the old man fell down. The only bad thing is that they dragged the lackey in. That’s simply a ridiculous episode. In the defence’s place I would have said straight out: he killed him, but he is not guilty, and the devil take you!”
“That is just what he did, only he didn’t say ‘the devil take you’.”
“No, Mikhail Semyonych, he almost did say it,” a third little voice put in.
“But, gentlemen, they acquitted an actress here in Lent who cut the throat of her lover’s lawful wife.”
“But she didn’t finish cutting it.”
“No matter, no matter, she began cutting it!”
“And what about the children, what he said about them? Magnificent!”
“Magnificent.”
“Well, and about mysticism, about mysticism, eh?”
“Oh, stop about mysticism,” someone else cried. “Think of Ippolit instead, of his fate from this day on! His prosecutor’s wife will scratch his eyes out tomorrow over Mitenka.”
“Is she here?”
“Here? If she were here, she’d have scratched them out here. She is sitting at home with toothache. He-he-he!”
“He-he-he!”
In a third group:
“And yet perhaps Mitenka will be acquitted.”
“Like as not, tomorrow he’ll smash up the whole Metropolis tavern and be drunk for ten days.”
“Oh, the devil!”
“The devil, yes, the devil; the devil was bound to be in it; where else should he be, if not here?”
“Gentlemen, eloquence, granted. But one can’t go breaking fathers’ heads with steelyards either. Otherwise where shall we end?”
“And the chariot, the chariot, remember?”
“Yes, he made a chariot out of a cart.”
“And tomorrow he’ll make a cart out of a chariot, ‘as need requires, all as need requires’.”
“Clever people they’ve become. Is there any justice in Russia, gentlemen, or is there none at all?”

But the bell rang. The jury had deliberated exactly an hour, neither more nor less. A profound silence reigned as soon as the public had sat down again. I remember how the jury came into the hall. At last! I will not give the questions point by point; I have forgotten them anyway. I remember only the answer to the first and chief question of the presiding judge, that is, “Did he kill with premeditation for the purpose of robbery?” (I do not remember the wording). Everything froze. The foreman of the jury, that very official who was the youngest of them all, pronounced loudly and clearly, in the deathly silence of the hall:
“Yes, guilty!”

And then on every point it went the same: guilty and guilty, and that without the slightest recommendation to mercy! No one had expected this; almost everyone had been sure at least of a recommendation to mercy. The deathly silence of the hall was not broken; literally everyone seemed turned to stone, both those who had longed for a conviction and those who had longed for an acquittal. But that was only for the first minutes. Then a terrible chaos arose. Among the male public many turned out to be very pleased. Some even rubbed their hands, not hiding their joy. Those who were displeased seemed crushed; they shrugged their shoulders and whispered, but as if they still had not taken it in. But, my God, what became of our ladies! I thought they would start a riot. At first they seemed not to believe their ears. And suddenly, through the whole hall, exclamations were heard: “But what is this? What is the meaning of this?” They leapt up from their seats. They must have thought that it could all be changed and done over again at once. At that instant Mitya suddenly stood up and, stretching out his hands before him, cried with a heart-rending wail:
“I swear by God and by his Last Judgement, I am not guilty of my father’s blood! Katya, I forgive you! Brothers, friends, spare the other one!”

He did not finish, but burst into sobs that filled the hall, loud and terrible, in a voice that was not his own, a new, unexpected voice that had suddenly come to him God knows from where. In the gallery above, in the farthest corner, there was a piercing woman’s scream: it was Grushenka. She had begged someone earlier and had been let into the hall again before the speeches began. Mitya was led away. The passing of sentence was put off till the next day. The whole hall rose in a commotion, but I did not wait or listen any longer. I remember only a few exclamations, on the steps, as people went out.
“He’ll get a whiff of the mines for twenty years.”
“No less.”
“Yes, sir, our peasants stood their ground.”
“And finished off our Mitenka!”
End of the Fourth and Last Part
## Epilogue · Chapter I · Plans to Save Mitya

On the fifth day after Mitya’s trial, very early in the morning, before nine o’clock, Alyosha came to Katerina Ivanovna to settle finally a certain matter of importance to them both, and having besides a message for her. She sat and talked with him in the very room in which she had once received Grushenka; and next to it, in another room, Ivan Fyodorovich lay in a fever, unconscious. Immediately after the scene in court, Katerina Ivanovna had had the sick and unconscious Ivan Fyodorovich carried to her house, disregarding all the future and inevitable talk of society and its condemnation. One of the two relatives who lived with her had left for Moscow immediately after the scene in court; the other had stayed. But even if both had left, Katerina Ivanovna would not have changed her decision and would have stayed to nurse the sick man and sit with him day and night. He was being treated by Varvinsky and Herzenstube; the Moscow doctor had gone back to Moscow, refusing to give his opinion on the possible outcome of the illness. The doctors who stayed, though they encouraged Katerina Ivanovna and Alyosha, evidently could not yet give firm hope. Alyosha visited his sick brother twice a day. But this time he had a special, most troublesome matter, and he foresaw how hard it would be for him to begin on it; and meanwhile he was in a great hurry: he had another urgent matter that same morning in another place, and he had to hurry. They had been talking for a quarter of an hour already. Katerina Ivanovna was pale, very tired, and at the same time in an extreme, morbid excitement: she sensed why, among other things, Alyosha had come to her now.

“Don’t worry about his decision,” she said to Alyosha with firm insistence. “One way or another, he will come to this way out all the same: he must escape! That unhappy man, that hero of honour and conscience (not that one, not Dmitri Fyodorovich, but the one lying behind that door, who sacrificed himself for his brother),” Katya added with flashing eyes, “told me the whole plan of the escape long ago. You know, he has already made contacts… I have told you something already… You see, it will probably happen at the third halting place from here, when the party of exiles is marched to Siberia. Oh, that is still a long way off. Ivan Fyodorovich has already been to see the head of the third halting place. Only it is not known who will be in charge of the party, and that cannot be known so far ahead. Tomorrow perhaps I will show you the whole plan in detail, which Ivan Fyodorovich left with me on the eve of the trial, in case anything happened… It was that very time when, you remember, you found us quarrelling that evening: he was already going downstairs, and I, seeing you, made him come back; do you remember? Do you know what we were quarrelling about then?”
“No, I don’t,” said Alyosha.

“Of course he hid it from you then: it was precisely about this plan of escape. He had revealed all the main points to me three days before; that was when we began to quarrel, and we quarrelled all those three days. We quarrelled because when he told me that in the event of a conviction Dmitri Fyodorovich would escape abroad together with that creature, I suddenly grew angry; I won’t tell you why; I don’t know why myself… Oh, of course I was angry then about the creature, about that creature, and precisely because she too would be escaping abroad with Dmitri!” Katerina Ivanovna suddenly exclaimed, her lips trembling with anger. “As soon as Ivan Fyodorovich saw then that I was so angry about that creature, he thought in a flash that I was jealous of Dmitri over her and that, therefore, I still went on loving Dmitri. And so our first quarrel came about. I would not give explanations; I could not ask forgiveness; it was hard for me that such a man could suspect me of my former love for that… And that, when I myself, long before, had told him straight out that I didn’t love Dmitri but loved only him! It was only from anger at that creature that I grew angry with him! Three days later, that very evening when you came in, he brought me a sealed envelope, which I was to open at once if anything happened to him. Oh, he foresaw his illness! He told me that the envelope contained the details of the escape, and that if he died or fell dangerously ill, I alone was to save Mitya. He left money with me too, almost ten thousand: those very ten thousand that the prosecutor, having learned from someone that he had sent them to be changed, mentioned in his speech. I was terribly struck all at once that Ivan Fyodorovich, still jealous of me and still convinced that I loved Mitya, had not, however, given up the idea of saving his brother, and was entrusting this business of saving him to me, to me myself! Oh, that was a sacrifice! No, you will not understand such self-sacrifice in all its fullness, Alexei Fyodorovich! I wanted to fall at his feet in reverence; but when I suddenly thought that he would take it only for my joy that Mitya was being saved (and he would certainly have thought so!), I was so irritated by the mere possibility of so unjust a thought on his part that I grew irritated again and, instead of kissing his feet, made another scene! Oh, I am unhappy! That is my character, a terrible, unhappy character! Oh, you will see yet: I shall do it, I shall bring things to the point where he too leaves me for another woman, with whom life is easier, like Dmitri; but then… no, then I shall not bear it; I shall kill myself! And when you came in then, and I called you and told him to come back, then, as he came in with you, I was so seized with anger at the hateful, contemptuous look he suddenly gave me that, you remember, I suddenly cried out to you that it was he, he alone who had convinced me that his brother Dmitri was the murderer! I slandered him on purpose, to wound him once more; he never, never assured me that his brother was the murderer; on the contrary, it was I, I myself who assured him of it! Oh, my fury is the cause of everything, everything! It was I, I who prepared that cursed scene in court! He wanted to prove to me that he was noble, and that even if I loved his brother, he would still not ruin him out of revenge and jealousy. And so he came out in court… I am the cause of everything; I alone am to blame!”

Katya had never made such confessions to Alyosha before, and he felt that she was now precisely at that degree of unbearable suffering when the proudest heart painfully crushes its pride and falls, defeated by grief. Oh, Alyosha knew another terrible cause of her present torment too, however she had hidden it from him all these days since Mitya’s conviction; but for some reason it would have been too painful for him if she had brought herself so low as to speak to him of that cause herself, now, at once. She was suffering for her “betrayal” at the trial, and Alyosha sensed that her conscience was drawing her to confess, precisely before him, before Alyosha, with tears, with shrieks, with hysterics, beating herself on the floor. But he feared that moment and wanted to spare the sufferer. All the harder became the message he had come with. He began to speak of Mitya again.

“Never mind, never mind; don’t be afraid for him!” Katya began again, stubbornly and sharply. “All that is only for the moment with him; I know him; I know that heart only too well. Be sure that he will agree to escape. And above all, it isn’t now; there will still be time for him to decide. By then Ivan Fyodorovich will have recovered and will manage everything himself, so that I shan’t have to do anything. Don’t worry, he will agree to escape. Why, he has agreed already: how can he leave his creature? And they won’t let her go to penal servitude, so how can he not escape? Above all, he is afraid of you; he is afraid you won’t approve of the escape from the moral side; but you must generously allow it to him, if your sanction is so indispensable here,” Katya added venomously. She was silent for a moment and smiled.

“He talks there,” she began again, “about some hymns, about a cross he must bear, about some duty; I remember, Ivan Fyodorovich told me a great deal about it then; and if you knew how he spoke!” Katya suddenly exclaimed with irrepressible feeling. “If you knew how he loved that unhappy man at the moment when he was telling me about him, and how he hated him, perhaps, at the same moment! And I, oh, I listened to his story and his tears then with a haughty smile! Oh, the creature! It is I who am the creature, I! It was I who gave him the fever! And that other one, the convicted one, is he ready for suffering?” Katya finished irritably. “Is such a man to suffer? Men like him never suffer!”

A sort of hatred and loathing contempt now sounded in these words. And yet it was she who had betrayed him. “Well, perhaps it is because she feels so guilty before him that she hates him at moments,” Alyosha thought to himself. He wanted it to be only “at moments”. In Katya’s last words he heard a challenge, but he did not take it up.

“That is why I asked you to come today: so that you would promise me to persuade him yourself. Or do you also think it would be dishonourable to escape, not valiant, or however it is… not Christian, perhaps?” Katya added with a still greater challenge.

“No, nothing. I will tell him everything…” Alyosha muttered. “He asks you to come to him today,” he suddenly blurted out, looking her firmly in the eyes. She started all over and drew back from him a little on the sofa.
“Me… is that possible?” she murmured, turning pale.

“It is possible, and it must be!” Alyosha began insistently, all animated. “He needs you very much, precisely now. I would not have begun on this and tormented you prematurely if it were not necessary. He is ill; he is like a madman; he keeps asking for you. He does not ask you to come to be reconciled; only that you should come and show yourself in the doorway. Much has happened to him since that day. He understands how incalculably guilty he is before you. He does not want your forgiveness: ‘I cannot be forgiven,’ he says himself; only that you should show yourself in the doorway…”
“You suddenly…” Katya murmured. “All these days I had a presentiment that you would come with this… I knew he would call for me!… It is impossible!”

“Let it be impossible, but do it. Remember, for the first time he is struck by how he insulted you, for the first time in his life; he never grasped it before so fully! He says: if she refuses to come, then ‘I shall be unhappy all my life now’. Do you hear: a convict for twenty years is still meaning to be happy; isn’t that pitiful? Think: you will be visiting a man ruined innocently,” broke from Alyosha with a challenge. “His hands are clean; there is no blood on them! For the sake of his countless future suffering, visit him now! Come; see him off into the darkness… stand in the doorway, that is all… For you must, you must do this!” Alyosha concluded, stressing the word “must” with incredible force.
“I must, but… I cannot,” Katya almost moaned. “He will look at me… I cannot.”
“Your eyes must meet. How will you live all your life if you don’t bring yourself to it now?”
“Better to suffer all my life.”
“You must come; you must come,” Alyosha stressed again inexorably.
“But why today, why now?… I can’t leave the sick man…”
“You can for a minute; it is only a minute. If you don’t come, he will be in a fever by night. I would not tell you an untruth; have pity!”
“Have pity on me,” Katya reproached him bitterly, and began to cry.
“Then you will come!” Alyosha said firmly, seeing her tears. “I will go and tell him that you are coming at once.”
“No, on no account tell him!” Katya cried out in fright. “I will come, but don’t tell him beforehand, because I will come, but perhaps I won’t go in… I don’t know yet…”
Her voice broke. She was breathing with difficulty. Alyosha got up to go.
“And what if I meet someone?” she suddenly said quietly, turning pale all over again.
“That is why it must be now, so that you meet no one there. There will be no one; I tell you truly. We shall be waiting,” he concluded insistently, and went out of the room.
## Epilogue · Chapter II · For a Moment the Lie Became Truth

He hurried to the hospital, where Mitya was now lying. On the second day after the verdict he had fallen ill with a nervous fever and been sent to our town hospital, to the prisoners’ ward. But the doctor Varvinsky, at the request of Alyosha and many others (Khokhlakova, Lise and so on), had put Mitya not with the prisoners but separately, in that very little room where Smerdyakov had lain before. True, there was a sentry at the end of the corridor, and the window had bars, and Varvinsky could feel easy about his indulgence, which was not quite legal; but he was a kind and compassionate young man. He understood how hard it was for someone like Mitya to step suddenly and directly into the company of murderers and swindlers, and that one had first to get used to it. Visits from relatives and acquaintances were permitted by the doctor, by the governor, and even by the police captain, all unofficially. But in these days only Alyosha and Grushenka had visited Mitya. Rakitin had tried twice to see him; but Mitya had insistently asked Varvinsky not to let him in.

Alyosha found him sitting on the bed, in a hospital dressing gown, slightly feverish, with his head wrapped in a towel soaked in water and vinegar. He looked at Alyosha as he came in with a vague look, but in his look there flashed, all the same, a kind of fright.

In general, ever since the trial he had become terribly thoughtful. Sometimes he would be silent for half an hour, seemingly thinking something over with difficulty and torment, forgetting whoever was there. And if he came out of his thoughtfulness and began to speak, he always began somehow suddenly, and invariably not about what he really needed to say. Sometimes he looked at his brother with suffering. With Grushenka he seemed to be more at ease than with Alyosha. True, he hardly talked with her at all, but as soon as she came in, his whole face lit up with joy. Alyosha sat down silently beside him on the bed. This time Mitya had been waiting anxiously for Alyosha, but he did not dare ask anything. He considered Katya’s consent to come unthinkable, and at the same time he felt that if she did not come, something quite impossible would happen. Alyosha understood his feelings.

“Trifon,” Mitya began fussily, “Trifon Borisych, they say, has wrecked his whole inn: he is lifting the floorboards, tearing off the planks; he has smashed the whole ‘gallery’, they say, into splinters; he is looking for treasure, those very fifteen hundred that the prosecutor said I had hidden there. As soon as he got back, they say, he started his antics at once. Serves the rogue right! The warder here told me yesterday; he is from there.”
“Listen,” said Alyosha, “she will come, but I don’t know when; perhaps today, perhaps in a few days; I don’t know that; but she will come, she will, that is certain.”

Mitya started; he was about to say something, but kept silent. The news had a terrible effect on him. It was plain that he longed tormentingly to know the details of the conversation, but that again he was afraid to ask now: anything cruel and contemptuous from Katya would have been like a knife thrust to him at this moment.
“This is what she said, among other things: that I must be sure to set your conscience at rest about the escape. If Ivan has not recovered by then, she will take it on herself.”
“You have told me that already,” Mitya remarked thoughtfully.
“And you have already repeated it to Grusha,” Alyosha remarked.

“Yes,” Mitya admitted. “She won’t come this morning,” he looked timidly at his brother. “She will only come in the evening. As soon as I told her yesterday that Katya was managing things, she was silent; and her lips twisted. She only whispered: ‘Let her!’ She understood that it is important. I didn’t dare question her further. She seems to understand now, doesn’t she, that the other one loves not me but Ivan?”
“Is that so?” broke from Alyosha.

“Perhaps it isn’t. Only she won’t come this morning,” Mitya hastened to point out once more. “I have given her an errand… Listen, brother Ivan will surpass us all. It is for him to live, not for us. He will recover.”
“Imagine, though Katya is trembling for him, she hardly doubts that he will recover,” said Alyosha.
